The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the $lang translation.

p.seg: Preface to the Nanhua Zhen Jing
Written by Guǒ Xiàng, styled Zǐxuán, of Hénán
Now, regarding Zhuangzi, one may say he understood the root,
thus he never concealed his unrestrained words.
Though his words did not conform to convention,
they resonated uniquely on their own.
When resonance lacks conformity,
even correctness becomes useless;
when words do not address practical matters,
even lofty ideas remain unactionable.
Compared to those who remain tranquil and unmoved, acting only when compelled,
there is indeed a difference—
yet this shows he knew the state of no-mind.
When the mind is non-active,
it responds according to stimuli,
adapting to the moment,
with words spoken only cautiously.
Thus, embodying transformation itself,
it flows through myriad generations, merging with things in obscurity.
How could it be that he merely set up debates, wandered alone, and discoursed beyond the mundane realm?
This is why his work, though unorthodox, stands as the foremost among the hundred schools.
Yet, though Zhuangzi may not have fully embodied this,
his words reach the ultimate.
They penetrate the order of heaven and earth,
articulate the nature of all things,
comprehend the changes of life and death,
and clarify the Way of inner sageliness and outer kingship.
Above, he knew that the creator has no substance,
below, he understood that things create themselves.
His words are vast and expansive,
their meaning profound and mysterious.
The ultimate of ultimates in the Way,
melds subtlety with elegance,
serenely unrestrained,
yet free without arrogance.
Hence it is said:
"Not knowing where righteousness should go,
wild and reckless in action,
yet treading the great path."
Holding food in mouth, joyful in tranquility,
belly full, wandering in primal chaos.
Ultimate benevolence reaches the point of no partiality,
filial piety and compassion end in universal forgetfulness,
ritual and music return to innate ability,
loyalty and trust emanate from heavenly light.
Using this light, their simplicity forms naturally.
Thus, the spiritual vessel transforms alone in the realm of dark mystery,
with a source deep and flow long.
Therefore, where its long waves ripple,
where its high winds fan,
it flows smoothly according to the nature of things,
fitting the desires of the people.
Expanding their narrow views, resolving their hang-ups,
even without the application of effortless effort,
arrogance and boastfulness dissipate.
So, reading his book,
one transcends and feels as if already aligned,
crossing the Kūnlún Mountains,
traversing the great void,
and wandering in the court of indistinct vagueness.
Even greedy and covetous individuals,
or those advancing with impatience,
glimpsing briefly its lingering fragrance,
tasting its overflowing streams,
catching faint echoes and shadows,
are enough to feel expansively free, forgetting physical form in self-contentment.
How much more for those who probe its distant sentiments and savor its eternal years!
Thus, they become continuous and remote, pure and far-reaching,
departing from the dust and grime,
and returning to the obscure ultimate.
Explanatory Preface to the Nanhua Zhen Jing
Written by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Xīhuá in the Táng Dynasty
Now, Zhuangzi is one who elucidates the deep roots of the Dào and virtue,
expounds the subtle meaning of double mystery,
articulates the tranquility of non-action,
clarifies the profound obscurity of solitary transformation,
bridges the nine streams of thought,
encompasses the hundred schools,
truly the supreme teaching within the realm,
indeed the subtle words beyond form.
This man, surname Zhuāng, given name Zhōu,
styled Zǐxiū,
was born in Méng County, Suīyáng, in the state of Sòng.
He studied under Master Chángsānggōng,
and received the title of Nánhuá Xiānrén.
During the early Warring States period,
at the end of the declining Zhōu dynasty,
he lamented the shallow pursuits of the common people,
grieved over the decline of the Dào and virtue,
and thus, with fervor and determination,
composed this discourse.
His words are grand and broad,
their meaning deep and far-reaching,
not for the hearing of inferior scholars,
how could those with shallow understanding fully grasp it!
The term "Zǐ" used here
is an honorable title for one with virtue.
The ancients called their teachers "Zǐ",
and it also denotes a book title.
It is not only the general name for the three sections,
but a common designation among the hundred schools.
As for the "Inner Chapters",
"inner" is named in relation to "outer",
and "chapter" means compiled bamboo slips.
In ancient times, they prepared bamboo by drying for slips,
and used leather straps to bind them.
Binding slips into chapters
is like connecting papers into scrolls today.
Thus Yuán Kǎi said:
"Major affairs are written on bound slips,
minor ones on simple tablets."
The inner chapters discuss the fundamental principles,
the outer chapters speak of events and deeds.
Though events are evident,
without principles, they cannot be understood;
though principles are subtle,
without events, they cannot be manifested.
Wishing first to clarify the wondrous principles,
he thus labeled the inner chapters at the front.
The inner chapters have profound principles,
so each is given a distinct title beyond the text.
Guǒ Xiàng then annotated them directly under the titles,
as with "Free and Easy Wandering" and "Discussion on Making All Things Equal".
From the outer chapters onward,
he took the first two characters of the chapter as the title,
such as "Webbed Toes" and "Horses' Hooves".
Regarding "Free and Easy Wandering",
interpretations vary through the ages.
Now, broadly outlining the main points,
I briefly provide three explanations.
The three are as follows:
First,
Gù Tóngbó said:
"Xiāo means to dissipate.
Yáo means distant.
Dissipating all burdens of action,
one sees distantly the principle of non-action.
Wandering in this manner,
it is called free and easy."
Second,
Zhī Dàolín said:
"Dealing with things but not being constrained by them,
thus carefree without awaiting anything;
mysterious response, unhurried yet swift,
thus remotely, there is nothing it does not accomplish.
Wandering the world in this way,
it is called free and easy wandering."
Third,
Mù Yè said:
"Free and easy is a name for unrestrained self-contentment.
With inner fullness of ultimate virtue,
one is always at ease;
responding to things with a forgetful heart,
there is nowhere one does not penetrate.
Wandering the world in this way,
it is called free and easy wandering."
The inner chapters clarify the fundamental principles,
the outer chapters discuss events and deeds,
the mixed chapters variably illuminate principles and events.
Though the inner chapters clarify principles,
they are not without events;
though the outer chapters discuss events,
they contain much subtle principle.
But in establishing teachings and dividing chapters,
it is based on the predominant focus.
The reason "Free and Easy Wandering" is placed first
is that those who have attained the Dào,
with wise virtue bright and acute,
find all they encounter fitting,
meeting things with free and easy ease,
thus using "free and easy" to name the chapter.
The sage who needs nothing,
reflects circumstances like a mirror,
possessing both the wisdom of expedience and reality,
thus able to equalize all realms greatly,
hence "Discussion on Making All Things Equal" follows.
Since pointing to horses' hooves and heaven-earth,
unifying all things,
the mind serene and calm,
one can nurture and preserve life,
thus "The Secret of Caring for Life" follows.
Having forgotten both good and evil,
with realm and wisdom both sublime,
following change and accepting transformation,
one can navigate the human world,
thus "In the World of Men" follows.
With inner virtue complete and full,
one can display virtue in fragmented ways,
externally engaging with things,
then rising and falling with things,
inner and outer darkly united,
thus "The Sign of Virtue Complete" follows.
Like still water reflecting,
engaging with things without a mind,
forgetting virtue and form,
the ultimate of uniting outer and inner,
one can guide and perfect the multitude,
thus "The Great and Venerable Teacher" follows.
The true sages of old,
knowing heaven and knowing humanity,
All use the two characters of the chapter titles as headings,
since there is no additional meaning,
I will not rearrange the chapters now.
Throughout history, eminent scholars,
recluses of the Jin and Han dynasties,
all have indulged in studying it,
providing explanatory commentaries.
Although their annotations leave no room for doubt,
and they all possess elegant expressions,
each was able to explore the hidden meanings.
I, Xuán Yīng, despite my mediocrity and ignorance,
have studied it since youth,
delving deeply and pondering meticulously for thirty years.
Based on the thirty-three chapters annotated by Zǐ Xuán,
I have compiled a comprehensive commentary totaling thirty volumes.
Although the wording and reasoning may be crude and unskilled,
it does convey some of the intended insights and directions.
I dare not presume to pass it on to future generations,
but merely record it for my own reference against forgetfulness.
The Authentic Classic of Southern Florescence with Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll One
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Inner Chapters, Free and Easy Wandering, First
In the Northern Darkness there is a fish,
its name is Kūn.
The size of the Kūn,
no one knows how many thousand lǐ it measures.
Subcommentary:
Míng means sea,
taking its vast and boundless expanse without shore,
thus it is called míng.
The Record of the Ten Continents by Dōngfāng Shuò says:
"In the míng sea, without wind, great waves rise a hundred zhàng."
Within the immense sea,
there exists this great fish,
wishing to clarify that the nature of things is spontaneous, hence it is marked as the chapter's beginning.
The Records of the Mysterious Middle says:
"In the east there is a great fish.
A traveler takes one day to pass its head,
seven days to pass its tail.
When it gives birth for three days,
the blue sea turns red because of it."
Thus we know that great beings are born in great places.
How could it be only the Northern Darkness?
It transforms into a bird,
its name is Péng.
Commentary:
The reality of the Péng and Kūn,
is something I do not know in detail.
The general meaning of Zhuāngzǐ,
lies in free and easy wandering and liberation,
acting through non-action and attaining self-fulfillment.
Therefore, he pushes to the extreme the expressions of small and large,
to illuminate the suitability of innate nature and lot.
Those who have attained broad perspective,
ought to grasp the essential convergence,
and disregard the specific寄托,
there is no need to meticulously generate explanations for every matter.
As long as it does not harm the overarching intention,
all can be briefly passed over.
Subcommentary:
The four seasons gallop like the wind,
the three lights roll up like lightning,
thus carrying mountains and peaks, it abandons the old,
lifting the boat in the valley, it hastens toward the new.
Therefore, transforming fish into bird,
wishes to clarify the great principle of transformation.
The back of the Péng,
no one knows how many thousand lǐ it measures.
Enraged, it takes flight,
its wings like clouds hanging from the sky.
Subcommentary:
Speaking of the fish's size,
shows the difficulty of knowing its head and tail;
speaking of the bird's back,
also indicates the immeasurability of its length.
Hence the text below says: none have known its length.
Beating its angry wings,
shaking and speeding its feathered robe,
desiring to whirl on the wind,
just about to strike the water.
Then it severs the clouds and vapors,
bearing the blue sky on its back,
soaring and hovering in flight,
brushing against the highest heavens,
casting shade and spreading shadows,
like descending clouds at the edge of the sky.
This bird,
when the sea moves, will migrate to the Southern Darkness.
The Southern Darkness,
is the Lake of Heaven.
Commentary:
If not the dark sea, it is insufficient to transport its body;
if not ninety-thousand lǐ, it is insufficient to support its wings.
Is this due to a fondness for the extraordinary?
Simply because a great being must spontaneously be born in a great place,
and a great place must also spontaneously produce this great being.
The principle is inherently natural.
Do not worry about its loss,
why then place mind within it?
Subcommentary:
Yùn means to turn or move.
Shì is a demonstrative reference.
Namely, this Péng bird, its form massive and heavy,
if not moving and turning within the sea,
has no means to elevate itself.
All this is inevitably so,
not by preference.
Moreover, as the form undergoes change and transformation,
the disposition also follows and alters.
In the past, as a fish,
it submerged and swam in the Northern Sea;
now, becoming a bird,
it ascends and soars to the Southern Darkness.
Although rising and sinking differ in nature,
the freedom and ease are one.
It is also like death and life, gathering and scattering,
whatever is encountered, one finds suitability therein.
Through a thousand changes, ten-thousand transformations,
none have ever not been oneself,
hence the transformation from fish to bird.
Moving from north to south:
the bird is a creature that traverses the void,
the south is the direction of opening brightness;
the fish is a creature that sinks and drowns,
the north is the place of dark obscurity;
wishing to express turning towards brightness and away from darkness,
abandoning stagnation and seeking progress,
thus citing south and north, bird and fish, to show the path of the Way.
As for the great sea and vast rivers,
their origin lies in the process of creation and transformation,
not made by human effort,
hence called the Lake of Heaven.
Qí Xié
is a recorder of the strange.
The words of Xié say:
"When the Péng migrates to the Southern Darkness,
the waters are struck for three thousand lǐ,
it whirls on the whirlwind up to ninety-thousand lǐ,
Commentary:
With large wings, it is difficult to lift off,
thus it whirls on the whirlwind and only then can ascend.
Ninety-thousand lǐ is necessary to be sufficient to sustain itself.
Since it has such wings,
how could it rise abruptly
and descend after just a few fathoms?
This is all inevitably so,
not by preference.
It leaves, using the June breath."
Commentary:
The great bird, once gone, takes half a year to reach the Lake of Heaven and rest;
the small bird, in one flight, takes half a morning,
dashes against the elm and sandalwood and stops.
Comparing their abilities, there is a difference,
but in fulfilling their natures, they are one.
Subcommentary:
Family name Qí, personal name Xié,
is a person's name,
also said to be a book title.
In the state of Qí there was this book of humorous and strange tales.
Zhì means to record.
Jī means to strike.
Tuán means to whirl or struggle.
Fúyáo is a whirlwind.
The book authored by Qí Xié,
records many strange and anomalous events.
Zhuāngzǐ quotes it as evidence,
to clarify that his own words are not empty.
The great Péng, intending to go to the Southern Darkness,
cannot rise abruptly,
therefore it lifts and strikes its two wings,
stirring and agitating three thousand [lǐ],
staggering as it moves,
only then able to leave the water.
Afterwards, twisting and turning sinuously,
beating angrily and circling,
supported by the wind and air,
shaken and lifted upward,
covering a path of ninety-thousand [lǐ],
a time span of half a year,
composed and will fulfilled,
only then does it speak of resting.
It is simply sufficient for itself,
how could it be sentimental about it?
The wild horses,
the dust and chaff,
all living things blowing each other with their breath.
Commentary:
These are all what the Péng relies upon to fly.
The wild horses
are the wandering vapors.
Subcommentary:
The Ěryǎ says:
"Outside the city is called the suburbs,
outside the suburbs is called the pastures,
outside the pastures is called the wild."
This speaks of the time of youthful spring,
when the yang energy stirs,
gazing distantly over the marshes and lakes,
it resembles galloping horses,
hence called the wild horses.
Stirred-up earth is called chén (dust),
the fine part of chén is called āi (chaff).
Between heaven and earth,
the breaths of living things blow upon each other,
thereby lifting the Péng.
The four kinds of living beings,
mixed and numerous,
the ten-thousand categories, varied and diverse,
their forms and natures different,
their provisions and dependencies suitably distinct.
Thus the Péng beats its sky-hanging wings,
entrusting itself to the wind and air to wander free and easy;
the cicada spreads its abruptly rising wings,
dashing against the elm and sandalwood to be self-fulfilled.
These all follow their nature and act,
receiving it from the process of creation and transformation,
not having sentiment about far or near,
how could they harbor intentions of pride or arrogance?
Those who embody this principle, to what can they speak of boasting or striving?
The blueness of the sky,
Is that its true color?
Or is it because the distance is boundless and without end?
When it looks down below,
It must also appear just like this!
Note:
Now observing the azure of the sky,
One ultimately does not know if this is indeed the sky's true color,
Or if the sky is so distant and limitless.
When the Peng bird looks down at the earth from above,
It is just like humans looking up at the sky from here.
Then it stops and plans to head south,
Meaning the Peng does not know the distance of the roads,
But simply goes forth with enough strength to carry itself away.
Explanation:
Looking up at the vault of heaven,
It is extremely remote;
The blue sky is high and far,
Beyond calculation or measure.
Vast and indistinct,
How could that be the sky's true color?
Yet the Peng dwells in the mid-heavens,
While humans reside on the lowly earth,
And the Peng's downward gaze
Is no different from humans' upward view.
Since humans cannot discern the sky's true color,
How could the Peng know the earth's distances?
Relying on its own strength to suffice,
It simply heads to the Southern Sea.
The Peng's planning and estimation
End right there.
Moreover, if the accumulation of water is not deep,
It will lack the strength to bear a large boat.
Pour a cup of water into a depression in the hall,
And a mustard seed can serve as a boat,
But place the cup there and it will stick fast,
For the water is shallow and the boat is large.
Note:
This all illustrates why the Peng flies so high—
It is because its wings are large.
For small entities, the resources needed are not great;
Thus for large entities, what is used cannot be small.
Therefore, principles have their utmost divisions,
And things have their fixed limits.
Each, being sufficient, matches its task,
And in succeeding, they are one.
But if one loses the master who forgets life,
And strives for existence beyond what is perfectly fitting,
Where actions do not lie in strength,
And movements do not match circumstances,
Then even with wings that ride the heavens, one cannot be without limit,
And flights that start abruptly cannot be without hardship!
Explanation:
"Moreover" is a borrowed term,
A word of casual brevity.
"Now" serves to open and develop, at the beginning of speech.
"Accumulation" means to gather.
"Deep" means profound.
"Cup" is a small vessel.
"Depression" means a muddy hollow,
Referring to a sunken spot in the hall's courtyard.
"Mustard" is a grass.
"Stick" means to adhere.
This begins an analogy.
Now, overturning a cup of water into a muddy depression in the hall,
Using a leaf as a boat,
It will float without hindrance;
But if one instead uses the cup as a boat,
It is certainly impossible.
Why?
Because the water is shallow and the boat large,
Causing it to stick to the ground and not move.
Thus, a large boat requires deep water,
While a small mustard seed does not need a vast flow.
If each fits its size appropriately,
Then all things can be carefree.
If the accumulation of wind is not thick,
It will lack the strength to bear large wings.
Therefore, at ninety thousand li, the wind is then below it,
Explanation:
This is the combined analogy.
If water is not deep and thick,
A large boat cannot float;
If wind is not lofty and strong,
Large wings have no means to soar to the heavens.
Thus, a small bird in half a morning
Darts up to the elm or sandalwood;
While the great Peng at ninety thousand li
Has the whirling wind blowing beneath it.
Only then does it ride the wind; bearing the blue sky on its back without any obstruction,
Only then does it plan to head south.
Note:
The reason it now plans to head south
Is not that it loves heights and admires distances,
But because if the wind does not accumulate, it would be blocked and unable to pass.
This is the carefreeness of the great Peng.
Explanation:
"Ride" means to rely upon.
"Obstruct" means to block.
"Hinder" means to stop.
Initially relying on the cyclone,
It could thus ascend;
With the wind piling up thickly,
Only then could it fly.
Thereafter, bearing the blue sky above,
And riding the wind's back below,
It soared straight to the heavens,
Not stopping until the sixth month.
Nets cannot reach it,
Arrows and snares do not threaten,
So how could calamities of obstruction or harm befall it!
Truly, because its resources and needs match appropriately,
It naturally attains its place.
To wander carefree to the Southern Sea—
Is that not fitting!
The cicada and the dove laugh at it, saying:
"We dart up and fly,
Reaching the elm or sandalwood;
Sometimes if we don't make it,
We just land on the ground.
Why go ninety thousand li to the south?"
Note:
If each is content in its nature,
Then even the great Peng cannot consider itself nobler than a small bird,
Nor does the small bird envy the heavenly lake,
For their glory and contentment are ample.
Thus, though small and large differ,
Their carefreeness is one.
Explanation:
The cicada
Appears in the seventh and eighth months,
Purplish-green in color,
Also called the shining cicada.
The dove is the pigeon-dove,
Which is today's turtledove.
"Dart" describes a sudden, swift motion.
"Reach" means to alight upon.
Or to dash toward.
"Sandalwood" is a sandalwood tree.
"Land" means to drop,
Or to pull,
Or to end.
"Why" means for what reason.
"Go" means to proceed to.
The cicada and dove, hearing of the Peng's vastness,
And how it relies on wind and water to fly high,
Thus mock its large form and toil,
And delight in their own small substance and ease.
Moreover, leaping no more than a few yards,
Dashing to the elm or sandalwood to perch,
If occasionally tired and not reaching the next grove,
They land, rest, and rise again,
Wandering carefree according to their nature,
Finding joy within.
Why must one traverse the earth for six months,
Travel ninety thousand li afar,
Endure the toil of journeying,
Just to head south—what for!
For the small to laugh at the large,
And for those who boast and strive yet are not carefree—such a thing has never been!
Those going to the wild green,
Eat three meals and return,
Their stomachs still full;
Those going a hundred li
Pound grain overnight for provisions;
Those going a thousand li
Gather three months' grain.
Note:
The farther one goes,
The more grain one gathers.
Thus, the larger the wings,
The thicker the accumulated air must be.
Explanation:
"Go" means to proceed to.
"Wild green"
Refers to the color of the countryside,
Which appears indistinct when viewed from afar.
"Full" means a satiated appearance.
Going to the countryside,
Returning after three meals,
The road being not far,
The belly remains full.
For a journey of a hundred li,
The distance somewhat farther,
One pounds grain
As preparation for one night's stay.
For a journey of a thousand li,
The road being long and far,
One gathers three months' grain
To suffice for the round trip.
Thus, Guo Xiang's note says:
"The farther one goes,
The more grain one gathers.
Thus, the larger the wings,
The thicker the accumulated air must be."
These two creatures,
What do they know!
Note:
The two creatures
Refer to the Peng and the cicada.
Comparing the large to the small,
is a means to equalize different inclinations.
The reason inclinations differ,
is it because they know they are different and thus differ?
All occur without knowing why, yet naturally so.
Naturally so,
not by deliberate action,
this is the general meaning of Carefree Wandering.
Commentary:
Guo Xiang's note states:
The two creatures refer to the roc and the cicada.
Comparing the large to the small,
is a means to equalize different inclinations.
Moreover, the great roc rides the whirlwind ninety thousand li,
while the small bird darts up only to the elm and sandalwood trees,
though the distances differ,
their satisfaction of nature is equal.
None know the length of the journey,
each takes what suffices and prevails by themselves,
their innate mechanisms operate spontaneously,
without knowing why.
Since they have no intention toward high or low,
how could they have attachment to superiority or inferiority!
The essence of Carefree Wandering,
lies here, does it not!
And calling the roc a creature—
the Da Dai Li records:
In the east, there are three hundred sixty scaled creatures,
with the winged dragon as their leader;
in the south, three hundred sixty feathered creatures,
with the phoenix as their leader;
in the west, three hundred sixty furred creatures,
with the qílín as their leader;
in the north, three hundred sixty armored creatures,
with the divine turtle as their leader;
in the center, three hundred sixty naked creatures,
with the sage as their leader.
Speaking comprehensively,
thus the roc is also called a creature.
Small knowledge cannot match great knowledge,
short lifespans cannot match long lifespans.
Note:
All things have their own nature,
each nature has its limit,
all are like lifespan and knowledge,
how could striving and admiration reach them!
From here down to Lièzǐ,
it successively lists the sizes of lifespans and knowledge,
each trusting its own aspect,
none sufficient to surpass the others.
Then it unifies them with the person who has no dependencies,
discarding that, forgetting self,
merging with all differences,
different aspects attain the same, and I have no merit or fame.
Therefore, unifying large and small,
means there is neither small nor large.
If small and large exist,
then even between the great roc and the quail,
or between the prime minister and the wind-rider,
all are equally encumbered things.
Equalizing life and death,
means there is neither death nor life.
If life and death exist,
then even between the great chūn tree and the ephemeral cicada,
or between Péngzǔ and the morning mushroom,
all are equally short-lived.
Thus, wandering where there is neither small nor large,
is boundless;
merging where there is neither death nor life,
is limitless.
If Carefree Wandering is tied to a specific aspect,
then even if set free to wander,
it will have limits,
unable to be dependency-free.
Commentary:
Things receive breath differently,
their endowments vary.
In knowledge, some are bright, some dim,
in lifespan, some short, some long.
Thus, listing the morning mushroom, the mínglíng tree, the prime minister, and Róngzǐ,
all are like lifespan and knowledge,
how could striving and admiration reach them!
Thus we know the natures of things differ,
and cannot be forcibly imitated.
How do we know it is so?
Commentary:
Xī means "how."
Rán means "so."
How do we know that lifespan and knowledge are as incomparable as this unraveling?
Posing the question hypothetically,
to lead to the following answer.
The morning mushroom knows not the end and beginning of the month,
the ephemeral cicada knows not spring and autumn,
these are short lifespans.
Commentary:
This answers the previous question.
The morning mushroom—
refers to what grows on dung and soil
in humid, rainy weather, steaming and sprouting,
born in shade and damp,
dies upon seeing the sun,
also called the "large mushroom."
Born in the morning, dead by evening,
hence called "morning mushroom."
The month's end is called huì,
the month's start is called shuò.
If it encounters shade,
it withers in a few days,
never lasting ten days,
thus it knows not huì or shuò.
The ephemeral cicada is a summer cicada,
born on wheat stalks,
also called "wheat-node."
Born in summer, dead by autumn,
thus it knows not spring or autumn.
The mushroom lives from morn to eve,
the cicada lives from summer to autumn,
this speaks of their brief lifespan,
hence called short lifespans.
South of Chǔ there is the mínglíng tree,
for which five hundred years make a spring,
five hundred years make an autumn;
in high antiquity, there was the great chūn tree,
for which eight thousand years make a spring,
eight thousand years make an autumn.
Commentary:
Mínglíng and great chūn,
are both names of trees,
taking leaf-growth as spring,
leaf-fall as autumn.
Mínglíng grows south of Chǔ,
considering two thousand years as one year.
Speaking of high antiquity—
refers to the time of Fúxī.
The great chūn tree,
lived since high antiquity,
considering thirty-two thousand years as one year.
Mínglíng blooms after five hundred years,
great chūn sheds leaves after eight thousand years,
both have extended springs and autumns,
hence called long lifespans.
And Péngzǔ is now especially renowned for longevity,
common people compare themselves to him,
is it not lamentable!
Note:
That lifespan and knowledge are incomparable,
is as vastly different as this.
Compared to what common people lament,
this too is lamentable.
Yet common people never lament this,
because each nature has its limit.
If one knows the limit,
then not a hair's breadth can be striven for,
what in the world is there to lament!
Things never desire the small from the large,
yet the small inevitably envy the large.
Thus, citing the differences between small and large,
each has its fixed lot,
not reachable by envy or desire,
then the burden of envy and desire can be ended.
Lament arises from burden,
burden ended, lament departs,
with lament gone, if life's nature is not at peace,
such a thing has never been.
Commentary:
Péngzǔ—
surname Jiān, name Kēng,
was a great-great-grandson of Emperor Zhuānxū.
Skilled in nurturing life,
able to harmonize the cauldron.
He presented pheasant soup to Yáo,
Yáo enfeoffed him at Péngchéng,
his Way could be ancestral,
hence called Péngzǔ.
He lived through the Xià and Yīn dynasties,
reaching about eight hundred years by the Zhōu era.
Tè means "especially."
Because of his long life,
his fame is uniquely known in the world.
And when common people compare themselves to Péngzǔ,
it is deeply lamentable.
That they do not lament—
is because Péngzǔ received a nature of distant longevity,
not of my kind of breath,
placed beyond words,
they dare not sigh in sorrow.
Thus we know life has its bounds,
not only is Péngzǔ a hair's breadth beyond reach,
thereby equalizing chūn and mushroom,
mixing Péng and early death,
each resting in their lot,
and life's nature is at peace.
Tāng's question to Jí was like this:
Note:
Tāng's question to Jí,
also says all things have their limits,
if left to them, all flows smoothly.
Thus Zhuāngzǐ considers the question correct.
Commentary:
Tāng,
He was a descendant of Emperor Kù,
from the lineage of Xiè,
with the surname Zǐ and given name Lǚ,
courtesy name Tiānyǐ.
His mother, Fúdū,
saw a white vapor piercing through the moon,
and conceived Tāng through its influence.
With a broad jaw and tapered forehead,
he stood nine feet tall.
Serving the Xià dynasty as a feudal lord,
he possessed sagely virtue,
and the feudal lords rallied to him.
Encountering Jié’s tyranny,
he was imprisoned at the Xiàtái.
Later freed,
he formed an alliance with the feudal lords at Jǐngbó,
confronted Jié at the ruins of Kūnwú,
and engaged in a great battle at the wilderness of Míngtiáo,
driving Jié to flee to Náncháo.
After defeating Jié,
Tāng offered the empire to Wùguāng,
who declined it.
Tāng then ascended the throne,
establishing his capital at Bó,
later changing it to Shāng,
becoming the founding ruler of Yīn.
Jí was
a worthy man of Tāng’s time,
also said to be an erudite scholar under Tāng.
Lièzǐ refers to him as Xià Jí.
The characters for Jí and Jí sound similar,
likely a scribal error.
As Jí was a worthy man,
Tāng treated him as a teacher,
hence Tāng inquired of Jí,
seeking the ultimate Way.
It is said that the natures of things differ,
each with its inherent disposition;
following this directly,
one should uphold and entrust to it.
Yīn Tāng sought further insight,
delving into profound mysteries.
Zhuāngzǐ approved of his questioning,
hence stating it is so.
North of the barren land,
there is a dark sea,
the Lake of Heaven.
Therein is a fish,
its breadth several thousand miles,
with none knowing its length,
named the Kūn.
Note:
"Xiū" means long.
The earth regards grass as its hair,
and in the cold, frozen north,
where plants do not grow,
it is called Qióngfà,
the so-called barren land.
The Kūn fish spans thousands in breadth,
with none knowing its length,
illustrating its immensity.
However, the dark sea, Kūn, and Péng
have appeared earlier in the text,
and now they are reiterated
precisely because the prior citation of Qíxié
suffices as a classical reference.
Now invoking Lièzǐ
further attests to its validity.
With earnest repetition,
the meaning is thus established.
Therein is a bird,
named the Péng,
its back like Mount Tài,
its wings like clouds hanging from the sky,
soaring on the whirlwind up ninety thousand miles,
piercing the clouds,
bearing the blue sky,
then heading south.
Note:
The Péng’s back is vast and colossal,
resembling lofty peaks.
The swirling wind twists and turns,
akin to a ram’s horn.
Ascending to graze the azure heavens,
cutting through the firmament,
it surges with unrestrained vigor,
charting a course to the Southern Sea.
Thus, in Yùkòu’s "Questions of Tāng," it is said, "How could the world know of such things?"
Great Yǔ encountered them in his travels,
Bóyì recognized and named them,
and Yíjiān recorded them upon hearing.
And so it heads to the Southern Sea.
The quail laughed at it, saying:
"Where is it going!"
"I leap up,
no more than a few fathoms high, then descend,
fluttering among the weeds and brambles—
this is the pinnacle of flight too.
So where is it going!"
This illustrates the distinction between small and great.
Commentary:
Each finds its fulfillment in its own nature,
reaching its utmost by being itself.
Previously, it was said that the two creatures have different wings,
hence their destinations differ.
One soars in the celestial lake,
the other spends its days among elms and sandalwoods—
each simply fulfills its form and is content,
unaware of the reasons.
Now speaking of the small-great distinction,
each has its innate essence,
beyond the reach of envy or aspiration,
each resting in its natural disposition,
not lamenting their differences,
hence it is reiterated.
Note:
"Qiě" means "about to,"
also a particle.
"Chì" means a small marsh.
"Yàn" means a sparrow.
Eight feet make a fathom.
"Áoxiáng" means frolicking.
The quail, a small bird,
roams freely in the marsh,
leaping and bounding,
content within the weeds and brambles,
thus it scoffs at the journey of ninety thousand miles,
delighting in its short flights—this indeed distinguishes the inherent differences in small and great natures,
discussing how each finds sufficiency without duality.
Thus, those whose knowledge qualifies them for one office,
whose conduct aligns with one village,
whose virtue matches one ruler,
and who gain trust in one state,
view themselves
much like this.
Commentary:
Just as the bird finds contentment in its own sphere.
Note:
"Gù" continues from the previous statement,
"fū" introduces what follows,
"guó" refers to the states of the five ranks,
"xiāng" is twelve thousand five hundred households.
Some, by their wisdom and efficacy,
are fit to hold an office;
some, through renowned reputation,
unite with their local community;
some, with vast virtue,
may face south as rulers,
securing the state,
pacifying the people.
These three types differ in endowment,
with varying strengths and weaknesses,
yet in their respective sufficiency,
they are inherently equal.
Viewing their own capabilities,
they are like the bird content in its own sphere.
Yet Sòng Róngzǐ still laughed at them.
Commentary:
Not yet equalized,
hence the laughter.
Note:
"Zǐ" is an honorific for the virtuous.
Surname Róng,
from the state of Sòng.
"Rán" means "thus."
Although Róngzǐ could forget possession,
he had not yet relinquished non-possession,
hence his laughter.
Those entrenched in officialdom,
clinging to rank and salary,
and even the detached,
still harbor mockery—
this is why they are not equalized.
Earlier, the small laughed at the great,
showing the great do not boast;
now the great laugh at the small,
and the small do not aspire.
Yet those unsettled in their nature and destiny
have not heard the principle.
Moreover, if the whole world praises him, he is not encouraged,
and if the whole world blames him, he is not discouraged.
Commentary:
Truly self-content.
Note:
"Jǔ" means all.
"Quàn" means to encourage.
"Jǔ" means dejection.
Róngzǐ followed his nature, embracing the Way,
aloof and transcendent;
even if all the world praised him,
it would not increase his encouragement,
and even if all the land criticized him,
it would not add to his discouragement,
truly self-content.
He settled the distinction between inner and outer.
Commentary:
Inner as self, outer as things.
Note:
Róngzǐ knew that inwardly, it is not the self,
and outwardly, it is not things.
Both inner and outer are relinquished,
both things and self are forgotten,
thus the distinction between inner and outer is settled without error.
He discerns the boundaries of honor and disgrace,
Comment:
honoring oneself and disgracing others.
Subcommentary:
forgetting encouragement and discouragement in praise and blame,
blending poverty and success in honor and disgrace,
thus he can reflect illumination upon his mind and wisdom,
and discern with profound mirror-like awareness the realm of things,
no longer making self inner and things outer,
nor honoring oneself and disgracing others.
This is all.
Comment:
Nothing can go beyond this either.
Subcommentary:
Sī means "this."
Yǐ means "to stop."
Sòng Róng's wisdom and virtue stop and are exhausted at this point.
As for him in the world, he was not anxious and striving.
Comment:
Being content within himself,
he was thus detached from the world.
Subcommentary:
Shuòshuò means "eagerly" or "anxiously."
Sòng Róng followed his nature in emptiness and tranquility,
acting directly according to principle,
never employing wisdom to seek,
nor forcing his mind for the Way,
dwelling beyond material things,
thus he was not one who strove anxiously.
Even so,
there was still something he had not established.
Comment:
He could only regard himself as right,
but was not able to be without any impossibility.
Subcommentary:
Shù means "to establish."
Master Róng abandoned existence to verify non-existence,
mired in one-sided stagnation,
thus the mind of non-dependence was not yet established,
and the joy of carefree wandering was still lacking in wisdom.
Now Lièzǐ rode upon the wind and traveled,
cool and skillful indeed,
Comment:
Lěngrán describes a light and exquisite appearance.
Subcommentary:
His surname was Liè, name Yùkòu,
a man of Zhèng.
He was contemporary with Duke Xū of Zhèng,
studied under Húqiūzǐ Lín,
and authored eight volumes.
He attained the Way of wind immortality,
rode the wind to wander,
coolly and lightly ascending,
thus praised as skillful.
Only after fifteen days would he return.
Comment:
If one still depends on something,
then even riding the wind to travel,
one cannot circulate everywhere in a single moment.
Subcommentary:
A xún is ten days.
Having attained wind immortality,
he traveled throughout the world,
every fifteen days,
returning home,
yet unable to ride on everything,
thus could not act in a single moment.
As for achieving blessings, he was not anxious and striving.
Comment:
He naturally rode the wind to travel,
not anxiously seeking it.
Subcommentary:
Zhì means "to obtain."
That Liè Yùkòu obtained the blessings of wind immortality
was due to being unaffected by heat or cold, mindless,
empty-hearted and following fate,
not involving forced emotions in choosing or rejecting,
nor anxiously seeking it.
To clarify the essence of practicing the Way,
the key lies in forgetting the mind.
If one employs forced wisdom and deliberation,
one is far from it.
Although this avoids walking,
there is still something he depends on.
Comment:
Without wind, he cannot travel,
this necessarily involves dependence.
Only one who rides on everything
is without dependence.
Subcommentary:
Riding the wind to lightly ascend,
though avoiding walking,
cannot advance without wind,
thus still requires dependence.
From officials below to Sòng Róng and Liè Yùkòu,
each listed with differing superiority in wisdom and virtue,
since none had completely forgotten,
all belong to the category of dependence.
Only by following the nature of all things,
wandering the path of transformation,
and being able to ride on everything without exception,
can one fully realize the subtle essence of carefree wandering.
As for riding the correctness of heaven and earth and harnessing the transformations of the six energies,
to wander in the infinite,
what would he depend on then!
Comment:
Heaven and earth
are the general name for all things.
Heaven and earth take all things as their substance,
and all things must take spontaneity as their correctness.
Spontaneity
means acting without action and being so of itself.
Thus the great roc's ability to fly high,
the quail's ability to stay low,
the long life of the great tree,
the brevity of the morning mushroom,
all these are what spontaneity enables,
not what forced action can achieve.
Acting without action and being so of itself,
this is why it is called correctness.
Thus riding the correctness of heaven and earth
means following the nature of all things;
harnessing the transformations of the six energies
means wandering the path of change.
Proceeding in this manner,
where could one go that has limits!
Whatever is encountered is ridden,
so what would one depend on!
This is the carefree wandering of the person of utmost virtue who mysteriously unites self and other.
If there is dependence,
then even Lièzǐ's lightness and skill
could not travel without wind,
thus one must obtain what one depends on before achieving carefree wandering,
let alone the great roc!
Only one who merges with things and follows the great transformation
can be without dependence and constantly free,
and not only free oneself!
Moreover, he accommodates those who have dependence,
enabling them not to lose what they depend on,
and when what is depended on is not lost,
then they become one with the great freedom.
Thus, dependence and non-dependence are what I cannot equalize.
As for each resting in its own nature,
the natural mechanism operating spontaneously,
receiving without knowing,
this is what I cannot differentiate.
If non-dependence is still insufficient to differentiate from dependence,
how much more so the great and small among the dependent!
Subcommentary:
Heaven and earth are the general name for all things.
All things
are different designations for spontaneity.
The six energies:
Jì Yí said:
dawn morning mist,
noon full sun,
sunset flying spring,
midnight vapor,
with heaven and earth's two energies making six.
Also Dù Yù said:
the six energies are
yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and light.
Also Zhī Dàolín said:
the six energies
are heaven, earth, and the four seasons.
Biàn means transformation.
Wūhū means "on what."
It means the sage without dependence,
empty-hearted and embodying the Way,
thus can ride the correct principle of the two modes (heaven and earth),
follow the spontaneity of all things,
harness the six energies to wander carefree,
and blend with all beings in transformation.
If nothing is not followed,
then where would one go that is not free!
Clearly penetrating the infinite,
on what would one depend!
Thus it is said:
The ultimate person has no self,
Comment:
Having no self, thus he follows things,
and by following things, he reaches the ultimate.
The spiritual person has no merit,
Comment:
Things have never owed their life to spontaneity,
yet necessarily delight in relying on intervention,
thus when principle reaches the ultimate, traces vanish.
Now, following without assisting,
uniting with the ultimate principle,
thus there is no merit.
The sage has no fame.
Comment:
The sage
is a name for one who has attained his nature,
not sufficient to name how it was attained.
Subcommentary:
"Ultimate" refers to his substance,
Divine speaks of its function,
sage speaks of its name,
thus regarding the substance it is called the ultimate,
regarding the function it is called divine,
regarding the name it is called sage,
but their reality is one.
Reaching the spiritual ultimate,
thus it is called the ultimate;
unfathomable as yīn and yáng,
thus it is called divine;
rectifying the names of all things,
thus it is called sage.
Above the single person,
there exist these three,
wishing to reveal the distinction in function and name,
thus there is the differentiation of three persons.
These three persons,
are precisely the ones mentioned earlier who ride the correctness of heaven and earth and command the transformations of the six energies.
Wishing to conclude the virtue of non-dependence of this person,
manifest his substance and function,
thus it is stated conversely.
Yáo offered the empire to Xǔ Yóu,
Commentary:
Yáo,
son of Emperor Kù,
surname Yīqí,
courtesy name Fàngxūn.
Mother Qìngdū,
impregnated by Kù sensing a red dragon,
height ten chǐ,
pointed above and full below,
eyebrows with eight colors,
feet stepping on the Wing star,
possessing sage virtue.
At fifteen succeeded as Marquis of Táng,
at twenty-one,
ascended the imperial throne replacing his elder brother,
capital at Píngyáng,
named Táotáng.
Reigned seventy-two years,
then passed it to Shùn.
Died at age one hundred twenty-eight,
buried at Yángchéng,
posthumous name Yáo.
According to naming rules:
assisting goodness and transmitting sageliness is called Yáo,
meaning he had the merit of transmitting to Shùn.
Xǔ Yóu, a recluse.
Surname Xǔ, name Yóu,
courtesy name Zhòngwǔ,
from Yángchéng, Yǐngchuān.
Lived in seclusion at Jīshān,
studied under Nièquē,
ate from the mountains,
drank from the rivers.
Yáo knew his worthiness,
offered the imperial position,
Xǔ Yóu heard this,
then washed his ears by the river,
Cháofù watering his calf,
led it away avoiding him saying:
You defile my water.
After death,
Yáo honored his tomb,
posthumous name Jīgōng.
He was Yáo's teacher.
Said: The sun and moon have risen yet the torchfire does not cease,
isn't its light rather difficult!
Timely rain has descended yet you still irrigate,
isn't its moisture rather laborious!
Commentary:
Torchfire,
means a flame torch,
also a small fire.
In Shénnóng's time it rained every fifteen days,
called timely rain.
Moreover with the sun and moon shining bright,
why borrow the light of a torch;
timely rain pouring down,
no need for laborious irrigation moisture.
Yáo being modest and capable of yielding,
withdrawing himself and advancing others,
thus spoke these words,
greatly praising Zhòngwǔ.
If you, sir, were established the empire would be well-governed,
yet I still preside over it,
I see myself as deficient.
I beg to offer the empire.
Commentary:
Govern, means to rectify.
Preside, means to rule.
Offer, means to give.
Yáo having studied under Xǔ Yóu,
thus called him "sir."
If Zhòngwǔ were established as son of heaven,
the world would surely achieve great peace,
yet I still act as ruler of things,
seeing myself as deficient and inadequate,
I beg to yield the imperial position to a worthy.
Xǔ Yóu said:
You govern the empire,
the empire is already well-governed,
Annotation:
He who can make the empire well-governed,
is one who does not govern the empire.
Thus Yáo governed it by not governing,
not by governing it to govern it.
Now Xǔ Yóu clearly states it is already governed,
thus there is nothing to replace.
Yet the governance truly comes from Yáo,
hence the words "you govern."
Should forget the words to seek what they illustrate.
Yet some say:
He who governs to govern,
is Yáo;
he who does not govern yet Yáo thereby governs,
is Xǔ Yóu.
This is greatly mistaken.
Governance arises from non-governance,
action emerges from non-action.
Sufficient to attribute to Yáo,
why borrow from Xǔ Yóu!
If saying only those who sit silently in mountain forests can be called non-action,
this is why Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ's discussions are rejected by those in power,
those in power inevitably remain in the realm of action without return,
this is the reason.
Commentary:
Govern, means to order.
Already, means completely.
Saying Yáo governed the empire,
long in peace,
all within the four seas and eight wildernesses,
completely tranquil,
why trouble to yield to me,
excessive polite words,
yet reading Zhuāngzǐ's text,
it贬低Yáo and promotes Xǔ,
while examining Guō Xiàng's annotation it贬低Xǔ and favors Yáo,
why?
To clarify that Fàngxūn is a great sage,
Zhòngwǔ a great worthy.
The paths of worthy and sage,
are far apart.
Thus Yáo bearing the screen at Fényáng yet losing the empire,
Xǔ Yóu not blending with customs stands alone on high mountains,
comprehensive illumination versus biased immersion,
clearly discernible.
Therefore Zhuāngzǐ drew on the traces of abdication,
hence the torchfire discussion;
Guō Xiàng examined the mind of non-dependence,
further presenting the non-governance theory.
Can be said to probe subtleties and seek obscurities,
thoroughly understanding text and fitting meaning,
should seek its intended illustration,
without any suspicion.
And I would still replace you,
would I be seeking fame?
Fame,
is the guest of reality.
Would I be seeking to be a guest?
Annotation:
He who takes responsibility upon himself,
responds to things and follows things,
has no opposition to things.
Thus Yáo has no opposition in the empire,
while Xǔ Yóu pairs with Jì and Qì.
Why say so?
He who merges with things darkly,
thus cannot be separated from the multitude of things.
Therefore responding mysteriously without mind,
only following what is felt,
floating like an unmoored boat,
east and west not of itself.
Thus no action not shared with the common people,
also no going not being the ruler of the empire.
Being ruler in this manner,
like heaven's natural height,
is the virtue of the ruler.
If aloofly standing atop high mountains,
not that he has attachment to self-preservation,
preserving a biased preference for one family,
how can he monopolize this!
This is but one thing among customs,
and an outer subject of Yáo.
If treating an inner ruler as an outer subject,
this has the name of ruler but not the reality of fulfilling rulership.
Commentary:
Xǔ Yóu aloof at Jīshān,
carefree at Yǐngshuǐ,
detesting the stench of glory and profit,
disgusted by filthy reputation,
yet Yáo earnestly invited,
still hoping he would replace himself.
If Xǔ Yóu valued the imperial throne,
he would seek the fame of ten thousand chariots.
But reality gives rise to fame,
fame arises from reality,
reality is the inner, the host,
fame is the outer, the guest.
Abandoning the host for the guest,
Seeking the external while bereft of the internal
is not what recluses value,
hence it is said, "I shall become a guest."
The wren nests in the deep forest,
occupying but a single branch;
the field mouse drinks from the river,
filling only its belly.
Annotation:
Each nature has its limit;
if satisfied within that limit,
then the world's wealth becomes superfluous.
Exegesis:
The wren,
a clever mother bird,
also called the artisan sparrow,
or the female craftsman,
also named the peach insect,
prefers deep places and skillfully builds nests.
The field mouse,
shaped like an ox in size,
also black in color,
with hoofed feet,
three hoof-tips per foot,
ears resembling elephant ears,
white tail tip,
enjoys entering rivers to drink.
Thus the bird, beyond one branch for nesting,
needs no dense forest;
the beast, beyond a full belly from drinking,
requires no vast waters.
How much more so for Xǔ Yóu, content in his humble hut,
disregarding golden palaces,
delighting in simple meals,
why toil for jade-like feasts!
"Return and rest, my lord—
I have no use for governing the world!"
Annotation:
Equally useless to all,
yet Yáo alone possesses it.
This clarifies that those embracing openness are boundless,
thus the world gladly supports them without weariness.
Exegesis:
"Yǔ" means I.
Xǔ Yóu, with few desires and pure integrity,
declined Yáo's abdication,
thus said to Yáo:
"You should swiftly return to the imperial carriage,
go back to the purple constellations;
the words of abdication
should now cease.
The honor of ruling the four seas
is useless to me;
the nobility of the imperial throne—
what purpose does it serve me?"
"Even if the cook does not manage the kitchen,
the priest does not overstep wine vessels and meat stands to replace him."
Annotation:
The cook and the priest
each remain in their duties;
birds, beasts, and all things
find sufficiency in what they receive;
Emperor Yáo and Xǔ Yóu
each find peace in their circumstances—
this is the ultimate truth of the world.
Each attaining their own truth,
what more is there to do?
Simply be content with oneself!
Thus, though the actions of Yáo and Xǔ differ,
in freedom they are one.
Exegesis:
The cook
refers to the person in charge of the kitchen,
equivalent to today's provision officer for meals.
The "shī"
is the spirit tablet in the grand temple.
The "zhù"
is today's court ritual officer.
Holding the prayer tablet, he addresses the spirit tablet and prays,
hence called "shī zhù."
Zūn are wine vessels.
Zǔ are meat vessels.
The cook and the priest
each have their designated roles.
Even if the cook is negligent,
unwilling to manage the kitchen,
the priest
will never overstep his position or abuse his duty,
abandoning the vessels to take over cooking.
Similarly, when Emperor Yáo abdicated,
ceasing to rule the world,
Xǔ Yóu did not leave his mountain forest
to assume the imperial throne.
Thus the annotation states: Emperor Yáo and Xǔ Yóu
each remained tranquil in their encounters.
Jiān Wú asked Lián Shū:
"I heard words from Jiē Yú—
Exegesis:
Jiān Wú and Lián Shū
are both ancient men who embraced the Dào.
Jiē Yú,
surname Lù, name Tōng,
courtesy name Jiē Yú,
a worthy of Chǔ,
a recluse.
Contemporary with Confucius,
he feigned madness and avoided office,
often engaging in farming.
The King of Chǔ, knowing his worth,
offered him a hundred yì of gold,
two carriages with four horses each,
all of which he declined.
Thereupon, carrying burdens with his wife,
they roamed mountains and seas,
none knowing their end.
Jiān Wú, hearing Jiē Yú's words,
found them wildly ungrounded,
so asked Lián Shū to inquire their meaning.
Saying 'I heard words from Jiē Yú'
means he heard Jiē Yú's speech.
Zhuāngzǐ entrusted three worthies to illuminate Yáo's singular sageliness.
The description of what was heard
is detailed below.
—vast but unanchored,
going forth without return.
I am startled and alarmed by his words,
like the Milky Way, without end."
Exegesis:
The words heard from Jiē Yú
are fearfully broad and unmoored,
once spoken as a rough outline,
with no depth to explore.
I privately heard them,
startled, doubtful, and terrified,
as if facing the celestial river in the sky,
distant and clear-high,
seeking its source and flow,
finding virtually no end.
"Greatly excessive,
unlike human sentiment."
Exegesis:
"Jìng tíng"
means excessive disparity.
It also describes a manner of going straight without looking back.
Meaning Jiē Yú's words do not align with convention,
often overly divergent,
not conforming to worldly feelings,
thus his grand statements do not fit reason.
Lián Shū said:
"What did his words say?"
Exegesis:
What was the intent of Lù Tōng's discourse?
Thus questioning Jiān Wú about what he heard.
He said:
"On the distant Gūyè Mountain,
there dwells a divine person.
Skin and flesh like ice and snow,
graceful as an untouched maiden."
Annotation:
These are all metaphorical expressions.
The divine person is what we now call a sage.
Though the sage may be in the court above,
his mind is no different from being in the mountains and forests—
how would the world recognize this!
Merely seeing him wear the yellow canopy,
bear the jade seal,
they think it enough to entangle his heart;
seeing him traverse mountains and rivers,
share the people's affairs,
they think it enough to weary his spirit—
how could they know the utmost perfection remains undiminished!
Now speaking of the kingly virtuous person and placing him on this mountain
aims to clarify that the world has no means to recognize him,
thus entrusting him beyond the farthest shores,
and pushing him beyond the reach of sight and hearing.
An untouched maiden
does not let external things injure the internal.
Exegesis:
"Miǎo" means distant;
the Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
"Gūyè Mountain is beyond the encircling sea,
where there are divine sage persons,
who restrain their mechanisms to respond to things.
When the time calls for courtesy and yielding,
they become Yáo and Shùn;
when the time calls for arms and conflict,
they become Tāng and Wǔ."
"Chuòyuē" means soft and weak.
"Chǔzǐ" is an unmarried maiden.
This says the sage's movement and stillness correspond,
thus emptiness and existence are both illuminated;
though residing in court corridors,
no different from mountains and forests,
harmonizing light with dust,
stained yet unstained.
Ice and snow signify purity,
gracefulness比喻softness and harmony.
The maiden is unharmed by things,
Gūyè speaks of its extreme remoteness.
This illuminates Yáo's abundant virtue,
profound and mysteriously subtle,
Therefore, it is entrusted beyond the farthest boundaries,
and extended beyond the reach of sight and hearing.
This is merely allegorical language;
why must there be an actual Gūyè?
One should forget the words to seek what they signify.
This is Jiānwú recounting what he heard in the past,
in response to Liánshū's words.
They do not eat the five grains,
but inhale the wind and drink the dew.
Note:
Though all eat the five grains, only they become divine beings,
showing that divine beings are not produced by the five grains,
but uniquely endowed with the wondrous breath of nature.
Explanation:
The five grains are:
millet, panicum, hemp, beans, and wheat.
It means that sacred and divine beings,
descending to live and responding to things,
possess pure and refined essences,
endowed with the finest energies of yīn and yáng.
Though they follow things to sustain themselves,
it is not due to the five grains;
relying on wind and dew for clarity and emptiness,
how could they be altered by the four seasons?
They ride on clouds and mists,
drive flying dragons,
and wander beyond the four seas.
Explanation:
Their wisdom illuminates and connects spiritually,
effortlessly following things,
hence it is said they ride on clouds and mists.
Without haste yet swift,
changing and manifesting without constancy,
hence it is said they drive flying dragons.
Dwelling upon all things,
yet their spirit transcends beyond the six directions,
hence it is said they wander beyond the four seas.
When their spirit is concentrated,
it makes things free from plagues and the yearly grains ripen.
I consider this insane and do not believe it.
Note:
Those who embody the spirit, dwell in spirituality, and exhaust principles to the utmost,
though silently in quiet halls,
mysteriously unite with what is beyond the four seas,
thus riding the two modes (yīn and yáng) and driving the six breaths,
harmonizing with the crowd and directing all things.
If there is nothing they do not accord with,
then they ride on floating clouds;
if there is no form they do not carry,
then they drive flying dragons.
Forgetting the self and attaining naturally,
though indifferent, they require nothing.
Sitting in forgetfulness, acting in forgetfulness,
acting through forgetfulness,
thus their movement is like dragging dry wood,
their stillness like gathering dead ashes,
hence it is said their spirit is concentrated.
When their spirit is concentrated, what is not concentrated attains naturally.
The world all judges based on what they see,
how could they ever believe this!
Explanation:
Concentrated means tranquil.
Plagues refer to diseases.
The ripening of the five grains means a fruitful year.
The sage's form is like dry wood,
mind like dead ashes,
essence and traces simultaneous,
movement and stillness both wondrous,
concentrated illumination silently connects,
empty mind benefits things.
Thereby making the four seasons follow in order,
the five grains abundant,
people free from disasters,
things without premature death.
The sage's presence in the world,
possesses such efficacy,
Jiānwú, not understanding the ultimate words,
called it insane and did not believe.
Liánshū said:
Indeed,
the blind cannot be shown the beauty of patterns and colors,
the deaf cannot be given the sounds of bells and drums,
is it only the physical body that has deafness and blindness?
Knowledge also has them.
Note:
Not understanding the ultimate words' extreme wonder,
and considering them insane and unbelievable,
this is the deafness and blindness of knowledge.
Explanation:
The blind,
means eyes without pupils,
dark as drum skin.
The deaf,
means ear ailment.
The blind,
means eye faculties impaired.
Seeing with eyes and hearing with ears,
are common conditions of beings,
being blind or deaf,
they cannot be shown sounds or colors.
Similarly, ultimate words and wondrous truths,
only those with suspended understanding can know,
foolish and confused individuals,
never comprehend in their lifetime,
truly due to obstacles of wisdom, blind and dark,
unable to illuminate and perceive.
Is it only physical form that has them?
Thus, hearing Jiēyù's words, they call them insane and unbelievable.
From here onward,
is Liánshū's response to Jiānwú's words.
These words of his,
are like the timely maiden.
Note:
Meaning what Jiēyù said,
naturally sought by things,
but those deaf and blind in knowledge,
say there is no such principle.
Explanation:
"This,"
is a pointing expression.
"Timely maiden,"
refers to a young maiden in her chamber.
Pointing to Jiēyù's words,
like a graceful maiden,
elegant, pure, and serene,
sought by the noble person.
But those deaf and blind in knowledge,
say there is no such principle.
Such a person,
such virtue,
will encompass all things as one,
the world seeks order,
who would laboriously trouble with the affairs of the world!
Note:
The sage's mind,
reaches the ultimate of the two modes,
comprehends the wondrous numbers of all things,
thus able to embody transformation and adapt to change,
nowhere inappropriate;
encompassing all things,
nothing not so.
The world, in chaos, seeks me,
I have no mind.
If I have no mind,
why not respond to the world?
However, those who embody mystery and reach the ultimate,
the way they unite the natures of all things and mold the transformations under heaven to achieve the fame of Yáo and Shùn,
always act through non-action,
who would laboriously trouble their spirit and weary their thoughts,
taking affairs as tasks,
only then able to accomplish?
Explanation:
"Zhī,"
is a grammatical particle,
also an exclamation of praise.
"Encompass" means to blend into one.
"Seek" means to request.
"Who" means which person.
"Such a person,"
praises Yáo as one with sage virtue,
praises Yáo's abundant virtue.
It means the sage's virtue unites with the two modes,
their way aligns with all beings,
blending all things into one,
controlling and directing all spirits.
The world's way is decadent,
the people are scattered and chaotic,
thus they seek a great sage to rule and pacify.
But like an empty boat or suspended mirror,
responding and sensing without mind,
who would trouble their form and weary their wisdom!
Managing and planning territories,
taking affairs as tasks,
only then able to handle affairs.
Thus Lǎozǐ said:
Act through non-action,
handle affairs through non-affairs.
Also said:
To take the world,
always through non-affairs;
when there are affairs,
it is insufficient to take the world.
Such a person,
nothing can harm them,
Note:
Being at ease with what harms,
then harm cannot harm.
Harm cannot harm,
and things also do not harm them.
Great floods reaching the sky do not drown them,
great droughts melting metal and stone, scorching earth and mountains, do not make them hot.
Note:
Nowhere not at ease,
thus wherever they are, it is suitable.
Life and death do not change them,
how much less drowning and heat!
Thus, the ultimate person is not entangled in calamities,
not because they avoid them,
but because reasoning directly forward, they naturally meet with good fortune.
Explanation:
"Jī" means "to arrive at."
One who has penetrated life and death,
then there is no death and no life;
who is suited to water and fire,
then does not drown nor burn.
Even if there were disasters like the Yang Nine melting metal,
or calamities like the Hundred Six flooding heavens,
chaotic as they may be from their side,
what are they to me!
Thus, Guǒ's commentary says:
"Death and life do not change oneself,
how much less between drowning and burning!"
This means that even their dust, grime, chaff, and husks could still mold and cast a Yáo or Shùn,
so who would be willing to take things as their business!
Commentary:
Yáo and Shùn are
merely names in worldly affairs.
Those who act for fame,
are not the true name.
Therefore, Yáo and Shùn,
how could they be just Yáo and Shùn?
They must have the substance of divine men.
What is now called Yáo and Shùn
only names their dust, grime, chaff, and husks.
Explanation:
Scattered is dust,
greasy is grime,
unripe grain is chaff,
grain skin is husk,
all are base things.
Melting metal is called casting,
molding clay is called pottery.
The rules of posthumous titles:
"Assisting goodness and transmitting sageliness is called Yáo,"
"Benevolent, sagely, prosperous, and bright is called Shùn."
Now, Yáo reached the root,
mysteriously transcending form and name,
blending traces and joining with the dust,
things delighted in his virtue,
hence established names and titles to manifest the sage's body.
However, names are coarse methods,
no different from chaff and husks;
posthumous titles are worldly affairs,
how do they differ from dust and grime!
Then, through feigning, flattering, and falsehood,
they forge that dust and grime into Yáo,
use this chaff and husk to mold and shape Shùn.
How could they know the mysterious substance,
how can it be spoken of!
Thus, who would be willing to take things as their business.
A man of Sòng procured ceremonial caps and went to the Yuè people,
but the Yuè people cut their hair and tattooed their bodies,
and had no use for them.
Explanation:
This is an analogy.
"Zī" means to trade.
The state of Yuè was close to rivers and lakes,
they cut their hair and tattooed their bodies
to avoid the harm of flood dragons.
"Zhāngfǔ" is the name of a cap.
Thus, Confucius, born in Lǔ,
wore robes with wide sleeves;
grew up in Sòng,
wore the Zhāngfǔ cap.
And Sòng was indeed the descendant of Wēizǐ,
Yuè was the offspring of Tàibó,
the two states traded back and forth,
hence the Zhāngfǔ caps were used as goods.
Moreover, Zhāngfǔ caps were originally for head adornment,
requiring coiled hair to support the cap,
but the Yuè people cut their hair and tattooed their bodies,
so the traded goods became useless.
Similarly, glory and splendor originally involve attachment,
wealth and honor arise from arrogance,
but Yáo, having embodied the Way and thoroughly forgotten,
could thus be useless to the world.
Therefore, Guǒ's commentary says:
"Yáo's having no use for the world
is just like the Yuè people having no use for the Zhāngfǔ caps."
Yáo governed the people of the world,
managed the policies within the seas,
yet went to see the four masters at the sunny side of the Miǎogūyè Mountain by the Fén River,
and profoundly lost his world.
Commentary:
Yáo's having no use for the world
is just like the Yuè people having no use for the Zhāngfǔ caps.
However, one who abandons the world
is surely revered by the world.
Though the world revered Yáo,
Yáo never possessed the world,
hence profoundly lost it.
And he once wandered his mind in the realm of absolute darkness,
though sitting atop all things,
he was always free and unfettered.
The four masters
are probably metaphorical to show that Yáo was not confined to being Yáo.
For Yáo was truly obscure,
his traces were Yáo.
Viewing the obscure from the traces,
inner and outer are different realms, not strange at all.
The world only sees Yáo as Yáo,
how could they recognize his obscurity!
Thus, seeking the four masters overseas,
and confining Yáo to what is seen,
thereby saying that those who flow with things
lose their means to be free and unfettered.
Yet they do not know that the most distant traces, when followed, become nearer,
and the highest places where one meets are actually lower.
If one sternly considers solitary height as the ultimate and not level with worldly burdens,
such are the valley hermits,
not those who are without dependence,
how can they suffice to speak of the ultimate and wander in the infinite!
Explanation:
"Govern" means to order principles,
"policies" mean customs and teachings,
this combines the metaphor.
The Fén River originates from Tàiyuán,
flows west into the Yellow River.
North of the water is called "yáng."
Then today's Píngyáng County in Jìnzhōu,
north of the Fén River,
was the former capital of Yáo.
"Profoundly" means
silent and vast,
a term for depth and distance.
"Lost" means to forget,
an expression of release and dispersion.
And the four masters
are the four virtues:
one is the root,
two is the trace,
three is neither root nor trace,
four is neither not-root nor not-trace.
It says Yáo reflected on the source of his mind,
saw the realm of the Way clearly,
transcended these four propositions,
hence it says he went to see the four masters.
The sage has no mind,
responding when stimulated,
thus able to order all states,
harmonize the nine lands.
Though again concentrating his spirit,
the four masters sat upright by the Fén River's sunny side,
governing all affairs,
yet profoundly he lost the world.
This is because root is trace,
substance is function,
emptiness and existence are both illuminated,
movement and stillness are simultaneous.
Thus, Gūshè is no different from Fényáng,
how could mountain forests differ from the imperial court?
People standardize what they see,
how could they ever believe this?
Mǎ Biāo took the four masters as Nièquē,
thus failing to reach the distant principle;
Liú Zhàng located the Fén River at the Shè Mountain,
further confusing recent matters.
The interpretation here
slightly differs from these.
Hence Guǒ's commentary says:
"The four masters
are probably metaphorical to show that Yáo was not confined to being Yáo."
The world only sees Yáo's traces,
how could they recognize his true self!
Huìzǐ said to Zhuāngzǐ:
"The King of Wèi gave me seeds of a large gourd,
Explanation:
Surname Huì, name Shī,
a man of Sòng,
served as chancellor of Liáng State.
"Said" means spoke.
"Gave" means bestowed.
"Gourd" is a type of calabash.
The King of Wèi is King Huì of Liáng.
Formerly residing in Ānyì,
the state was called Wèi,
later forced by powerful Qín,
moved to Dàliáng,
changed again to Liáng,
usurping the title of king.
Huìzǐ used this metaphor of the large gourd
to ridicule Zhuāngzǐ's writings,
though their themes were vast and grand,
they were not pertinent to practical affairs,
hence these words to provoke each other further.
I planted them, and when they grew, the fruit could hold five dàn,
used to hold water,
but its firmness could not support itself.
Explanation:
"Planted" means cultivated.
"Fruit" means the gourd.
Huì Shī, having obtained the gourd seeds,
cultivated them to maturity,
produced a very large gourd,
containing five dàn.
Yet using this gourd to hold water,
it was hollow and brittle, not firm,
thus could not support itself.
Split it to make dippers,
then they were too flat and had nothing to hold.
It is not that it isn't enormously large,
but I smashed it because it was useless.
Explanation:
"Pŏu" means to split or divide it.
"Piáo" is a ladle.
"Huòluò" means flat and shallow.
"Xiāorán" means hollow and large.
"Pŏu" means to break by striking.
If used to hold water,
it is hollow and brittle, unable to bear its own weight;
if split to make a ladle,
it is too flat and shallow to hold much.
Everyone deems it useless,
so it is broken and discarded.
This criticizes Zhuāngzǐ's words as failing to address urgent needs of the time,
similar to this statement,
and should thus be eliminated.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
You are truly unskilled in using the large!
There was a man of Sòng skilled at making an anti-chap medicine,
whose family for generations made their living by bleaching silk floss.
Note:
The medicine could prevent hands from chapping,
so they often bleached silk floss in water.
Explanation:
"Píng" means to float.
"Pì" means to bleach.
"Kuàng" is silk floss.
"Shìshì" means generations.
The people of Sòng waded in water in deep winter,
bleaching silk floss to make textiles,
their hands developing sores,
chapped like a tortoise's shell,
so generation after generation,
they passed down this medicine,
keeping their hands from chapping,
enabling them to bleach silk floss in water constantly,
preserving this livelihood,
never failing or ceasing.
It is also said:
"Pì" means to separate;
"Kuàng" is raw silk.
Meaning to separate it in water.
A visitor heard of this,
and offered to buy the formula for a hundred pieces of gold.
Explanation:
One piece of gold is one cun square and weighs one jīn.
A traveling visitor from another state happened to hear of it,
requested to buy the technique for hand sores,
and thus paid the price of a hundred gold pieces.
The man gathered his clan and deliberated:
For generations, we've bleached silk floss,
earning no more than a few pieces of gold.
Now we can sell the technique for a hundred gold in one morning,
let's agree to it.
Explanation:
"Yù" means to sell.
Since the valuation was high,
he gathered the clan to discuss.
Generations of bleaching
yielded meager profits;
selling the technique in one morning
brings immense wealth.
With one voice,
all said to agree.
The visitor obtained it,
and used it to persuade the King of Wú.
When Yuè posed a threat,
the King of Wú made him a general.
In winter,
engaging in naval battle with the Yuè people,
he greatly defeated them,
and was granted a fief of land.
Explanation:
Wú and Yuè were northern neighbors,
their lands bordered by rivers and sea,
weapons often clashed,
necessitating the use of warships.
In deep winter, soldiers
often had chapped hands.
The visitor, endowed with great talent
and innate wisdom,
having obtained the formula,
persuaded the King of Wú.
When Yuè invaded Wú,
the king appointed him as commander.
Relying on this famed medicine,
the soldiers' hands did not chap.
As soon as the banners were raised,
the Yuè forces fell into disarray.
Achieving this great victory,
he returned in triumph,
his merits outstanding,
and was enfeoffed with land.
The ability to prevent chapping is the same,
yet one used it to gain a fief,
while another could not avoid bleaching silk floss,
showing the difference in its application.
Explanation:
"Huò" indicates uncertainty.
The formula itself is not skilled,
but its users differ.
Thus, the traveler gained a marquisate with it,
while the man of Sòng used it for bleaching,
demonstrating the disparity in skillful and unskillful use.
Now you have a gourd large enough to hold five shí,
why not make it into a great buoy to float upon rivers and lakes,
instead of worrying that it's too flat and shallow to hold anything?
This shows your mind is still tangled like overgrowth!
Note:
Overgrowth does not grow straight.
This passage illustrates that each thing has its proper use;
if used appropriately,
where can one not wander freely?
Explanation:
"Lǚ" means to bind with ropes.
"Zūn"
is lacquered like a wine vessel,
tied with ropes,
used to cross rivers and lakes,
what southerners call a "waist boat."
"Péng,"
a type of grass,
is twisted and not straight.
"Fū" is an exclamation.
A large gourd floating on rivers and lakes
can save one from drowning;
profound teachings circulating in the world
can deliver the deluded masses.
Yet Huìzǐ, with a tangled mind,
unable to grasp the profound truth directly,
foolishly raised the analogy of smashing it,
criticizing Zhuāngzǐ's writings,
for improper use, deeply lamentable.
Huìzǐ said to Zhuāngzǐ:
I have a large tree,
people call it a "chū."
Explanation:
The chū is like the cork tree or lacquer tree,
smelling very foul,
an undesirable wood.
Names in the world
are generally illusory,
people smelling it together,
unsure of its true nature,
hence said to be called "chū."
Its main trunk is gnarled and unfit for the ink-line,
its small branches curled and unfit for the compass and square.
Planted by the road,
carpenters do not glance at it.
Explanation:
"Yōngzhǒng" means knotted and tumorous.
"Juǎnqū" means not straight.
The compass makes circles, the square makes angles.
"Tú" is the road.
The chū tree,
a useless timber,
with a gnarled trunk,
twisted branches,
untouched by the ink-line,
unfit for circles or squares,
standing by the roadside,
carpenters do not even look at it.
Now your words,
grand but useless,
are similarly rejected by all.
Explanation:
The tree, being gnarled and useless,
is ignored by carpenters;
your words, far-fetched and impractical,
are shunned by all.
This is the analogy.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
Have you not seen the wildcat?
It crouches low,
awaiting careless prey;
leaping east and west,
unavoiding of heights or depths;
it falls into traps,
and dies in nets.
Explanation:
"Xīng" is a wildcat.
"Tiàoliáng" means running and jumping.
"Pì,"
a method,
refers to mechanisms like traps.
"Wǎnggǔ" are nets and snares.
Have you not seen how a wildcat catches mice?
Crouching low,
it waits for arrogant, careless mice;
leaping east and west,
unavoiding of high or low ground,
it falls into mechanical traps,
and dies in nets.
All are deluded by small gains,
failing to plan for greater matters.
Similarly, kneeling and bending in false reverence,
clinging to sagely traces,
feigning emotions and distorting nature,
to seek temporal advantages.
Though one may have achieved their desires before,
they are bound to face peril and ruin later.
Figures like Shāng Yāng, Sū Qín, and Zhāng Yí
exemplify this very truth.
How is this different from a cat catching rats,
only to die in a trap itself?
Now consider the yak,
as large as a cloud hanging from the sky,
capable of grand feats,
yet unable to catch a mouse.
Note:
The yak, similar to the bison,
originates from the southwestern tribes,
with a massive form.
Viewed from afar in the mountains,
it resembles clouds on the horizon,
