Note: Without emotions, therefore entrust to things. Subcommentary: Compare to that spiritual truth, absolutely without nature and consciousness; already forgetting sentient beings and self, how can there be right and wrong? This explains being without human emotions.
How minute! That by which he belongs to humans.

Note: Physical appearance like a human. Subcommentary: "Belong" means connected. Traces noisy and stingy, form connected to human groups, not different from things - therefore called minute. This concludes having human form.
How vast! Alone completing his heaven.

Note: Without emotions, therefore vastly nothing not entrusted. That which nothing is not entrusted - what emotional beings cannot achieve. Therefore, without emotions and alone completing heaven. Subcommentary: "Vast" means lofty and great appearance. Vastly great teaching, ten thousand realms all forgotten; wisdom and virtue lofty and profound, concentrated illumination broad and far-reaching - therefore praising the great man alone completing natural truth. This concludes being without human emotions.
Huìzǐ said to Zhuāngzǐ: "Is a human originally without emotions?"

Subcommentary: Previous text said: "Having human form, without human emotions." Huì Shī quotes this to doubt Zhuāngzǐ's statement: "Humans must originally be without emotional concerns?" However, the two worthies Zhuāng and Huì both wandered hearts beyond, therefore often received this as topic for discussion.
Zhuāngzǐ said: "Yes."
Subcommentary: "Yes" means thus. Approving his question, therefore answered "Yes."
Huìzǐ said: "Being human yet without emotions - how can he be called human?"
Subcommentary: If without nature and wisdom, how named as human? This is Huì Shī's advancing reproachful words questioning Zhuāngzǐ.
Zhuāngzǐ said: "The Way gives him appearance; heaven gives him form - how can he not be called human?"

Note: Human life is not born from emotions; what life knows, how could it be known by emotions? Therefore, having emotion toward becoming Lí Kuàng, one cannot; yet Lí Kuàng through having no emotions were clear and bright. Having emotion toward becoming sages and worthies, one cannot; yet sages and worthies through having no emotions were sage and worthy. How could it be only that sages and worthies are absolutely distant and Lí Kuàng difficult to admire? Even the lowly foolish, deaf and blind, and chickens crowing, dogs barking - did they have emotion toward becoming so? Also ultimately could not. Not asking far and near, though departing from oneself by one part, between Yán and Kǒng ultimately cannot get it. Therefore, closing off from the myriad things, instead take from one's own person - ears and eyes cannot exchange tasks to complete work; hands and feet cannot replace offices to achieve function. Therefore, the infant at beginning of life does not use eyes to seek milk, not use ears toward brightness, not use feet to handle things, not use hands to seek walking. How could the hundred parts have no fixed offices, physical appearance no constant master, and yet be controlled solely by emotion? Subcommentary: "How" means why. The empty penetrating Way gives him appearance; the natural principle gives him form. Leaving aside his physical substance, form and appearance already possessed - how can he not be
The Nanhua True Classic Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Seven, Part One
Commentary by Guō Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá of the Táng Dynasty Inner Chapters, The Great and Venerable Teacher, Number Six
To know what Heaven does and to know what humanity does is the ultimate.

Commentary: To know that what Heaven and humanity do are both natural means internally letting go of one's self and externally merging with things, mysteriously united with the multitude, entrusting to it without anything not being reached. Subcommentary: "Heaven" means what is natural; "ultimate" is the name for reaching the pinnacle. What Heaven does refers to the darkening and brightening of the three luminaries, the generation and cessation of the four seasons, the stretching and rolling of wind and clouds, and the cold and warmth of thunder and rain. What humanity does refers to using hands to grasp, feet to walk, eyes to see, ears to hear, the mind to know skill and clumsiness, and all that is carried out. To know that what Heaven does is entirely spontaneous, unrelated to cultivation or creation, how could it come from knowledge or effort? Therefore, internally letting go of one's self, externally merging with things, greatly observing all, mysteriously united with the multitude, exhausting principle and fulfilling nature—this is called the ultimate.
To know what Heaven does is to be born of Heaven.

Commentary: "Heaven" means what is natural. Those who act with purposeful action cannot act, yet acting happens through spontaneous acting. Those who know with purposeful knowing cannot know, yet knowing happens through spontaneous knowing. Spontaneous knowing means not knowing, yet not not knowing; thus, knowing arises from not knowing. Spontaneous acting means not acting, yet not not acting; thus, acting arises from not acting. Since acting arises from not acting, therefore, not acting is taken as the master. Since knowing arises from not knowing, therefore, not knowing is taken as the essence. Thus, the true person discards knowing yet knows, does not act yet acts, is born naturally, and attains through sitting in forgetfulness. Hence, knowing is called cut off and acting is named removed. Subcommentary: Clouds moving, rain falling, rivers' sources, mountains and valleys—these are not related to human effort; this is being born of Heaven. The ability to know and what is known are both natural. This explains the previous "know what Heaven does."

To know what humanity does is to use the known of one's knowledge to nurture the unknown of one's knowledge, to end one's natural years without being cut off midway—this is the flourishing of knowledge.

Commentary: In human life, though the body is but seven feet tall, the five constants are necessarily complete. Thus, though the body is small, it is served by all heaven and earth. Therefore, all that exists in heaven, earth, and the myriad things cannot be absent for a single day. If one thing is lacking, then the living have no means to live; if one principle is not reached, then natural years have no way to end. However, what the body possesses, knowledge may or may not know; principles that exist may or may not be acted upon. Thus, what knowledge knows is few, while what the body possesses is many; what action does is little, while principles that exist are vast. Those above cannot treat it as a vessel and seek its completeness. What people know need not be the same, yet what they do dare not differ; if they differ, then artifice is formed. If artifice is formed and the true is not lost, this has never happened. Some delight in knowledge without tiring, thereby burdening their hundred body parts; what they delight in is but one limb, yet all roots are harmed. This is using what they know to harm what they do not know. As for the flourishing of knowledge, knowing what humanity does has its portion, thus entrusting without forcing; knowing what humanity knows has its limits, thus using without dissipating. Therefore, if what is known does not trap itself with boundlessness, then within the unified body, the known and unknown darkly meet and are entirely preserved. This is using what is known to nurture what is unknown. Subcommentary: What humanity does refers to the four limbs and hundred body parts, each having their functions. "The known of knowledge" means knowing oneself regarding form, thus taking form as the known. "The unknown of knowledge" means being able to know form oneself but not sound, thus taking sound as the unknown. Then, the eyes act for the hands and feet, and the feet act for the ears and nose in walking; though again without mind, they act for each other, and the work of aiding each other is accomplished. Thus, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, four limbs, hundred body parts alternately employ each other, each having their roles. The brightness and darkness of the mind also have their limits; using what is within their portion, ultimately not forcing knowledge—this is using the known of one's knowledge to nurture the unknown of one's knowledge. Therefore, one can exhaust one's natural years without untimely cut-off. Those who can be like this may be called having the flourishing beauty of knowledge.
Even so, there is distress.

Commentary: Though knowledge is flourishing, it is not like discarding knowledge and entrusting to Heaven, which is without distress. Subcommentary: Though knowledge is flourishing and beautiful, there are still afflictions and burdens; it is not like forgetting knowledge and entrusting to solitude.
Knowledge has something it awaits, and only then is it appropriate.

Commentary: Those who know are unable to have no "can" and no "cannot," thus necessarily have something they await. If one is born by entrusting to Heaven, then encountering things, it is appropriate. Subcommentary: Knowledge necessarily confronts objects; without objects, it is not appropriate. Objects, since their production and cessation are uncertain, things also await gain and loss, impermanent. Only when both object and knowledge are forgotten, both ability and object dismissed, can one have no "can" and no "cannot," and only then be without distress.
What it awaits is specifically undetermined.
Commentary: Having something to await means it is undetermined. Subcommentary: What is awaited is specifically undetermined.
How can we know that what I call Heaven is not human? Or that what I call human is not Heaven?

Commentary: My life having limits is Heaven; the mind wanting to increase it is humanity. However, this is what humanity calls it; things are none other than Heaven. "Heaven" means what is natural. If all are natural, then order and chaos, success and failure, encountering or not encountering, are not human doings—all are natural. Subcommentary: Examining closely the self, entrusting distantly to things, the functioning of knowledge and ability is none other than natural. Thus, knowing that Heaven and humanity, in principle, return to non-duality, therefore what is called Heaven is human, what is called human is Heaven. How could the ordinary multitude comprehend this meaning? The "I" spoken refers to Zhuangzi himself. This erases the distinction between human and Heaven, mixes and unites things and self.
Moreover, only after there is a true person is there true knowledge.

Commentary: Only after there is a true person is the knowledge under heaven all able to attain its truth and not be confused. Subcommentary: The sage indeed can darkly unite with the true and merge with the Way, forget self and discard things, embrace this sagely virtue, and only then have this true knowledge. Thus, merging into one with the true person and without afflictions or burdens—the state of true knowledge is listed in the text below.
What is called a true person?
Subcommentary: Assuming a question to reveal the meaning.
The true persons of old did not oppose the few.

Commentary: If all few are not opposed, then what is followed is many. Subcommentary: "Few" means small. Leading with the ancient to govern the present, honoring the root and suppressing the branches, emptying the heart and entrusting to things, greatly following the multitude of lives—even if meeting with slight smallness, they would not oppose or resist.
They were not mighty in success.

Commentary: Not relying on their success to place themselves before things. Subcommentary: Acting without relying, nurturing without controlling—how could they be mighty, occupying achievements, wanting to place themselves before things?
They did not scheme over scholars.

Commentary: Releasing the mind straight forward, and the multitude of scholars naturally joined; it was not through planning and scheming that they were brought. Subcommentary: Empty and even, forgetting and淡泊, the scholars naturally returned; it was not due to exercising the mind in planning and recruiting. If so, when missing, they did not regret; when hitting, they did not self-attain. Commentary: Simply fully appropriate without error, not taking gain and loss to heart. Subcommentary: When the time of Heaven had passed, they never had regretful thoughts; when fate by chance was appropriate, they did not take self-attainment as beauty.
If so, they climbed high without trembling, entered water without getting soaked, entered fire without heat—this is knowledge able to ascend and reach the Way, like this.

Commentary: Speaking of the ability to ascend to the Way is like this far. Principle is inherently fully preserved, not fearing death. Thus, the true person walking on land is not avoiding soaking, keeping away from fire is not fleeing heat, having no error is not arranging appropriateness. Therefore, though not taking heat as heat, they never rush into fire; not taking soak as soak, they never tread water; not taking death as death, they never lose life. Thus, life—how is it born? It is born. Completion—how is it completed? It is completed. Therefore, entrusting to it without anything not reached—this is the true person. How could they have intentions about what they encounter? Subcommentary: "Trembling" means fear; "soaked" means wet; "ascend" means rise; "reach" means arrive. The true person penetrates the non-duality of life and death, embodies that safety and danger are one; thus, they can enter water, enter fire, never介意ing, climb high, tread danger—how could they again be startled or fearful? Persons of true knowledge have this ability and function, ascend to the mysterious Way, thus attaining such a state.
The true persons of old, in their sleep, did not dream.

Commentary: Without intentional thought. Subcommentary: Dreaming is emotional intention and妄想. The true person has no emotional worry, cuts off thought and thinking; thus, though sleeping in silent泊, they do not dream, and upon awakening, are always at ease without worry.
In their waking, they were without worry.
Commentary: Meeting what they encounter, they are at ease. Subcommentary: As above.
In their eating, they did not savor.
Commentary: Principle dictates they eat, that is all. Subcommentary: Mixing traces in the human world, sharing the dust and eating, not indulging in flavors, thus not knowing sweetness and beauty.

Commentary: It comes from within the root origin. Subcommentary: "Heels" means the roots of the feet. The true person's mind-nature is harmonious and slow, wisdom illumination concentrated and still; even the breath is also again slow and delayed, coming from the heels, clarifying its depth and stillness.
The multitude's breath comes from the throat. Those who are submissive, their words are like obstructed.

Commentary: The breath is not peaceful and smooth. Subcommentary: "Throat" means the throat; "obstructed" means hindered. Ordinary people's minds race and compete, speech and panting only come from the throat; emotions are agitated, breath hurried, unable to be deep and still. Bending and rising, the breath is not harmonized; within the throat, it is always as if obstructed.
Those whose desires are deep, their heavenly mechanism is shallow.

Commentary: Deep roots and utmost stillness, then returning to one without desire. Subcommentary: Those who indulge in various dusts and have heavy emotions and desires have their natural mechanism and spirit shallow and dull. If wisdom illumination were deep and far, how could it be so?
The true persons of old did not know to delight in life, did not know to hate death.

Commentary: They embodied transformation. Subcommentary: Qi gathers as life; life is my time. Qi disperses as death; death is my following. Since they are darkly merged with transformation, they do not hold delight or hatred in their hearts.
Their emerging was not joyful, their entering was not resistant.

Commentary: Vastly and calmly entrusting to it. Subcommentary: When the time responded to emerge into life, originally without emotion for joy; when the time responded to enter death, how could they have intention to resist or avoid?
Carefree they went, carefree they came, that is all.

Commentary: Entrusted to the ultimate principle, thus going and coming without difficulty. Subcommentary: "Carefree" describes being unbound. Carefree, transforming alone, entrusting to principle and wandering freely; though again death goes and life comes, never with intention or attachment.
They did not forget their beginning, did not seek their end.

Commentary: Both end and beginning, transformation and change, are forgotten. How could they only inversely forget life and still secretly probe seeking the meaning of death? Subcommentary: "Beginning" is birth; "end" is death. Both life and death are dismissed, never attached or滞留; how could they only uniquely forget life and partially seek death? End and beginning are equalized, meeting whatever, thus at ease.
They received it and delighted in it.
Commentary: Not questioning what is received; encountering it, nothing is not suitable. Subcommentary: Delighting in what is encountered.
They forgot and returned it.
Commentary: Returning it does not come from consciousness—it reaches the ultimate. Subcommentary: Returning to the unborn.
This is called not using the mind to discard the Way, not using humanity to aid Heaven. This is called the true person.

Commentary: Human life is still—this is the nature of Heaven. Stirred by things and moving—this is the desire of nature. Things stirring humans are endless; humans chasing desires are without restraint—then heavenly principle is extinguished. The true person knows that using the mind turns away from the Way, aiding Heaven harms life; therefore, they do not do it. Subcommentary: "This is called" points to the previous text, summarizing its meaning. "Discard" means abandon. Speaking of the above wisdom and virtue, forgetting life—this may be called not using a grasping and rejecting mind to abandon the empty and penetrating Way, also not using human emotions to differentiate and add to the natural portion. Those who can be like this are named true persons.
If so, their mind is resolved.

Commentary: Where they dwell, they are at ease—this is resolve. Subcommentary: If like the previous not discarding the Way, etc., the mind is怀ing resolve and操守, able to cause such. Thus, the Laozi says: "Those who force action have resolve."
Their countenance is still.
Commentary: Though acting, without harming stillness.
Their forehead is broad.

Commentary: "Broad" describes the appearance of great simplicity. Subcommentary: "Forehead" means the brow; "broad" means the appearance of great simplicity. The true person descends into the world, outstanding qi different from ordinary; not only wisdom illumination empty and bright, resolve power vast and universal, but also威严 appearance leisurely and elegant,相貌 dignified and solemn; sun-angle moon-mystery—this is the category.
Chilly, they are like autumn.
Commentary: Killing things is not to be威严.
Warm, they are like spring.
Commentary: Generating things is not to be humane.
Joy and anger penetrate the four seasons.

Commentary: Those who embody the Way and merge with change share warmth and severity with cold and heat, yet never have a mind. However, having the appearance of warmth and severity, the節制 of generation and killing, thus temporarily named joy and anger. Subcommentary: The sage has no mind; feeling, thus responding.威严 and grace suit affairs, leniency and severity meet opportunity; same as plain autumn descending frost, originally without mind for肃杀; like green spring's growth and nurture, how could they have intention for humane grace? Thus, the true person is like thunder moving, wind blowing, trees flourishing, flowers blooming; covering and carrying harmonize with the two modes; joy and anger penetrate the four sequences.
With things, they have appropriateness, and none know their limit.

Commentary: No mind toward things, thus not seizing things' appropriateness; no thing not appropriate, thus none know their limit. Subcommentary: The true person responds to the world, meets feelings, timely interacts with things; necessarily having appropriate convenience, yet empty mind and compassionate love, always good at saving people; measure equal to the great void, thus none know their limit.
Thus, when the sage uses arms, they destroy states yet do not lose the people's hearts.

Subcommentary: Yao attacked Congzhi, Yu attacked Youhu, Cheng Tang ended Xia, Zhou Wu attacked Yin—all above harmonized with Heaven's time, below accorded with human affairs. Therefore, they raised arms, lamented the people and punished crimes; though again destroying states, they did not lose the common people's joyful hearts.
Benefits and grace extend for ten thousand generations, yet they do not act from loving people.

Commentary: Following what the people's hearts desire to destroy, they destroy them, thus not losing the people's hearts. The bright sun ascending heaven illuminates all six directions—not from loving people do they illuminate them. Thus, the sage in the world, warm like spring sunlight naturally harmonious—thus those receiving moisture do not thank; chilly like autumn frost naturally descending—thus those withering and falling do not resent. Subcommentary: Benefiting things, enriching grace, matters equal to spring sunlight; how could it be only one time? It extends for ten thousand generations. Like straw dogs to the common people, thus without biased love emotions.
Therefore, delighting in penetrating things is not the sage.
Commentary: The sage has no delight; simply, nothing blocks it and things naturally penetrate. Subcommentary: Hanging a mirror high in the
Zhuānxū obtained it and dwelt in the Dark Palace.

Note: Zhuānxū was the grandson of Huángdì, also known as Emperor Gāoyáng, and also called the Dark Emperor. He was capped at age twelve, assisted Shǎohào at fifteen, and ascended the throne at twenty. He mined copper from Yǔshān to cast a tripod cauldron, capable of summoning the spirits of the four seas, possessing supernatural powers. He passed away at ninety-seven, having attained the Way, and became the Emperor of the North. Dark is the color of the north, hence he dwelt in the Dark Palace.
Yǔqiáng obtained it and stood at the North Pole.

Note: Yǔqiáng is the name of a water deity, also known as Yǔjīng. With a human face and bird body, he rides a dragon and travels. He and Zhuānxū are both descendants of Xuānyuán. Although he attained the Way, he did not hold an imperial position but became a water deity. Water's position is in the north, hence his location is called the North Pole.
Xīwángmǔ obtained it and sits at Shàoguǎng; none know her beginning, none know her end.

Note: Shàoguǎng is the name of a mountain in the western extremity. Xīwángmǔ is the essence of the Great Yin, with a leopard's tail and tiger's teeth, fond of laughter. During Shùn's time, she sent an envoy to present a jade ring; during Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's time, she offered green peaches. Her appearance is that of a sixteen or seventeen-year-old girl, very dignified and constant. She always sits in the western Shàoguǎng Mountain, neither dying nor being born, hence none know her beginning or end.
Péngzǔ obtained it, reaching up to the time of Yǒuyú and down to the Five Hegemons.

Note: Péngzǔ was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Zhuānxū, enfeoffed at Péngchéng. His Way could be ancestral, hence called Péngzǔ. He was skilled in nurturing life and attained the Way. The Five Hegemons are: Kūnwú as the Hegemon of Xià; Dàpéng and Shǐwéi as Hegemons of Yīn; Qí Huán and Jìn Wén as Hegemons of Zhōu—together making five. Péngzǔ attained the Way, thus achieving longevity, from Yǒuyú up to Yīn and Zhōu down, totaling eight hundred years.
Fù Yuè obtained it and became the minister of Wǔ Dīng, encompassing the entire realm. He rides the Eastern Cord, straddles Jī and Wěi, and is ranked among the constellations.

Commentary: The Way has no capability. This speaks of obtaining it from the Way to illuminate that it is self-attained. Self-attained means the Way cannot make one attain it. If I have not attained it, I also cannot make it attained. Thus, all who attain it do not rely externally on the Way nor internally on themselves, but dig it out spontaneously and transform independently. The difficulty of life is like transforming independently and attaining it spontaneously. Since one has attained life, why worry about not attaining life and striving for it? Therefore, striving for life indeed cannot fully preserve life, because life does not come from oneself, and striving for it harms one's true life. Note: Wǔ Dīng is the name of a Yīn king, titled Gāozōng. Gāozōng dreamed of obtaining Fù Yuè and sent seekers throughout the realm, finding him at Fùyán in Héběi County of Shǎnzhōu, where he was building walls. He became minister to Wǔ Dīng, bringing peace and prosperity. Fù Yuè is the essence of a star, and the star Fù Yuè is located above Jī and Wěi. Jī and Wěi are among the twenty-eight constellations, sustaining the east, hence said to ride the Eastern Cord, straddle Jī and Wěi, and stand in line with stars like Jiǎo and Kàng, thus ranked among the constellations.
Nánhuá Zhēnjīng Commentary, Chapter Seven.
The Southern Florescence True Classic Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll 8, Part 2
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty
Nánbó Zǐkuí asked Nǚyǔ, saying: "Your years are long, yet your complexion is like that of a child. Why is this?"

Subcommentary: Kuí should be the character Qí; it is a mistake. This is the same Nánbó Zǐqí from the "Human World" chapter. Nǚyǔ is an ancient person who embraced the Dào. 'Rúzǐ' is like a young child. Nǚyǔ had long heard the ultimate Dào, thus he could conserve and nurture life. Though his years were old, he still had the complexion of a child and the appearance of retained vitality. Since he was different from ordinary people, Zǐkuí thus asked how he achieved this.
He said: "I have heard the Dào."
Commentary: Having heard the Dào, he lets it live spontaneously; thus his vital energy and complexion are whole.
Subcommentary: He answers, saying:
"Having heard the Dào, I thus attained the preservation of life. Therefore, I reversed aging and returned to childhood; my complexion is like that of a稚子."
Nánbó Zǐkuí said: "Can the Dào be learned?"
Subcommentary: Observing that his appearance and complexion were already different from ordinary people, his heart cherished admiration, thus he inquired about his methods and arts.
He said: "No! How could it be! You are not the right person."

Subcommentary: "È! È kě!" means it is not possible. Nǚyǔ's spirit and mind were inwardly tranquil, his form and appearance outwardly radiant. Zǐkuí, seeing he had such countenance, joyfully requested to learn, but [Nǚyǔ], disliking his questioning, thus suppressed him, saying he was not the right person.
"Now, Bǔliáng Yǐ has the talent of a sage but not the Dào of a sage. I have the Dào of a sage but not the talent of a sage."

Subcommentary: Bǔliáng: his family name was Jī, his personal name Yǐ. Emptying the mind and concentrating on tranquility constitutes the Dào; intelligent and sharp wisdom constitutes talent. This says Liáng has the talent for external application but lacks the inwardly concentrated Dào; Nǚyǔ has the Dào of emptiness and tranquility but lacks intelligent and sharp talent. Each is stuck on one side, not yet achieving comprehensive excellence. However, comparing talent with the Dào, talent is inferior and the Dào is superior.
"I wish to teach him; perhaps he will indeed become a sage! If not, telling the Dào of a sage to one with the talent of a sage is also easy. Yet I still guard it and tell him."

Subcommentary: 'Shù' means to aspire, 'jī' means near, 'guǒ' means resolute. When superior persons hear the Dào, they still rely on diligent practice. If one does not diligently practice the Dào, there is no way to attain it. Therefore, although receiving instruction, one must cultivate and learn, aspire to draw near the mysterious Dào, and resolutely become a sage. If it were not so, telling and showing would be very easy; why would it require cultivation and guarding, making achievement difficult? However, Nǚyǔ had long heard the ultimate Dào, his inner mind concentrated and still. Now wishing to transmit and tell it, he still guarded it himself; how much more so for a beginner—there is no room for laziness! Even if one speaks with the mouth and hears with the ear, what benefit is there? Therefore, it is not that knowing is difficult, but that practicing is difficult.
"After three days, he was then able to externalize the world."

Commentary: 'Externalize' means to forget. Subcommentary: 'Externalize' means to forget and let go. Being a teacher is not easy; transmitting the Dào is extremely difficult. Just as he was about to teach others, he concentrated his spirit, stilled his thoughts, cultivated and guarded it. After three full days, his mind was already empty and still, observing that all myriads are empty. Thus, heaven above and earth below were all considered non-existent.
"Having externalized the world, I again guarded it for seven days, and then was able to externalize things."

Commentary: 'Things' are what are needed morning and evening, closely related to oneself, difficult to forget. Subcommentary: The myriad realms of the world are distant and sparse, thus easy to forget. Things that support the body are intimate, thus difficult to dismiss. Guarding for seven full days, he then dismissed them. Thus, Guǒ's commentary says: 'Things are what are needed morning and evening, closely related to oneself, difficult to forget.'
"Having externalized things, I again guarded it for nine days, and then was able to externalize life."

Commentary: Completely forgetting. Subcommentary: Destroying the body, leaving the form, sitting in forgetfulness, losing the self. Having applied the mind for a long time, the forgetting and dismissing gradually deepened.
"Having externalized life, he was then able to have a 'morning clarity'."

Commentary: Forgetting life, then one does not detest death; not detesting death, thus wherever one encounters, one is at ease, open and without obstruction, seeing the opportunity and acting—this is 'morning clarity'. Subcommentary: 'Morning' is dawn; 'clarity' is brightness. Viewing death and life as one, simultaneously forgetting self and things, wisdom shines forth openly, like the morning sun first rising; therefore it is called 'morning clarity'.
"Having morning clarity, he was then able to 'see the solitary'."

Commentary: Wherever encountered, be at ease with it, forgetting the connections of before and after—this is 'seeing the solitary'. Subcommentary: Now, the ultimate Dào is concentrated and still, mysteriously transcending words and images; it is not non-existent, not existent, not ancient, not modern, goes alone, comes alone, absolutely unopposed, absolutely independent. Seeing this superior state is called 'seeing the solitary'. Therefore, the classic says: 'Silent and unchanging.'
"Seeing the solitary, he was then able to have 'no past and present'."

Commentary: Going together with the solitary. Subcommentary: Following the daily renewal of the creator, going along with all changes, not being shifted by external circumstances, thus there is no difference between past and present.
"Having no past and present, he was then able to 'enter the deathless and un-born'."

Commentary: Now, being attached to life, therefore there is death; detesting death, therefore there is life. Thus, having no attachment and no detesting, one can then have no death and no life. Subcommentary: 'Past and present' are merged. Now, the differences of past and present in time, the distinctions of life and death in phenomena—these are the views of deluded people, an inverted perspective. Since time operates anew, operating anew means no present, no past, thus phenomena also neither go nor come, have no death, no life. Who can merge with this principle? It is only someone like Nǚyǔ's disciple!
"What kills life does not die; what gives life does not live."

Subcommentary: 'Kill' means to extinguish; 'death' is also extinction. This means this so-called death has never been extinguished; this so-called life has never been born. Since life can enter the deathless and un-born, one embodies the phenomena's lack of birth and extinction. Since phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, how can emotions have any joy or detestation? Let it be, and there is nothing not suitable.
"As a thing, there is nothing it does not escort."
Commentary: Let it escort itself, thus there is nothing it does not escort.
"There is nothing it does not welcome."

Commentary: Let it welcome itself, thus there is nothing it does not welcome. Subcommentary: 'Escort' means to send off. Now, the Dào as a thing saves and aids without fixed methods. Although again not extinguishing, not living, it also again lives and extinguishes. Thus, it welcomes endless life and escorts immeasurable death.
"There is nothing it does not destroy."
Commentary: Let it destroy itself, thus there is nothing it does not destroy.
"There is nothing it does not complete."

Commentary: Let it complete itself, thus there is nothing it does not complete. Subcommentary: Not escorting yet escorting, there is nothing it does not destroy and extinguish; not welcoming yet welcoming, there is nothing it does not generate and complete.
"Its name is 'disturbance-tranquility'."

Commentary: Now, one who is merged with things, when things disturb, is also disturbed, yet has never not been tranquil. Subcommentary: 'Yīng' means disturbance; 'níng' means tranquil stillness. Now, the sage compassionately saves, the Dào aids all living beings. The wondrous source is nameless, following things to establish names. Moving yet constantly still, though disturbed, yet tranquil.
"'Disturbance-tranquility' means being disturbed and only then achieving completion."

Commentary: If things disturb and one alone is not disturbed, then one fails. Therefore, being disturbed and letting it be, then there is nothing not perfectly achieved. Subcommentary: Only after being able to harmonize the light and merge with the dust, moving yet constantly still, can one then follow things' disturbances, skillfully lending and generating completion.
Nánbó Zǐkuí said: "Where did you alone hear this?"

Subcommentary: Zǐkuí found it strange that Nǚyǔ's discussion of the Dào was so sublime and wondrous, thus he asked where he alone heard it. From here below, there are nine levels in total: the first six concern teaching, the last three concern principle. All are the words by which Nǚyǔ informed Zǐkuí.
He said: "I heard it from the Son of Auxiliary Ink."

Subcommentary: 'Zhū' means 'from'. 'Fù' means auxiliary, secondary. 'Mò' means writing brush and ink. 'Hànmò' means written words. Principle can generate teaching, thus written words are called auxiliary. Now, fish must rely on the trap to be caught; principle also relies on teaching to become clear. Therefore, he heard it from writing, meaning he first understood through written words.
"The Son of Auxiliary Ink heard it from the Grandson of Repeated Recitation."

Subcommentary: Copying a text is called 'Auxiliary Ink'; reciting from memory is called 'Repeated Recitation'. At first, one relies on the text to generate understanding, thus one holds and reads it. Next, one gradually awakens to its principle, therefore one repeatedly recites it. Moreover, teaching arises from principle, thus it is called 'Son'; recitation arises from teaching, thus it is named 'Grandson'.
"The Grandson of Repeated Recitation heard it from Clear Vision."

Subcommentary: 'Zhān' means to see, also to reach. Reciting meticulously and skillfully, accumulating effort over a long time, one gradually sees the ultimate principle, the spiritual repository becomes clear.
"Clear Vision heard it from Whispered Assent."

Subcommentary: 'Niè' means to ascend, also to whisper privately in the ear. Having recited deeply and exquisitely, through teaching one awakens to principle, the mind gives rise to joy, privately assenting. Whispering privately in the ear, having heard the Dào, not yet daring to practice it publicly, is also gradually ascending to superior wonder and mysterious feeling.
"Whispered Assent heard it from Required Service."

Subcommentary: 'Xū' means must; 'yì' means use, also practice. Although again privately assenting in the heart, wisdom's illumination gradually brightens, one must rely on teaching, follow cultivation, diligently practice without laziness. Understanding but not practicing the Dào, there is no way to attain it.
"Required Service heard it from Song."

Subcommentary: 'Ōu' means singing ballads. Having awakened to principle through teaching, practicing according to understanding, one thereby causes majestic virtue to manifest clearly, songs and ballads fill the roads.
"Song heard it from Profound Obscurity."

Commentary: 'Profound Obscurity' names non-being, yet it is not non-being. Subcommentary: 'Xuán' is a name for deep and far; 'míng' is a designation for secluded stillness. Since virtuous conduct is inwardly harmonized and fine reputation outwardly revealed, one gradually reaches the ultimate emptiness, arriving at Profound Obscurity.
"Profound Obscurity heard it from Vast Thrice-Transcended."

Commentary: Now, ascending through names to reach non-being, one must attain non-being beyond names. Therefore, although Profound Obscurity is still not the ultimate, one further pushes and entrusts to Vast Thrice-Transcended—this is also the mystery within mystery. Subcommentary: 'Cān' means three; 'liáo' means transcendence. The first transcends existence; the second transcends non-existence; the third transcends both existence and non-existence; therefore it is called 'thrice-transcended'. Now, the state of Profound Obscurity, though wondrous, is not the ultimate. Therefore, reaching the thrice-transcended, one just then creates the doubly profound.
"Vast Thrice-Transcended heard it from Doubtful Beginning."

Commentary: Now, the principle of nature has that which is achieved through accumulated practice. Generally, one ascends from near to far, refines the coarse to the subtle. Therefore, only after seven levels does one reach the name of non-being; after nine levels does one doubt that non-being is the beginning. Subcommentary: 'Shǐ' means the root. Now, the Dào transcends the four propositions, leaves behind those hundred negations; the path of names and words is cut off, the place of mind and knowledge is extinguished. Although again thrice-transcended, one has not exhausted its wonder. Beyond the thrice-transcended lies the fundamental root of the Dào, called the realm of double mystery, the gate of all wonders. Its meaning is also difficult to obtain and express in words. Therefore, having no root yet taking a root, the root has nothing to be rooted in; doubtfully named as the root, there is also nothing that can be the root; therefore it is called 'Doubtful Beginning'.

Zǐsì, Zǐyú, Zǐlí, and Zǐlái, four people talking together, said: "Who can take non-being as the head, life as the spine, death as the rump? Who knows that death, life, existence, and extinction are one body? We will be friends with him."

Subcommentary: Zǐsì and the other four—their basis is not detailed. Observing their minds and traces, all are beyond-the-world scholars. Their feelings are like plain water; they formed a pure friendship, narrating their unreserved harmony in empty mystery, forgetting words in the ultimate Dào. Now, a person arises from emptiness and non-being; non-being is prior, thus take non-being as the head. From non-being generates being; life comes next, thus take life as the spine. Having life, then death; death is last, thus take death as the rump—this is also so. Though the rump and head are different, originally they are one body; and death and life, though different, originate from one body. Whoever can reach this meaning, wherever encountered is suitable—how can there be preferences of existence and extinction, joy and detestation, between them? Whoever knows this, we will be friends with him.
The four looked at each other and laughed, unreserved in their hearts, and thereupon became friends with each other.
Subcommentary: Where the eye falls, the Dào is present; therefore they looked at each other and laughed. All conformed to the mysterious principle; therefore they were unreserved in their hearts.
Soon after, Zǐyú fell ill; Zǐsì went to inquire after him.
Subcommentary: Being ill, one must go inquire. Acting according to principle, not contrary to being beyond the world.
He said: "Great indeed is the Creator! That he would make me into such a contorted thing!"

Subcommentary: 'Wěi' means great. 'Creator' is like the transforming creator. 'Jūjū' describes a cramped, contracted, unextended appearance. Now, the great furnace, the great smelter, the creator is without bias—how could he intentionally make my single body into a cramped, contracted ailment? Speaking thus, it is none other than fate. Zǐyú, understanding principle, sighed with these words.

"Hunchbacked, my back sticking out, above I have five pipes [protruding vertebrae?], my chin hidden at the navel, shoulders higher than the top of my head, a topknot pointing to the sky. The energies of yīn and yáng are in disharmony."

Commentary: 'Lì' means to encroach and disorder. Subcommentary: Hunchbacked, bent at the waist, back bones protruding. Since he is bent over and cannot look up, the five viscera are all above. His head low, thus his chin is hidden at the navel; his shoulders hunched high, thus they are higher than the top of his head. And the cervical vertebrae are curved, the large bone like a topknot. The two energies, yīn and yáng, encroach and disorder, unregulated, thus causing his one body to meet this severe illness.
"His mind was at leisure and without affairs."

Commentary: He did not consider it a trouble. Subcommentary: Death and life are still one body; how could illness and suffering again occupy his mind? Therefore, though hunchbacked and contorted, his spirit and mind were leisurely and carefree, completely not considering it an affair.
Dragging himself, he looked into a well and
Moreover, we all consider ourselves as "I".

Note: Whether in life, death, or transformation, I am always "I". Since all are "I", what have I lost? Never having lost "I", why should I worry? Without resistance, I weep when others weep; without sorrow, I weep but without grief. Commentary: In my life and death, all are "I" — never not "I". What have I lost? If one takes attachment to "I" as intention, where is it not "I"?
How can we know what I call "I"?

Note: There is nothing that is not "I", thus mysteriously unifying inner and outer, permeating past and present, renewing daily with transformation — how could one know where "I" resides? Commentary: Yong means ordinary. Common people have shallow understanding — how could they know what I call "I" exists everywhere? Even through thousands of changes, "I" remains constant. Whether new "I" or old "I", what is there to like or dislike?
Furthermore, you dream of being a bird and soar in the sky, dream of being a fish and dive into the depths.
Note: This means going everywhere with self-attainment.
Do we know whether the speaker now is awake or dreaming?

Note: When dreaming, one believes oneself awake — how can we know the present is not a dream? Or know it is not awakening? The transformation between dream and awakening knows no fixed direction, thus the changes of life and death are not worth regretting at any moment. Commentary: Li means to reach. Being fish or bird follows nature's freedom; facing life or death, one remains self-attained. Since fish and birds have no superiority, why cling to victories in life and death? Mengsun profoundly understood this source, thus never minding it. Moreover, we don't know whether our discussion of fish and birds occurs in awakening or dream. People in dreams believe themselves awake — why can't present awakening be within a dream? Thus we know dream, awakening, life and death cannot be fixed.
Reaching comfort doesn't wait for laughter; offering laughter doesn't wait for arrangement.

Note: When all one reaches is comfort, one forgets comfort itself, thus not awaiting laughter. Pai means shifting. Ritual demands sorrow in weeping, joy in laughter — when sorrow and joy remain in heart, one cannot shift with comfort. Now Mengsun is constantly comfortable, thus weeping without sorrow, moving along with transformation. Commentary: Zao means to reach. Xian means good. Pai means shifting. Wherever one goes is comfort — this is comfort itself. Constant comfort — why wait for laughter to then be happy? If one awaits good things to move oneself before comfort, this cannot follow changes and transformations, shifting with things. Now Mengsun is constantly comfortable, thus weeping without sorrow.
Accept arrangement and depart with transformation, then enter the solitary unity with Heaven.

Note: Being content with shifting and going with transformation, thus entering solitude and becoming one with Heaven. From here upward to Zisi, the ultimate is one, but their mourning practices differ, hence their songs and weeping vary. Commentary: Wherever one is, is comfort; thus accepting whatever shifts, never not "I", and going with transformation — such a person can enter the profound mysterious gate, the natural unity.
Yi'erzi visited Xuyou. Xuyou said: "What did Yao provide you?"

Note: Zi means to supply or aid. Commentary: Yi'er was an ancient worthy. Zi means to provide assistance. Yi'er first visited Emperor Yao, then saw Zhongwu. The question: "Emperor Yao, greatly sage, with lofty virtue — having visited him, what teachings and aiding methods did he provide? Please relate them."
Yi'erzi said: "Yao told me: 'You must personally practice benevolence and righteousness, and clearly speak right and wrong.'"

Commentary: Gong means personally. Benevolence means kindness nurturing things; righteousness means decisive judgment cutting falsehood. Right means clearly rewarding good; wrong means clearly punishing evil. These four are valued in human relations — you must personally practice them and clearly speak them to others. This recounts Yao's teaching.
Xuyou said: "Then why have you come here?"
Commentary: Er means you. Xi means what. Zhi is a particle. Yao's teachings have already harmed you greatly — why come again?
"Since Yao has tattooed you with benevolence and righteousness, and cut off your nose with right and wrong, how will you wander the path of carefree meandering and transformation?"

Note: This means using form-teaching self-harms and maims, unable again to wander the field of self-attainment, the path of non-attachment. Commentary: Qing means tattooing the forehead. Yi means cutting off the nose. Zisui means放任纵任. Zhuanxi means transformation. Tu means path. Benevolence, righteousness, right and wrong harm true nature — their damage is like physical punishment. You, already tattooed and nose-cut by Yao, constrained in nature — how can you again wander carefree,逍遥放荡, comfortably self-attained in the path of transformation? Meaning you cannot do so again.
Yi'erzi said: "Even so, I wish to wander in its outskirts."

Note: Not daring again to tread the central path, but wishing to wander its edges. Commentary: Though I suffered this damage, my humble heart remains undiminished. Not daring to confront the heart-path, I wish to tread the path's outskirts.
Xuyou said: "Not so. The blind cannot share in the beauty of eyebrows, eyes, and countenance; the sightless cannot share in viewing blue, yellow, and ceremonial patterns."

Commentary: The blind have eyes but see not; the sightless have no eye-slits, like drum-skins. Fu means axe-pattern; Fu means two '己' back-to-back. The blind and sightless, eyes already ruined, cannot see colorful patterns nor appreciate eyebrows and complexion — like Yi'er, tattooed and nose-cut by Yao, emotion and wisdom already injured, how could he love profound mystery and observe all wonders?
Yi'erzi said: "Wuzhuang lost her beauty, Juliang lost his strength, Huangdi forgot his wisdom — all were within the furnace and hammer."

Note: Meaning things under heaven don't necessarily form themselves; natural principle also requires forging to become vessels. Thus these three all heard the Dao and then forgot their pursuits. This uses borrowed words to dismiss the burdens of action. Commentary: Wuzhuang, ancient beauty, heard the Dao and ceased adornment, forgetting her beauty. Juliang, ancient strongman, heard the Dao and embraced femininity, forgetting his strength. Huangdi, Xuanyuan, had sage wisdom but heard the Dao and forgot it. Lu means furnace; Chui means hammer. These three forgot their pursuits through hearing the Dao, uniting with truth — like worldly objects forged in furnace to become useful. Why not the natural principle? Could you teach me to complete my Dao? Thus we know natural creation lies within furnace — meaning there is cultivation and forging.
"How do we know the Creator won't heal my tattoos and restore my nose, letting me ride completion to follow you, sir?"

Note: Spontaneous going-forward is natural; going and harming nature, then able to reform — also natural. How do we know my nature won't heal tattoos and restore nose, letting me ride the achievable Dao to follow you? Wanting to reject without teaching恐怕不是造物之至. Commentary: Creator means造化物. Though harmed by benevolence, righteousness, right and wrong — how know within creation, my nose won't be restored, tattoos healed, letting me reform and follow you for improvement? To reject without teaching would contradict the Creator.
Xuyou said: "Alas! It cannot be known. I'll tell you the general outline."

Commentary: Yi is a sigh. The ultimate Dao is profoundly mysterious, beyond words and images, unknowable by mind — hence sighing "cannot be known". But since you earnestly seek, I cannot remain silent. Though unspeakable fully, I'll outline it for you.
"My teacher! My teacher! It粉碎万物而不为义, benefits all ages without being benevolent."

Note: All occurs spontaneously, without deliberate love or action — where could benevolence and righteousness lodge? Commentary: "My teacher" means the ultimate Dao. The ultimate Dao cannot be known by mind, but I'll outline its essence — it is my teacher. Zhe means to crush. Like autumn frost crushing all things — does it intentionally cut to be righteous? Spring energy nurturing all things — does it intentionally love to be benevolent? It is so without being so. Xuyou learns from the ultimate Dao — since it is thus, why must you personally practice benevolence and righteousness? This roughly tells Yi'er the method to heal tattoos and restore nose.
"Older than antiquity yet not aged."
Note: Daily renewal.
"Covers and carries heaven and earth, carves all forms without being skillful."

Note: Natural, thus not skillful. Commentary: Before all phenomena, this Dao existed — wisdom and virtue complete, thus metaphorically called older, yet truly not old. Since no oldness exists, how can aging be? To clarify: not old yet older, aged yet not aged — thus older than antiquity yet not aged. Though heaven covers and earth carries, Dao is their source; all forms carved rely on creation, equally endowed with nature — thus skill vanishes. Since no age, no skill, no right, no wrong — what do you clearly speak?
"This is where it wanders."
Note: Wandering in non-action, learning from no-teacher. Commentary: Where my teacher's heart wanders ends here — this concludes the earlier meaning of my teacher.
Yan Hui said: "I have improved."

Note: Considering decrease as improvement. Commentary: Yanzi, receiving Confucius' teaching, devotedly sought the Dao, felt self-improvement, presented understanding to teacher. Decreasing has benefit of emptiness, thus decrease is improvement.
Confucius said: "What do you mean?"
Commentary: Having said improved — what meaning?
He said: "I have forgotten benevolence and righteousness."
Commentary: Forgotten all-encompassing benevolence, dismissed cutting-falsehood righteousness — this is called improvement.
He said: "Good, but not yet."

Note: Benevolence is the trace of universal love; righteousness is the achievement of completing things. Loving isn't benevolence, but benevolence-trace appears; completing isn't righteousness, but righteousness-achievement emerges. Preserving benevolence and righteousness不足以知爱利之由 — without heart-mind, thus forgetting is possible. But only forgetting achievements and traces — thus not yet mysteriously penetrating. Commentary: Benevolence and righteousness forgotten — principle gradually understandable, but mind still shallow, thus not yet.
Another day, again meeting, he said: "I have improved."
Commentary: Another day means different day. Empty understanding renews daily — again meeting, further improvement described below.
He said: "What do you mean?"
Commentary: What meaning in "improved"?
He said: "I have forgotten rituals and music."
Commentary: Rituals head disorder; music tools of excess — heavier burdens, next forgotten.
He said: "Good, but not yet."
Note: Rituals are bodily functions; music tools of joy-forgetting. Forgetting tools not equal to forgetting why tools exist. Commentary: Empty forgetting gradually possible, but not yet ultimate.
Another day, again meeting, he said: "I have improved." He said: "What do you mean?"
Commentary: Same as previous explanation.
He said: "I sit in forgetfulness."
Commentary: Empty mind unattached, thus able to sit straight and forget. Sitting forgetfulness meaning detailed below.
Confucius, startled, said: "What is sitting forgetfulness?"
Note: Cu means startled appearance. Forgetfulness so deep, thus startled exclamation. What does sitting forgetfulness mean?
Yan Hui said: "I dismantle limbs and body, dismiss keen hearing and clear vision."

Commentary: Hui means destroy, discard. Chu means remove, reject. Though hearing belongs to ears, sight to eyes, their use originates in heart-spirit. Realizing the body isn't real, all realms empty — thus able to destroy four limbs and hundred parts, dismiss keen hearing, clear vision, heart-wisdom.
"Leaving form, abandoning knowledge, identical with great penetration — this is called sitting forgetfulness."

Note: Sitting forgetfulness — what isn't forgotten? Forgetting traces and why traces exist — inwardly unaware of self, outwardly unknowing of heaven and earth, then expansively united with transformation as body, penetrating all. Commentary: Great penetration like great Dao. Dao penetrates and generates all things, thus called great penetration. Outwardly separating from body — all empty, this explains dismantling limbs. Inwardly removing heart-consciousness — blankly unknowing, this explains dismissing keenness. Then like dead wood, cold ashes, darkly identical with great Dao — such improvement called sitting forgetfulness.
Confucius said: "Identity means no preferences."
Note: Nothing not identical, then never uncomfortable; never uncomfortable — what to like or dislike?
"Transformation means no constancy."

Note: Identical with transformation, only transformation directs — thus no constancy. Commentary: Since identical with great Dao, no right/wrong, like/dislike; darkly in transformation, thus not stubbornly guarding constancy.
"You truly are worthy! I, Qiu, ask to follow you."
Commentary: Guo means decisive. Er means you. Forgetfulness so — certainly greatly worthy. Though I your teacher, I fall behind you — following to learn is my wish. Humble retreat to advance Yan Hui.
Ziyu and Zisang were friends. After ten days of pouring rain, Ziyu said: "Zisang is probably ill." He wrapped food and went to feed him.

Note: These two acted for each other without acting. Now wrapping food to feed — entrusting to heavenly principle, spontaneous, not acting for each other then going. Commentary: Rain beyond three days called downpour. Dai means near. Zisang poor, during downpour near starvation — this unquestioned between beyond-worlds friends. Going by principle, though wrapping food, no sense of acting for each other.
Reaching Zisang's door, he heard something like singing, like weeping, playing zither: "Father? Mother? Heaven? Man?" The voice couldn't bear the strain, hurriedly reciting verse.

Commentary: Ren means endure. Qu means hasty. Zisang, starving, thus plucked zither asking: "This poverty and hunger — from whom? From parents? From man?" This singing-weeping words. Voice couldn't endure, also hastily versifying.
Ziyu entered, saying: "Your song-verses — why like this?"

Note: Suspecting emotional attachment, thus hasty departure far from principle. Commentary: Unified in life-death, forgetting sorrow-joy, in non-acting mutual beyond-worlds friendship. Now your song-verses seem resentful — thus entering startled, asking reason.

He said: "I ponder what brought me to this extreme, but cannot find it. Parents surely didn't want me poor! Heaven covers impartially, earth carries impartially — how could heaven and earth privately impoverish me? Seeking who did this, I find nothing. Yet reaching this extreme — it is fate!"

Note: All things natural, non-acting. Commentary: Parents loving, don't wish hunger/cold; heaven-earth impartial, why alone impoverish me? Considering rulers, all natural; seeking origins, no trace — what brought me to this extreme is my endowed fate. What regret?
Nanhua Zhen Jing Zhu Shu Juan Zhi Ba
The Nanhua Zhenjing Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Nine, Part Three
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá of the Táng Dynasty Inner Chapters, The Seventh: Responding to Emperors and Kings
Nièquē asked Wángní four questions and four times received no answer.

Subcommentary: The four questions and four unknowing responses refer to the four questions in the "Equalizing All Things" chapter. The way of emperors and kings lies in forgetting knowledge; hence, this principle is placed at the beginning of the chapter. Lǎozǐ says: "Governing the state without wisdom is the virtue of the state."
Nièquē, leaping up, was greatly delighted. He went and told Púyīzǐ. Púyīzǐ said, "Have you only now come to know it?"

Subcommentary: Púyīzǐ was a worthy man of Yáo's time. At eight years old, Shùn took him as teacher and yielded the throne to him, but he did not accept it. He is also known as Bèiyīzǐ. Nièquē grasped the profound meaning of unknowing and, leaping with joy, went to tell Púyīzǐ, bewildered by the deep meaning of Wángní. Púyīzǐ, a great sage beyond the mundane, attained the ultimate principle of forgetting words. The principle of unknowing is long-standing; have you only now come to know it?
Yǒuyúshì did not reach Tàishì.

Commentary: Both Yǒuyúshì and Tàishì are traces of worldly affairs, not the source of traces. The source of traces is traceless. Who in the world knows this? It has never been named; how could there be any victory or defeat? Yet, the traceless rides the changes of the multitude, belonging to all ages. As ages have perils and safety, traces have their limitations. Subcommentary: Yǒuyúshì is Shùn. Tàishì is Fúxī of Tàihào. In the era of the Three Sovereigns, customs were pure and harmonious; in the time of the Five Emperors,风气 became competitive. With competitiveness, wisdom was used to nurture things; with purity and harmony, truth was preserved to guide the universe. The meaning of "not reaching" can be understood from this.
Yǒuyúshì still stored up benevolence to attract people; he indeed gained people, but never emerged from the realm of the non-human.

Commentary: To deem what people like as right and what they dislike as wrong—people are confined to the realm of right and wrong. One who can emerge from the realm of the non-human must enter the realm where there is no non-human. Thus, there is no gain or loss, no approval or disapproval—how could it be merely storing benevolence to attract people? Subcommentary: Shùn stored up benevolence and righteousness to attract scholars and commoners, winning the hearts of the people. This was not forgetting oneself and naturally uniting with the world; thus, he emerged from the realm of right and wrong. Some texts read "zāng" as "good," meaning good at benevolence and righteousness to attract people's hearts.
Tàishì lay down leisurely and awoke contentedly.

Subcommentary: "Leisurely" describes a relaxed manner; "contentedly" a self-satisfied appearance. In Fúxī's time, pure customs still existed, so he lay down peacefully and leisurely, and upon waking, was joyful and self-content.
At one time, he took himself for a horse; at another, for an ox.

Commentary: Being thus, how could there be distinction between human and non-human? This can be said to emerge from the realm of the non-human. Subcommentary: Forgetting self and others, dismissing right and wrong, whether horse or ox, he responded to others' calls. Since even human and beast had no fixed identity, how could there be right and wrong?
His knowledge was true and trustworthy.
Commentary: Letting it know by itself, thus true and trustworthy. Subcommentary: Following his true knowledge, his feelings were without falsehood, thus genuinely trustworthy.
His virtue was utterly genuine.
Commentary: Letting it attain by itself, thus without falsity. Subcommentary: Taking non-virtue as virtue, his virtue had no virtue, thus it was not false.
And he never entered the realm of the non-human.

Commentary: Not entering the realm of right and wrong, he transcended the age of Yǒuyúshì. Subcommentary: Since he followed his true feelings and his virtue was genuine, he could transcend the realm of intellectual knowledge and not enter the domain of right and wrong.
Jiānwú visited the mad Jiēyú. The mad Jiēyú said, "What did Rìzhōngshǐ tell you?"

Subcommentary: Jiānwú and Jiēyú have been explained previously. Rìzhōngshǐ is the name of a worthy man, Jiānwú's teacher. Since he is your teacher, what did he instruct? This is Jiēyú initiating the question.
Jiānwú said, "He told me that a ruler should use his own devised laws, righteousness, and measures to govern people. Who would dare not obey and be transformed?"

Subcommentary: "Shì" means to use. He taught me the way of rulership and the method of transforming things: one must use one's own wisdom to govern and employ benevolence and righteousness to guide customs. Then, who among the common people would not obey? How dare the distant masses not submit to transformation?
The mad Jiēyú said, "This is deceptive virtue."

Commentary: Using oneself to control things causes things to lose their truth. Subcommentary: Using oneself to control things leads to the loss of their true nature—a deceptive virtue, not the true Way.
In governing the world, it is like crossing the sea by digging a river or making a mosquito carry a mountain.

Commentary: Entrusting appropriateness to all things, then affairs accomplish themselves without effort. Using one person to control the world, then achievements are none and the task is unbearable. Subcommentary: The vast sea, broad and deep, is hard to traverse; digging it into a river is certainly impossible. Similarly, the great Way is distant and vast, profoundly hard to know; carving it into righteousness is a difficult task. Also, a mosquito is extremely small, a mountain extremely high; making it carry the load is beyond its capacity. Governing with small wisdom and great schemes is analogous.
Does the sage govern by governing externally?
Commentary: He completes what is within his innate nature. Subcommentary: He governs according to what is within his portion, certainly not externally. Governing externally means not governing.
He rectifies and then acts.
Commentary: Each rectifies its life and nature. Subcommentary: He follows their correct nature and then acts to transform.
He is firm in enabling them to do what they can, and that is all.

Commentary: He does not do what they cannot. Subcommentary: "Firm" means steadfast. Following their true nature, he employs those capable in affairs, stopping within their portion, not venturing beyond.
Moreover, birds fly high to avoid the harm of arrows and nets; mice dig deep burrows under the sacred mound to avoid the calamity of smoke and digging.

Commentary: Even birds and beasts each have means to preserve themselves. Thus, if emperors and kings leave them to themselves without acting, they accomplish themselves. Subcommentary: "Zēng" means nets; "yì" means shooting with rope-attached arrows. "Xīshǔ" are small mice; "shén qiū" is the altar mound. Birds fly high to escape nets; mice dig deep to avoid smoke. All follow their nature spontaneously—do they wait to be taught to avoid harm? Since birds and mice are thus, so are humans. Hence, know that devising righteousness and laws is highly deceptive.
And how could you be unaware that these two creatures know?

Commentary: He says, "Are you unaware that these two creatures each preserve themselves without waiting for teaching?" Subcommentary: "Ér" means you. Have you not known that these two creatures avoid harm and preserve themselves without being taught? Since they burrow deep and fly high, how could they be ignorant? How much more so for humans, to devise laws and righteousness, deceptively manipulating living beings—is this not deluded?
Tiāngēn wandered to the south of Yīn Mountain, came to the Liǎo River, and happened to meet Wúmíngrén. He asked, "May I ask about governing the world?"

Subcommentary: Tiāngēn and Wúmíngrén are allegorical names for this dialogue. "Yīn yáng" means south of Yīn Mountain; the Liǎo River is within Zhào territory. "Zāo" means to encounter. Tiāngēn wandered by the mountains and rivers, happened to meet Wúmíngrén, and asked him—his intention was to inquire about governing the world.
Wúmíngrén said, "Begone! You are a vulgar man. Why do you ask so unpleasantly?"

Commentary: Asking about governing the world means not starting from the Great Beginning and not ending in Profound Obscurity. Subcommentary: You are a vulgar man, should quickly leave. The intent of your question greatly displeases my heart.
I am about to join with the Creator as a companion.

Commentary: Letting people act by themselves. Subcommentary: The Creator makes people, each sufficient in their innate nature—why labor to devise methods and intend to govern? Since I am one with the Great Thoroughfare, I let things be without assisting.
When weary, I ride the bird of faintness and vagueness, go beyond the six extremes, wander in the land of Nothingness, and dwell in the wilds of vast emptiness.

Commentary: "Faintness and vagueness" refers to the fragmented multitude. Riding the fragments, galloping through all things, thus one can always pass through without narrow obstructions. Subcommentary: "Faintness and vagueness" means profound and deep; "vast emptiness" denotes breadth. The bird is chosen for its traceless, light ascent. "Six extremes" is like the six directions. The sage governs the world with tranquility and non-action, greatly conforming to the nature of things, akin to the Creator. When he rests from action and returns to the root, weary of the world, he rides the profound and distant great Way, ascends the void and extinguishes traces, transcends the six directions to roam freely, wanders in Nothingness to be carefree, concentrates spirit and wisdom on Mount Shè, dwells in clarity and emptiness in the wilds. Thus, what need is there to govern the world? This is the meaning of non-action.
Why do you use the art of governing the world to disturb my heart?

Commentary: If all are let loose in the field of self-attainment, then without governing, they govern themselves. Subcommentary: Letting go and allowing, all things transform themselves—what art is needed to govern and disturb my heart? Why such action?
He asked again.
Subcommentary: Tiāngēn, not yet understanding, requested resolution of doubts again.
Wúmíngrén said, "Let your mind wander in simplicity."
Commentary: If one follows nature without adornment, then it is simple.
Merge your breath with indifference.

Commentary: Indifferently quiet in nature and stopping. Subcommentary: Let your spirit wander in the realm of tranquility, merge your form and breath in the land of solitude. Only when both form and spirit are empty and quiet, then the world transforms itself without need for governance.
Follow the natural course of things without any personal bias, and the world will be governed.

Commentary: Following nature's spontaneous generation is impartiality; the mind wanting to benefit is partiality. Allowing partiality indeed cannot fully generate life; following impartiality completes it. Subcommentary: Following the nature of the Creator's things, conforming to the innate nature of spontaneity, without personal bias or devising methods and intentions to govern—let go and allow, then self and others are complete.

Yángzǐjū saw Lǎodān and said, "Suppose there is a person here: swift as an echo, strong and resolute, penetrating and clear in understanding things, tireless in learning the Way. Can such a one be compared to an enlightened king?"

Subcommentary: Yáng Zhū, styled Zǐjū, asked Lǎozǐ about the Way of enlightened kings. Suppose there is a person inherently intelligent, with sharp and swift wisdom like an echo's response, handling affairs with strength and decisiveness, discerning things thoroughly and clearly, diligent in learning the Way without weariness. Can such a person be compared in virtue to an enlightened king or sage emperor?
Lǎodān said, "In the eyes of a sage, such a one is like a petty official easily changed, tied by skills, toiling his body and alarming his mind."

Commentary: Such effort does not allow self-preservation, insufficient to compare with a sage ruler. Subcommentary: Comparing that person to a sage ruler, he is like a petty official easily changed, toiling to alter his appearance, his skills and cleverness tying his spirit, laboring to change his form, and being alarmed in mind due to ties.
Moreover, the stripes of tigers and leopards attract hunters; the agility of monkeys and the skill of dogs catching foxes bring them leashes. Can such be compared to an enlightened king?

Commentary: These are all tied by their patterns and skills, not involved in emptiness to驾驭 the boundless. Subcommentary: "Jí" means leash. "Yuánjū" are macaques. Tigers and leopards have patterned skins, hence attract hunters; macaques, due to agile jumping, are often leashed; dogs, for catching foxes, often have collars. If swift persons are likened to sage emperors, then these three creatures can be compared to enlightened kings.
Yángzǐjū, startled, said, "May I ask about the governance of an enlightened king?"
Subcommentary: Having asked incorrectly, he was alarmed, changed expression, and respectfully inquired about the principle of enlightened king's governance.
Lǎodān said, "The achievements of an enlightened king cover the world but seem not his own."

Commentary: Without an enlightened ruler, the world cannot attain self-fulfillment. Now self-fulfillment is truly the achievement of the enlightened king. Yet, the achievement lies in non-action and returns to the world, all attaining self-responsibility, thus seeming not the enlightened king's achievement. Subcommentary: The sage governs, achievements matching the Creator, covering like heaven, bearing like earth, yet success without claiming, thus not done by himself.
He transforms and lends to all things, and the people do not depend on him.

Commentary: The enlightened king fulfills the nature of things, so everyone says, "I am so myself," and does not know to depend on the enlightened king. Subcommentary: Guiding the people to abandon evil, lending all things to bestow blessings, his mysterious achievements subtly pervade, used daily without awareness. The people say, "We are so naturally," not relying on the ruler's virtue.
He has but does not proclaim fame, making things rejoice in themselves.

Commentary: Though his achievements cover the world, he does not proclaim them as his own fame, so things all feel self-attained and rejoice. Subcommentary: "Mò" means without; "jǔ" means to display. He attributes achievement to things, not displaying his name, making things self-rejoicing and content.
He stands in the unfathomable.
Commentary: He dwells in the path of change, daily renewing without fixed direction.
And wanders in non-being.

Commentary: Being one with all things, his wandering is in emptiness. If not merging with things, then conflicting with things leaves no leisure—how could he wander in emptiness? Subcommentary: "Non-being" is the mysterious source. Establishing virtue and achieving merit, spiritually unfathomable, and since traces are the root, he always wanders in the ultimate.
In Zhèng, there was a spirit-medium named Jìxián.
Subcommentary: In the state of Zhèng, there was a miraculous shaman very efficacious, coming from Qí, named Jìxián.

He knew people's life, death, survival, perish, fortune, misfortune, longevity, and brevity, predicting to the year, month, ten-day period, or day, as if divine. The people of Zhèng, seeing him, all fled and ran away.

Commentary: They dislike hearing their own death day. Subcommentary: Divining auspicious and inauspicious, never erring, fixing times accurately, verified like spirits. Not wishing to hear misfortune in advance, they flee and avoid.
Lièzǐ saw him and was enchanted. Returning, he told Húzǐ.

Subcommentary: Lièzǐ's story is in the "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter, not repeated here. Húzǐ is a Daoist adept of Zhèng, named Húzǐ, called Lín, Lièzǐ's teacher. Lièzǐ saw Jìxián's minor arts verified like spirits, admired him heartily, enchanted as if drunk. Returning, he fully reported to his teacher.
He said, "At first, I thought your Way was ultimate, but there is one more ultimate."

Commentary: He means Jìxián's ultimacy surpasses the master's. Subcommentary: "Fūzǐ" is Húzǐ; "zhì" means ultimate. Initially, I received your teaching as ultimate; now seeing Jìxián, his Way is even more ultimate than yours. This is Lièzǐ's enchanted words.
Húzǐ said, "I have given you the patterns but not the reality. How could
The Southern Florescence True Canon, Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Ten, Part Four
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters, "Webbed Toes," the Eighth
Webbed toes and extra fingers
—do they arise from inborn nature?
Yet they are excesses to inherent virtue.
Subcommentary:
"Webbed" means joined;
it also means large;
it refers to the big toe and the second toe being connected,
merged into one toe.
"Extra finger"
means beside the thumb, an additional finger grows, making six fingers.
"Arise from inborn nature"
means these webbed or extra fingers
both receive from what is so of themselves,
existing within the natural allotment of life and inborn nature.
"Excess" means extra.
"Virtue" refers to the five virtues: humaneness, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and fidelity.
This says that Zēng and Shǐ received inborn natures with these five virtues,
stored in the five organs,
and are not surplus in their inborn nature.
Attached wens and hanging tumors
—do they arise from physical form?
Yet they are excesses to inborn nature.
Commentary:
What is long is not considered surplus,
what is short is not considered insufficient;
this means both webbing and wens arise from physical inborn nature, not borrowed from external things.
Yet whether webbed or not,
each is sufficient in itself,
but these alone are webbed or extra,
so among the multitude, they are considered excessive,
hence called "excess."
But the confused may say they are not of inborn nature,
and thus wish to cut them off and discard them;
this means the Way is not preserved in some places,
virtue is not upheld in some aspects,
and people have discarded talents,
things have discarded uses;
how can this be the intention of perfect governance?
Things have their small and large,
capabilities have their few and many;
what is large is webbing, what is many is a wen.
The distinction of webbing and wens
exists in all things;
if none are entrusted with responsibility,
this is to discard the inborn nature of all things entirely.
Subcommentary:
Attached, excess flesh,
suspended, small tumors,
both receive physical form and only exist afterward,
so they arise from physical form and are excesses to inborn nature.
For example, Lí and Kuǎng received inborn natures of intelligence,
arrayed in their organs,
not relying on borrowed learning,
thus they are not excesses to inborn nature.
Those who extensively apply humaneness and righteousness in their use
array them in the five organs!
But this is not the correctness of the Way and its virtue.
Commentary:
Those who merge with things have no excess.
Thus, those who extensively apply humaneness and righteousness,
though arrayed in the five organs,
are merely the correctness of one school,
unable to be without fixed methods with things and each correct in their life and inborn nature,
hence it is said not the correctness of the Way and its virtue.
The degree of methods, few or many,
has no fixed limit in the world.
Yet the difference of few and many
each has its determined allotment;
even a hair's breadth deviation
cannot be striven for,
so each guards its own method,
and whether few or many, all attain self-fulfillment.
But some, hearing that many cannot correct the few,
thus wish to discard the many and entrust the few,
this is to discard the entire world,
is it not delusional?
Subcommentary:
"Methods" refer to ways and techniques.
It says that the virtue of Zēng and Shǐ, with inborn natures rich in humaneness and righteousness, arrayed in the organs and applied in use,
this is merely the knowledge of one school,
unable to greatly merge with all things.
Those who can merge with things
thus respond to humaneness and righteousness without being bound by righteousness,
respond to few and many without being few or many,
undergoing a thousand changes, ten thousand transformations,
endless with things,
without partial attachments,
hence this is the correctness of the Way and its virtue.
Therefore, webbing on the feet
connects useless flesh;
extra on the hands
grows useless fingers;
Commentary:
Simply due to life and inborn nature, it cannot be otherwise,
not because of usefulness that it is so.
Subcommentary:
The webbed, joined toes
are of no benefit to walking,
so though this connection exists,
it ultimately becomes useless flesh;
the extra growth on the fingers,
since it does not aid grasping,
though this flesh stands,
it is ultimately a useless finger.
This aims to clarify that what is received from natural inborn nature exists,
not born for the sake of aiding function.
Extensive methods, webbed or extra, in the dispositions of the five organs,
lead to excessive and deviant conduct in humaneness and righteousness,
Commentary:
The dispositions of the five organs
are simply extensive in methods,
and those with few wrongly admire them,
