leading to excess and deviation,
losing the utmost appropriateness within the body.
Subcommentary:
Those like Zēng and Shǐ,
with inborn natures rich in humaneness and righteousness,
with these dispositions,
web the organs.
Those with sparse inborn natures
force their natures to admire them,
boast of this as conduct,
seek heavenly principle,
since it is not following inborn nature,
it becomes excessive and deviant.
"Excessive" means obsessive stagnation;
"deviant" means an improper appearance.
And they extensively apply intelligence in their use.
Commentary:
The use of intelligence
each has its inherent allotment,
so extensive methods are not considered surplus,
sparse methods are not considered insufficient.
Yet stirred by emotions and desires,
none do not despise the sparse and value the extensive;
seeing what is valuable and forcing themselves to admire it,
they then exceed their original use and constrain their natural inborn nature.
If they forget what they value and preserve their plain allotment,
then they are not excessive to their inborn nature and different methods are all complete.
Subcommentary:
It says that Lí and Kuǎng's plain allotment
is extensive in intelligence,
those with sparse inborn natures
force their dispositions to admire it,
using this as their method,
is it not mistaken?
Therefore, those webbed in sight
confuse the five colors,
indulge in patterns and ornaments,
is it not the dazzling blues, yellows, and brilliant ceremonial robes?
And Lí Zhū is such a one.
Subcommentary:
Axe-shaped pattern is called "fǔ."
Two "jǐ" characters back-to-back are called "fú."
The five colors
are blue, yellow, red, white, and black.
Blue and red form patterns,
red and white form designs.
"Dazzling" describes a blinding appearance.
Is it not Lí Zhū?
It is he.
"Yǐ" is an auxiliary word.
Lí Zhū, also named Lí Lóu, was a clear-sighted man from the time of the Yellow Emperor,
able to see a hair at a hundred miles.
Those extensive in hearing
confuse the five tones,
indulge in the six pitch-pipes,
is it not the sounds of metal, stone, silk, bamboo, Huángzhōng, and Dàlǚ?
And Shī Kuàng is such a one.
Commentary:
Those with ears and eyes
never trouble themselves by admiring deafness and blindness,
the trouble often lies in hoping to be like Lí and admiring Kuàng;
thus Lí and Kuàng, though inborn with intelligence,
are precisely the ones who confuse the ears and eyes.
Subcommentary:
The five tones are gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ.
The six pitch-pipes are Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Gūxiǎn, Ruíbīn, Wúyì, Jiázhōng, and others.
The six pitch-pipes are yang,
the six tones are yin, totaling twelve.
Metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, clay, leather, wood—
these are the eight sounds.
"Is it not"
means clinging to these sounds,
is it not Shī Kuàng?
Shī Kuàng,
courtesy name Zǐyě,
was a music master to Duke Píng of Jìn,
extremely knowledgeable in tones and pitch-pipes.
It says that Lí and Kuàng, these two, had plain allotments of intelligence,
and ordinary, ignorant people wrongly generated hope and admiration,
losing their original inborn natures,
how could they not be troubled?
Thus, Lí and Kuàng's intelligence
is precisely what confuses the ears and eyes.
Those extra in humaneness
pluck up virtue and block inborn nature to gather fame and reputation,
making the world clamor to uphold unattainable standards—is it not so?
and such were Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Yú.
Commentary:
Now Zēng and Shǐ had natures inherently strong in benevolence,
while those without such inherent strength forcibly admired them,
and in admiring them practiced benevolence,
thus their benevolence became artificial.
The world never admires Jié or Zhí yet must admire Zēng and Shǐ,
thus Zēng and Shǐ's pipe-and-drum stirring of the world,
causing it to lose its true nature,
is worse than that of Jié or Zhí.
Sub-commentary:
"Branching in benevolence"
means originally having many branches of benevolence and righteousness,
like naturally growing an extra finger from one's hand.
Employing the five virtues,
they become biased and stagnant in depravity,
thereby obstructing their true nature.
Using this to interact with things,
to gather fame and reputation,
they make all living beings rush about in competition,
like reed pipes and drumming,
able to move things to admiration and aspiration.
Now Zēng and Shǐ had natures strong in benevolence and righteousness,
while those without such strength forcibly admired them,
abandoning their shortcomings to emulate their strengths,
thus it is said they followed unattainable standards.
"Promoting" means pulling up;
it refers to elevating artificial virtue,
blocking their true nature.
"Zēng" refers to the family name Zēng,
personal name Shēn,
courtesy name Zǐyú,
a disciple of Zhòngní.
"Shǐ" refers to the family name Shǐ,
personal name Qiū,
courtesy name Zǐyú,
a minister of Duke Líng of Wèi.
These two both possessed natures of benevolence and filial piety, hence they are cited.
Those with doubled-up disputation,
piling tiles and tying knots, stringing phrases together,
letting their minds wander among hardness-whiteness and sameness-difference,
exhausting themselves for the praise of useless words—is this not so?
and such were Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí.
Commentary:
Those who parade their clever arguments,
reaching for perilous rhetoric,
never allow thought for the mouths of blockheads,
but must compete in argument between Yáng and Mò,
thus Yáng and Mò become the masters who confuse the multitude of words.
Sub-commentary:
"Yáng" refers to the family name Yáng,
personal name Zhū,
courtesy name Zǐjū,
a man of Sòng.
"Mò" refers to
personal name Dí,
also a man of Sòng, serving as a senior official of Sòng;
because he practiced the way of Mò,
he was called Mò.
These two were both followers of disputation,
possessing naturally argumentative natures,
both capable of lofty talks and perilous rhetoric,
stirring up inherent natures,
stubbornly clinging to right and wrong;
like concealing and hiding phrases in knots,
making them hard to understand,
their minds' wandering place of study
lies solely in the doctrine of hard-white,
between sameness-difference and right-wrong,
never leaving the realm of criticizing others.
"Straining"
means self-reliance,
also describes exerting effort.
"Praise" means glorifying.
Followers of Yáng and Mò,
both pride themselves on minor learning,
dazzling the crowd,
boasting with useless words,
confusing the multitude of things.
Then, are Yáng and Mò not the teachers who confuse the multitude?
It is said they are precisely these Yáng and Mò.
Thus these are all paths of doubled-up side branches,
not the ultimate correctness of the world.
Commentary:
These several masters all follow their innate natures,
truly doubling up side branches themselves,
each being a correctness of their own school.
But using one correctness to correct ten thousand,
then the ten thousand become incorrect.
Thus the ultimate correct does not use itself to correct the world,
but lets the world each attain its own correctness.
Sub-commentary:
These several masters all had natural intelligence, benevolence, and disputation,
like joined toes or
extra fingers growing beside,
endowed from their original nature,
how could it be artificial!
Thus know that following nature in abundant benevolence
is the path of doubled-up side branches.
But foolish and confused followers,
abandon themselves to emulate things,
seeking beyond their allotment,
following without cease.
Thus stirring up inherent natures
comes from these several people,
using one to correct ten thousand,
hence not the ultimate way and correct principle of the world.
That which is truly correct
does not lose the essence of innate nature and destiny.
Commentary:
When each thing follows its nature,
that is true correctness.
From here onward observing,
the ultimate correctness can be seen.
Sub-commentary:
Using the correct principle of spontaneity
to correct the innate nature and destiny of all living beings,
thus it is called correct.
Each thing attains itself,
thus it is said not to lose.
Spontaneity means my spontaneity,
innate nature and destiny also mean my innate nature and destiny,
how far are they!
Thus "truly correct" means
correcting through not correcting,
speaking of correctness and not-correctness.
From here upward,
clarifies the error of forcing nature;
from here downward,
reveals the attainment of following nature.
Thus the joined is not considered doubled,
Commentary:
Using the branch to correct the joined,
then the joined is called doubled.
and the branching is not considered extra;
Commentary:
Using the joined to correct the branch,
then the branch is called extra.
Sub-commentary:
Using the branch to correct the joined,
then the joined is called doubled,
but the joined is truly not doubled;
using the joined to view the branch,
then the branch is called extra,
but the extra is truly not extra.
The long is not considered excessive,
Commentary:
Using the short to correct the long,
then the long is called excessive.
The short is not considered insufficient.
Commentary:
Using the long to correct the short,
then the short is called insufficient.
Sub-commentary:
The long refers to Zēng, Shǐ, Lí Kuàng, Yáng, Mò,
all endowed with innate nature,
accumulating benevolence and righteousness,
intelligence and eloquent disputation,
compared to the common crowd,
thus called long,
following nature in action,
thus not excessive.
The short refers to
the multitude falling short of these like Zēng and Shǐ,
thus called short,
yet also with natural mechanism self-deploying,
thus not insufficient.
Therefore, a duck's leg though short,
lengthening it brings worry;
a crane's leg though long,
shortening it brings sorrow.
Commentary:
Each has its own correctness,
cannot use this to correct that and reduce or augment it.
Sub-commentary:
"Duck" means small duck.
"Crane" refers to birds like the gray crane.
"Leg" means foot.
The principle of spontaneity
nurtures all forms,
though again long and short differ,
each form is fully adequate for its role,
all attain carefree wandering.
But some wish to cut the crane's long to lengthen the duck's short to make them equal,
greatly violating creation,
contravening and losing innate nature, hence worry and sorrow.
Thus an inherently long nature should not be cut,
an inherently short nature should not be lengthened,
with nothing to remove worry.
Commentary:
Knowing one's innate allotment should not be cut or lengthened and accepting it,
then without removing worry, worry removes itself.
Sub-commentary:
Receiving nature and form, all have their limits,
long and short, bright and dark,
originally differ in allotment.
This is like the duck and crane,
not to be cut or lengthened.
Thus,
if each abides within their inherent nature, though making no effort to dispel worries,
worries will depart of themselves.
Alas, are benevolence and righteousness not part of human nature?!
Commentary:
Now benevolence and righteousness naturally belong to human disposition,
one should simply follow them.
Why do those benevolent people have so many worries?
Commentary:
To fear that benevolence and righteousness are not part of human nature and worry about it,
truly can be called having many worries.
Subcommentary:
"Alas" is a sound of sighing and lamentation.
Now the sentiment of benevolence and righteousness arises from heavenly principle,
follows nature and is possessed by it,
not through imitation or emulation.
Those benevolent people,
such as the followers of Zēng and Shǐ,
do not comprehend the true essence,
arbitrarily promote encouragement and reward,
claiming that the way of benevolence and righteousness can be learned and achieved.
Zhuāngzǐ deeply lamented this delusion,
hence he uttered this sigh of "alas."
Reaching beyond one's inherent nature to attract external things,
thus it is called having many worries.
"Are they not part of human nature?" means that they indeed are part of human disposition.
Moreover, for those with webbed toes,
cutting them apart causes weeping;
for those with an extra finger,
biting it off brings crying.
These two cases,
one having an excess in count,
the other a deficiency in count,
share the same worry.
Commentary:
Calling it deficient,
thus they weep when it is cut;
considering it excessive,
thus they cry when it is bitten off.
In this manner,
though the myriad beings differ vastly, there is no place to release worries.
Only if each is content with their innate nature,
not cutting the webbed or biting off the extra,
then all can be accomplished without harm,
and what worry remains?!
Subcommentary:
"Biting off" means to sever by gnawing.
"Cutting" means to separate or dissect.
"Excess in count"
refers to having an extra sixth finger.
"Deficiency in count"
refers to webbing making four distinct toes.
Now webbing and extra digits are two things,
naturally arising, one should simply let them be,
not judging them as too many or too few.
Yet some cannot forget their indifference,
stubbornly clinging to right and wrong,
calling the extra as excessive,
the webbed as deficient,
arbitrarily wishing to cut the webbed and bite off the extra,
to conform to the count of five.
Since this injures natural creation,
it causes weeping and crying,
thus though cutting and biting differ,
the worry is the same.
The benevolent people of today
strain their eyes and worry about the world's troubles;
Commentary:
If the traces of universal love are esteemed, then the eyes of the world become disordered.
By esteeming these traces, causing troubles to arise and then worrying about them,
this is to plunge people into difficulty and then rescue them.
Yet the present age precisely calls this benevolence.
Subcommentary:
"Straining" means the eyes are disordered.
"Benevolence" refers to the traces of universal love.
"Today" means the latter ages.
It is said that followers of Zēng and Shǐ,
practicing this universal love,
consequently cause some to abandon themselves to imitate others,
opening paths of hope and opportunism,
thus the function of eyes and ears becomes disordered.
When eyes and ears are disordered, troubles and difficulties arise,
then worrying about their chaos,
they try to save it with benevolence and righteousness.
They do not realize that the troubles and difficulties arise
from the traces of the sages.
Those without benevolence
cut off the genuine feelings of their nature and destiny to greedily seek honor and wealth.
Commentary:
Now honor and wealth become objects of greed
because there are those who esteem them.
If there were no esteemed traces,
then people would be content with their lot,
measuring their strength to accept their roles,
how could there be cutting off oneself to imitate others, greedily seizing unwarranted hopes?
Subcommentary:
"Greedily" means coveting wealth.
Those who inherently do not embrace benevolence and righteousness
are called people without benevolence.
Their intent is to greedily seek profit and emolument,
stealthily acquiring honor and wealth,
thus they sever their own innate nature,
lose the genuine feelings of their allotted destiny,
and force their nature and feign feelings,
abandoning themselves to pursue external things.
This truly arises because the traces of the sages are esteemed,
hence such flaws occur.
Thus it is known that to embrace simplicity and return to purity,
one must renounce and discard benevolence and righteousness.
Therefore, alas, are benevolence and righteousness not part of human nature?!
Subcommentary:
This reiterates the previous point.
Since the Three Dynasties and below,
how clamorous and noisy the world has been!
Commentary:
Now benevolence and righteousness are naturally human disposition.
But since the Three Dynasties and below, arbitrarily and clamorously, abandoning true disposition to pursue traces,
as if racing to keep up,
is this not having many worries?!
Subcommentary:
"Since" means from.
The Three Dynasties are Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu.
"Clamorous" means uproar and din.
Now benevolence and righteousness
arise from innate disposition.
But since the Three Dynasties and below,
abandoning disposition to follow traces,
clamorously competing and chasing,
how extremely foolish!
Thus, the Xià practiced benevolence,
the Yīn practiced righteousness,
the Zhōu practiced rites,
which is the very form of this clamor.
Moreover, to rely on the hook, line, compass, and square to correct things
is to whittle away their nature;
Subcommentary:
The hook is for curves;
the line is for straightness;
the compass is for circles;
the square is for angles.
Now things depend on the hook, line, compass, and square to become curved, straight, round, or square,
this is not innate nature.
This illustrates that people who depend on the traces of teaching to become benevolent and righteous
lack genuine feelings.
Now genuine spontaneity follows nature and acts,
not relying on artificial learning.
Thus, forcing nature and feigning feelings,
abandoning oneself to imitate things and practice benevolence and righteousness
is to diminish, damage, and harm the innate nature.
To rely on cords, bonds, glue, and lacquer to make things firm
is to violate their inherent virtue;
Subcommentary:
"Bonds" mean to bind and restrain.
"Firm" means solid.
"Violate" means to harm.
"Virtue" means true wisdom.
Now to depend on rope bonds and constraints,
glue and lacquer for firmness,
this relies on external things,
not true solidity.
This metaphorically refers to learning from Zēng and Shǐ to practice benevolence,
which is forced and artificial,
not true nature.
Since it goes against the original nature,
it harms their virtue.
To twist and bend rites and music,
to coax and soothe with benevolence and righteousness,
in order to comfort the hearts of the world,
this loses their constant spontaneity.
Subcommentary:
"Twist" means to bend.
"Bend" means to cut or reshape.
"Coax and soothe" means like coddling and soothing.
To bend the straight into curves,
applying the patterned rites with ornamentation;
to cut the long to fit the short,
performing indulgent and excessive music;
coddling with partiality in the name of benevolence,
coaxing with rigid adherence to righteousness.
Using these to falsify the genuine,
to comfort the minds of things,
thus causing things to lose their authenticity,
and people to forget their root.
Then, abandoning the root to chase the branch,
they lose their true constant natural nature.
This summarizes the errors of the preceding text,
to introduce the correctness in the following text.
The world has a constant spontaneity.
Constant spontaneity means: the curved not using a hook,
the straight not using a line,
the round not using a compass,
the square not using a square,
attaching and joining not using glue or lacquer,
binding and restraining not using ropes or cords.
Subcommentary:
Now the myriad things of the world,
each have their constant lot.
For instance, the péng grass is curved, hemp is straight,
the head is round, the feet are square.
Water freezes in winter and melts in summer,
fish gather in spring and scatter in autumn,
this arises from natural spontaneity,
not by relying on external things,
how could hooks, lines, compasses, squares, glue, lacquer, or ropes be applied to them!
As it is with form,
so it is with nature.
Thus we know that rites, music, benevolence, and righteousness
disrupt the constant principles of Heaven.
Another explanation:
"fù lí" (附離),
"lí" means to rely upon.
Hence the Hàn Shū states:
During Emperor Āi's time, those who attached themselves to the Dǒng clan,
all rose from humble origins to positions of two thousand shí,
with the annotation stating:
"Lí" means to rely upon them.
Therefore, all under Heaven spontaneously come into life yet do not know how they live,
uniformly attain yet do not know how they attain.
Commentary:
All things have their constant nature,
if left to themselves without interference,
then people would obliviously attain naturally without self-awareness.
Subcommentary:
Spontaneous generation of things,
receiving vital energy and assuming form,
some square, some round,
now curved, now straight,
nourishing and maturing them,
each sufficient in its nature,
none can discern why it is so,
all unaware of the cause,
how could they intentionally engage in reasoning
or emotionally cling to gain and loss!
This shows that forced postures and artificial compassion
lose their constancy.
Thus, past and present are not dual,
and cannot be diminished.
Commentary:
Being one with things, therefore there is no duality with things and constant completeness.
Subcommentary:
To perceive beginning and end as non-unified
is the delusion of ordinary feelings;
to witness past and present as non-dual
is the clear illumination of sagely wisdom.
Therefore, not generating yet generating,
not knowing how they generate,
not attaining yet attaining,
not knowing how they attain;
although times may differ between past and present, the principle remains undiminished,
through all transformations and changes,
the inconstant is uniquely constant.
Then why should benevolence and righteousness continuously adhere like glue, lacquer, or ropes to wander within the realm of Dào and Dé?
Commentary:
Attaining by following the Dào,
then embracing simplicity and going alone,
continuously relying on external things has no place
within it.
Subcommentary:
"Xī" (奚) means "why".
"Liánlián" (連連) means continuously.
As for Dào and Dé,
they are neither existent nor non-existent,
neither generated nor extinguished,
cannot be sought through sagely wisdom,
how could they be grasped through form and name!
Yet types like Zēng and Shǐ,
with natures excessive in benevolence,
leading others by themselves,
stagnate in reputation and doctrine,
bound as if by ropes,
stubbornly fixed like glue and lacquer,
mind after mind continuing,
unceasingly connected.
Embracing this conduct
to roam freely in the land of Dào and Dé
is like learning squareness through roundness,
fish admiring birds,
vainly hoping for the reputation of eminence,
ultimately without practical achievement,
not forgetting the fish and rabbit while clinging to the trap,
and losing oneself like discarded straw dogs,
why value this!
It bewilders all under Heaven!
Commentary:
Continuous benevolence and righteousness
only suffice to confuse things,
causing them to lose their authenticity.
Subcommentary:
The teachings of benevolence and righteousness,
the traces of intelligence and hearing,
contradict the Dào of spontaneity,
and disrupt the minds of all under Heaven.
Minor confusion changes directions,
major confusion changes nature.
Commentary:
Exchanging east and west
does not harm the substance;
esteeming benevolence and upholding righteousness,
losing their constancy,
leading to fatal grounds,
is great confusion.
Subcommentary:
Taking south as north
is still minor delusion;
stagnating in traces and losing authenticity,
is greater confusion.
How do we know it is so?
Subcommentary:
"Rán" (然) means "so".
This poses a hypothetical question to introduce the following text.
Since Yú's time, invoking benevolence and righteousness to扰乱天下,
all under Heaven have rushed about pursuing benevolence and righteousness,
Commentary:
Not harming things
is not for benevolence's sake,
yet benevolent traces appear;
causing all principles to be appropriate
is not for righteousness' sake,
yet righteous achievements emerge;
thus being appropriate and unharming
does not come from invoking benevolence and righteousness.
Yet all under Heaven rush about,
abandoning themselves to pursue others, losing their constancy.
Thus, disordered minds do not arise from ugliness but always from beauty,
worldly disturbances do not emerge from evil but always from benevolence and righteousness,
therefore benevolence and righteousness
are tools to扰乱天下.
Subcommentary:
"Yú shì" refers to Shùn.
"Zhāo" means to seek.
"Náo" means to disturb.
Before Táng Yáo's time,
simplicity and genuineness were still preserved;
after Yú Shùn,
pure customs gradually dissipated,
hence using benevolent and righteous sagely traces
to comfort the common people,
causing all beings in the universe
to deludedly rush about,
losing their innate nature,
chasing after sagely traces.
Is this not using benevolence and righteousness to change their nature?
Commentary:
Although Yú's time had no intention to change,
the nature of all under Heaven was already altered.
Subcommentary:
From this perspective,
is it not using benevolent and righteous sagely traces to扰乱天下,
causing all living beings
to abandon the root for the branch and alter their innate nature?
Therefore, let us attempt to discuss it:
since the three dynasties and below,
all under Heaven have used external things to change their nature.
Commentary:
Before the three dynasties,
there truly were traces of non-action.
Traces of non-action
are also esteemed by those who act,
esteeming them causes loss of natural simplicity.
Thus, even sages have unavoidable circumstances,
some exchanging the nature of effortless rule for toilsome labors,
how much more so ordinary people!
Subcommentary:
Before the Five Emperors,
the wind of non-action still prevailed;
after the three dynasties,
teachings of action gradually arose.
Simplicity and refinement differed across ages,
steps and paces varied with times,
leading to abandoning oneself to imitate others,
easily losing true nature,
pursuing external things without return,
is it not lamentable!
The commentary says "exchanging the nature of effortless rule for toilsome labors":
"pán yí" means wounds or injuries.
It refers to Xià Yǔ weathering wind and rain,
hands and feet calloused,
exchanging such hardships
for the undertaking of non-action,
if those above are thus,
the common people below follow suit.
Petty people sacrifice themselves for profit,
scholars sacrifice themselves for fame,
great officers sacrifice themselves for their families,
sages sacrifice themselves for all under Heaven.
Commentary:
Dwelling like quails and eating like fledglings,
moving like birds without pattern,
why regret not sacrificing!
Thus, constantly merging with the world,
only adapting to changes,
their traces are traces of sacrificing for the world;
encountered circumstances may sometimes involve changes like wounds or bare shanks,
their traces are traces of harming nature.
Yet even when ranging over the eight extremes, spirit and energy remain unchanged,
hands and feet wounded but the residing form undisturbed,
then what is sacrificed?
Nothing is sacrificed.
Therefore, they do not pursue what is conventionally pursued,
yet their actions appear to conform with the worldly pursuits.
Note:
Pursuit (xùn) means to follow,
to strive for,
to seek,
to chase after,
referring to dedicating oneself to follow it.
Petty men covet profit,
upright men value fame,
officials sacrifice for a single family,
emperors strive across the four seas,
though what they pursue differs,
the alteration of their inherent nature is the same.
However, the sage is constantly in harmony with the world,
though his actions appear as pursuit,
hence there may be physical afflictions like scars, baldness, or leg injuries,
yet they never burden his spirit.
Thus, these several individuals,
though their undertakings differ,
and their reputations carry different labels,
in harming their nature by sacrificing their persons in pursuit,
are one and the same.
Note:
The "several individuals"
refer to the four persons mentioned earlier in the text.
"Undertakings"
means their pursuits of profit, fame, or the world differ.
"Reputations"
means the different labels of petty men, officials, and sages.
It says these four persons,
though their undertakings differ,
and their reputations have different labels,
meaning though the four differ,
in damaging their lives by chasing after external things with their persons,
they are ultimately no different.
Zāng and Gǔ,
two men herding sheep together both lost their sheep.
Note:
This continues the previous analogy to lead into the following text.
Mencius said:
Zāng is a man good at learning;
Gǔ is a youth.
Yáng Xióng said:
Zāng refers to a male servant or slave;
Gǔ is from a respectable family.
"Herd" means to tend.
"Lost" means to misplace.
It says these two were engrossed in their tasks,
and both lost their sheep.
Asked what Zāng was doing,
he was holding a bamboo slip and reading;
asked what Gǔ was doing,
he was playing at dice games.
These two men,
their tasks were different,
but in losing the sheep, they were the same.
Note:
Xī means "what."
Cè are bamboo slips.
The ancients had no paper,
all wrote books on bamboo slips.
Moving five passes and throwing the jade piece is called "bó"
not throwing the jade piece is called "sāi."
Asking Zāng and Gǔ,
reveals the difference between reading and gaming,
but in herding and losing sheep,
there is truly no difference.
Bóyí died for fame at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain,
while Dào Zhí died for profit atop Dōnglíng.
Note:
What follows combines the analogies.
Bóyí and Shūqí
were both sons of the lord of Gūzhú.
Gūzhú
was descended from Shénnóng,
with the surname Jiāng.
Bóyí,
personal name Yǔn,
courtesy name Gōngxìn;
Shūqí,
personal name Zhì,
courtesy name Gōngyuǎn.
Yí was older but born of a concubine,
Qí was younger but the legitimate heir,
their father often favored Qí,
and frequently praised him to Yí.
When their father died,
the brothers yielded to each other,
neither inheriting the title.
Hearing King Wén had the Dào,
they went to Zhōu.
Encountering King Wǔ attacking Zhòu,
they grasped his horse's bridle to remonstrate,
but their advice was not heeded,
so they entered Shǒuyáng Mountain,
gathering ferns for food,
refusing to eat grain,
and eventually starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain.
The mountain is in Pǔzhōu, east of the county.
Thirty lǐ south of Pǔzhōu city,
one can see the temple and tomb of Yí and Qí,
with dense, towering trees.
Dào Zhí
was the younger cousin of Liǔxià Huì,
personal name Zhí,
leading nine thousand followers,
often acting as a great robber,
hence named "Robber."
Dōnglíng
is a mountain name,
also said to be Tàishān,
within Qízhōu's boundaries,
fifteen lǐ from Dōngpíng,
where Zhí died.
These two men,
though what they died for differed,
in damaging their lives and harming their nature, they were the same.
Note:
Bóyí pursued fame,
dying at the foot of Shǒuyáng;
Dào Zhí coveted profit,
perishing atop Dōnglíng.
Though what they pursued—fame or profit—differed,
in terms of damage and harm,
there was no distinction.
Why must Bóyí be right and Dào Zhí wrong?
Commentary:
What the world values is life,
now pursuing it excessively,
both damage their lives,
then the right or wrong of what they pursue
is not worth further discussion.
Note:
According to世俗 views,
there is good and evil;
viewed from the Dào,
what is right or wrong?
Thus, Dào Zhí is not necessarily wrong,
and how can Bóyí alone be right?
The whole world is in pursuit.
Those who pursue rén and yì,
are called gentlemen by convention;
those who pursue goods and wealth,
are called petty men by convention.
Note:
This summarizes the preceding text to form the subsequent meaning.
But the Dào has been lost for a long time,
and nothing is truly appropriate.
Now, everyone in the世俗 is pursuing,
how could it be only Yí and Zhí!
Following rén and yì,
never departs from fame;
chasing goods and wealth,
certainly aims at profit.
Only fame and profit,
are the roots of damaging life,
they are not the natural principle,
but arise from世俗 sentiments,
thus gentlemen and petty men,
cannot be firmly distinguished.
Their pursuit is the same,
so there are gentlemen among them,
and petty men among them;
but in damaging life and harming nature,
then Dào Zhí is just like Bóyí,
so why distinguish between gentleman and petty man among them?
Commentary:
The world all considers not harming life as good,
now equally harming life,
then though what they pursue differs,
it is not worth further consideration.
Why is life harmed?
Why is nature altered?
All due to esteeming the traces of wúwéi.
If one knows that traces arise from wúwéi and are formed, then one abandons esteem and excess and returns to the ultimate harmony with oneself.
Yáo and Jié would both be equal in self-attainment,
so how can gentleman and petty man be distinguished?
Note:
Wù means "why."
In their pursuit of fame and profit,
there is a distinction between gentleman and petty man;
but in damaging life and harming nature,
there is truly no difference between Dào Zhí and Bóyí.
This is because世俗 people invert things,
unrelated to the true ultimate.
On what basis to choose a gentleman,
on what basis to distinguish a petty man?
It means there is no difference.
Moreover, those who bind their nature to rén and yì,
even if as accomplished as Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiú,
are not what I call good.
Commentary:
To tie this to that is "binding."
Binding nature to rén,
is merely pursuing rén,
hence not good.
Note:
Binding means to tie.
"Zāng" means goodness.
"Wú" is how Zhuāngzǐ refers to himself.
To abandon oneself and imitate others,
gaining things but losing one's self,
is the artificial sentiment of the common flow.
Therefore, to bind my innate nature,
learning their benevolence and righteousness,
even if achieving the traces of sages,
like Mò Dí and Yáng Zhū,
goes against one's inherent nature,
thus it is not what Lùnshēng considers good.
To subordinate one's nature to the five flavors,
even if as proficient as Yú'ér,
is not what I call zāng;
Note:
Following one's nature to understand flavors is true goodness.
Subcommentary:
Mèngzǐ said:
Yú'ér
was a man of Qí who recognized flavors.
Shīzǐ says: Yú'ér blended ginger and cinnamon,
to prepare food for his lord.
Without natural simplicity,
imitating others to gain knowledge,
even if as proficient as Yú'ér,
is not true goodness.
To subordinate one's nature to the five sounds,
even if as proficient as Shī Kuàng,
is not what I call keen hearing;
to subordinate one's nature to the five colors,
even if as proficient as Lí Zhū,
is not what I call clear sight.
Note:
Not entrusting it to oneself but subordinating it to others,
then even if proficient like them,
one's self is already lost.
Thus, each should employ their own ears and eyes,
without being tied to Lí Zhū or Shī Kuàng,
that is true keen hearing and clear sight.
Subcommentary:
Lí Zhū and Shī Kuàng,
endowed with keen sight and hearing,
followed their nature and could do so,
not through learning.
Now, to force one's nature and fake emotions,
abandoning oneself to imitate others,
even if achieving proficiency,
is not worthy of being called good.
What I call zāng,
is not referring to benevolence and righteousness,
but being good in one's own virtue;
Note:
Good at self-attainment,
forgetting benevolence yet being benevolent.
Subcommentary:
Dé means attainment.
Those who comprehend the mysterious Dào,
do not change their nature to follow others,
how could they cling to used straw dogs,
or dwell in the transient huts of former kings!
Thus, one should know their own knowing,
attain their own attainment,
considering this as goodness,
is it not appropriate!
What I call zāng,
is not what is called benevolence and righteousness,
but following the true condition of one's nature and life;
Note:
Calling benevolence and righteousness good,
then harming oneself to pursue them,
this in turn is not benevolent to one's own nature and life.
If one is not benevolent to oneself,
how can they be to others!
Therefore, by following one's nature and life,
one can then extend to others,
extending to others without burdening oneself,
both others and self share in self-attainment,
this can be called good.
Subcommentary:
Zēng Shēn, Shǐ Yú, Yáng Zhū, Mò Dí,
these four practiced benevolence and righteousness,
likely following their nature and emotions,
endowed by heavenly mandate,
like extra digits,
not acquired through learning.
Yet some see Zēng and Shǐ's benevolence and righteousness,
and say imitating them can lead to success;
hear of Lí Zhū and Shī Kuàng's keen senses,
and claim that similar achievement is possible;
how can they know it's the work of creation and nurture!
Thus Wáng Bì commented on the Yì,
"Not making emotions conform to nature,
how can one long practice what is forced,"
refers to this.
What I call keen hearing,
is not hearing others,
but hearing oneself;
what I call clear sight,
is not seeing others,
but seeing oneself.
Note:
To renounce Lí Zhū and Shī Kuàng,
and trust one's own hearing and sight,
then the keen senses of all directions are fully preserved.
Subcommentary:
To admire Lí Zhū and Shī Kuàng,
seeing and hearing as they do,
mind and spirit race,
ears and eyes exhaust and perish,
this is foolish darkness,
how can it be called keen hearing and clear sight!
If one hears what the ears hear,
sees what the eyes see,
preserving one's lot and embracing truth,
not straying outward,
then all things are heard and seen clearly.
Not seeing oneself but seeing others,
not attaining oneself but attaining others,
is to gain what others gain without gaining one's own gain,
to suit what suits others without suiting what suits oneself.
Note:
This is abandoning oneself to imitate others,
even if imitating them perfectly,
one's self is already lost.
Subcommentary:
Not being able to see what one's eyes see but seeking Lí Zhū's clarity,
not knowing what one's knowledge knows but straining to admire Shǐ Yú's righteousness,
this is fake emotions learning others' attainments,
not following nature to attain one's own.
Then, with artificial learning outwardly displayed,
imitating others to please people,
the heart toils in pretense,
thus not suiting what suits oneself.
To suit what suits others without suiting what suits oneself,
whether Dào Zhí or Bó Yí,
is equally depraved and perverse.
Note:
If losing one's nature is considered depravity,
then although the paths of loss differ,
the loss itself is the same.
Subcommentary:
Yín means stagnation.
Pì means deviation.
To preserve one's lot and follow nature,
is the correct path;
to esteem fame and love victory,
is depraved deviation.
Thus, abandoning oneself to chase things,
opening paths of hope and luck,
whether Bó Yí's goodness,
or Dào Zhí's evil,
are equally depraved and perverse.
Repeating "suiting what suits others"
is to conclude the former and lead to the latter, enhancing the literary flow.
I am ashamed regarding the Dào and Dé,
thus above, I dare not uphold the conduct of benevolence and righteousness,
and below, I dare not engage in depraved and perverse actions.
Note:
Ashamed of not embodying the Dào and Dé,
acknowledging no trace of dark return,
thus renouncing conduct,
forgetting fame and profit,
leisurely as wind and dust,
forgetting self and others,
just like this.
Subcommentary:
The empty and penetrating Dào,
the virtue of ultimate forgetting,
transcends benevolence and righteousness,
without profit or fame.
And Zhuāngzǐ wonderfully embodied the center of the circle,
roaming the mind beyond things,
his will and conduct transcending
benevolence, righteousness, and judgments of right and wrong;
embodying the natural state of non-being,
ashamed of not acting according to the Dào and Dé.
Speaking of "above and below,"
shows the superiority of benevolence and righteousness over depravity.
Saying "I am ashamed and dare not,"
indicates humility.
Guǒ Xiàng's note says "leisurely as wind and dust":
cóngróng means relaxed and unrestrained;
while "wind and dust,"
movement without intent.
Chuī means wind;
lěi means dust;
like the movement of a clear breeze,
lightly lifting fine dust.
Nánhuá Zhēnjīng Zhù Shū, Scroll Ten
The Southern Florescence True Classic Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll 11, Continuation 5
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters, "Horse Hooves" Number Nine
Horses,
their hooves can tread on frost and snow,
their hair can ward off wind and cold,
they chew grass and drink water,
lift their legs and leap,
this is the true nature of horses.
Commentary:
Both inferior and fine horses are content with their own bodies and sufficient.
Subcommentary:
Chewing means with the teeth.
Treading means stepping on;
warding off means resisting;
lifting means raising.
Now, hooves tread on frost and snow,
hair wards off wind and cold,
when hungry, they chew grass,
when thirsty, they drink water,
at ease and content with their nature,
they lift their legs and jump about,
seeking what is endowed by the Creator,
so how could their true nature desire to be tethered, hobbled, or placed in stables and subjected to human care?!
Moreover, all things vary,
each relying on their innate disposition,
arranged and following their nature,
each attains carefree ease,
without pride or striving,
thus their lives can be preserved.
Even if there were raised platforms and grand halls,
they would have no use for them.
Commentary:
The true nature of horses
is not to avoid saddles and hate being ridden,
but simply not to envy glory and splendor.
Subcommentary:
Raised means nurturing.
It refers to the towers and pavilions where noble people nurture and protect themselves.
It is also said:
Raised platforms are like spiritual altars.
Grand,
means large,
proper,
that is, the main hall of the proper residence.
This means that by nature,
horses delight in the open fields,
even if there are high towers and grand halls,
they have no use for them.
How much more so for clear and empty scholars,
and simple, honest people,
who enjoy thatched huts,
and are content with jar windows,
even if there are vermilion pillars and carved rafters,
what are they to me?!
Then along came Bó Lè,
who said:
"I am good at managing horses."
He branded them,
clipped them,
trimmed their hooves,
and bridled them,
tethered them with halters and hobbles,
and lined them up in stables with bedding,
and two or three out of ten horses died;
Commentary:
If one intentionally manages them,
then they are not well managed.
Managing them as a good practice
is actually not good.
Subcommentary:
The Lièzǐ says:
His surname was Sūn,
given name Yáng,
courtesy name Bó Lè,
a man skilled at managing horses during the time of Duke Mù of Qín.
Branding means searing with hot iron.
Clipping means cutting their hair;
trimming means paring their hooves;
bridling means putting on a headstall.
Halter means tying with a rope hobble;
hobble means binding the front two legs.
Stable means the trough and manger;
bedding,
is made by weaving wood into planks,
placed under the horse's feet,
to remove dampness,
what is called a horse bed.
Now, not allowing horses to follow their true nature,
but arbitrarily branding and clipping them,
already goes against the natural principle,
and many have died.
Moreover, being unattached to things,
is how life and nature remain safe and intact;
intentionally managing them,
causes natural lifespans to be cut short.
He starved them,
thirsted them,
galloped them,
urged them,
aligned them,
ordered them,
with the worry of bit ornaments in front,
and the threat of whips behind,
and the deaths among the horses had already surpassed half.
Commentary:
Now, a good charioteer
aims to fully utilize their abilities.
Fully utilizing abilities lies in letting them fulfill themselves,
yet instead, he drives and forces their steps,
demanding uses beyond their capacity,
thus they cannot endure and many die.
If instead, one employs the strength of both inferior and fine horses,
according to their natural slowness or speed,
even if their footprints reach the edges of the eight wildernesses,
the nature of all horses would be preserved.
Yet some, hearing of following the nature of horses,
say it means releasing them and not riding them;
hearing of the style of non-action,
then claim that walking is not as good as lying down;
how can they go so far without returning?!
This misses Zhuāngzǐ's intent by far.
Subcommentary:
Bit means the mouthpiece.
It refers to adorning the bridle with precious items.
A whip with leather is called a whip,
without leather is called a switch,
both are horse rods.
Now, galloping and urging excessively,
starving and thirsting abnormally,
aligning them with yoke and crossbar,
ordering them with bridle and reins,
threatening them with whip and switch,
and seeking abilities beyond their allotment,
thus inferior horses cannot endure,
and deaths have surpassed half.
Sagely wisdom in managing things
inflicts similar damage.
A potter says:
"I am good at managing clay,
the round ones match the compass,
the square ones match the square."
Subcommentary:
Molding earth is called pottery.
Pottery means transforming,
also a workshop.
Clay means adhesive,
also earth.
This means the potter is skilled at blending water and earth to make earthenware,
applying circles and squares,
that must match the compass and square.
A carpenter says:
"I am good at managing wood,
the curved ones match the hook,
the straight ones match the line."
Subcommentary:
Hook means curved.
Line means straight.
This means the carpenter, with his skill and cleverness,
is good at managing wood,
the curves and straightness of the wood
must match the hook and line.
Now, is it the nature of clay and wood to want to match compass, square, hook, and line?
Subcommentary:
The nature of earth and wood,
endowed by the Creator,
does not seek curves or straightness,
how could it crave circles and squares?
Potters and carpenters
arbitrarily judge good and bad.
Yet generation after generation praises them, saying Bó Lè is good at managing horses, and potters and carpenters are good at managing clay and wood,
this is also the error of those who govern the world.
Commentary:
The world considers those who follow nature without adding artifice as unskilled in management,
bending the curved straight,
harshly training inferior horses to act like fine ones,
able to use compass and square to forcibly twist their nature,
until death and only then stopping,
and then calling it good management,
is that not an error?!
Subcommentary:
This summarizes the preceding text to combine its analogies.
Yet worldly feelings are foolish and confused,
considering management as good,
and non-management as false,
nothing is more false than this.
In my opinion, those who are good at governing the world are not like this.
Commentary:
Governing by not governing
is the good governance.
Subcommentary:
Like this means such.
Zhuāngzǐ says:
"In my opinion, those good at governing the world
are not like the potters and carpenters mentioned before."
The method of good governance
is listed in the text below.
Those people have a constant nature,
weaving for clothing,
To plow and eat,
this is called shared virtue;
Note:
The virtue of the people,
differs slightly but is largely the same.
Thus, what cannot be eliminated from human nature
is clothing and food;
what cannot be abandoned in affairs
is farming and weaving;
these are universally recognized as fundamental in the world.
Those who uphold this way
achieve the utmost in non-action.
Explanation:
Those people are the common masses.
It means all living beings possess a true constant nature without relying on external things.
Virtue is what is attained.
By following their true constant nature,
all things are self-sufficient,
hence shared virtue.
Guǎng Xiàng says,
what cannot be eliminated from nature is clothing and food,
what cannot be abandoned in affairs is farming and weaving,
these are what the world agrees upon as fundamental,
upholding this way,
non-action is perfected.
Unified and without partiality,
it is called heavenly freedom.
Note:
Let it be free and it naturally unifies,
not due to partiality,
hence called heavenly freedom.
Explanation:
Partiality means bias.
Call means to name.
Heaven means naturalness.
The empty and penetrating single way nurtures all living beings,
raising and cultivating them,
without bias or partiality.
If one intentionally governs things,
it contradicts their natural state;
simply let them be free,
then all things are self-sufficient,
thus named heavenly freedom.
Therefore, in the age of perfect virtue,
their walking is steady,
their gaze is upright.
Note:
This is the appearance of self-sufficiency within,
with nothing external sought.
Explanation:
Steady,
means a contented heart.
Upright,
means a tall and straight appearance.
In the most pristine and harmonious age,
the time of initial perfect virtue,
hearts were free from right and wrong,
actions forgot self and others.
Thus, preserving truth and inner fulfillment,
they dwelt steadily in non-action;
not seeking externally,
they roamed upright in emptiness and tranquility.
At that time,
mountains had no paths or tunnels,
marshes had no boats or bridges;
Note:
Not seeking undeserved profits,
so they were content with their own households.
Explanation:
Path means trail;
tunnel means road.
Boat means vessel.
At that time,
it was the age of perfect virtue.
People knew to keep to their roles,
all things were simple and genuine,
no cutting or seizing,
hence paths could be forgotten,
no coming or going,
thus boats and bridges were abandoned.
All living beings,
connected in their communities;
Note:
In chaotic simplicity, all attain alike,
then the whole world is indifferent,
how could states differ or families vary!
Explanation:
In the age of chaotic simplicity,
it was pure, harmonious, and indifferent.
Thus, insentient万物,
joined together in shared neighborhoods;
sentient群生,
belonged together in common towns;
how could states have different policies or families unusual customs!
Birds and beasts formed flocks,
plants and trees grew lush.
Note:
Satisfied with their nature and stopping there,
no desire to devour or conquer,
thus things remained whole.
Explanation:
Flying birds and running beasts unharmed,
thus they formed flocks;
vegetables, grasses, fruits, and trees uncut,
they achieved lush growth.
Therefore, birds and beasts could be led on a leash to wander,
and magpie nests could be climbed to peek into.
Note:
Harmless to creatures,
thus creatures are tame.
Explanation:
People had no intent to harm creatures,
creatures had no fear of people.
Thus, mountain birds and wild beasts
could be leashed and roamed with;
magpie nests,
could be climbed and peered into.
In the age of perfect virtue,
they lived together with birds and beasts,
mingled with all things,
how could one distinguish gentlemen from petty persons!
Explanation:
Those following deviant paths are petty persons,
those walking the upright way are gentlemen.
Yet dwelling in nests and caves,
they made no distinction from birds and beasts;
eating freely and with full bellies,
blending with all creatures without difference:
how then to know gentlemen,
how to discern petty persons!
Alike in lack of knowledge,
their virtue does not depart;
Note:
Knowledge leads to departing from the way through contrived goodness.
Explanation:
Since there is no mind of discrimination,
they are alike in the principle of no knowledge.
Nor do they risk virtue to seek action,
thus they embrace unity without departure.
Alike in lack of desire,
this is called plain simplicity;
Note:
Desire leads to departing from nature through adornment.
Explanation:
Alike in the initial lack of desire,
all things are pure and honest;
unlike the superficial extravagance of later ages,
people are all simple and genuine.
In plain simplicity, the people's nature is attained.
Note:
No trouble from knowledge and desire.
Explanation:
The reason living beings lose their nature
is all due to clinging to desires.
Since there is no desire and plain simplicity,
true nature is not lost,
thus it is called attainment.
This sentence summarizes the beauty of perfect virtue described before.
But when sages appear,
Note:
Sages are
the traces of the people's attained nature,
not the source of those traces.
This mention of sages appearing
means the emergence of their traces.
Straining to act benevolently,
striving to be righteous,
and the world begins to doubt;
indulging in music,
forcing etiquette,
and the world begins to divide.
Note:
Once the traces of sages become prominent,
then benevolence and righteousness are not genuine, and rituals and music depart from nature,
merely attaining outward form.
With sages come these flaws,
what can I do about it!
Explanation:
From here upward,
clarifies the virtue of purity and simplicity;
from here downward,
criticizes the failures of sage traces.
When sages appear,
it refers to those after the Five Emperors who practiced sage traces.
Straining
means the appearance of exerting force.
Striving,
means a posture of self-importance.
Indulgence is a heart of extravagance,
forcing is behavior of contortion.
When the way of purity and simplicity fades,
hypocrisy and artifice arise.
Striving relies on righteousness that judges wrongs,
straining boasts of benevolence with bias,
indulgence values extravagant and wanton music,
forcing upholds flashy and superficial rituals,
then the world becomes divided,
the people grow doubtful,
disrupting heaven's order,
beginning from this point.
If unhewn wood remained intact,
who would make sacrificial vessels!
If white jade remained unbroken,
who would create guī and zhāng tablets!
Explanation:
Unhewn wood refers to whole timber.
Remaining intact means uncarved.
Shú means "who."
Xī zūn
are wine vessels
carved with ox heads
for ancestral temple sacrifices.
Guī tablets have pointed tops and square bases,
while zhāng tablets are half-guī.
These are brief analogies
illustrating artificial governance.
If the Dào and Dé remained unabolished,
what need would there be for rén and yì!
Explanation:
This combines the analogies.
In the era of the Great Dào,
right and wrong weren't distinguished;
in the age of supreme Dé,
likes and dislikes weren't discussed.
Without preferences, human desires naturally cease;
without distinctions, essence and manifestation are forgotten.
Hence the Lǎojīng states: "When the Great Dào is abandoned,
rén and yì appear."
If innate nature remained undivided,
what use would there be for rituals and music!
Explanation:
Rituals regulate behavior,
music harmonizes hearts.
If emotions remain undisturbed,
what need to harmonize hearts!
If nature remains undivided,
why labor to regulate behavior? Thus we know harmonizing hearts and regulating behavior arise from the Dào's decline.
If the five colors weren't confused,
who would create patterns!
If the five tones weren't disordered,
who would apply the six pitch-pipes!
Commentary:
All these transform simplicity into ornament,
abandoning the root to exalt the branch,
damaging and discarding
heavenly purity.
Though the world values them,
they are not truly valuable.
Explanation:
Patterns emerge from contrast,
music values harmony.
If colors and tones
don't interact and manifest,
then musical scales and embroidered patterns
cannot achieve their functions.
This restates the analogy
to prove the previous point.
Damaging unhewn wood to make vessels
is the craftsman's crime;
destroying the Dào and Dé to establish rén and yì
is the sage's fault.
Commentary:
Craftsmen have their compass and square measurements,
sages have their admirable traces.
Explanation:
This summarizes the preceding meaning.
Craftsmen damage plain wood to make sacrificial vessels,
sages destroy the non-action Dào with rén and yì traces -
since the harm is the same,
their culpability should be equal.
Horses,
living on land, eat grass and drink water;
when pleased, they rub necks together;
when angry, they turn back-to-back and kick.
Horses' knowledge stops here.
Commentary:
Guiding their true knowledge,
riding their natural movements,
enables traversing ten thousand miles
without losing equine nature.
Explanation:
Mí means rubbing,
following. Tì means kicking.
Yǐ means "stop."
Creatures' joy and anger
derive from natural endowment,
acting according to nature,
not through artificial pretense.
Thus when pleased they rub necks in harmony,
when angry they kick back-to-back,
and horses' understanding perfectly ends here,
eating grass and drinking water,
happiness contained within.
When yokes are added to them,
and browbands整齐 them,
then horses learn to stand stubbornly, twist from yokes, violently struggle, cunningly spit bits, and stealthily loosen bridles.
Explanation:
Héng, the crossbar before the carriage shaft.
È, the wood on horse's neck.
Yuè tí,
on the forehead above the skull,
moon-shaped.
Jiè means solitary.
Ní means side-glancing.
Yīn means bending.
Zhì means resisting.
Màn means charging.
Guǐ means deceitful.
Qiè means stealing.
Horses' true knowledge
only enjoys freedom;
they don't seek adornment,
how could they crave glory!
Once moon-brands are added,
and crossbars整齐 them,
contravening their natural disposition,
unable to endure hardship,
deceit consequently sprouts:
side-glancing, bending necks from yokes,
resisting those controlling them.
"Stealing bridles" means secretly loosening headstalls,
"cunning bits" means spitting out bridles.
Truly because their true nature is damaged,
they develop countless pretenses.
Thus horses' knowledge reaching thievery
is Bó Lè's crime.
Commentary:
Horse natures differ yet uniform use is demanded,
hence some exhaust their strength and develop artifices.
Explanation:
Tài means crafty deceit.
Horses' true knowledge
suits open country;
when driven excessively,
deceitful hearts emerge -
these cunning thieving artifices
are Bó Lè's culpability.
In Hèxū's time,
people dwelled without knowing their tasks,
walked without knowing destinations,
mouths full, they played;
bellies full, they wandered;
people's abilities stopped here.
Commentary:
This was people's true capability.
Explanation:
Zhī means "go to."
Hèxū
was an ancient sovereign;
also said to have radiant virtue
making people flock to him,
hence called Hèxū,
probably Yándì.
In the Dào-practicing era,
the non-action age,
minds free from attachments,
they dwelled without purposeful action;
acting according to nature,
they wandered without destinations.
With mouths full, they played,
no different from infants;
with bellies full, they roamed,
indistinguishable from children.
This most pristine age
had people thus capable.
Until sages arrived,
bending with rituals and music to "rectify" worldly forms,
elevating rén and yì to "comfort" worldly hearts,
then people began striving for knowledge,
competing for profit,
unstoppably.
This too is the sages' fault.
Commentary:
Their faults all arise from admirable traces.
Explanation:
Bending and twisting,
practicing rituals and music to "correct" physical forms;
suspending rén and yì high,
making people aspire to "comfort" their hearts;
then they began self-important striving,
loving knowledge and developing deceit;
scheming for wealth and position,
competing endlessly.
Alas!
Such are the faults of sage traces.
Nánhuá Zhēnjīng Commentary Volume 11
The Southern Florescence True Canon Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Twelve, Part Six
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters, Chapter Ten: "Opening Trunks"
To prepare against thieves who open trunks, rifle bags, and break into boxes,
one must bind with cords and fasten locks and bolts securely.
This is what the world calls wisdom.
Subcommentary:
胠 (qū) means to open;
篋 (qiè) means a trunk;
囊 (náng) means a bag;
攝 (shè) means to gather or secure;
緘 (jiān) means to tie or seal;
縢 (téng) means cord or rope.
扃 (jiōng) refers to the crossbar or latch;
鐍 (jué) refers to the lock and key.
Now, preparing against thieves who open trunks and rifle bags,
or break into boxes to steal goods,
these are petty thieves,
not great robbers.
How should one prepare defenses against them?
What methods should be used?
One must gather and secure trunks and bags,
tying them with cords and ropes,
and fasten locks and bolts firmly,
to prevent careless storage.
This is the shallow wisdom of the world.
Yet when a great robber arrives,
he shoulders the box, lifts the trunk, and carries the bag as he hurries away,
worrying only that the cords, locks, and bolts might not be secure enough.
If so, then is not what was earlier called wisdom
merely storing up gains for the great robber?
Commentary:
This shows how wisdom cannot be relied upon.
Subcommentary:
Binding with cords and fastening locks securely
is to guard against petty thieves.
But when a great robber arrives,
shouldering and carrying things away as he goes,
he fears only that the ropes and latches might not be strong enough.
The earlier preparations for defense
instead become resources for the robber.
Thus, worldly wisdom cannot be relied upon.
Therefore, let us try to discuss this:
Is there any instance of what the world calls wisdom
that does not store up gains for great robbers?
Is there any so-called sage
who does not guard things for great robbers?
Subcommentary:
Those who embody the Dào, the great worthies,
speak without fixed assertions.
Wishing to elucidate the principle of forgetting words,
they say, "Let us try to discuss this."
They say:
Worldly people
possess shallow and superficial wisdom;
the sages who display traces
have not penetrated deeply into principle.
Although their intention is to guard and restrict,
they instead accumulate for the robbers;
though they govern the world,
they end up guarding for the robbers.
If one believes there are those who do not do so,
it is to clarify: how could there be any who do not store and guard for great robbers?
This means they inevitably store up for robbers.
How do we know it is so?
Subcommentary:
This poses a hypothetical question
to elucidate the meaning and purpose.
In the past, in the state of Qí, neighboring villages were within sight of each other,
the sounds of chickens and dogs were within hearing,
the areas where nets were spread,
and where plows and hoes tilled,
extended over two thousand li.
Subcommentary:
Qí
was the domain of the descendants of Tàigōng,
enfeoffed in the land of Yíngqiū.
By the time of Duke Huán, who assembled the feudal lords nine times,
unifying and rectifying the world,
the people were prosperous,
unsurpassed in the three Qí regions.
Thus, the sounds of chickens and dogs were within hearing,
neighboring villages were within sight of each other,
nets were spread for hunting and fishing,
plows and hoes tilled to cultivate agriculture.
The territory was vast,
over two thousand li,
and in terms of prosperity and excellence,
it indeed led among the feudal lords.
耒 (lěi) means plow.
耨 (nòu) means hoe.
Throughout the four borders of the state,
the establishment of ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
and the governance of hamlets, villages, districts, and rural areas—
were these not all modeled after the sages?
Subcommentary:
Humans cannot be established without land,
nor eat without grain.
Thus, an enclosed area for sacrificing to the soil is called shè (社),
and for sacrificing to grain is called jì (稷).
Jì refers to the foremost of the five grains.
Shè
means "to spit forth,"
indicating it can produce all things.
The Simǎ Rules state:
Six chǐ make a bù (step),
a hundred bù make a mǔ (acre),
a hundred mǔ make a fū (holding),
three fū make a wū (homestead),
three wū make a jǐng (well-field),
four jǐng make a yì (village).
It also says:
Five families make a bǐ (group),
five bǐ make a lǘ (neighborhood),
five lǘ make a zú (clan),
five zú make a dǎng (party),
five dǎng make a zhōu (district),
five zhōu make a xiāng (canton).
Zhèng Xuán says:
Twenty-five families make a lǘ,
twenty-five hundred families make a zhōu,
twelve thousand five hundred families make a xiāng.
闔 (hé) means to combine or encompass.
曷 (hé) means "what" or "how."
Throughout the four borders,
within the three Qí regions,
the establishment of these ancestral temples and other matters
all imitated Yáo and Shùn, following the sages,
to set the laws and rules for governing the state.
Yet Tián Chéngzǐ one day killed the ruler of Qí and stole his state.
Commentary:
Those who model themselves on the sages
only imitate their traces.
Now, traces
are things that have passed,
not tools for responding to change.
Why should they be esteemed and clung to?
To cling to formed traces and apply them to the boundless,
when the boundless arrives, the traces become stagnant.
Thus, one guards the state only to have it guarded for others.
Subcommentary:
Tián Chéngzǐ,
also known as Chén Héng, a minister of Qí,
was the seventh-generation descendant of Jìng Zhòng.
Initially,
Jìng Zhòng went to Qí
and received a fief in Tián,
thus changing the clan name to Tián.
In the fourteenth year of Duke Āi of Lǔ,
Chén Héng assassinated his ruler,
who was Duke Jiǎn.
He annexed territories from Ānpíng to Lángyé,
making them his own fief.
By the time of Tàigōng Hé, the great-grandson of Héng,
he moved Duke Kāng of Qí to the seacoast
and established himself as the Marquis of Qí.
From Jìng Zhòng to Duke Zhuāng,
nine generations in total controlled the government of Qí;
from Tàigōng to King Wēi,
three generations served as Marquis of Qí;
altogether, twelve generations.
Zhuāngzǐ
lived during the time of King Xuān.
Now, not counting King Xuān,
it is said to be twelve generations.
Did he steal only the state?
He also stole the laws of the sages' wisdom along with it.
Commentary:
If he had not stolen the sagely laws,
he would have had no means to seize the state.
Subcommentary:
What Tián Héng stole
was not merely the state of Qí.
He first stole the sagely wisdom,
thus gaining the allegiance of the feudal lords.
This shows that the traces of benevolence and righteousness
merely become the basis for robbery.
Thus, Tián Chéngzǐ had the name of a robber,
yet enjoyed the security of a Yáo or Shùn.
Subcommentary:
Tián Héng usurped the state of Qí,
thus gaining the reputation of a great robber;
yet his position was elevated among the feudal lords,
and he enjoyed the security and comfort of a Táng or Yú ruler.
Small states dared not criticize him,
large states dared not punish him,
and for twelve generations, his family held Qí.
Subcommentary:
The states of viscounts and barons
dared not criticize or condemn;
the states of earls and marquises
how could they launch campaigns against him?
Thus, his lineage continued uninterrupted,
and his ancestral temple endured distantly.
The generations spanned twelve,
as explained earlier.
Then, did he not steal the state of Qí,
and along with it, the laws of the sages' wisdom to guard his robber's person?
Commentary:
This means that the sagely laws are merely tools for people to use;
they are not sufficient to be instruments of complete adequacy.
Commentary:
They appropriate the state by cloaking themselves in benevolence and righteousness,
and preserve themselves by relying on sagely wisdom.
This reiterates the preceding text,
to conclude its meaning.
Let us attempt to discuss this:
Are there any among those whom the world calls the most wise
who do not accumulate for the great robbers?
Are there any among those called the most sage
who do not guard for the great robbers?
Commentary:
Reiterating the previous meaning,
to introduce what follows.
How do we know it is so?
Commentary:
Posing a hypothetical question
to elaborate its purpose.
In the past, Lóng Páng was beheaded,
Bǐ Gān was disemboweled,
Cháng Hóng was torn apart,
and Zǐ Xū's body was left to rot,
thus these four men, despite their worthiness, could not avoid execution.
Annotation:
This says that tyrannical and chaotic rulers
can also wield the authority of a ruler to execute worthy men without anyone daring to resist,
all due to the ways of the sages.
Had there been no sagely ways,
how could Jié and Zhòu have maintained their positions to unleash their poison,
making the world look on with fear?
Commentary:
Lóng Páng,
surname Guān,
was a worthy minister of Xià Jié,
killed by Jié.
Bǐ Gān,
a prince,
remonstrated with Zhòu,
who cut out his heart to examine it.
Cháng Hóng,
a worthy minister of King Líng of Zhōu.
The Garden of Stories says:
When Shū Xiàng of Jìn had Cháng Hóng killed,
Cháng Hóng frequently appeared in Zhōu,
and through a group sent a letter,
Cháng Hóng said to Shū Xiàng:
You raise Jìn's troops to attack Zhōu,
to depose the Liú clan and establish the Shàn clan.
The Liú clan said to the ruler:
This is Cháng Hóng.
So he was killed.
"Torn apart" means ripped open.
It is also said:
"Torn apart" means disemboweled;
"rot" means decayed, shattered.
This says Zǐ Xū suffered execution,
his body floated on the river,
left to decay.
These four men all had loyal and worthy conduct,
yet could not escape execution,
because the immoral men,
relying on the position of rulers,
and the authority of sagely traces,
thus could trample the loyal and good,
and unleash their poison.
So Zhí's followers asked Zhí:
Do robbers also have a way?
Commentary:
Hypothetically using Zhí's followers to raise the question.
Zhí said:
How could there be anywhere without a way!
Commentary:
This answers the previous question.
The way is omnipresent,
where is it not the way!
Where the way exists,
is detailed below.
To accurately guess the treasures in a room,
is sageliness;
entering first, is courage;
exiting last, is righteousness.
Knowing what can and cannot be done, is wisdom;
dividing equally, is benevolence.
One who lacks these five and can become a great robber
has never existed in the world.
Annotation:
These five are meant to prohibit robbery,
but instead become tools for robbers.
Commentary:
The treasures in the room's storehouse,
storing wealth and valuables,
the robber conjures a reckless thought,
estimates and calculates,
hitting the mark unfailingly,
as if divinely inspired,
hence called sageliness.
Joining forces with one heart,
not avoiding resistance,
striving to enter first,
is that not courage!
Arrows and stones flying,
disregarding life and death,
competing to exit last,
is that not righteousness!
Knowing when to act;
when to stop,
recognizing safety and danger,
assessing misfortune and fortune,
succeeding when advancing,
is his wisdom.
Valuing righteousness over wealth,
taking little, yielding much,
dividing goods equally,
is his benevolence.
These five are the aforementioned sageliness, courage, righteousness, wisdom, and benevolence.
To be a robber,
one must possess these five virtues;
without the five virtues,
robbery cannot succeed.
Thus, to become a great robber without sagely wisdom
has never existed in the world.
From this perspective,
the good cannot establish themselves without the way of the sages,
nor can Zhí practice his ways without the way of the sages;
Commentary:
The way of the sages
refers to the five virtues.
Reasoning thus,
if the good do not practice the five virtues,
they have no means to establish themselves and follow the way,
and robbers like Zhí without sagely wisdom,
how could they carry out their theft!
Since the good in the world are few and the bad many,
the sages benefit the world little and harm it much.
Annotation:
How true these words!
Though true,
we cannot do away with sages,
as the world's wisdom cannot be entirely eliminated,
so the sagely way is needed to restrain it.
If all wisdom remains and only sagely wisdom is abolished,
then the harm to the world would be greater than with sages.
Thus, though the harm of having sages is great,
it is still better than the chaos without sages.
Though better than without sages,
it is not as harmless as abolishing all.
Alas,
all under heaven seek profit but cannot eliminate their wisdom;
how deluded and misguided they are!
Commentary:
The paths of good and evil
both stem from sagely wisdom.
Bó Yí upheld integrity and became famous,
while Robber Zhí indulged in greed and cruelty for gain.
But Zhí's followers are many,
and Bó Yí's kind are few,
so we know sagely traces benefit the world little and harm it much.
Hence it is said,
when the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold;
when Lǔ's wine is thin, Hán Dān is besieged;
when sages are born, great robbers arise.
Annotation:
The loss of lips does not intend to chill the teeth, yet they chill;
the thin wine of Lǔ does not intend to besiege Hán Dān, yet it is besieged;
the birth of sages does not intend to raise great robbers, yet they arise.
This is natural mutual production,
an inevitable trend.
Though sages do not establish esteem for things,
they cannot prevent things from being esteemed.
Thus, regardless of people's nobility or baseness,
or the truth or falsehood of affairs,
if they emulate the sagely methods,
the world swallows its voice and silently submits,
which is what Jié and Zhí rely on to become great robbers.
Commentary:
The Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuǒ Zhuàn say,
"With the lips gone, the teeth feel cold,"
referring to Yú and Guó.
Hán Dān is a city of Zhào.
It is said King Xuān of Chǔ held a court assembly with the feudal lords,
and Duke Gōng of Lǔ arrived late with thin wine.
King Xuān was angered,
and intended to humiliate him.
Duke Gōng said:
I am a descendant of the Duke of Zhōu,
practicing the rites and music of the Son of Heaven,
with merits to the Zhōu house.
Now I bring wine and lose propriety,
and you blame its thinness,
is that not too much!
He then left without bidding farewell.
King Xuān was enraged,
and raised troops to attack Lǔ.
King Huì of Liáng always wanted to attack Zhào,
but feared Lǔ would rescue it.
Now that Chǔ and Lǔ had conflict,
Liáng then besieged Hán Dān, and Hán Dān was besieged.
Similarly, when sages are born,
they do not intend to raise great robbers, yet great robbers arise,
forced by circumstance.
To attack the sages,
Release thieves and robbers,
and the world begins to be governed.
Annotation:
The sage is
what the world esteems.
If one abandons what is esteemed and preserves simplicity,
discards prohibitions and replaces them with few desires,
this is how to strike down the sage while our simplicity remains intact,
release thieves and robbers while their wickedness naturally ceases.
Thus the ancients said:
"Guard against depravity and preserve sincerity,
not in keen observation;
cease extravagance and remove ornament,
not in severe punishments."
This is what it means.
Subcommentary:
Strike means to hit.
Sage here refers to the traces of sageliness.
The sage
has wisdom that encompasses all things,
and the Way that benefits the world.
Now speaking of striking down
also implies贬斥仁义 and rejecting sageliness and wisdom.
Not valuing hard-to-obtain goods,
thus releasing thieves and robbers,
without relying on severe punishments,
the world becomes peaceful.
When rivers dry up, valleys become empty;
when hills are leveled, abysses become filled.
When the sage is dead,
then great robbers do not arise.
Annotation:
Drying rivers does not intentionally empty valleys, yet valleys become empty;
leveling hills does not intentionally fill abysses, yet abysses become filled;
eliminating sageliness does not intentionally stop robbers, yet robbers stop.
Thus stopping robbers lies in removing desires,
not in displaying sagely knowledge.
Subcommentary:
When wisdom emerges, cunning and falsity arise;
when traces of sageliness perish, great robbers cease.
Just as rivers drying makes valleys empty,
hills leveling makes abysses filled,
how could this be intentionally arranged?
It is the inevitable outcome.
Dead means ceased.
The world is peaceful and without affairs.
Annotation:
Not only do robbers cease,
but all traces of contention and esteem are removed.
Subcommentary:
Affairs means matters.
Eliminate sageliness and discard wisdom,
the world is peaceful,
people sing and drum on earthen jars,
thus there are no purposeful affairs.
If the sage does not die,
great robbers will not stop.
Even if valuing sages to govern the world,
this actually greatly benefits a robber like Dào Zhi.
Annotation:
If one values sages to govern the world,
then villains like Jié and Dào Zhi also utilize their methods.
What is utilized is valued,
thus the benefits cannot be slight.
Subcommentary:
In the age of simplicity,
tranquil and non-action,
all things return to their roots,
every person returns to their destiny,
how could they wait for teachings and traces to become mysteriously united?
When sagely wisdom is not forgotten,
great robbers then arise;
even if valuing sagely methods again,
to govern the world,
it is no different from greatly benefiting Dào Zhi.
Why?
The reason Xià Jié could unleash his harm and poison,
and Dào Zhi could indulge his greed and cruelty,
is because they relied on the traces of sageliness.
Had there been no traces of sageliness,
how could Xià Jié occupy the imperial throne,
poisoning the common people?
How could Dào Zhi command thousands of followers,
rampaging across the world?
Since what is relied upon is valued,
the benefits are not slight;
reasoning from this,
the fault lies with sagely wisdom.
Create dou and hu measures to measure things,
and they will steal the measures along with the goods;
create steelyards and balances to weigh things,
and they will steal the weights along with the goods;
create tallies and seals to establish trust,
and they will steal the seals along with the trust;
create benevolence and righteousness to correct people,
and they will steal righteousness along with the correction.
Annotation:
What troubles petty thieves
is what great robbers utilize and benefit from.
Subcommentary:
Hú is
today's hán,
used to measure the quantity of things.
Quán,
is the weight of a scale,
héng is the beam of a scale,
used to balance the weight of things.
Fú are
split into two pieces,
joined to form one,
like today's bronze fish or wooden tallies.
Xǐ are
the jade seals of kings,
held to summon and command the world.
Benevolence is kindness;
righteousness is appropriateness;
the king's kindness covers the people,
acting appropriately and setting examples,
thus nurturing and rearing the common folk.
These eight things
are the sharp tools of the world,
none can be without the others.
The sage establishes teachings to rectify states and families,
but Tián Chéng used them to steal the state of Qí;
is this not harming petty thieves while benefiting great robbers?
How do we know it is so?
Those who steal hooks are executed,
those who steal states become lords;
in the gates of lords, benevolence and righteousness reside—
then is this not stealing benevolence, righteousness, and sagely wisdom?
Subcommentary:
Hooks are
belt hooks.
The rise of sagely traces
originally aimed to punish evil and encourage good.
Now privately stealing a belt hook
invites punishment and execution;
publicly seizing the state of Qí
instead gains lordship;
without benevolence and righteousness,
there is no way to lead the masses.
Thus speaking,
is this not stealing sagely traces and robbing the state?
"How do we know it is so?"
is a rhetorical question;
"Those who steal..." below
is the rhetorical answer.
Thus those who follow great robbers,
proclaim themselves lords,
steal benevolence and righteousness along with the benefits of dou, hu, steelyards, balances, tallies, and seals—
even the reward of carriages and crowns cannot encourage them to stop,
the threat of axes and execution cannot prohibit them.
Annotation:
Carriages, crowns, axes, and execution
are heavy forms of reward and punishment.
Using heavy rewards and punishments to prohibit robbery,
yet great robbers further follow and steal them,
then they are instead used by robbers.
What is used is heavy,
thus accomplishing their great robbery.
Great robbers
must act with benevolence and righteousness,
balance with steelyards,
trust with tallies and seals,
encourage with carriages and crowns,
intimidate with axes and execution,
steal these public instruments,
then lordship can be obtained and proclaimed.
Therefore benevolence, righteousness, rewards, and punishments
are only sufficient to execute hook stealers.
Subcommentary:
Follow means to pursue.
Encourage means to urge.
Prohibit means to stop.
Xuān means carriage.
Miǎn means crown.
The establishment of sagely traces
originally aimed to cease wickedness and deceit,
yet Tián Héng then used their way to steal the state of Qí,
steelyards, balances, tallies, and seals
all possessed by him,
boldly proclaiming himself a lord,
