peacefully facing south as ruler,
how could he be urged by carriages and crowns,
or intimidated by axes and execution?
Small ones are called axes,
large ones are called yuè.
Also said: axes adorned with gold.
This greatly benefits Dào Zhi and makes him impossible to prohibit—
this is the fault of the sage.
Annotation:
That Dào Zhi cannot be prohibited
is because the benefits of what he steals are heavy.
The reason the benefits are heavy
is because the sage does not make them light.
Thus the solution lies in devaluing goods,
not in valuing the sage.
Subcommentary:
The reason Dào Zhi could command nine thousand followers and rampage across the world
is also because he relied on the five virtues.
Without sagely wisdom,
how could it be so!
Thus we know that driving horses to plunder people,
which cannot be restrained,
originates from the fault of the sages establishing laws.
Therefore it is said:
Fish cannot leave the depths,
the sharp instruments of the state cannot be shown to others.
Commentary:
Fish that lose the depths are captured by people,
sharp instruments used become resources for robbers,
hence they cannot be shown to others.
Subcommentary:
"Leave" means to lose.
"Sharp instruments" refer to the traces of the sages.
"Show" means to make clear.
Fish that lose water are harmed and captured by creatures,
sharp instruments shown to others are seized by people,
hence it is not permissible.
Those sages,
are the sharp instruments of the world,
Commentary:
Now the sages,
truly can cut off sageliness and abandon knowledge to return to merging with the ultimate of things,
each thing's ultimate merges,
then their traces are traces that benefit things.
Instruments are like traces,
what can be grasped and used is called an instrument.
Subcommentary:
Sages refer to Yáo, Shùn, Wén, Wǔ, and others.
They are not that by which the world is illuminated.
Commentary:
Showing sharp instruments to the world,
thereby supplies its robbers and thieves.
Subcommentary:
Now the sages governing the world,
respond to things according to the time,
yielding deference or armed conflict,
action and withdrawal are not uniform,
cannot be rigidly held,
clearly shown to the world,
if held and practiced,
must lead to their弊端,
such as the cases of Yān Kuài and Bái Gōng are examples.
Therefore cut off sageliness and abandon knowledge,
then great thieves cease;
Commentary:
Remove what they rely on,
then without applying prohibitions they stop by themselves.
Subcommentary:
Abandoning and cutting off the sagely,
the things of the world each keep their place,
then thieves naturally subside.
Discard jades and destroy pearls,
petty thieves do not arise;
Commentary:
Devalue what they treasure,
then without adding punishments they cease by themselves.
Subcommentary:
Hide jades in mountains,
conceal pearls in rivers,
not valuing precious treasures,
how could there be theft and excess!
Burn tallies and break seals,
and the people become simple and rustic;
Commentary:
Eliminate what the deceitful rely on,
then there is no means to practice their cunning.
Subcommentary:
Tallies and seals,
represent sincerity and trust.
Deceitful and crafty individuals,
rely on and use them,
hence burning and destroying them,
can return to simplicity and revert to淳朴, returning to rusticity.
Smash measures and break scales,
and the people do not contend;
Commentary:
For small fairness is what great unfairness relies on.
Subcommentary:
Measures and scales,
are used to gauge amount,
weigh lightness and heaviness.
Once subjected to theft via measures,
they instead become resources for thieves.
Smashing and breaking them,
accords with the ancient's wisdom of guarding,
hence there are no contentious disputes.
Utterly destroy the sagely laws of the world,
and only then can the people begin to be discussed with.
Commentary:
Externally there is nothing to feign,
then internally my simplicity is wholly preserved,
and there are no words of self-loss.
Subcommentary:
"Utterly" means exhaust.
"Destroy" means ruin.
Sagely laws,
refer to the five virtues.
Having destroyed the Three Kings,
and ruined the Five Emperors,
temporary lodgings all exhausted,
straw dogs not displayed,
forgetting the trap and the snare,
things and self merge in the ultimate,
only then can one begin to discuss the realm of profound subtlety,
and deliberate on the far reaches of the Dào and virtue.
Pluck out and confuse the six pitch-pipes,
melt and break off reed-organs and zithers,
plug the ears of blind music-master Kuàng,
and the world begins to...
Eliminate patterned elegance,
scatter the five colors,
glue shut the eyes of Lí Zhū,
and the world begins for people to contain their hearing;
melt and break off reed-organs and zithers,
plug the ears of blind music-master Kuàng,
and the world begins for people to contain their acute hearing;
eliminate patterned elegance,
scatter the five colors,
glue shut the eyes of Lí Zhū,
and the world begins for people to contain their sharp sight;
Commentary:
Now sounds and sights, Lí and Kuàng,
are what those with ears and eyes value.
Receiving life has its allotment,
and if led by what is valued,
then life's mandate is lost.
If instead destroy what they value,
abandon that and trust oneself,
then acute hearing and clear sight are each preserved,
and people contain their genuineness.
Subcommentary:
"Pluck out" means pull out.
"Melt" means dissolve.
Reed-organ's shape is similar to the shēng,
both have pipes set in a gourd,
with reeds at the pipe ends.
The zither is eight feet one inch long,
one foot eight inches wide,
with twenty-seven strings,
created by Fú Xī.
Now the ear indulges in gōng and zhǐ notes,
admires music-master Kuàng's acute hearing;
the eye stagnates in dark and yellow,
hopes for Lí Zhū's sharp sight;
thereby the heart-mind races,
ears and eyes are exhausted and lost.
Then pulling out pipes and breaking strings,
melting metal and cutting off weaving;
destroy the "Yellow Blossom" melody,
abandon the "White Snow" song;
eliminate the patterned elegance of ceremonial robes,
scatter the red and purple hues.
Hence glue shut Lí Zhū's eyes,
remove the source of feigning and imitation;
plug music-master Kuàng's ears,
take away the leader that confuses the multitude.
Thereafter people all attain self-sufficiency,
things do not cause me loss,
exhaust the ear's hearing and instead hear without sound,
indulge the eye's ability to see and inwardly see without color,
natural mechanism unfolds by itself,
the ultimate of non-action,
how could there be brightness and darkness, superiority and inferiority among them!
Therefore the world is harmonious and peaceful,
the myriad things share the same virtue.
Following one's own hearing and sight,
hence people contain their acute hearing and clear sight.
"Contain" means to harbor and nurture.
Destroy and eliminate marking cords and discard compass and square,
break the fingers of artisan Chuí,
and the world begins for people to have their own skill.
Therefore it is said:
Great skill seems clumsy.
Commentary:
Now with the simplicity of spiders and dung beetles,
spinning webs and rolling balls,
not seeking from craftsmen,
then the myriad things each have their ability.
Although abilities differ,
yet what they practice dare not differ,
then it seems skillful yet is clumsy.
Hence those skilled at employing people,
enable the square to be square,
the round to be round,
each fulfilling their capability,
people secure in their nature,
not demanding the myriad people to have artisan Chuí's skill.
Thus various skills by not being mutually capable seem clumsy,
yet the world all having its own ability is great skill.
Now using their own ability,
then compass and square can be discarded and the marvelous artisan's fingers can be broken.
Subcommentary:
Marking cord, for curves;
plumb line, for straight;
compass, for circle;
square, for right angle;
artisan Chuí was a worker under Yáo,
creating the methods of compass and square;
It is also said that Shùn had ministers.
Lì,
means to break,
to cut.
Artisan Chuí possessed innate skillfulness,
employing the hook and line,
cutting and carving different forms,
narrating and creating compass and square,
thus causing the common people of the world,
to be enticed and imitate,
abandoning themselves to chase after things,
truly originating from this.
If one discards the compass,
and abandons the line,
breaks and cuts off Chuí's fingers,
then everyone within their own nature,
would possess such skill.
Just like the spider's web or the dung beetle's ball,
how could they be related to human efforts of pride and aspiration,
if it's the natural skill of heaven!
This matter originates from the Lǎozǐ.
Eliminate the conduct of Zēng and Shǐ,
gag the mouths of Yáng and Mò,
reject and discard benevolence and righteousness,
and the virtue of the world will begin to merge in profound unity.
Note:
Remove those who lead the masses into disorder,
then everyone under heaven will return to their simplicity and unite in profound virtue.
Explanation:
Xuē means to remove.
Qián means to shut.
Rǎng means to reject.
Xuán,
means origin,
the Way.
Zēng Shēn was extremely filial,
Shǐ Yú was loyal and upright,
Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí,
possessed great eloquence by nature.
Those four individuals,
with their innate dispositions,
caused the learners of the world,
to abandon themselves and imitate others,
thereby creating disorder among the masses,
losing their original nature.
Thus, eliminate the conduct of loyalty and faithfulness,
shut the mouths of frivolous debaters,
reject forced benevolence,
discard strained righteousness.
Thereby, things do not lose their authenticity,
people all attain self-fulfillment,
following their nature and preserving principle,
thus merging in unity with the profound Way.
If people contain their clarity,
then the world will not be dissipated;
if people contain their acuity,
then the world will not be burdened;
Explanation:
Shuò means to melt away or scatter.
Lèi means worry or distress.
Only because one flaunts their intelligence,
do worries and distress thus gather,
causing the common people to be overturned and scattered.
If one can hold and embrace intelligence within, without displaying it outwardly,
then all things will be content and joyful, without worries or distress.
If people contain their knowledge,
then the world will not be confused;
if people contain their virtue,
then the world will not be perverse.
Explanation:
If one can know what is within their own nature,
nurture virtue without being dissipated,
they will surely tread the correct path of the central pivot,
wander within the universe without confusion,
how could there be inversion, sorrow, or perversity among them!
Those like Zēng,
Shǐ,
Yáng,
Mò,
Shī Kuàng,
Artisan Chuí,
Lí Zhū,
all established their virtues outwardly and thereby dazzled and confused the world,
Note:
These several individuals,
endowed with multiple talents,
thus caused the world to leap and imitate them.
Imitating them leads to loss of self,
the loss of self is due to them,
thus they become the source of disorder.
The great trouble of the world,
is the loss of self.
Explanation:
The aforementioned individuals,
all possessed extraordinary innate dispositions,
but failed to conceal their light and hide their brilliance,
instead stirring waves and blending with the vulgar,
seeking fame outwardly,
establishing virtue externally,
drawing others to follow themselves,
dazzling the multitude.
The world loses its virtue and does not return to the root,
the origin of losing oneself,
stems from this.
Thus, laws are of no use.
Note:
As for the application of laws,
vision does not exceed what is seen,
thus all eyes are clear;
hearing does not exceed what is heard,
thus all ears are acute;
scholars do not exceed their abilities,
thus all skills are adept;
knowledge does not exceed what is known,
thus all natures are content;
virtue does not exceed what is attained,
thus all virtues are appropriate.
Why establish what is beyond one's innate nature,
causing the world to rush about and unable to return to themselves!
Explanation:
To act in accordance with nature,
action must stem from nature,
this is the wonder of the method.
But followers of Zēng and Shǐ,
using themselves to draw others,
bring no benefit to the present age,
instead harm the future,
even if such laws are established,
they are ultimately of no use.
Do you alone not know about the age of perfect virtue?
In the past, in the times of Róngchéngshì,
Dàtíngshì,
Bóhuángshì,
Zhōngyāngshì,
Lìlùshì,
Líchùshì,
Xuānyuánshì,
Hèxūshì,
Zūnlúshì,
Zhùróngshì,
Fúxīshì,
Shénnóngshì,
at that time,
people used knotted cords,
Note:
Sufficient to record essentials only.
Explanation:
The above twelve rulers,
were all ancient sovereigns.
At that time, there were no historical records,
so the exact sequence is unknown.
They carved wood to make tallies,
knotted cords to show trust,
there was peace and harmony between high and low,
and human hearts were pure and simple.
Thus the Yìjīng says,
In high antiquity, they governed by knotted cords,
later sages replaced them with written documents and tallies.
They found their food sweet,
their clothing beautiful,
Note:
Being suitable, it was always sweet;
being appropriate, it was always beautiful.
If one thinks of extravagance,
then there is never satisfaction.
They enjoyed their customs,
were content in their dwellings,
Explanation:
Staying within their lot,
thus sweet;
rejecting ornament, thus beautiful; blending in unity,
thus joyful;
serene and detached,
thus content in dwelling.
Neighboring states were within sight of each other,
the sounds of chickens and dogs were heard,
yet the people grew old and died without visiting each other.
Note:
The ultimate of having no desires.
Explanation:
Borders and towns were adjacent,
the distance between them not far,
the sounds of chickens and dogs barking,
could be heard connecting.
Yet their natures were each self-sufficient,
with no desires from the world,
they ended their lives according to heaven's decree,
without visiting each other,
the ultimate of non-action.
In such a time,
then perfect order was achieved.
Explanation:
Without desires or wants,
embracing the Way and holding virtue,
such a time as this,
was it not perfect!
Now it has come to the point where people crane their necks and stand on tiptoe saying,
'There is a worthy person in such a place,'
and packing provisions, they rush to him,
thus abandoning their parents at home and neglecting their duties to their rulers;
Footprints connect to the borders of the feudal lords,
and carriage tracks intertwine beyond a thousand miles.
Annotation:
Even the traces of perfect governance
still lead to such flaws.
Explanation:
Yíng means to carry supplies.
Likewise, the ethos of ultimate principle,
spread as teachings,
values this superficial refinement,
making people learn it.
With the path of honoring the worthy opened,
seeking teachers and visiting the Way,
lifting heads and stepping forward,
traveling far to other places,
tracks and ruts cross paths,
where footprints reach,
carrying provisions and trading goods,
undaunted by a thousand miles,
internally abandoning parents and being unfilial,
externally leaving lords and being disloyal.
The traces of perfect governance
thus lead to such flaws.
This is the fault of those above favoring knowledge.
Annotation:
Those above refer to rulers who favor knowledge.
Knowing and favoring it,
thus they have this fault.
Explanation:
Honoring the traces of perfect governance,
favoring the wisdom of governing things,
thus leads to this.
If those above truly favor knowledge without the Way,
then the world falls into great chaos.
Explanation:
If the rulers above cannot be effortless and tranquil,
pure and empty, in harmony with the Way,
but use knowledge and ability to govern things,
things will inevitably be harmed,
thus leading to great chaos.
Lǎojūn said: governing a state with knowledge
is the state's thief.
How do we know it is so?
Explanation:
A hypothetical question
to reveal the reason.
When knowledge of bows, crossbows, traps, and ingenious devices is abundant,
birds are thrown into chaos in the sky;
when knowledge of hooks, bait, nets, and fish traps is abundant,
fish are thrown into chaos in the water;
when knowledge of sharpened stakes, snares, and animal traps is abundant,
beasts are thrown into chaos in the marshes;
Annotation:
The denser the attacks,
the more cunning the evasion,
so even birds and beasts cannot be controlled by knowledge,
let alone humans!
Thus, those who govern the world must not rely on knowledge;
relying on knowledge has no subtlety.
Explanation:
A small net with a handle,
shaped like the constellation Bì,
thus named Bì.
Shooting arrows with strings attached
is called yì.
Gǔ and zēng
are both types of nets.
Gǒu,
a curved beam,
is also a fish trap.
Xuē gé are sharpened stakes,
like today's deer antler barriers,
used with ropes and nets to catch animals.
Jū fú,
are hare nets.
Using knowledge to govern things
inevitably leads to turmoil,
so those who govern a state must not use knowledge.
When knowledge of deceit, poison, sophistry, hard-and-white debates, and arguments on similarity and difference abounds,
the common people are confused by disputation.
Annotation:
What those above value in abundance,
those below cannot be content with having little of,
for pursuing much with little innate nature leads to confusion.
Explanation:
Cunning and fraudulent deceit,
gradually poison and harm things.
Xié huá,
means tricky,
also crafty and sly.
Xiè gòu means fraud and deceit.
The wisdom of sophistry and hard-and-white debates,
the rhetoric of deceptive arguments on similarity and difference,
truly damages the true principle,
and benefits not worldly teachings,
so from afar, it seems like stammering,
and foolish commoners are confused by petty arguments.
Thus, the world is often in great chaos,
and the fault lies in favoring knowledge.
Explanation:
Měi měi means a dim, confused appearance.
Forgetting oneself and letting things be,
then the world is clear and peaceful;
holding to traces and using knowledge,
then the world falls into great chaos.
Thus, we know the dim confusion above and below
stems from favoring knowledge.
Thus, all under heaven know to seek what they do not know but do not know to seek what they already know,
Annotation:
Not seeking what is known but seeking what is unknown
is to abandon oneself and imitate others without stopping at one's own lot.
Explanation:
What is known
is within one's lot;
what is unknown
is beyond one's lot.
Abandoning the inner to seek the outer,
how is this not confusion?
All know to condemn what they consider bad but do not know to condemn the means they consider good,
Annotation:
Considering their own good as good
is the source of contention and rivalry.
Explanation:
What is considered bad
is like Jié and Zhí;
the means considered good
are the traces of sages.
Robber Zhí practiced what is considered bad to occupy the eastern mound,
while Tián Héng practiced the traces of sages to steal the state of Qí.
Thus, whether like Zāng or Gǔ in their tasks,
losing sheep leads to the same outcome,
or whether like Jié or Zhí in different actions,
the harm to their nature is equal.
Foolish commoners
rashly judge right and wrong,
but good and bad
truly cannot be fixed.
Thus, great chaos arises.
So above, it obscures the brightness of the sun and moon,
below, it melts the essence of mountains and rivers,
in the middle, it ruins the progression of the four seasons;
even the soft-bodied insects
and delicate floating things
all lose their nature.
How extreme is the chaos caused by favoring knowledge under heaven!
Annotation:
For fortune, misfortune, regret, and distress
arise from action.
And the action of knowledge
can truly shake heaven and earth,
governing all living beings,
so rulers
how can they not forget their knowledge?
Explanation:
Thus,
continuing from the above.
Simply because of using knowledge and holding to traces above,
the world falls into great chaos.
Bèi means to disrupt.
Shuò means to melt.
Duò means to ruin.
Creatures clinging to the ground are called chuǎn ruǎn,
those flying in the air are called xiào qiáo,
all light and small things.
Holding to traces and using knowledge
inevitably causes severe harm,
thus able to stir yin and yang,
shake heaven and earth,
causing eclipses of the sun and moon,
collapse and drying up of mountains and rivers,
disorder in the progression of heat and cold,
untimeliness of wind and rain,
whether flying, running, in water or on land,
all lose their inherent nature,
so poisonous is favoring knowledge to things,
reaching such an extent.
This has been so since the three dynasties onward,
abandoning the simple, honest people and delighting in the fawning, cunning ones,
discarding tranquil, effortless non-action and delighting in the garrulous teaching,
and garrulous teaching has already thrown the world into chaos!
Annotation:
Zhūn zhūn
means teaching others based on oneself.
Explanation:
Zì means from.
The three dynasties
refer to Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu.
Zhǒng zhǒng,
simple, honest people.
Yì yì,
a light and cunning appearance.
Shì means to discard.
Zhūn zhūn,
teaching others based on oneself.
In the era of ultimate purity in high antiquity,
the age of simplicity,
modeled after the round heaven in clarity and emptiness,
emulating the square earth in tranquility,
and as a community,
shared the lack of knowledge with birds and beasts.
When it came to the dispersal of simplicity and departure from purity,
straying from the Way and turning against virtue,
the traces of the Five Constant Virtues by the sages had already become evident,
and the Three Dynasties employed wisdom even more excessively;
abandoning the plain and unadorned scholars of integrity,
favoring the frivolous and cunning flatterers,
discarding the self-contentment of desirelessness,
delighting in the intentional instruction of others,
they had already thrown the world into chaos—
how could one not lament this!
The Commentary and Subcommentary on the True Classic of Nánhuá, Volume Twelve
The Southern Florescence True Classic: Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll 13, Part 7
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters: "Let It Be, Give It Free Reign" Number 11
I have heard of letting the world be and giving it free reign,
but I have not heard of governing the world.
Commentary:
Giving free reign so that it is self-so brings order;
governing it brings chaos.
Human life is straightforward;
if nothing agitates it,
then life's destiny is not transgressed,
and desires and aversions are not disordered.
If those above cannot be non-active,
then what those above do, the people all rush toward,
thus there arise seductive allurements, fond desires, and the people's nature becomes dissipated.
Therefore, what is valued in sage-kings
is not valuing their ability to govern,
but valuing their non-action and letting things act of themselves.
Subcommentary:
"Give free reign" means to be lenient.
"Let be" means to be self-so.
"Govern" means to control and rule.
The allegorical words say:
I hear that when the various worthies and sages let things be,
self-so and leniently giving free reign,
then the world is clear and tranquil;
if one establishes teachings to rule the common people,
things lose their nature,
like Bó Lè taming horses.
Letting them be
is for fear that the world would dissipate its nature;
giving them free reign
is for fear that the world would shift its virtue.
Subcommentary:
Nature is
the principle endowed at birth;
virtue is
the name for meritorious conduct;
therefore, the words about letting be and giving free reign are presented
to prevent the faults of shifting and dissipation.
If one does not follow nature and let it be self-so,
there is fear that things will become dissipated and aberrant, losing their nature.
If one does not give them free reign,
there is further fear of imitating others,
and their virtue shifting and changing.
If the world does not dissipate its nature,
and does not shift its virtue,
is there then anyone who governs the world?
Commentary:
Without governance, there is no shifting or dissipation.
Subcommentary:
With nature correct and virtue settled,
why labor to administer governance and rule them?
Having governance falls short of having no governance;
having action falls short of having non-action.
In the past, when Yáo governed the world,
he made the world joyful so that people delighted in their nature;
this is not tranquility.
When Jié governed the world,
he made the world distressed so that people suffered in their nature;
this is not pleasure.
Commentary:
Although Yáo let the world be and gave it free reign,
his traces were still governing.
Though order and chaos differ,
in their causing the loss of later generations' tranquility and pleasure,
making things compete, esteem, fear, and despise without being self-possessed, they are the same.
Therefore, praising Yáo and condemning Jié
is不如 forgetting both.
Subcommentary:
"Tranquility" means quiet.
"Pleasure" means joy.
"Distressed" means sorrow.
Yáo approached people with virtue,
people sang and struck the ground in joy,
but this went against quiet nature;
Jié harmed things with cruelty,
things encountered sorrow and distress,
going against their joyful pleasure.
Though Yáo and Jié's governance differed in this way,
in causing things to lose their nature, they were equal.
Not being tranquil and not being pleased
is not virtuous.
What is not virtuous and yet can be long-lasting
does not exist in the world.
Commentary:
Only tranquility, pleasure, and self-possession
can be long-lasting.
Subcommentary:
Yáo approached people without tranquility,
Jié dealt with things without pleasure,
not conforming to the pure and harmonious nature;
to wish to be long-lasting
is something the world has never had.
When people are greatly joyful,
it leans toward yang;
when greatly angry,
it leans toward yīn.
When both yīn and yáng are leaned upon,
the four seasons do not arrive properly,
the harmony of cold and heat is not achieved,
and instead, it harms people's physical forms!
It causes people's joy and anger to lose their proper place,
and their dwelling to be without constancy.
Subcommentary:
"Lean upon" means to assist.
Joy emerges from the hún (ethereal soul),
anger emerges from the pò (corporeal soul),
humans are endowed with yīn and yáng,
sharing the same qì with the two modes (heaven and earth).
Yáo made the hundred families joyful,
leaning upon yáng's warmth and expansiveness;
Jié made people angry,
assisting yīn's harshness and severity.
When people's joy and anger are excessive,
heaven then loses its regularity,
midsummer is not hot,
deep winter has no frost.
Once the harmonious qì is lost,
add to that heavenly disasters,
people suffer many illnesses and ailments;
is this not instead harming the physical form?
One cannot have action and create methods,
it will inevitably lead to ruin and harm.
Deliberations and thoughts do not come from self-possession,
and the middle way is not achieved in pattern.
Commentary:
These are all of the kind of Yáo and Jié,
making things' joy and anger excessive,
leading to such troubles.
Humans within heaven and earth
are most capable of using spiritual awareness, joy, and anger to disturb the multitude of living beings and agitate yīn and yáng.
Therefore, in the space between gain and loss,
when joy and anger gather in the hearts of the hundred families,
then the harmony of cold and heat is ruined,
the nodes of the four seasons become disordered,
all measures become dim and lost,
and the ten thousand affairs fall prematurely.
Subcommentary:
Being stuck in joy and anger,
then causes the hundred families' deliberations and thoughts to lose authenticity,
already deviating from the law of established regulations,
thus they are ruined.
Thereupon, the world begins with arrogance, reproach, aloofness, and fierceness,
and afterward, there are the actions of Robber Zhí, Zēng Shěn, and Shǐ Qiú.
Therefore, using the whole world to reward the good is insufficient,
Commentary:
Coveting reward leads to goodness,
thus rewards cannot supply enough.
Using the whole world to punish the evil is inadequate,
Commentary:
Fearing punishment leads to cessation,
thus punishment cannot overcome.
Subcommentary:
"Arrogance" means deceit and falsity.
"Reproach" means blaming and questioning.
"Aloof" means solitary.
"Fierceness" means ferocity.
Thereupon, with deceitful falsity and reproach,
standing aloof and not blending with the group,
individually harboring fierceness and ferocity,
lightly encroaching upon things,
starting from Yáo,
afterward came the evil of Robber Zhí,
the goodness of Zēng Shěn and Shǐ Qiú,
good and evil being thus prominent,
reward and punishment are attached.
Coveting reward, one performs good;
fearing punishment, one ceases evil;
using all the world's axes and halberds is insufficient to punish evil;
emptying the storehouses of the cosmos is insufficient to reward good.
"Adequate" means sufficient.
Therefore, the greatness of the world is insufficient for reward and punishment.
Subcommentary:
If one forgets reward and punishment,
and entrusts to authenticity, then sufficiency is present.
From the three dynasties downward,
clamorously they ultimately take reward and punishment as their task;
how could they have leisure to settle the genuine state of their life's destiny?
Commentary:
Forgetting reward and punishment, they become good of themselves;
then the life's destiny is greatly sufficient.
Reward and punishment are what sage-kings use to match merit and fault,
not to display encouragement and fear.
Therefore, when principle is utmost, they discard them,
then the utmost unity can be returned to.
But from the three dynasties downward,
they then sought their traces and deeds,
thus clamorously competing with the traces,
ultimately taking what is寄托 as their task;
how could they have leisure to settle the genuine state of their life's destiny?
Subcommentary:
"Clamorous"
means noisy uproar,
that is, competing and chasing.
People fear the execution by axe and halberd,
and also covet the reward of high carriage and official cap;
hearts harboring a hundred worries,
affairs arising from ten thousand origins,
clamorously competing and chasing without knowing cessation.
Since the Xià and Yīn dynasties,
such practices have gradually spread,
rewards and punishments create turmoil,
keeping people busily occupied all day long,
how could there be any leisure to settle one's innate nature and destiny!
Moreover, do you delight in visual clarity?
This is indulgence in colors;
do you delight in acute hearing?
This is indulgence in sounds;
Subcommentary:
"Delight" means being affected by something.
"Indulgence" means becoming obsessed and stagnant.
Seeking detachment and admiring breadth,
one becomes mired in sounds and colors.
Do you delight in benevolence?
This disrupts virtue;
do you delight in righteousness?
This contradicts principle;
Subcommentary:
Virtue has no likes or dislikes,
partial affection thus disrupts virtue;
principle has no right or wrong,
imposing judgments thus violates principle.
"Contradict" means to oppose.
Do you delight in ritual?
This assists in artifice;
do you delight in music?
This assists in excess;
Subcommentary:
Ritual involves
bowing, kneeling, bending, and clasping hands,
elaborate formalities of elevation and reduction.
Music includes
the Xiánchí and Dàxià,
the pitch pipes and eight tones.
Delighting in ritual aids flashy skills and abilities,
loving music further assists the licentious sounds of scales and melodies.
Do you delight in sageliness?
This assists in craft;
do you delight in knowledge?
This assists in flaws.
Commentary:
When conforming to principle, there is no delight,
delighting in it leads to the disasters of indulgence and contradiction.
"Assist" means to aid.
Subcommentary:
Delighting in traces of sageliness
aids the arts and skills of the world;
loving clever schemes
increases the flaws of right and wrong.
If the world is to settle the genuine state of its innate nature and destiny,
these eight things
may exist,
or may perish;
Commentary:
Existence or perishing does not matter,
let each follow its allotted share,
then the innate nature and destiny will be settled.
Subcommentary:
The eight are:
clarity of sight and hearing, benevolence, righteousness, ritual, music, sageliness, and knowledge.
This means people's endowments differ,
their innate dispositions vary.
For those like Lí Kuàng, Zēng Shěn, and Shǐ Qiū, who inherently possess these,
they may preserve them;
but for the masses, whose innate share originally lacks them,
striving and admiring distorts genuineness,
so they may let them perish.
If the world is not to settle the genuine state of its innate nature and destiny,
these things
will begin to coil and cramp, disrupting the world.
Commentary:
If one insists on preserving these eight,
then one cannot follow spontaneity and naturalness,
hence the coiling and cramping.
Subcommentary:
"Coiling"
describes a state of not being relaxed and free.
"Cramping"
denotes a hurried appearance.
All living beings in the world,
knowing only what is beyond their share,
unable to rest content,
coil and constrain themselves,
boast and embellish human affairs,
cramp and rush hastily,
racing and chasing after things,
all because they do not forget these eight,
leading to such flaws.
Yet the world begins to honor and cherish them,
how extreme is the delusion of the world!
Commentary:
Not being able to discard them is already a mistake.
But to further honor them as valuable,
is that not profoundly deluded?
Subcommentary:
The aforementioned eight
disrupt the constant norms of heaven,
not being able to forget and discard them is already great delusion.
Yet to further respect them,
using them as models,
is deeply regrettable.
How could one merely pass by and discard them?
Instead, one fasts and purifies to speak of them,
kneels and sits formally to present them,
drums, sings, and dances for them,
what can I do about such a situation?
Commentary:
It is not merely passing by and leaving them behind,
but treasuring them to such an extent.
Subcommentary:
The meaning of these eight items
is like that of straw dogs—after they have passed,
they should not be gathered again.
Yet people observe fasts and prohibitions,
speak of them explicitly and adhere to rituals,
rulers and ministers kneel and sit,
presenting them to each other,
drumming the songs of Jiǔsháo,
dancing to the melodies of Dàzhāng.
They treasure temporary lodgings
to such a degree;
Zhuāngzǐ himself laments,
helpless against it.
Therefore, when a gentleman has no choice but to oversee the world,
nothing is better than non-action.
Through non-action, the genuine state of innate nature and destiny is then settled.
Commentary:
Non-action does not mean folding hands and remaining silent,
but simply letting each be as they are,
then the innate nature and destiny are settled.
"Having no choice"
does not mean being forced by threats or punishments,
but holding to the Dào and embracing simplicity,
trusting in the inevitable ultimate,
and the world naturally submits.
Subcommentary:
The gentleman is a sage;
having no choice but to oversee the world,
he constantly practices non-action.
Although he practices non-action,
it is not about folding hands and silence;
whether active or still, he is without deliberate mind,
and the genuine state of innate nature and destiny is never unsettled.
Therefore, one who values his person for the sake of governing the world
can be entrusted with the world;
one who loves his person for the sake of governing the world
can be given the world.
Commentary:
If one lightly risks one's body chasing profit,
abandons oneself to pursue things,
then one cannot even settle oneself,
what then of the world?
Subcommentary:
Valuing one's person and disdaining profit,
keeping oneself inner and things outer,
preserving and cherishing one's essence and spirit,
not being agitated by the world—
such a one can be placed above all things,
entrusted with transforming the world.
Therefore, if a gentleman can avoid dissipating his five organs,
and avoid displaying his keen senses;
Commentary:
Dissipation and display cause harm.
Subcommentary:
The five organs
are the abode of the essence and spirit;
keen senses are the functions of ears and eyes.
If one discriminates the affections and consciousness of the five organs,
and displays the functions of keen senses,
then the essence and spirit race wildly within,
and the ears and eyes are exhausted and lost without.
He remains still as a corpse but appears as a dragon,
silent as an abyss but with the sound of thunder,
Commentary:
In action or withdrawal, silence or speech,
he is always without deliberate mind and leaves it to spontaneity.
Subcommentary:
The sage is tranquil as a dead corpse in stillness,
yet active like a flying dragon in the sky;
how could there be a difference between stillness and activity in principle and teaching?
Thus, tranquil yet active,
still as a corpse but appearing as a dragon,
silent as an abyss but with the sound of thunder.
This aims to clarify that stillness and activity, activity and stillness,
principle and teaching, teaching and principle,
are neither identical nor different.
The spirit moves and heaven follows,
Commentary:
The spirit conforms to things and moves,
heaven follows principle and acts.
Subcommentary:
"Spirit"
refers to what subtly activates all things,
being both active and still at once.
Virtue matches the vast heavens,
accommodating and nurturing all beings.
Composed and non-interfering, all things drift like dust.
Note:
As wandering dust moves on its own.
Explanation:
"Lěi" means dust.
Composed and self-so,
non-acting and empty-tranquil,
like wind stirring fine dust,
floating objects in clear sky,
the yang energy drifting,
following its course without personal control.
Why should I bother governing the world!
Note:
Just let things follow their natural course.
Explanation:
When things and self blend as one,
both merging with spontaneity,
why laboriously bother
to impose governance!
Cuī Jù asked Lǎo Dān:
"If not governing the world,
how can people's hearts be good?"
Lǎo Dān replied:
"You must not disturb people's hearts!"
Note:
Disturbing them harms their innate goodness.
Explanation:
Surname Cuī,
given name Jù,
unknown origins.
Having asked:
"If indulging without governance,
how achieve goodness?"
Answer:
Indulging and letting be,
naturally accords with principle;
creating rules to manage things
disturbs people's hearts.
As explained below.
Hearts suppress what's low and promote what's high,
Note:
Suppress it and it sinks,
promote it and it rises,
showing how easily swayed they are.
Explanation:
Hearts suppress others to lower positions,
promote themselves to higher,
all common tendencies.
Imprisoned between high and low,
Note:
Without suppression or promotion,
then security is found.
Explanation:
Hearts drowning in highs and lows,
pulled by circumstances,
like confined prisoners,
harassed and distressed.
Gentle softness tames the rigid strong.
Note:
Being gentle and soft
makes the rigid strong yield.
Explanation:
"Chuò yuē" means soft and weak.
Affecting weakness in disposition,
seeking to subdue the strong.
Honor wounds through carving,
its heat scorching fire,
its cold freezing ice.
Note:
The heat of scorching fire,
the cold of freezing ice,
both born from accumulated joy and anger.
If uncarved, unpolished,
each preserving its simplicity,
how could ice or fire exist!
Explanation:
"Lián" means pursuing fame.
"Guì" means harming.
Carving and polishing reputation,
wanting to lead others.
If anger arises against feelings,
cold freezes ice;
if joy follows the heart,
heat rivals scorching fire.
Its speed, between bowing and rising, twice reaches beyond the four seas,
Note:
Moved by customs.
Explanation:
The heart chasing circumstances,
in a single thought's moment,
already spans all directions,
let alone between bowing and rising,
twice reaching the four seas!
Its dwelling is deep and still,
its movement hangs to heaven.
Note:
Still, it can be like deep abyss;
moving, it ties to heaven and leaps.
Explanation:
The desiring heart,
leaves without fixed standard.
Occasionally still,
like flowing water meeting deep pool;
touched by circumstances, moving,
resembling heaven's suspension;
unceasingly active,
it ties to heaven and leaps.
Frenzied and proud, beyond restraint,
is it not the human heart!
Note:
The changes of human heart,
leave nothing undone.
Following and letting go,
it quiets and flows naturally;
controlling and restraining it,
it rebels and grows frenzied.
"Fèn jiāo" means
an unstoppable force.
Explanation:
Suppressing low, promoting high,
likes, dislikes, joy, anger,
frenzied outbursts and arrogance,
impossible to restrain—
is it not the human heart!
Long ago, Huángdì first disturbed hearts with benevolence and righteousness,
Note:
Huángdì didn't create benevolence and righteousness,
but merging with things,
their traces naturally appeared.
Once traces appeared,
later generations' hearts inevitably pursued them,
thus Huángdì's traces disturbed things.
Explanation:
Huángdì established norms fitting the times,
nurturing people with kindness,
different from forced benevolence
or imposed righteousness.
Later rulers,
clinging to these tracks,
people called them sages,
disturbing hearts began here.
Flaws arose from later kings,
fault lies not with Huángdì.
Yáo and Shùn thus had no fat on thighs,
no hair on shins,
nourishing the world's form,
tormenting their organs for benevolence,
straining their energy to establish laws.
Yet still they couldn't overcome all,
Explanation:
"Bá" means white flesh.
Yáo and Shùn followed Huángdì's path,
hearts and bodies worn thin,
thighs lean without white flesh,
shins bare without fine hair,
nourishing the world's form,
settling all beings' natures,
organs tormented within,
energy strained without,
practicing benevolence as standard,
establishing laws as model,
yet still couldn't avoid exiling the wicked,
thus failing to overcome all.
Yáo then exiled Huān Dōu to Chóng Shān,
cast Sān Miáo to Sān Wēi,
banished Gòng Gōng to Yōu Dū,
this shows failing to overcome the world.
Explanation:
Dì Hóng's unworthy son,
called "Chaos" by the world,
namely Huān Dōu,
allied with Gòng Gōng,
exiled to southern wilds.
Jìnyún's unworthy son,
called "Glutton" by the world,
namely Sān Miáo.
As Yáo's feudal lord,
granted land of Sān Miáo.
Country left of Dòngtíng Lake,
right of Pénglí Lake,
in Yùzhāng,
near Southern Mountain.
Sān Wēi,
mountain name,
in western wilds,
modern Qínzhōu's western Qiāng.
Shǎohào's unworthy son,
called "Monstrous" by the world,
namely Gòng Gōng,
Yáo's water official.
Yōu Dū in the north,
modern Yōuzhōu.
Shàngshū records Gǔn's execution,
this text complements it.
All four harbored wickedness,
disobeying Yáo's transformation,
thus cast to four wilds,
this shows Yáo's failure to overcome the world.
Thus the Four Fiends were dealt with by Shùn,
and when people today praise Yáo,
it is because at that time Shùn was acting in Yáo's position.
When this extended to the Three Sovereigns, the world was greatly alarmed.
Commentary:
The names Yáo and Shùn as emperors
are merely their traces;
I lodge in these traces, but the traces are not me,
so the alarm comes from the world itself.
The more the world is alarmed,
the cruder the traces become;
the difference between crude and subtle
is like the difference between a smooth and rugged path—
does the traveler therefore constantly change his feet?
Thus the sage is one,
yet there are differences like Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ.
To understand these differences
is to recognize the names of eras and generations,
which are insufficient to name the reality of the sage.
So, are Yáo and Shùn
merely one Yáo and one Shùn?
Therefore, even with a compassionate expression
and the traces of benevolence and righteousness,
the source of these traces remains whole.
Subcommentary:
"Extend" means to prolong.
From Huángdì extending to Yáo and Shùn,
the traces of sageliness stagnated,
and things became disturbed and chaotic,
reaching the Three Sovereigns,
when the alarm grew even greater.
Below were Jié and Zhí,
Subcommentary: Jié and Zhí acted with the conduct of petty men, thus below,
while Zēng and Shǐ acted with the conduct of gentlemen, thus above.
Above were Zēng and Shǐ,
and both Confucians and Mohists arose.
Subcommentary:
This means Confucians and Mohists clung to traces,
and right and wrong arose because of it.
Thereupon, joy and anger mutually doubted,
Subcommentary:
approving joy and disapproving anger,
doubting and distrusting each other.
The foolish and wise deceived each other,
Subcommentary:
the wise adorned themselves to startle the foolish,
mutually deceiving and insulting.
Good and bad mutually condemned,
Subcommentary:
the good and the not good
condemning each other.
Deceit and trust mutually ridiculed,
Subcommentary:
deceit being false and trust real,
they ridiculed each other.
And the world declined;
Commentary:
None could attain self-fulfillment in harmony.
Subcommentary:
Entangled and conflicting continuously,
the cosmos declined.
Great virtues differed,
and innate natures became scattered;
Commentary:
Establishing minor differences without stopping at distinctions.
Subcommentary:
Joy, anger, right, and wrong,
blazing fiercely on the path,
thus lives were cut short prematurely,
and innate natures scattered.
"Scattered" means disordered.
The world favored knowledge,
and the common people exhausted themselves in seeking it.
Commentary:
Knowledge is boundless, yet they favored it,
so there was nothing to supply their demands.
Subcommentary:
If sages exhaust limitless knowledge,
how could the common people not be drained?
Thereupon, axes and saws were used to cut,
ink-lines to kill,
and mallets and chisels to execute.
Commentary:
Carving and polishing innate natures,
it ultimately came to this.
Subcommentary:
The ink-line
straightens crooked wood;
rituals and norms
show people honor and disgrace;
the mallet and chisel
bore holes in wood;
punishments and laws
execute people's bodies and heads.
Craftsmen wield axes and saws to damage wood,
sages use rituals and laws to harm the Way.
The world was in great turmoil and chaos,
the crime lying in disturbing people's hearts.
Thus the worthy hid beneath the great mountains and steep cliffs,
while the rulers of ten thousand chariots worried and trembled in their ancestral temples.
Commentary:
If one follows nature and occupies the appropriate position,
then the worthy and foolish embody their true feelings, and the noble and humble fulfill their roles,
ruler and minister, high and low,
none failing to reach their utmost,
and the world would be without worry.
These traces,
however, disturbed the hearts of the world,
making them rush about uncontrollably.
Thus those of medium wisdom and below
all adorned their natures outwardly to dazzle the masses,
hating the straightforward and despising the upright,
with followers leading each other.
Therefore, those who embraced authenticity lost their footing,
while those who exalted falsity stole the reins of power,
causing rulers to worry above
and people to suffer below.
Subcommentary:
"Turmoil"
means trampling upon one another.
Another interpretation says chaos,
the cosmos in great disorder,
the crime stemming from sagely wisdom.
The way of the gentleman waned,
hiding traces in forests and marshes,
while rulers, though in their temples,
constantly worried and trembled,
lacking good assistance,
fearing the state would collapse.
In the present age, those condemned to death lie piled upon each other,
those in cangues push against one another,
and the executed are seen everywhere,
Subcommentary:
"Condemned"
means decisively sentenced to death.
"Cangues"
are shackles,
clamping feet and necks,
all called cangues.
During the era of the Six States and the decline of the Zhōu,
truly due to sagely traces,
tattooing, nose-cutting, and the five punishments
filled the roads with cangues,
the condemned piled upon each other,
and mutilated bodies littered the paths.
Piled upon each other and seen everywhere,
showing their multitude.
Yet Confucians and Mohists began to strut and bare their arms among the shackles.
Alas,
how extreme!
Their lack of shame and ignorance of disgrace is utterly extreme!
Commentary:
Due to pedantic Confucians clinging to traces,
they brought about this disaster.
Not considering discarding traces and returning to oneness,
but instead baring arms to use traces to govern traces,
can be called the height of shamelessness and ignorance of disgrace.
Subcommentary:
"Strutting"
describes exerting effort.
Sagely traces are tools that harm things,
yet Confucians and Mohists again bare arms beyond their bounds,
exerting effort among the shackles,
holding to traces and enforcing teachings,
trying to save the ills of the era—
how can such chaos ever end?
Hence, he sighs in astonishment,
lamenting their obstinate ignorance unceasingly,
feeling shame but no disgrace.
I do not know if sagely knowledge is not the fastener of cangues,
or benevolence and righteousness the tenon of shackles.
Commentary:
Cangues use fasteners as pins,
and shackles use tenons for function.
Sagely knowledge and benevolence
are traces far from crime.
Traces far from crime make people esteem them,
and esteeming them breeds arrogance and deceit,
from which arise tools to guard against evil—
this has never not happened.
Thus, abandoning what is esteemed ends crafty deceit,
and without crafty deceit, cangues and shackles are discarded;
what need for tenons and fasteners then?
Subcommentary:
"Fasteners"
are wedge pins for shackles.
"Tenon hole" is the aperture.
Inserting an object into the hole is the tenon.
Shackles without wedges are not firm,
fetters without holes are useless.
Similarly, laws and institutions cannot stand without sagely traces,
and Jié and Zhí cannot act without benevolence and righteousness;
sagely traces are the source of disturbance,
benevolence and righteousness the root of harm.
How can we know that Zēng and Shǐ are not the heralds of Jié and Zhí?
Commentary:
"Heralds"
are the fiercest arrows,
meaning Zēng and Shǐ are tools used by Jié and Zhí.
Subcommentary:
Hāo,
an arrowhead with holes that produces a fierce sound.
Sagely wisdom becomes the tool for stealing a state,
benevolence and righteousness the resources for violence and cruelty.
Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiú are utilized by Jié and Zhí like fierce arrows,
hence the saying.
Thus it is said: "Eradicate sageliness and discard knowledge, and the world will be greatly ordered."
Commentary:
Emulate that by which they cause disturbance.
Subcommentary:
Eradicate the tools for stealing a state,
discard the resources for violence and cruelty,
then within the cosmos there will be clarity and peace,
meaning great order.
When the Yellow Emperor had been established as the Son of Heaven for nineteen years,
his commands were implemented throughout the world,
Subcommentary:
His virtuous influence and decrees
were greatly implemented within the cosmos.
Hearing that Guǎngchéngzǐ was atop Mount Kōngtóng,
he went to see him,
Subcommentary:
Mount Kōngtóng
is in the northern region of Liángzhōu.
Guǎngchéng
is an alternative name for Lǎozǐ.
He said:
"I have heard that you, my master, have attained the ultimate Way,
I dare to ask about the essence of the ultimate Way.
I wish to take the essence of heaven and earth,
to assist the five grains,
and to nourish the people,
Subcommentary:
The five grains
are millet, broomcorn millet, beans, hemp, and wheat.
He desires to take the principles of the deep and obscure,
the essential qi of heaven, earth, yīn, and yáng,
to aid in completing the five grains,
and thereby nourish the common people.
I further wish to govern yīn and yáng,
to fulfill the lives of the multitude,
how should this be done?"
Subcommentary:
Suì means to follow or accord with.
He wishes to model officials and divide duties after yīn and yáng,
accord with the nature of the multitude of lives,
and asks how to do so.
Guǎngchéngzǐ said:
"What you wish to ask about
is the substance of things;
Commentary:
To ask about the essence of the ultimate Way
can be said to be about substance.
Subcommentary:
Ér means you.
Wishing to sow and plant the five grains,
and to officiate over the two modes (yīn-yáng),
what you ask is crude and shallow,
not going beyond form and substance,
deviating from the profound and mysterious essence.
This is a criticism.
What you wish to govern
is the remnant of things.
Commentary:
Not allowing them to be so of themselves but wishing to govern them,
hence it is remnant.
Subcommentary:
If you insist on setting up offices and dividing duties,
pulling things to follow yourself,
you already go against creation and transformation,
and will inevitably cause injury and damage.
Since you govern the world,
cloud vapors do not wait to gather before raining,
grasses and trees do not wait to yellow before falling,
the light of the sun and moon has increasingly become desolate.
Subcommentary:
Zú means to gather.
Dividing officials and imitating yīn and yáng,
having a mind to govern the myriad things,
will inevitably lead to calamities.
Rain and wind become unregulated,
heat and cool lose their proper sequence,
clouds do not gather before rain falls,
trees are still green when they are cast down;
comets clash and eclipses occur,
the three lights (sun, moon, stars) become dim and obscure,
human minds are disturbed,
the celestial phenomena become desolate and negligent.
And with the petty mind of a flatterer,
how could you be sufficient to discuss the ultimate Way!
Subcommentary:
Jiǎn jiǎn
describes a narrow and inferior appearance.
You are a flattering and sycophantic person,
your mind is narrow and inferior,
how could you discuss the ultimate Way!
The Yellow Emperor withdrew,
relinquished the world,
built a separate chamber,
spread white rushes as a mat,
lived in seclusion for three months,
then went again to seek him out.
Subcommentary:
The Yellow Emperor withdrew,
purified and unified his mind,
abandoned the honorable position of the ninth fifth (imperial throne),
built a separate chamber,
avoided noise and clamor,
used white rushes for cleanliness,
lived in leisure for a period of time,
then went again to request the Way.
Yāo means to go to or visit.
Guǎngchéngzǐ lay with his head to the south,
the Yellow Emperor, from a lower position, advanced on his knees,
bowed twice, touched his head to the ground, and asked:
"I have heard that you, my master, have attained the ultimate Way,
I dare to ask,
how can one govern the body so as to be long-lasting?"
Guǎngchéngzǐ rose abruptly,
and said:
"An excellent question!
Commentary:
If everyone cultivates themselves and does not govern the world,
then the world will be ordered,
hence he approves of it.
Subcommentary:
If one makes people govern things,
things will inevitably be disturbed and troubled,
if each governs their own body,
the world will be clear and correct,
hence he approves.
Jué rán means to rise quickly.
Come!
I will tell you about the ultimate Way.
The essence of the ultimate Way
is deep and obscure;
the ultimate of the ultimate Way
is dim and silent.
Commentary:
Deep, obscure, dim, and silent
all mean complete non-being.
Why is it
that Zhuāng and Lǎo repeatedly refer to non-being?
To clarify that what generates things is non-being, and things generate themselves.
They generate themselves,
they are not generated for a purpose,
so what action is there regarding what is already generated?
Subcommentary:
The ultimate Way is subtle and refined,
the mind and spirit are unfathomable,
hence it is described as deep and far-reaching,
dim, silent, mysteriously transcendent.
Do not look, do not listen,
embrace spirit with stillness,
and the form will naturally become correct.
Commentary:
Forget looking and you will naturally see,
forget listening and you will naturally hear,
then the spirit is not disturbed and the form is not deviant.
Subcommentary:
Eyes and ears have no external seeing or hearing,
embrace and preserve spirit and vitality,
external conditions cannot disturb it,
mind and form unite,
naturally merging with the correct Way.
Be still, be clear,
do not labor your form,
do not shake your essence,
then you can achieve long life.
Commentary:
Allow it to move spontaneously,
hence remain still and not die prematurely.
Subcommentary:
Clarify the spirit and quiet the thoughts,
the body without labor,
not attached to external conditions,
spirit and vitality constantly tranquil,
mind at leisure, form at ease,
long life and enduring vision.
Eyes see nothing,
ears hear nothing,
mind knows nothing,
your spirit will guard the form,
and the form will achieve long life.
Commentary:
These all follow the nature and act spontaneously,
hence long life.
Subcommentary:
Allow seeing and hearing but have nothing seen or heard,
since the sense faculties and objects are already empty,
the mind is also tranquil and quiet,
illuminated without knowledge or thought,
responding to opportunities constantly tranquil,
spirit serene, guarding the form,
one can achieve long life and enduring vision.
Be careful within yourself,
Commentary:
Preserve your authenticity.
Subcommentary:
Forget the mind,
and preserve the true self.
Close off your external senses,
Commentary:
Guard your innate nature.
Subcommentary:
Cease seeing and hearing,
to guard your innate nature.
Excessive knowledge leads to ruin.
Commentary:
Knowledge has no bounds,
hence it causes ruin.
Subcommentary:
If one is not cautious with intellectual concerns,
the spirit and mind become fatigued,
and the ears and eyes are exhausted externally,
how can one not be ruined?!
I will lead you to the heights of great brightness,
reaching the source of utmost yang;
I will guide you into the gate of profound darkness,
reaching the source of utmost yin.
Commentary:
To reach the origins of yin and yang,
is to ascend to the heights of great brightness,
and enter the gate of profound darkness.
Subcommentary:
Yang represents movement.
Yin represents stillness.
"Suì" means to emerge.
When the perfect person responds to movement,
their wisdom illuminates like the sun and moon,
hence it is called great brightness.
The source of utmost yang,
signifies descending from the root to the traces,
hence it is said to emerge.
When there is no stimulation,
it is deeply rooted, still, and concentrated.
The source of utmost yin,
also means gathering traces back to the root,
hence it is called entering the gate of profound darkness.
Guǎngchéng showed Huángdì the two meanings of movement and stillness,
thus employing the two gates of yin and yang.
Heaven and earth have their officials,
yin and yang have their storehouses,
Commentary:
Simply let them be.
Carefully guard your own self,
and all things will naturally flourish.
Subcommentary:
The officials of heaven,
refer to the sun, moon, and stars,
which can illuminate the four directions,
and uphold all things,
hence called officials.
The officials of earth,
refer to metal, wood, water, fire, and earth,
which can sustain animals and plants,
and carry all beings,
also called officials.
The two energies of yin and yang,
spring, summer, autumn, and winter,
each have their own roles,
like storehouses or organs.
All can follow their nature,
with nothing unfit,
why oppose creation
to establish more governance?!
Simply be non-active,
carefully guard your own self,
and all things
will naturally prosper;
why trouble your mind,
bringing sorrow upon yourself?!
I hold fast to the One and abide in harmony,
thus I have cultivated myself for twelve hundred years,
and my form has never decayed.
Commentary:
Attaining the ultimate of fulfilling one's nature and destiny,
reaching the pinnacle of longevity.
Only by not dying prematurely can one influence other things.
Subcommentary:
Preserving a serene and single-minded heart,
abiding in the wondrous way of centrality and harmony,
nurturing and cultivating the self,
though having years of longevity,
ultimately without a day of aging.
Huángdì bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
Guǎngchéngzǐ can be called Heaven!
Commentary:
Heaven is non-action.
Subcommentary:
Admiring the purity and loftiness of the sage's way,
which can unite in virtue with the mysterious Heaven.
Guǎngchéngzǐ said:
Come!
I will tell you.
Those things are endless,
yet people all think they have an end;
Subcommentary:
Death, life, and transformation,
the principles of things are endless,
but ordinary people, foolish and deluded,
believe there are beginnings and ends.
Those things are unfathomable,
yet people all think they have a limit.
Commentary:
They merely see one transformation.
Subcommentary:
All things are unfathomable,
with thousands of changes and myriads of transformations,
but foolish people, confused and attached,
believe there are boundaries and limits.
Those who attain my way,
above become sovereigns and below become kings;
Commentary:
The titles of sovereign and king
follow the times, whether above or below,
but in attaining the way of adaptability to respond to the endless,
it is one and the same.
Subcommentary:
Attaining the way of spontaneity,
if encountering an era of simplicity above,
one becomes like Fúxī and Shénnóng;
if meeting a decadent age below,
one responds as Tāng and Wǔ.
The paths of sovereigns and kings differ in ease and difficulty,
but the way is one.
Those who lose my way,
above see light and below become earth.
Commentary:
Losing the endless way,
they then cling to one transformation and cannot harmonize above and below,
hence their views differ with perspective.
Subcommentary:
Losing the way of non-action,
and stagnating in a mind of desire,
in life they perceive light,
in death they simply become earth.
Confused and attached to life and death,
unable to harmonize above and below,
hence there are two designations.
Now all flourishing things are born from earth and return to earth,
therefore I shall leave you,
Commentary:
Earth is without a mind.
Born from mindlessness,
thus one should return to guard mindlessness and go alone.
Subcommentary:
All things flourish,
all are born from the earth,
and when they wither and fall,
return to the earth.
All things in the world,
arise from non-being,
and in death return to emptiness and stillness.
Life and death are not two,
not stagnating in one direction,
now I shall leave you to follow what is fitting.
Enter the gate of the endless,
to wander in the fields of the limitless.
Commentary:
To be one with transformation.
Subcommentary:
Returning to the root of dark stillness,
entering the gate of the endless;
responding to changes between heaven and earth,
wandering in the fields of the limitless.
I share light with the sun and moon,
I endure as heaven and earth.
Commentary:
All is left to them.
Subcommentary:
"Cān" means to be the same.
Sharing brightness with the three luminaries,
enduring as long as the two realms (heaven and earth),
how could it be merely twelve hundred years?!
Approach me,
and be merged!
Distance yourself from me,
and be obscured!
Commentary:
The coming and going of things,
are all unnoticed.
Subcommentary:
The sage is mindless like a mirror,
when stimuli arise,
they respond and coincide mysteriously,
if no stimuli arise,
then they are obscure and conceal their traces.
Others all die,
yet I alone remain!
Commentary:
Regarding life and death as one,
then wherever one goes, one remains.
Subcommentary:
Unifying life and death,
clarifying transformation,
there has never been not-me,
neither coming nor going,
I alone remain.
Who holds life and death?
Hence they worry and fear them.
Yúnjiàng was traveling east,
passing by a branch of Fúyáo when he happened to meet Hóngméng.
Hóngméng was just slapping his thighs and hopping about in play.
Note:
Yúnjiàng is the commander of clouds.
Hóngméng is the primordial energy.
Fúyáo,
the tree spirit,
lives in the Eastern Sea.
Also said to be the wind.
Zāo means to encounter.
Fǔ means to pat.
Quèyuè means to jump.
This is a parable.
Now, energy is the origin of living things,
clouds are the source of rain and moisture,
trees belong to the realm of spring sun,
and the east is the direction of benevolence.
Citing these four matters,
it shows that a ruler governing things
should prioritize virtue and kindness.
Yúnjiàng saw him,
Note:
Surprised by his unusual demeanor and appearance,
his movements different from the ordinary,
thus inquired about the reason for his journey,
hoping to learn the way of managing things.
He halted in astonishment,
stood still firmly,
and said:
Old man, who are you?
Old man, why are you doing this?
Note:
Tǎng means a look of shock and doubt.
Zhì means motionless.
Sǒu is a term for an elder.
Hóngméng continued slapping his thighs and hopping without cease,
replying to Yúnjiàng,
"Wandering!"
Note:
Roaming freely through natural transformations.
Yúnjiàng said:
I wish to ask something.
Hóngméng looked up at Yúnjiàng and said:
Ah!
Yúnjiàng said:
The energy of heaven is not harmonious, the energy of earth is stagnant,
Note:
The two energies neither descend nor ascend,
causing stagnation.
The six energies are not in harmony,
Note:
Yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and light,
these are the six energies.
The four seasons are not in order.
Note:
Spring, summer, autumn, and winter,
their seasonal cycles are disrupted in sequence.
Now I wish to combine the essence of the six energies to nurture all living beings,
how should I do this?
Note:
I want to blend the essence of the six energies to nourish all things,
hence the question.
Hóngméng slapped his thighs, hopped, and shook his head, saying:
I do not know!
I do not know!
Note:
All things follow nature inherently;
if one intentionally tries to govern them,
it will surely disrupt creation,
hence he shook his head and did not answer.
Yúnjiàng could not get an answer.
Another three years later,
traveling east,
he passed through the wilderness of the state of Sòng and happened to meet Hóngméng again.
Yúnjiàng was overjoyed,
hurried forward and said:
Has Heaven forgotten me?
Has Heaven forgotten me?
Bowing twice and kowtowing,
he wished to hear from Hóngméng.
Note:
Thus, as if addressing Heaven,
saying twice "forgotten me,"
hoping he recalls the past.
Hóngméng said:
Drifting along,
not knowing what to seek;
Commentary:
Yet naturally attaining what is sought.
Note:
Floating through life,
without greed or grasping.
Unrestrained,
not knowing where to go;
Commentary:
Yet naturally arriving where to go.
Note:
Acting without conscious intent,
without fixed direction.
The wanderer is surrounded by myriad things,
observing the genuine reality.
Commentary:
For one who is inwardly content,
all seen is naturally correct.
Note:
Hóngméng's mind wanders in vastness,
encountering many things,
with the wisdom to observe,
knowing that what is observed is without falsehood.
Yāngzhǎng means numerous.
What do I know!
Commentary:
That is all there is to it.
Note:
Drifting and unrestrained,
with an empty mind accepting things,
each thing finds its own correctness,
what more should I know!
Yúnjiàng said:
I too consider myself unrestrained,
yet the people follow wherever I go;
I have no choice regarding the people,
now they emulate me.
Commentary:
For riding things does not create traces, yet traces naturally appear;
unrestrainedness does not attract people, yet people come of their own accord,
hence they imitate and it is unavoidable.
Note:
I am like Hóngméng,
without intent to govern the world,
yet compelled to face the people,
who then follow my traces,
thus becoming imitators of things.
I wish to hear a word from you.
Note:
Desiring to hear the essential meaning,
hoping to resolve deep doubts.
Hóngméng said:
Disturb heaven's constant order,
go against the nature of things,
and the profound heaven will not succeed;
Commentary:
If one follows the nature of things without interference,
then nature is not opposed and order is not disturbed,
silent accomplishment and natural attainment follow.
Note:
Disrupting the natural constant way,
opposing the true nature of things,
then deceit arises,
and natural transformation fails.
Scatter the herds of beasts,
and birds cry out at night;
Commentary:
They are separated from their inherent tranquility.
Note:
As imitation traces become evident,
harm to things and disasters arise,
beasts then panic and scatter in groups,
birds take fright and call at night.
Disaster reaches the grasses and trees,
calamity affects the insects.
Commentary:
All suffer harm as a result.
Note:
Grasses and trees wither without frost,
disaster extends to insects.
Kūn,
means bright,
awakening to the sun's warmth.
Alas,
the fault of governing people!
Commentary:
Where there are traces of governance,
disorder is born from it.
Note:
With heaven's governance thus destroyed,
it is the fault of governing people.
Yúnjiàng said:
Then what should I do?
Note:
Wishing to learn the method of non-governance.
Hóngméng said:
Alas,
how poisonous!
Commentary:
Meaning the fault of governing people runs deep.
Note:
Lamenting repeatedly the severe harm and ruin.
Yī, a sighing sound.
Lightly, lightly, return now.
Commentary:
Xiānxiān describes the manner of rising or sitting.
Displeased that he cannot let go completely and freely,
thus sending him away to return.
Note:
Xiānxiān means a light, elevated manner.
Disapproving of Yúnjiàng's governance of things as causing calamity,
Thus he feigned lightness of action,
advising him to cease his tracks and return to the root.
Yúnjiàng said:
"I have encountered a celestial difficulty,
and wish to hear one word."
Hóngméng said:
"Alas!
Nourish your heart.
Commentary:
When the heart is harmed by its use,
then to nourish the heart,
is it not by not using the heart?!
Subcommentary:
The method of nourishing the heart
is listed in the following text.
You simply abide in non-action,
and things transform themselves.
Subcommentary:
Tú means only.
Simply abide with a heart of non-action and things transform themselves.
Cast off your physical form,
expel your intelligence,
and forget principles along with things;
Commentary:
Neither principles nor things are held in mind,
but darkly entrusted to spontaneity,
then through non-action they transform themselves.
Subcommentary:
Lún means principle.
Casting off the physical form
is forgetting the self.
Expelling intelligence
is forgetting the heart.
Forgetting both body and mind,
dispelling both things and self,
this is nourishing the heart.
Become one with the primordial vapor,
Commentary:
Having no boundary with things.
Subcommentary:
Míngxìng is the qì of spontaneity.
Vastly expanding body and mind to become one,
naturally uniting with the substance.
Loosen the heart and release the spirit,
be blank and without a soul.
Commentary:
Sitting in forgetfulness and following solitude.
Subcommentary:
Hún means fondness of knowledge and action.
Explaining and releasing means dispelling and cleansing.
Mòrán means without knowledge;
cleansing the heart and spirit,
like dead ashes and withered trees,
having no knowing soul.
The myriad things are numerous,
each returns to its root,
each returns to its root without knowing it;
Commentary:
Returning without knowing,
this is true return.
Subcommentary:
Yúnyún means numerous.
Numerous comings and goings,
birth and extinction do not leave spontaneity,
returning to the root is clear,
how could one use knowledge and only then return to destiny?!
In a state of primordial chaos,
throughout life do not leave it;
Commentary:
Primordial chaos is without knowledge and allows self-return,
thus able to never leave its root throughout life.
Subcommentary:
Primordial chaos without knowledge and following solitude, through a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations,
does not leave spontaneity.
If one knows it,
that is to leave it.
Commentary:
Knowing and then returning,
is contrary to returning.
Subcommentary:
Using knowledge to admire the root of life,
is to leave the nature of spontaneity.
Do not ask its name,
do not spy on its essence,
things naturally generate themselves.
Commentary:
Spying and asking means losing their self-generation.
Subcommentary:
The Dào is beyond names and words,
principles transcend emotions and thoughts.
If one uses names to inquire about the Dào,
uses emotions to spy on principles,
is that not far off!
Being able to dispel emotions and forget names,
entrusting to solitary transformation,
things attain the principle of life.
Yúnjiàng said:
"Heaven bestowed virtue upon me,
showed me silence;
I sought it with my own person,
and now I have obtained it."
Commentary:
Knowing and not being silent,
often leads to self-loss.
Subcommentary:
Bestowing words of Dào and virtue,
showing the practice of mysterious pointing,
since establishing myself,
only now have I realized.
Bowing twice and touching his head to the ground,
he rose, took leave, and departed.
Worldly people
all like others who agree with them and dislike those who differ from them.
Subcommentary:
People stained by habits,
confused and stubborn for a long time,
rejoice at agreement and fear,
dislike and detest disagreement.
Desiring those who agree with them,
and not desiring those who differ from them,
is because they take surpassing the multitude
as their heart.
Commentary:
The heart desires to stand out from the group to become prominent among the masses.
Subcommentary:
Affirming oneself and negating others,
liking agreement and disliking difference,
must mean wanting to display one's own merit and fame,
to surpass the multitude.
Those who take surpassing the multitude as their heart,
how can they ever truly surpass the multitude?!
Commentary:
Since everyone takes surpassing others as their heart,
this is precisely why they remain ordinary people.
If I also wish to surpass the multitude,
then I am no different from the multitude and cannot stand out from them.
Since all take surpassing each other as their heart,
while I alone go nowhere without being the same,
this is greatly different from the multitude and makes me the master of the multitude.
Subcommentary:
If people compete to surpass the multitude as their heart,
this is a common vulgar sentiment,
how can one alone transcend beyond the group?!
Merging with their light and dust,
one becomes greatly different from the multitude and becomes outstanding among them.
Relying on the multitude to pacify what one hears,
is not as good as the multitude's skills, which are many.
Commentary:
What one person hears,
is not as numerous as the multitude's skills,
thus relying on the multitude brings peace.
If one does not rely on the multitude,
then the thousands and millions of the multitude,
all become one's enemies.
Subcommentary:
Using the multitude's skills,
relying on the multitude's knowledge,
then there is no conflict or competition.
This is called: the clear-sighted see for you,
the wise plan for you.
But those who wish to rule over others' states,
this is seizing the benefits of the Three Sovereigns without seeing their calamities.
Commentary:
Those who wish to rule over others' states,
not relying on the multitude's self-action but acting through themselves,
this is merely seeking the benefit of the Three Sovereigns' rule over things without seeing the calamity of acting through oneself.
However, the benefit of the Three Sovereigns,
was it because they acted?
They relied on the world's self-action and followed it.
Subcommentary:
Using one's own biased views to rule a state,
merely seeks the benefit of the Three Sovereigns' rule over things,
not knowing it brings the great calamity of losing one's life.
This is gambling with others' states,
how many gambles do not result in losing others' states?!
Subcommentary:
Jiǎo means to seek.
Using the benefits of imperial kingdoms to seek what is not one's portion,
for the fortunate meeting of one person,
never fails to result in personal destruction.
Not one in ten thousand survives,
thus it is said, how many?
Those who preserve others' states,
are less than one in ten thousand;
while those who lose others' states,
not one succeeds but ten thousand have more than enough losses.
Commentary:
Oneself and the world
are mutually dependent in formation.
Now if one person alone monopolizes control over the world,
then the world becomes blocked,
how can oneself be open?!
Thus not only does one not succeed,
but the ten thousand directions have more than enough losses.
Subcommentary:
With a gambling heart becoming an imperial ruler,
speaking of preservation, not one succeeds,
speaking of destruction, there is more than enough failure.
Alas,
those who possess land do not know this!
Commentary:
This line laments that the ruler does not realize how opportunism becomes a flaw.
Those who possess land,
possess the great entity.
Commentary:
The ninth and fifth positions are revered and lofty,
the four seas vast and immense,
this is called the great entity.
Those who possess the great entity,
must not be treated as things;
things
Annotation:
If one cannot use things but is instead used by things,
then one is merely a thing,
how could one master things?!
If one cannot master things,
then one is unworthy of possessing the great entity.
Commentary:
If one merely seeks the domains of the Three Sovereigns,
but cannot let things act spontaneously,
one instead becomes used by things.
If one is already a thing oneself,
how could one master things?!
This is absolutely impermissible.
By not being a thing,
one can thus master things.
Annotation:
Those who use things,
are not used by things.
Not being used by things,
this means not being a thing;
not being a thing,
thus one masters all things under heaven,
enabling each to attain its own nature.
Commentary:
One is not used by things but uses things.
Understanding that the master of things is not a thing,
how could this apply only to governing the people under heaven?!
Passing through the six directions,
roaming across the nine provinces,
Annotation:
Using the spontaneous action of all under heaven,
thus traversing all things without exhaustion.
Commentary:
The sage comprehends spontaneity,
penetrates the workings of creation,
operates through the minds of the people,
uses the senses of all living beings,
thus knowing that the master of things is not a thing.
How could it only mean wearing the yellow canopy,
sitting in Fényáng,
bearing the jade seal,
and ruling the world?
Surely one should also traverse the six directions,
ascend the great purity,
soar beyond the nine provinces,
and wander to Gūyè.
Going alone and coming alone,
this is called solitary possession.
Annotation:
Others all distinguish themselves, yet one alone roams with the multitude,
this is going alone and coming alone.
Possessing this solitude alone,
can be called solitary possession.
One who possesses solitude,
is deemed supremely noble.
Annotation:
Mystically uniting with the multitude,
not seeking nobility among them,
yet the multitude cannot but regard one as noble,
this is supreme nobility.
If instead one holds to biased views and considers oneself uniquely different,
then even if aligned in principle,
one remains merely a thing among the common,
rejecting solitary possession.
Unable to possess solitude,
yet desiring to greedily usurp high positions,
wrongfully seizing what is not one's due,
how could the multitude submit to such a one?!
Thus, this is not supreme nobility.
Commentary:
Others all distinguish themselves, yet one alone roams with the multitude,
this is going alone and coming alone.
Possessing this solitude alone,
can be called solitary possession.
Wishing to stand out, yet one alone roams,
the multitude lacks this ability,
hence it is named solitary possession.
One who possesses solitude,
the people gladly support,
the masses bear and uphold.
With such a one as ruler,
