this can be called most honored and noble.
The teaching of the great person,
is like form to shadow,
sound to echo.
Annotation:
The minds of the people,
are form and sound;
the teaching of the great person,
is shadow and echo.
What intention does the great person have toward the world?
It is merely like shadow and echo following form and sound.
Commentary:
The great person is the sage.
Responding without intention,
responding without using the mind,
thus the minds of the people,
are form and sound;
the teaching of the great person,
is shadow and echo.
When questioned, respond to it,
exhausting all they hold within,
Annotation:
Enabling each thing to fully express what it holds within.
Commentary:
The sage's mind follows the stimuli of things,
responses also match the opportunity,
exhausting the inner thoughts of things.
Becoming the counterpart of the world.
Annotation:
The questioner is the host,
the responder thus is the counterpart.
Commentary:
Counterpart means mate.
The first stimulus is the host,
the responder is the mate.
Abiding in soundlessness,
Annotation:
In stillness, awaiting things.
Commentary:
Abiding means stillness.
When there is no stimulus,
the mind is like a withered tree,
still and without echo.
Acting without fixed direction.
Annotation:
Transforming along with things.
Commentary:
Acting means responding to the opportunity.
Meeting the opportunity without fixed direction.
Leading you to return to the bustling activity,
Annotation:
Bustling activity means spontaneous movement.
Lifting and carrying all things,
enabling them to return to their nature of spontaneous movement,
this is the ultimate of non-action.
Commentary:
Bustling activity means spontaneous movement.
Meeting the opportunity without fixed direction,
yet still wishing to lead and carry you multitude of beings,
enabling you to return to your original nature,
then non-action is perfected.
To wander without bounds;
Annotation:
Journeying with transformation,
thus without bounds.
Commentary:
Wandering,
the mind wanders together with nature,
thus without traces of boundaries.
Entering and exiting without side,
Annotation:
Mystically united without outward appearance.
Commentary:
Entering and exiting amidst the dust of life and death,
mystically united with the creator,
no edges are visible.
Together with the day, without beginning;
Annotation:
Together with daily renewal,
thus without beginning.
Commentary:
Renewing with each day,
thus without end or beginning.
The form and body,
conform to the great unity,
Annotation:
Its appearance is no different from heaven and earth.
Commentary:
Form means praise;
body means physical form.
The sage's virtuous form and body,
unite with the duality of heaven and earth and the great way,
externally not peering into the cosmos,
internally not possessing one's own self.
In great unity, there is no self.
Annotation:
Having a self prevents great unity.
Commentary:
Uniting with the two realms,
identifying with the great way,
then both things and self are forgotten.
Without self,
how can there be possession?!
Annotation:
What is difficult to eliminate under heaven is the self.
Since the self is already eliminated,
then the multitude of existents need not be possessed again.
Commentary:
Since the self is nonexistent,
how can things exist!
Those who perceive existence,
were the exemplary persons of old;
Note:
They were merely capable of glorifying their names.
Explanation:
Practicing benevolence and righteousness,
and ordering the relationships between ruler and minister,
does not depart from being an exemplary person through purposeful action.
Those who perceive nonexistence,
are friends of heaven and earth.
Note:
Perceiving nonexistence means allowing them to live in solitude.
Explanation:
Perceiving the wondrous principle of non-action,
and seeing the true nature of spontaneity,
heaven and earth are not existent, all things are ultimately empty,
turning from existence into nonexistence,
thus they are called friends.
What is lowly yet cannot be left unutilized,
are things;
what is humble yet cannot be left unrelied upon,
are the people;
Note:
Following their nature and utilizing them leads to order,
opposing their nature and oppressing them leads to chaos.
The reason why the people and things are considered humble and lowly,
is precisely because they are not followed and utilized.
Thus, those who utilize the lowly become noble,
those who rely on the humble become honored,
this is an inevitable correspondence.
Explanation:
Although the people reside in low positions,
each has their own capabilities;
although things are light and lowly,
all bear useful materials.
No material is discarded as useless,
no person is abandoned as unusable,
then all may flourish.
What is hidden yet cannot be left undone,
are affairs;
Note:
Affairs are concealed within them,
thus they are hidden.
They each act on their own,
thus they cannot be left undone but should simply be followed and utilized.
Explanation:
Hidden means concealed.
Affairs may be apparent or obscure,
natures may be skillful or clumsy,
some are apparent here,
some hidden there,
some skillful at this,
some clumsy at that,
but one should simply utilize them,
to harmonize all affairs.
What is coarse yet cannot be left unstated,
are laws;
Note:
Laws are the traces of wondrous affairs,
how can one disregard the wondrous affairs because the traces are coarse!
Explanation:
Laws refer to teachings and instructions.
Comparing teachings with principle,
principle is subtle while laws are coarse,
using the analogy of traps and snares,
thus they must be stated.
What is distant yet cannot be left unupheld,
is righteousness;
Note:
It should be upheld when appropriate,
which is why it is considered distant.
Explanation:
Although righteousness is far removed from the Dào,
if it accords with principle,
one should decide to adopt it.
What is intimate yet cannot be left unexpanded,
is benevolence;
Note:
Intimacy tends to be partial,
thus only when expanded does it become benevolence.
Explanation:
Although intimacy involves partial affection and narrow scope,
universal and extensive love,
is great benevolence.
What is regulated yet cannot be left unaccumulated,
is ritual;
Note:
Ritual regulations,
suffer from being fixed on one thing,
thus embodying them in everything,
they accumulate and become comprehensive.
Explanation:
Accumulated means深厚 (thick, substantial).
Regulated means文 (pattern, refinement).
Ritual values mutual interactions,
human sentiments are ornate and shallow,
thus externally displaying courtesy and deference,
internally cultivating substantial accumulation,
this is true ritual.
What is harmonious yet cannot be left unexalted,
is virtue;
Note:
In lowly affairs,
even if harmonious, it is not virtue.
Explanation:
Harmonious means compliant.
Those who cultivate the Dào,
blend their light with the world,
are humble and compliant towards things,
yet their will and conduct are pure and lofty,
soaked but not stained—such is their virtue.
What is unified yet cannot be left unchanged,
is the Dào,
Note:
In difficult affairs,
even if unified, it is not the Dào,
how much more so if not unified!
Explanation:
The wondrous origin is a single qì,
penetratingly generating all things,
extremely simple and easy,
is this not only the Dào!
What is divine yet cannot be left unacted,
is heaven.
Note:
If stubbornly refusing to act,
even if divine, it is not heaven,
how much more so if not divine!
Explanation:
Divine workings are unfathomable,
manifesting and concealing without fixed method,
responding to opportunities without obstruction,
accordant with heavenly spontaneity.
Thus the sage observes heaven but does not assist,
Note:
Simply following its spontaneous action.
Explanation:
The sage observes the natural wondrous principle,
greatly conforming to all things without assisting their inherent natures.
The following explains the previous text.
Accomplishes through virtue without being burdened,
Note:
Spontaneously uniting with the lofty.
Explanation:
Enabling circumstance and awareness to merge darkly,
superior virtue being already accomplished,
naturally there are no flaws or burdens.
Emerges from the Dào without planning,
Note:
Unplanned yet unified,
thus serving as the foundation.
Conforms with benevolence without relying on it,
Explanation:
The Lǎojīng says,
act but do not rely.
Benevolent kindness and broad love,
value being appropriate,
thus there is no reliance.
Is close to righteousness without accumulating it,
Note:
Following nature and residing distantly,
is not accumulation.
Explanation:
The former king's temporary lodge,
cannot be treasured,
the already displayed straw dogs,
how could they be accumulated and retained!
Responds to ritual without taboos,
Note:
Spontaneously responding to ritual,
not due to taboos.
Explanation:
The wondrous origin is serene,
its traces respond to ritual,
how could it be constrained by taboos!
Engages with affairs without declining,
Note:
Affairs are engaged through principle,
capability or incapability borne by oneself,
acting when response requires action,
without any refusal or decline.
Explanation:
Mixing with customs and riding the waves,
engaging with things according to affairs,
responding to opportunities without seizing,
also without refusal or decline.
Aligns with laws without chaos,
Note:
Govern the coarse with the subtle,
thus there is no chaos.
Explanation:
Following the nature of things,
aligning them with laws,
thus there is no chaos.
Relies on the people without taking them lightly,
Note:
Relying on their spontaneous action,
not using them lightly.
Commentary:
The people are the foundation of the state;
when the foundation is secure, the state is at peace.
Therefore, one should not dare to rely on or use it lightly.
It follows things without departing from them.
Annotation:
To follow and entrust oneself to them,
without abandoning the foundation.
Commentary:
Complying with the hearts of the common people,
following the nature of all things,
even when applying laws and teachings,
do not let them interfere with the inherent nature.
Things are not worth doing,
yet one cannot refrain from doing them.
Annotation:
As for action,
is it done merely because it is worth doing?
It arises from the essence of this action itself,
hence it cannot be stopped.
Commentary:
The endowment of life in things,
their functions are myriad and diverse,
like the dung beetle rolling its ball,
or the spider spinning its web,
these come from natural instinct,
not from artificial learning.
Thus, what is inherently absent cannot be forced into being,
but what is within one's nature cannot be left undone.
Those who do not understand Heaven
are not pure in virtue;
Annotation:
Not comprehending spontaneity leads to forced action,
and forced action results in impure virtue.
Commentary:
Being ignorant of the principles of nature
leads to shallow and impure virtue.
Those who are not in harmony with the Dào
have no basis for anything;
Annotation:
If one cannot empty oneself to receive things,
then every affair will miss its opportunity.
Commentary:
Blocking the nature of the Dào, which is empty and profound,
thus facing a wall in every matter, truly there is no way to proceed.
Those who do not understand the Dào,
how pitiful they are!
Commentary:
Ignorant of the principles of Heaven and humanity,
confused about the duties of ruler and subject,
their actions are topsy-turvy,
deeply lamentable.
What is called the Dào?
There is the Dào of Heaven,
and the Dào of humanity.
Acting through non-action and holding reverence
is the Dào of Heaven;
Annotation:
Residing above and entrusting all things to their spontaneous action.
Commentary:
Without affairs and without action,
revered and lofty above,
this aligns with the natural Dào of Heaven.
Acting through action and bearing burdens
is the Dào of humanity.
Annotation:
Those who are burdened by action
cannot follow their innate attainment.
Commentary:
Holding office and engaging in action,
burdened with numerous and繁杂 affairs,
this is the Dào of human relations.
The ruler
embodies the Dào of Heaven;
Annotation:
By aligning with Heaven's way of entrusting things,
one naturally resides above all things.
Commentary:
The ruler, positioned above, entrusts affairs to others,
in accordance with the non-action of the Dào of Heaven.
The ministers
embody the Dào of humanity.
Annotation:
Each fulfills their appointed role.
The Dào of Heaven and the Dào of humanity
are far apart from each other,
Annotation:
The ruler practices non-action and delegates to the百官,
the百官 have their duties, and the ruler does not interfere.
Both achieve self-attainment through non-interference,
thus the way of the ruler is leisurely,
the way of the minister is laborious,
between labor and leisure,
they cannot be discussed on the same day.
Commentary:
The ruler's position is尊高,
delegated to stewards;
the minister's way is humble,
serving with utmost sincerity;
hence the ruler's way is leisurely,
the minister's way is laborious,
they cannot be mentioned in the same breath.
This must be carefully observed.
Annotation:
Without careful observation, the roles of ruler and minister become disordered.
Commentary:
The Dào of Heaven involves the ruler's non-action,
the Dào of humanity involves the minister's engagement in affairs.
There is a distinction between尊卑,
differences in labor and leisure,
each guarding their own duties,
then both ruler and minister achieve non-action.
If one fails to discern the principles,
then labor and leisure are misplaced,
and the roles of ruler and minister become混乱.
The two principles (Heaven and Earth) give birth and nurture,
transforming endlessly,
among forms and substances,
they are the most vast,
constantly renewing and changing,
with thoughts and moments推移,
truly equal and balanced,
as it is said, they bring things to maturity and nourish them.
The Commentary on the Nánhuá Zhēnjīng, Volume Thirteen.
The Southern Florescence True Classic: Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll 14, Part 8
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters: "Heaven and Earth" Twelve
Though Heaven and Earth are vast,
their transformations are uniform;
Comment:
Uniform in acting through non-action and transforming spontaneously.
Subcommentary:
Now, the two principles (Heaven and Earth) give birth and nurture,
covering and supporting without end;
among forms and substances,
they are the most extensive and great;
yet renewing and transforming ceaselessly,
their appearance remains unchanged;
with each thought shifting and fading,
they are truly uniform and equal,
this is what is called "stabilizing" them.
Thus it is said, "Heaven and Earth and I are born together."
Though the myriad things are numerous,
their governance is one;
Comment:
Taking self-attainment as governance.
Subcommentary:
Now, the four kinds of births and the myriad things,
their categories are most numerous,
yet in following their nature and attaining self-realization,
this principle is singular,
this is what is called "nourishing" them.
Thus it is also said, "The myriad things and I are one."
Though the multitude of people is large,
their master is the ruler.
Comment:
Under Heaven has diverse minds,
but the mindless is the master.
Subcommentary:
The black-headed masses and common soldiers,
though their number is great,
he who is master and ruler,
is but one person.
Being mindless and following along,
he fittingly holds this position.
The ruler originates in virtue and is completed by Heaven,
Comment:
Taking virtue as the origin,
nothing fails to attain it.
Those who attain do so spontaneously,
thus attaining without gratitude,
thereby completing Heaven.
Subcommentary:
Origin means foundation.
Now, the ruler governs people and things,
he must take virtue as the basis;
things each attain themselves,
thus fully realizing their natural nature.
Hence it is said,
"The rulers of the profound antiquity in governing the world,
did so through non-action,
merely the virtue of Heaven."
Comment:
They followed the movements of spontaneity.
Subcommentary:
Profound means distant.
The rulers of antiquity
refer to the sovereigns before the Three Sovereigns.
It says the sage rulers of profound antiquity
governed the world through non-action,
indeed, what did they do!
This cites antiquity to prove the present,
completing the meaning of Heavenly virtue.
Viewing speech through the Dào, the rulers of the world are correct,
Comment:
Those who are non-active
naturally become rulers,
not through devious means.
Subcommentary:
Using the principle of empty penetration,
observe the responses of things,
and the rulers who follow non-action and accord
do not use depraved and crooked words,
thus their principles align with the kingly Dào.
Viewing distinctions through the Dào, the righteousness of ruler and minister becomes clear,
Comment:
Each fitting their own role,
then non-action is for the higher position,
action for the lower position.
Subcommentary:
Now, the way of the ruler is non-action,
while the way of the minister involves affairs,
noble and humble, labor and ease,
their principles are inherently different.
Just as the head naturally resides above,
the feet naturally below,
viewing through the Dào,
distinctions and righteousness become clear.
Viewing abilities through the Dào, the officials of the world are well-governed,
Comment:
Officials each fittingly govern according to their abilities.
Subcommentary:
Now, officials have high and low ranks,
abilities have superior and inferior,
if abilities match their posts, then things are not privately attained,
thus the officials of the world are well-governed.
Viewing broadly through the Dào, the responses of the myriad things are complete.
Comment:
Through non-action,
the world each responds with its own non-action.
Subcommentary:
Now, the great Dào produces things,
their natures and dispositions differ,
each following their own course,
all are fully provided for,
some running, some flying,
all respond to their functions,
not knowing the reason why,
how could they deliberate!
Thus viewing universally through principle,
the responses of all things are complete.
Therefore, what penetrates Heaven and Earth is virtue;
Comment:
If the myriad things all attain without exception,
then Heaven and Earth penetrate.
Subcommentary:
Penetrate means to be the same.
Being the same as the two principles' covering and supporting,
born together with Heaven and Earth—this is virtue.
What moves through the myriad things is the Dào;
Comment:
If the Dào does not block their paths,
then the myriad things naturally attain their movement.
Subcommentary:
The ultimate principle is without obstruction,
allowing things to come and go freely,
moving together with the myriad things,
thus it is called the Dào.
Those who govern people above, engage in affairs;
Comment:
Causing each person to naturally attend to their own affairs.
Subcommentary:
Though governing people,
it follows their inherent nature,
things each follow their abilities,
all finding their own suitability,
thus affairs are properly handled and the world is governed.
Those with abilities that manifest as arts, possess skill.
Comment:
Skill
is what the myriad things do not use.
Subcommentary:
Following their inherent nature,
they naturally possess arts and abilities,
not relying on external actions,
thus it is true skill.
Skill is subsumed under affairs,
affairs are subsumed under righteousness,
righteousness is subsumed under virtue,
virtue is subsumed under the Dào,
the Dào is subsumed under Heaven.
Comment:
Now, the root and branches subsume each other,
like arms and hands enclosing each other,
thus when the body is harmonious, all joints are comfortable,
when the Heavenly Dào is smooth, root and branches both flow freely.
Subcommentary:
Subsume
means to include,
to assist,
to return to.
Now, the skill of artistic ability
must include affairs.
If not including affairs,
how can skill be applied!
If affairs are improperly handled,
skill becomes useless.
Though acting through righteousness,
one cannot violate virtue;
though possessing this virtue,
one must emulate the Dào's empty penetration;
thus called empty penetration,
ultimately returning to the method of spontaneity.
This is how affairs and principles include each other,
though their functions differ.
Therefore, it shows that the root can encompass the branches,
the meaning from shallow to deep.
Hence it is said:
"Those in antiquity who nurtured the world,
being without desire, the world was sufficient,
being non-active, the myriad things transformed,"
Subcommentary:
Now, subsuming Heaven is why they were non-active,
subsuming the Dào is why they were without desire.
Thus the ancient emperors who nurtured the multitudes,
what did they do?
Indeed, being without desire, the common people were each sufficient,
being non-active, the myriad things transformed spontaneously.
"Deeply tranquil, the hundred clans were settled."
Subcommentary:
When one rules with folded hands in profound stillness,
the common people become virtuous in every household.
Thus the ancient classic says: "When I love stillness, the people naturally become upright."
The Record states:
"By comprehending the One, all things are accomplished."
Commentary:
The One refers to the Dào.
Since affairs arise from principle,
principle must encompass affairs;
the root can contain the branches,
therefore knowing the One,
all things are accomplished.
This saying appears in the Xīshēng Jīng,
and Zhuāngzǐ quotes it as evidence.
"Without mental striving, even ghosts and spirits submit."
Annotation:
Through non-action of the One, all principles are upheld.
Commentary:
When one's traces blend with human affairs,
while the mind verifies natural principles,
and thoroughly penetrates the source and boundaries,
mysteriously reaching the profound mystery,
then in the visible realm, one becomes the focus of people's devotion,
and in the hidden realm, even ghosts and spirits submit.
The Master said:
"The Dào
is what covers and carries all things;
how vast and great it is!
The noble person cannot but empty their mind of it."
Annotation:
Having a mind obstructs its naturalness,
thus one should empty and remove it.
Commentary:
The Master refers to
Lǎozǐ.
Zhuāngzǐ studied under Lǎo Jūn,
hence calling him 'Master'.
Emptying means
removing,
cleansing.
The empty and penetrating Dào
encompasses everything without exception;
heaven and earth rely on it for support,
all things obtain it for transformation and life.
Is there anything not following from this?
It is the ultimate root of things.
Praising its vast and magnificent greatness,
to exhort the rulers of the age:
Should they not emulate the Dào's non-action,
and wash away the burden of having a mind?!
Acting through non-action is called Heaven,
Annotation:
Not performing this action,
yet this action performs itself -
this is the Way of Heaven.
Commentary:
Acting through non-action
means following one's nature in movement.
Heaven's mechanism operates spontaneously,
therefore it is called Heaven.
This is action through non-action.
Speaking through non-speech is called Dé,
Annotation:
Not uttering these words,
yet these words speak themselves -
this is true virtue.
Commentary:
Silent without speech yet responding limitlessly,
like a mirror hung in a high hall,
reflecting whatever comes before it;
whether speaking or silent, there's no difference -
therefore it is called virtue.
This is speaking through non-speech.
Loving people and benefiting things is called benevolence,
Annotation:
This means following the true nature of life's circumstances.
Commentary:
Compassion like clouds moving,
love like rain falling;
the mind without partial attachment,
virtuous influence spreading widely;
cherishing all life -
therefore it is called benevolence.
Making different things one is called greatness,
Annotation:
All things and forms
maintain their proper places;
not pulling others to conform to me
achieves true greatness.
Commentary:
Though carving numerous forms
with different natures and dispositions,
following their innate qualities,
all harmonize with nature;
accepting without forcing separation
is therefore called greatness.
Acting without eccentricity is called breadth,
Annotation:
Mystically uniting self and other,
then all things naturally find accommodation,
thus creating abundance.
Commentary:
Concealing one's light and traces,
blending with common customs and waves;
if establishing virtue doesn't differ from others,
how could one's conduct be special compared to things?!
With mind without boundaries,
like a million-acre lake,
providing shelter for all living beings - this may be called breadth and tolerance.
Embracing all differences is called wealth.
Annotation:
Because I make no distinctions,
I can uniquely possess this multitude.
Commentary:
Occupying the imperial position,
commanding ten thousand chariots' prestige,
accepting all things' differences,
following the common people's variations,
so all natures are fulfilled -
therefore one can richly possess the world.
Thus holding virtue is called discipline,
Annotation:
Virtue is
humanity's guiding principle.
Commentary:
Being able to maintain one's inherent virtuous conduct
may be called the guiding principle of all things.
Virtue accomplished is called establishment,
Annotation:
What is achieved without virtue
cannot be called establishment.
Commentary:
Only when virtuous conduct is accomplished
can one establish achievements and aid things.
Following the Dào is called completeness,
Annotation:
The Dào is not partial to things.
Commentary:
Following means complying.
Only by complying with the empty and penetrating
can virtuous conduct become sufficient.
Not letting things break one's will is called perfection.
Annotation:
This is inner self-attainment.
Commentary:
Breaking means bending.
Unifying praise and blame,
mixing honor and disgrace,
not letting worldly things bend one's integrity -
this is complete virtue.
When the noble person understands these ten aspects,
they embrace them as the greatness of mind's function,
Annotation:
When the mind is great,
it can accommodate all affairs.
Commentary:
Embracing means containing.
The noble and worthy person,
mastering the previous ten matters,
can then contain all affairs,
with mind and nature being broad and great.
Abundantly, they become where all things flow toward.
Annotation:
Virtuous influence overflowing abundantly,
allowing all things to come and go spontaneously.
Commentary:
Flowing means going toward.
With mind and nature broad and leisurely,
virtuous influence overflowing abundantly,
therefore one becomes where all living beings flow toward.
Being thus,
one stores gold in mountains,
stores pearls in deep waters,
Annotation:
Not valuing hard-to-obtain things.
Commentary:
If acting as described above,
this constitutes non-action;
since not coveting glory and splendor,
naturally not treasuring precious goods.
Thus pearls born in water
are left stored in the deep without seeking;
gold coming from mountains
is kept hidden in peaks without pursuing.
Not profiting from goods and wealth,
Annotation:
One can even forget oneself,
how much more so goods and wealth?!
Commentary:
Even obtaining pearls and jade,
one still doesn't covet them for personal gain;
constantly using goods and wealth,
how could one still seek profit from them?!
Not approaching nobility and wealth;
Annotation:
These come and go incidentally,
the mind always stays far from them.
Commentary:
Whether such incidental things come or go,
one neither grieves nor delights,
Thus externally, they keep distant from high positions and official carriages,
and internally, they do not draw near to wealth and honor.
They do not delight in longevity,
nor grieve over premature death:
Annotation:
This is what is called liberation from bondage.
Explanation:
Even if one's lifespan were extended forever,
they would not consider it a delight;
if one's life were cut short prematurely,
they would not consider it a cause for sorrow.
They do not glory in success,
nor feel ashamed in poverty;
Annotation:
They forget longevity and premature death in their heart,
how much more so the distinctions between poverty and success!
Explanation:
Wealth, honor, glory, and advancement,
they do not consider as splendor;
poverty, low status, obstruction, and hardship,
they do not consider as shameful.
Longevity and premature death have never occupied their thoughts,
how could feelings of glory and shame
be allowed to linger in their hearts!
They do not seize the benefits of the whole world as their private share,
Annotation:
They leave everything to the myriad things.
Explanation:
Though shining upon the cosmos,
ruling over all under heaven,
with the precious treasures of the four seas
all tied to one person's actions,
they do not profit from goods and wealth,
but entrust them to the myriad states.
How could they constrain and take for themselves,
using them as a private share!
They do not regard ruling the world as a position of prominence for themselves.
Annotation:
Suddenly, they are unaware that glory rests upon them.
Explanation:
Sheltering the common people,
leading all under heaven,
yet attributing achievement to things,
forgetting their own wealth and honor,
thus they do not consider themselves great and glorious.
Prominence means being manifest,
Annotation:
Not being prominent means being silent and still.
Explanation:
Manifest means to display.
Even if sitting in Fényáng,
losing their hold on the world,
they must still manifest wisdom;
how could it be said they conceal their light!
The myriad things are one storehouse,
death and life share the same form.
Annotation:
Shedding all, they have no fixed abode.
Explanation:
Forgetting self and others,
thus the myriad things can be seen as one storehouse;
being oblivious to changes,
thus death and life share the same appearance.
Death and life bring no change to oneself,
how much less the distinctions between poverty, success, premature death, and longevity!
The Master said:
As for the Dào,
how deep it dwells,
how clear and pure it is.
Explanation:
The ultimate principle is profound and mysterious,
comparable to the deep sea;
limpidly clear and pure,
it illuminates even the eyebrows and temples.
Deep, then, describes its dwelling in silence and profound clarity;
clear and pure, then, describes how even in movement it remains eternally clean.
Some versions also use the character for "lord."
If metal and stone do not obtain it,
they have no means to sound.
Annotation:
Sound manifests from silence.
Explanation:
Sound manifests from silence,
response arises from authenticity.
Thus, metal and stone have sound,
but do not ring unless struck.
Annotation:
This is used as a metaphor for those who embody the Dào: they respond only after things stimulate them.
Explanation:
Strike means to hit.
Within metal and stone,
musical notes are inherently stored;
if they are not struck,
they ultimately produce no sound.
Similarly, the heart of the utmost person
truly holds sage virtue,
and if things do not stimulate,
there is no way for the sage's response to manifest.
Earlier, deep water was used to illustrate the ultimate Dào;
here, metal and stone are borrowed to reveal the sage's heart.
Who can fix the myriad things!
Annotation:
Response and stimulus have no fixed direction.
Explanation:
Compare it to a bright mirror,
or an empty valley;
when things come, then it responds,
responding without a heart of its own.
Since things vary infinitely in length and brevity,
responses also vary without fixed shape.
Those who possess kingly virtue,
move with simplicity and are ashamed to be versed in affairs,
Annotation:
They proceed according to their nature,
not fond of being versed in affairs.
Explanation:
Simplicity means authenticity.
To move means to go.
Kingly and great, they are neither arrogant nor boastful,
proceeding with authentic nature;
since they embrace simplicity with purity and loftiness,
they are ashamed to be versed in worldly affairs.
They establish themselves in the origin and their understanding connects with the spiritual.
Annotation:
With the foundation established, understanding does not oppose it.
Explanation:
The spiritual means
the unfathomable function.
Constantly abiding in principle above,
it goes forth and responds to things.
The unfathomable spiritual
understands and connects with things;
this subtle function
must rely on
the intent to show that the root can generate function, and function does not contradict the root.
Thus, their virtue is vast,
Annotation:
Embracing simplicity and connecting with the spiritual,
then it becomes even more vast.
Explanation:
Being pure, simple, and non-acting,
proceeding with authentic nature,
with spiritual understanding connecting to things,
yet constantly established in the origin,
function does not contradict the substance,
movement does not harm stillness.
With virtuous conduct like this,
how could they not be the most centered and great!
When their heart emerges,
it is because things seek it.
Annotation:
It emerges only after things seek it,
not initiating before things.
Explanation:
To seek means to request.
The utmost sage has an empty heart,
and thus self and others respond;
unless things seek the sage's virtue,
there is no way for the sage's heart to manifest.
The emergence of the sage's heart
truly comes from things seeking it.
They wish to harmonize without initiating,
not leading things.
Thus, form cannot live without the Dào,
life cannot be clear without virtue.
Explanation:
Form means
the seven-foot body;
life means
the hundred-year lifespan;
virtue means
the wisdom that can clarify;
the Dào means
the realm that can be penetrated.
The Dào can penetrate and give life to the myriad things,
thus without the Dào, there is no life;
virtue can reflect and illuminate the source of principle,
thus without virtue, there is no clarity.
The Lǎojīng says,
the Dào gives them life,
virtue nurtures them.
Preserving form and exhausting life,
establishing virtue and illuminating the Dào,
is this not the work of kingly virtue!
Explanation:
To preserve means to accept.
To exhaust means to fully experience.
Accepting the beauty or ugliness of one's appearance,
experiencing fully the longevity or premature death of one's lifespan,
establishing great virtue to rectify the times,
using the ultimate Dào to penetrate things.
Who can be like this,
if not one with kingly virtue!
How vast and expansive!
Suddenly emerging,
vigorously moving,
and the myriad things follow them!
This is called the person of kingly virtue.
Annotation:
Suddenly and vigorously both describe the manner of responding without a heart.
Movement arises without intent,
thus all things follow it,
so vast and boundless it is.
Therefore, it can preserve forms and exhaust life,
establish virtue, illuminate the Way, and achieve kingly virtue.
Commentary:
Vast and boundless,
denotes breadth and evenness.
Unconscious, spontaneous—the appearance of no-mind.
Things respond and move,
emerging when the moment arrives,
following and entrusting to things,
and thus things comply.
As if possessing all excellences,
hence it is kingly virtue.
Look, yet it is obscure;
listen, yet it is soundless.
Commentary:
The ultimate Way is profound and mysterious,
the sage's mind is concentrated and still,
not a form that can be seen with eyes,
beyond sound that can be heard with ears.
Within the obscure,
alone one sees the dawn;
within the soundless,
alone one hears harmony.
Annotation:
If seeing and hearing are not anchored in stillness,
then there is obscurity and disharmony.
Commentary:
Although again obscure and formless,
it can mold all phenomena,
and though silent without echo,
it can harmonize the eight tones.
To clarify that function arises from substance,
its capability is thus.
Therefore, deep within depth, it can embody things;
Annotation:
Only by exhausting its origin can one master things.
Commentary:
Being both existent and non-existent,
both still and responsive,
letting go again and again,
hence deep within depth.
Then, exhausting principle and fulfilling nature,
thus it can embody all things.
Divine within divinity, it can be essence;
Annotation:
Only by reaching ultimate compliance can one fully embody subtlety.
Commentary:
Divine,
is the name for the unfathomable.
Responsiveness and stillness interpenetrate,
existence and non-existence thoroughly understood,
thus neither measurable nor immeasurable,
nor not measurable,
but the divine essence of subtlety.
Therefore, in its interaction with all things,
though utterly non-existent, it supplies their needs;
Annotation:
I remain firm and entrust all to them,
then their needs are self-supplied.
Commentary:
Letting go again and again,
is called utter non-existence.
Yet interacting with things without fixed method,
responding appropriately to the moment,
despite myriad differences,
seekers are supplied,
like a mirror hung high in a hall,
reflecting whatever comes.
It extends freely yet gathers to its abode,
whether large or small,
long or short,
far-reaching.
Annotation:
All are allowed freely,
converging to their ultimate point.
Commentary:
Extend, means to let loose.
Abode, means convergence.
If the substance is thus utterly non-existent,
it can respond to needs fittingly,
hence able to follow the times and entrust,
responding to things in myriad ways,
essential in convergence without stagnation.
Thus whether large or small,
suddenly short or long,
even far-reaching,
those who come,
according to their circumstances,
all have their needs met,
like prescribing medicine for the illness,
in principle, always appropriate.
The Yellow Emperor journeyed north of the Chìshuǐ River,
ascended the Kūnlún Mountains and looked south,
upon returning,
lost his dark pearl.
Annotation:
This allegorically illustrates how truth is attained.
Commentary:
Red is the color of the south,
the heart is the organ of the south.
Water's nature is flowing,
positioned in the north.
Analogous to the deluded mind clinging to appearances,
dark and unillumined,
hence said north of the Chìshuǐ.
Kūnqiū represents the body.
South is the direction of clarity,
looking signifies observation,
dark denotes profundity and distance,
pearl signifies precious treasure.
To clarify that all beings in the world,
without exception, delude mind and body,
chasing after attachments,
unaware,
dark as the north,
restless as flowing water,
losing truth and the Way,
truly stems from this.
Now, to return to the origin and source,
seek truth and inquire of the Way,
thus looking south signifies illumination and discernment,
losing upon return signifies returning to destiny,
so first clarify where truth is lost,
then show the method of attaining the Way.
The method revealed,
is listed below.
He sent Knowledge to search but it couldn't find it;
Annotation:
Using knowledge is insufficient to attain truth.
Commentary:
Search, means to seek.
Thus, beyond thought, it cannot be sought by mind.
He sent Lìzhū to search but it couldn't find it;
Commentary:
Not a form,
it cannot be grasped by eyes.
He sent Chīgòu to search but it couldn't find it either.
Annotation:
With clever speech and argument,
one strays further from truth.
Commentary:
Chīgòu means disputation.
Beyond words, it cannot be sought by debate.
Then he sent Xiàngwǎng,
and Xiàngwǎng found it.
Commentary:
Wǎngxiàng means without intent.
Beyond sound and form,
beyond thought and deliberation,
thus Knowledge and Lìzhū reached their limits and returned,
Chīgòu with debate,
striving forcefully, lost truth,
only Wǎngxiàng, without intent,
alone obtained the dark pearl.
The Yellow Emperor said:
How strange!
Xiàngwǎng could actually find it?
Annotation:
Clarifying that attaining truth is not by using the mind;
Xiàngwǎng, thus, is truth itself.
Commentary:
Lílóu deluded in nature,
relying on sharp sight, lost the Way,
Xuānyuán awakened to principle,
marveled that Wǎngxiàng obtained the pearl.
Encouraging all students,
can one not depart from form, discard wisdom, renounce acuity, and dismantle the body?
Yáo's teacher was XǔYóu,
XǔYóu's teacher was Nièquē,
Nièquē's teacher was Wángní,
Wángní's teacher was Pīyī.
Commentary:
The four above,
all were recluses in Yáo's time,
weary of the dusty world,
embracing the Way and virtue,
pure and honest, cleansing themselves,
unlike ordinary people,
Yáo knew their worth,
wished to yield the empire to them.
Zhuāngzǐ shows a lineage of transmission,
hence lists their teachers.
Yáo asked XǔYóu:
Can Nièquē align with heaven?
Annotation:
Meaning to become the Son of Heaven.
I rely on Wángní to invite him.
Annotation:
Wishing to use his teacher to summon him.
Commentary:
Align, means to match.
Rely, means to depend on.
Yáo said:
Nièquē, being virtuous,
has the merit to match the heavenly position,
hoping through Wángní,
to remotely compel his attendance.
Unable to resolve the matter of governance,
he consulted Xǔ Yóu.
Xǔ Yóu said:
Perilous indeed is the state of the world!
Commentary:
"Jí" means peril.
Subcommentary:
"Dài" means imminent.
"Jí" means peril.
If one were to yield the throne to Nièquē,
abdicating the ten-thousand-chariot kingdom,
the signs of peril and ruin
would not be far off.
As for Nièquē's character,
he is intelligent, perceptive, and wise,
quick-witted and sharp,
his nature surpassing others.
Commentary:
Being overly intelligent and sharp
makes others look up to him enviously,
frequently harming the people.
Subcommentary:
"Ruì" means sagely.
"Jǐ" means agile.
"Mǐn" means swift.
Now, when a sage governs the world,
he lets the tassels of his crown obscure his vision,
and stuffs yellow silk in his ears,
thereby blocking out sharp sight and hearing,
not wishing to see and hear too much.
But now Nièquē internally harbors sagely wisdom,
externally dazzles with intelligence,
his words are sharp and debates swift,
his strategies vast and far-reaching,
his virtuous conduct and innate cleverness,
all his actions surpass others.
Since his traces are so conspicuous,
they are bound to become a source of trouble.
The manifestation of peril and ruin
is detailed below.
Moreover, he uses the human to receive the heavenly.
Commentary:
Using knowledge to seek a return to his natural state.
Subcommentary:
The loss of authenticity by things
has long since occurred.
To use the methods of mind and intellect
to restore their original state
means the natural disposition is lost far beyond recovery.
He is meticulous in prohibiting faults,
but does not know from what faults arise.
Commentary:
Now, faults arise from intelligence and knowledge,
yet he employs knowledge to prohibit them,
thus his faults only multiply.
Therefore it is said,
the absence of faults lies in abandoning knowledge,
not in forcefully prohibiting them.
Subcommentary:
That from which faults arise
is knowledge.
This means Nièquē only knows to meticulously prohibit the faults and troubles of the common people,
but does not know that troubles arise from knowledge.
Should he be matched with Heaven?
He would rely on the human and lack the heavenly.
Commentary:
If the world were given to him,
he would then cause later generations to rely on knowledge and lose their authenticity.
Subcommentary:
If given the position of Heaven,
and set to rule over the multitude of beings,
he would certainly operate through mind and intellect,
and delight in the principles of Heaven,
causing all things to lose themselves,
no longer possessing their natural disposition.
He would take his own self as fundamental and differentiate forms.
Commentary:
Taking the myriad things as fundamental,
then the multitude of changes can be unified and different forms can be made the same.
This trace
would then cause later generations to follow his example in controlling things,
and the myriad things would become disordered.
Subcommentary:
"Fāng" means "about to".
Now, the sage has no fixed mind,
but follows and relies on things.
But now Nièquē takes his own person as fundamental,
leading things to make them return,
causing the different forms under heaven
to follow his transformation.
The loss of nature by things
truly stems from this.
The troubles of later generations
begin from this.
He would esteem knowledge and rush about like fire.
Commentary:
When the worthy hold positions ahead,
then knowledge and views are esteemed by those following,
leading to competitive rushing like fire.
Subcommentary:
Being unable to forget knowledge and rely on things,
but esteeming knowledge to govern the world,
he would then follow traces,
abandon himself and imitate others,
dashing and rushing about,
swift as fire.
He would become the initiator of labors.
Commentary:
About to initiate the beginning of toilsome service for later generations.
Subcommentary:
"Xù" means beginning.
"Shǐ" means toil/service.
Unable to be non-active,
and relying on knowledge to control things,
the toils and labors of later generations
begin from this.
He would become an obstacle to things.
Commentary:
Would then cause later generations to be constrained and control things.
Subcommentary:
"Gāi" means to obstruct/hinder.
Unable to use the Way to connect with people,
he instead relies on knowledge to obstruct things.
He would look around and things would respond.
Commentary:
Would then cause later generations to point and command to move things,
making them respond to superior duties.
Subcommentary:
About to look around to the four directions,
pacifying and securing the ten thousand states,
making the common people
respond to his transformative methods.
He would respond to the needs of the multitude.
Commentary:
Would then cause later generations to be unable to forget goodness,
and to benefit from humaneness in responding appropriately.
Subcommentary:
Using the knowledge of a single self
to respond to the needs of the multitude of things,
since it is not mindless,
inevitably leads to peril.
He would transform along with things.
Commentary:
Would then cause later generations to chase after things,
unable to find contentment within.
Subcommentary:
Applying his own knowledge
to the multitude of things,
making the various beings follow his transformation,
things thus lose their nature,
and he himself also gains nothing.
And he has never been constant.
Commentary:
All these were fitting for their time,
but if one receives their benefit today,
one will inherit their harm tomorrow.
Hence it is said he has never been constant.
Subcommentary:
Governing things with knowledge,
policies come from many sources,
earlier ones bear his virtue,
later ones suffer his弊端,
already deviating from the pure antiquity,
thus there is no constancy.
How could he be sufficient to match Heaven?
Even so,
he has a clan,
he has an ancestor.
Commentary:
His affairs can be categorized and thus ancestor-like and emulated.
Subcommentary:
"Zú" means a retreat/haunt.
Now Nièquē dwells in mountain retreats,
holding his aspirations high,
unable to blend with the traces of the world,
he is insufficient to match Heaven.
Yet among the common flow,
few are his peers,
thus his aspirations are lofty and far-reaching,
truly worthy of emulation.
He can be the father of the multitude,
but cannot be the father of the multitude's father.
Commentary:
The father of the multitude's father
is that which leaves traces.
Subcommentary:
"Fù" means ruler.
This means Nièquē, lofty and non-active,
not leveling with the vulgar,
although his way can be narrated,
may suitably be the father of the multitude,
but cannot be the father of fathers.
The father of fathers is Yáo.
Now Yáo, residing above the myriad things,
yet his mind roams to the mountains of Gūyè,
when he went to see the Four Masters,
he was right in the land of Fényáng.
Thus, being still, he moves;
moving, he is still.
Non-action is action,
To act through non-action and possess through non-possession,
being and non-being arise simultaneously,
movement and stillness imply each other,
thus one can become the sovereign among sovereigns,
the father among fathers.
What is called exhausting principles and fulfilling nature,
mysterious and even more mysterious,
makes one the father of all living beings,
thus it is fitting indeed.
Hence Guǒ Xiàng's commentary states,
"The father's father is that by which traces are formed."
Governance
is the leader of chaos,
Commentary:
This means not only does order have its master,
but chaos also has its leader.
Explanation:
"Leader" means master.
If one uses cunning to manage affairs,
though there may be order at the time,
chaos will inevitably follow later.
Both paths take cunning as their leader.
This is the calamity facing north,
Commentary:
Jié and Zhòu did not kill virtuous ministers themselves,
but relied on the traces of sage wisdom to bring disaster.
Explanation:
Jié and Zhòu relied on sage wisdom to kill virtuous ministers,
thus sage wisdom is the calamity facing north.
This is the harm facing south.
Commentary:
Tián Héng did not kill the ruler himself,
but borrowed benevolence and righteousness to harm him.
Explanation:
Tián Héng borrowed benevolence and righteousness to kill his lord,
thus benevolence and righteousness are the harm facing south.
The commentary states,
"Tián Héng did not kill the ruler himself,
but borrowed benevolence and righteousness to harm him."
Yáo observed at Huà.
The border guard of Huà said:
Ah,
O sage!
Please allow me to offer blessings to the sage.
Explanation:
Huà
is a place name,
present-day Huàzhōu.
The border guard
refers to the person guarding the borders at Huà.
"Ah" is an exclamation of admiration.
The border guard saw that Yáo possessed the virtue of a sage,
illuminating the world,
and wished to pray for his constant wealth,
hoping he would enjoy abundant blessings.
May the sage live long.
Yáo said:
I decline.
May the sage be wealthy.
Yáo said:
I decline.
May the sage have many sons.
Yáo said:
I decline.
Explanation:
Wealth, longevity, and many sons
truly bring numerous troubles,
and those who can embody this
abandon non-action.
Thus, through these two individuals,
the three afflictions are illuminated.
The meaning of declining
is explained below.
The border guard said:
Longevity,
wealth,
and many sons
are what people desire.
You alone do not desire them,
why is this?
Explanation:
These three matters mentioned earlier
contain what people greatly desire.
You alone decline them,
what is your reasoning?
Yáo said:
Many sons bring many fears,
wealth brings many affairs,
longevity brings many humiliations.
These three things
are not means to cultivate virtue,
thus I decline.
Explanation:
With numerous descendants,
worries and fears increase greatly;
with abundant wealth and goods,
affairs and business become truly numerous;
with extended lifespan,
one encounters difficulties and humiliations.
These three are insufficient to nourish the virtue of non-action,
but rather add to the burdens of action,
hence all are declined.
The border guard said:
At first I thought you were a sage,
but now I see you are merely a noble man.
Explanation:
I said you illuminate both being and non-being,
thus embodying the way of the sage;
now that you abandon being for non-being,
you are merely a noble man.
Heaven gives birth to the myriad people,
and must assign them duties.
With many sons assigned duties,
what fears could there be!
Commentary:
All things find their place and aspirations are settled.
Explanation:
Heaven and earth create and transform the myriad things,
each with their own abilities,
assign offices according to talent,
what worries and fears could there be!
Be wealthy and let others share in it,
what affairs could there be!
Commentary:
Entrust it to the world,
thus there are no affairs.
Explanation:
When the common people are prosperous,
and the four seas are abundant,
entrust it to the multitude without keeping it private,
this is the affair of non-action.
As for the sage,
he dwells like a quail
Commentary:
Without intention yet naturally at peace.
and eats like a fledgling,
Commentary:
Relying on things yet content.
Explanation:
The quail
is the common quail,
living in the wild without fixed abode.
The fledgling
is a young bird,
who must look to its mother for sufficient food.
The sage lives frugally and simply,
comparable to the quail;
his provisions barely sufficient,
like the fledgling bird.
Since he has no mind for extravagance,
how could he have attachment to flavors!
He moves like a bird without leaving traces;
Commentary:
Acting according to nature,
not following constant paths.
Explanation:
"Traces" means visible marks.
The sage extinguishes his mind and wisdom, merging with things in obscurity,
just like a bird in flight,
leaving no tracks to be seen.
When the world possesses the Way,
he prospers together with all things;
Commentary:
Acting wildly and recklessly yet naturally treading the great path.
Explanation:
When fortune is clear and peaceful,
he governs the millions;
when things come to affect him,
he responds timely with prosperity.
Guǒ Xiàng's commentary says "acting wildly and recklessly,"
which seems to contradict the text's meaning.
When the world lacks the Way,
he cultivates virtue and retreats into seclusion;
Commentary:
Even the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ,
if they accord with heaven and respond to human needs,
are not without seclusion.
Thus, acting through non-action yet leaving nothing undone
is not without seclusion.
Explanation:
"Seclusion" is pronounced xián.
When times are turbulent,
he blends with the masses and conceals his light,
cultivating virtue and hiding his traces,
preserving his path of life,
retiring contentedly to leisure,
roaming freely beyond the world.
This is what is called being free in both concealment and manifestation,
employing or setting aside according to the time.
After a thousand years, weary of the world,
he departs and ascends as an immortal;
Commentary:
The ultimate person exhausts the length of lifespan,
embracing the changes of exhausted principles,
his life is a natural movement,
his death is a transformation among things,
thus it is said he wearies of the world and ascends as immortal.
Explanation:
The sage understands the non-duality of life and death,
penetrates the oneness of transformation and change,
Thus they could fulfill the natural span of life's length or brevity,
and, weary of the clamorous world, vanish and ascend.
Why must one have the ascent at Dǐnghú,
to be deemed an immortal alone?
Or the longevity of Ānqī,
to be called a thousand years old!
Ride those white clouds,
and reach the land of the divine;
Note:
When the vital breath disperses,
it goes everywhere.
Explanation:
The ethereal spirit ascends,
merging indistinguishably with the Great One,
riding clouds and harnessing the breath,
arriving at the homeland of the Heavenly Emperor.
The three afflictions do not approach,
the body remains free from calamity;
then what disgrace could there be!
Explanation:
The three afflictions
refer to the earlier mentions of wealth, longevity, and many sons.
For one who drives the creator to come and go,
and rides change to wander freely,
the three afflictions are fundamentally void,
the seven-foot body comes from non-existence,
thus calamities and disgraces
are hardly worth mentioning!
The border keeper left.
Yáo followed him,
saying:
I beg to ask.
Explanation:
After the request was spoken,
the border keeper then departed.
Yáo, just realizing his error,
thus asked for a response.
The border keeper said:
Retreat now!
Explanation:
Since the doubts have been resolved,
you should quickly retreat and return.
When Yáo governed the world,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo was established as a feudal lord.
When Yáo passed it to Shùn,
and Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo resigned his lordship to farm.
Explanation:
Bóchéng Zǐgāo,
it is unknown where he was from,
likely a man of the Way.
When Yǔ went to see him,
he was farming in the wild.
Yǔ hurried to a lower position,
stood and asked him,
saying:
In the past when Yáo governed the world,
you, sir, were established as a feudal lord.
Yáo passed it to Shùn, Shùn passed it to me,
yet you, sir, resigned your lordship to farm.
May I ask,
what is the reason for this?
Explanation:
In the era of Táng and Yú,
he faced south and was called a lord,
but by the time of the Xià,
he retreated to farm in the wild.
His positions changed so drastically,
what meaning lies therein?
Zǐgāo said:
In the past when Yáo governed the world,
he gave no rewards, yet the people were diligent;
he imposed no punishments, yet the people were awed.
Explanation:
Rewards and punishments
are means to show encouragement and awe.
But Yáo governed with non-action,
and all things followed his transformation,
so the people needed no praise or rewards to encourage themselves toward goodness,
nor required penalties to fear and avoid wrongdoing.
This reveals his sage brilliance,
his virtue was such.
Now you use rewards and punishments, yet the people remain unvirtuous,
virtue declines from this point,
penal laws are established henceforth,
the chaos of future generations begins here.
Explanation:
Even with widespread rewards and punishments,
the people still lack virtue,
as supreme virtue has declined,
thus penal codes proliferate,
so we know future chaos
starts from this.
Why do you not go away?
Do not disrupt my work!
He tilled diligently without looking back.
Note:
In Yǔ's time, the three sages succeeded one another,
governance perfected and virtue complete,
yet merits and beauties gradually faded,
so historical records have nothing to document,
and even Confucius could not inquire about it,
thus although they possessed the world, they were not attached to it,
this is having it as if not having it.
So examining their times, Yǔ was the best,
considering the individuals, though there were three sages,
they were essentially one Yáo.
When there were no sages,
the world's heart suddenly turned to Qǐ.
For one who is perfectly impartial and appropriately positioned,
entrusts the world to the people,
taking and giving not for oneself,
thus losing it, one does not seek it,
gaining it, one does not decline it,
suddenly going,
carefreely coming,
therefore receiving criticism from men of integrity yet being listed among the three kings,
is not strange.
Zhuāngzǐ uses this to illustrate Yáo's shortcomings,
shortcomings that began with Yáo and faults completed with Yǔ,
how much more so for later ages without sages!
He entrusts distant traces to Zǐgāo,
making him abandon and not govern,
intending to end sagehood and return to oneness,
discarding knowledge to attain utmost tranquility.
But its reality is unheard of.
Zhuāngzǐ's words
cannot be questioned from a single perspective;
sometimes using Huángdì's traces to criticize Yáo and Shùn's legs,
how could he only honor Yáo and disdain Yǔ!
Thus we should set aside the寄托,
and record his intent to abolish sages and discard wisdom.
Explanation:
Hé means why.
Luò means to disrupt.
Yìyì describes the manner of plowing.
Bóchéng addressed Yǔ as Fūzǐ.
Why do you not go away, sir!
Do not disrupt my farming tasks.
Thereupon he plowed with effort,
without looking back again.
The three sages' succession
had essentially no superiority or inferiority,
but as simplicity and refinement differed across eras,
their traces varied.
Guō Xiàng's note that shortcomings began with Yáo and faults completed with Yǔ
aims to clarify that having sages is不如 not having them,
and having action is不及 non-action,
thus he elevates distant traces
to illustrate abolishing sages and discarding wisdom.
In the great beginning, there was non-being,
non-being had no name;
Note:
Because there was non-being,
there was nothing to name.
Explanation:
Tài means great;
chū means beginning.
When the primal breath first sprouts,
it is called the great beginning,
meaning its breath is vast,
capable of being the origin of all things,
hence named the great beginning.
At the time of the great beginning,
there was only this non-being,
not yet any being.
Since being did not yet exist,
where could names be placed!
Thus non-being had no name.
From this arose the One,
having the One but not yet formed.
Note:
The One
is the beginning of being,
the most subtle,
and because it is most subtle,
it does not yet have the form of physical principles.
The arising of the One
originates from the ultimate One,
not from non-being.
Yet why does Zhuāngzǐ repeatedly refer to non-being at the beginning?
What is the reason?
The beginning
means not yet born but obtaining life,
the difficulty of obtaining life,
yet it does not rely above on non-being,
nor depend below on knowledge,
suddenly and spontaneously gaining this life,
so why strive for life after being born, thereby losing its self-generation!
Explanation:
The One corresponds to the Dào,
having the name of One but not the forms of the myriad things.
When things attain it and are generated,
it is called dé;
Note:
Non-being cannot generate things,
yet it is said that things attain it and are generated,
which is to clarify that things' generation is self-attained,
and entrusting them to self-attainment
can indeed be called dé.
Commentary:
Virtue (dé) is
attainment (dé),
meaning to attain this.
That by which things attain life,
externally does not rely on things,
internally does not originate from the self,
neither non-existent nor existent,
neither self nor other,
unknowable in its origin of life,
thus it is called virtue.
The unformed possesses distinctions,
yet is seamless and continuous,
this is called destiny;
Commentary:
Though without form or substance,
it receives substance with inherent nature,
yet these distinctions of length and brevity,
are so seamless without gaps,
thus it is called destiny.
Through stillness and movement things are generated,
things form with inherent principles,
this is called form;
Commentary:
"Liú" means stillness.
Yáng moves, Yīn is still,
energies rise and descend in fusion,
distributing through the three realms (heaven, earth, humanity),
transforming and generating all things,
things achieve completion,
with life principles fully present,
this is called form.
Forms preserve spirit,
each having its norms,
this is called nature.
Annotation:
Virtue, form, destiny, and nature,
are named according to transformations,
yet in their spontaneity, they are one.
Commentary:
"Tǐ" means substance;
"bǎo" means to preserve.
Receiving form and substance,
preserving spirit and essence,
forms then have ugliness and beauty,
spirits have foolishness and wisdom.
Following appropriate norms and rules,
each differing from the other,
with inherent nature fixed,
and unchangeable,
thus it is called nature.
Cultivating nature returns to virtue,
virtue at its peak aligns with the origin.
Annotation:
Constantly achieving it spontaneously without action.
Commentary:
Following this endowed nature,
returning to the virtue of primordial life,
thus reaching the state of virtue,
aligns with the Tàichū (primordial beginning).
Alignment leads to emptiness,
emptiness leads to vastness.
Annotation:
Not aligning with the origin,
but acting with purpose midway,
then the heart harbors things,
and with things contained, the virtue of nurturing becomes small.
Commentary:
Aligning with Tàichū,
the mind becomes empty and open;
the mind being empty,
thus can encompass vastness.
Uniting with the chirping of birds;
Annotation:
Speaking without intent, yet speaking spontaneously,
aligns with bird chirps.
Commentary:
"Huì" means a bird's beak.
The mind being empty,
actions also merge with things,
thus speech aligns with bird chirps.
Bird chirps have no intent for right or wrong,
how could sage's words harbor emotions of hate or love!
Chirping united,
aligns with heaven and earth.
Annotation:
Heaven and earth also move spontaneously without intent.
Commentary:
Speech aligning with bird chirps,
virtue also aligns with heaven and earth.
Heaven and earth have no intent in covering and bearing,
the sage has no intent in speech,
thus uniting with heaven and earth.
This union is seamless,
like foolishness, like obscurity,
Annotation:
Achieving union through sitting in oblivion,
not through deliberate examination.
Commentary:
"Mín" means union.
The sage internally corresponds to ultimate principles,
externally conforms to all beings,
only traces and the root,
completely united,
thus called seamless.
This is blending with the vulgar and riding the waves,
merging with the dust of all things,
appearing foolish,
and also obscure.
Another explanation:
Aligning with bird chirps,
and aligning with heaven and earth,
is also seamless.
This is called mysterious virtue,
aligning with the great conformity.
Annotation:
Virtue is mysterious and what it conforms to is great.
Commentary:
Summarizing what preceded,
praising its beauty and abundance.
Such a person,
can be said to possess profound and mysterious virtue,
thus aligning with Tàichū,
greatly conforming to all under heaven.
Confucius asked Lǎo Dān:
Some people govern the Dào as if imitating each other,
making the unacceptable acceptable,
the untrue true.
Annotation:
As if imitating and emulating,
forcing the unacceptable to be acceptable,
the untrue to be true,
this distorts their inherent nature.
Commentary:
Learning from Lǎo Dān,
hence asking for answers on every matter.
Speaking generally without specifics,
thus saying "some people."
Implementing governance and transformation,
making people imitate,
controlling things based on self,
things lose their nature,
thus what is acceptable to oneself,
may be unacceptable to things,
what is true to oneself,
may be untrue to things,
what is acceptable or true to things,
to oneself may be the same.
Disputers say,
separating hardness and whiteness is as clear as hanging in the sky.
Annotation:
Meaning it is highly evident and easy to see.
Commentary:
Hardness and whiteness,
refers to Gōngsūn Lóng's theory of guarding whiteness.
Followers of Kǒng Chuān,
firmly upheld this theory,
unmatched at the time,
with no rivals under heaven.
Now disputers say:
I can separate the theory of hardness and whiteness,
not considering it sophistry,
with clear and eloquent argument,
like hanging the sun and moon in the sky.
Thus Guō Xiàng's annotation says it is highly evident and easy to see.
Can such a person be called a sage?
Commentary:
Concluding the previous question.
Such a person,
can they be considered a sage?
Lǎo Dān said:
These are but petty clerks, skilled yet bound, laboring their bodies and alarming their minds.
Commentary:
"Xū" means mutual.
Meaning they exchange right and wrong to contend,
using these skills to bind themselves,
thus exhausting their bodies,
and alarming their minds.
This answers the previous question.
"Jì" (skill),
some texts use "zhī" (branch),
meaning the exchange of right and wrong,
branches and leaves diverging.
A dog trained to catch foxes becomes anxious,
nimble monkeys are taken from the mountains and forests.
Annotation:
Meaning these all lose their natural state.
Commentary:
"Yuán jū",
means macaques.
Dogs trained to catch foxes,
often wear collars for hunting,
since not free,
thus become anxious.
Monkeys originally dwell in mountains and forests,
roaming freely in openness,
but for their agility in grabbing,
lose their natural abode.
"Lí" (fox),
some texts use "māo" (cat).
The bamboo rat.
Hill,
I tell you,
what you cannot hear and what you cannot speak.
Many are those with heads and feet but without hearts and ears,
Note:
Heads and feet
refer to beginning and end.
Without hearts and ears,
means they transform naturally.
Subcommentary:
Ruò,
ér,
both mean "you."
Heads and feet,
refer to end and beginning.
Reason transcends speech and debate,
thus they cannot hear or speak.
Moreover, it cannot be known through mental deliberation
or heard through the ear's faculty,
hence it is said they lack hearts and ears.
All that have mechanism but no emotion,
are called having end and beginning,
thus it is said they are many.
None can be expressed in words,
nor fully known through the heart,
why do you so often employ the abilities of apes and monkeys,
exalting debates as lofty as suspended dwellings,
making things emulate yourself,
is this not excessive?
Those with form and those without form or shape all existing together—this is entirely nonexistent.
Note:
This means those with form are prone to change,
and cannot coexist with those without form or shape.
Thus, those skilled in governing the Way
do not cling to the old self,
but follow along with the daily renewal of transformations.
Subcommentary:
Those with form,
are the body;
those without form,
are the mind.
You say both mind and body exist,
but when I observe through principle,
I see they are entirely empty.
Their movement,
is stillness;
their death,
is life;
their decline,
is rise.
This, too, is not due to any cause.
Note:
This means movement and stillness, death and life,
flourishing and decline, fall and rise,
have never been constant,
all occur spontaneously,
not because of any deliberate use that makes them so,
thus letting them be leads to natural attainment.
Subcommentary:
Times involve motion and stillness,
things undergo death and life,
affairs experience rise and fall,
these six
are the natural principles,
with no known reason for being so.
How could they be related to human emotions or deliberate thought,
or achieved through imitation and effort?
Simply allow and follow them,
and things will naturally align.
Governance lies with people,
Note:
It does not depend on the ruler acting arbitrarily.
Subcommentary:
Each person follows their nature in action,
their innate mechanism operates spontaneously,
not directed by the ruler's guidance.
Forget things,
forget Heaven,
this is called forgetting oneself.
Note:
When both Heaven and things are forgotten,
not only is the self forgotten,
what else remains?
Subcommentary:
Not only are material affairs empty,
but also heavenly principles are nonexistent.
Only when both affairs and principles
are both forgotten,
can one reach the ultimate state of neither existence nor nonexistence.
Those who forget themselves
are said to have entered into Heaven.
Note:
What people cannot forget
is themselves;
if even the self is forgotten,
what else is there to recognize?
This is to be unknowing and unlearned, merging with the natural.
Subcommentary:
Enter means to unite with.
Moreover, the most difficult thing to forget in the world
is oneself;
if even oneself can be forgotten,
then what thing in the world is worth preserving?
Thus, knowing that both self and things are forgotten,
one can mysteriously unite with the natural Way.
Jiǎng Jiān Wǎn met Jì Chè and said:
The ruler of Lǔ said to Wǎn:
"I request instruction."
Unable to decline the command,
I have already advised him,
but unsure if it was appropriate,
I venture to offer it for your consideration.
Subcommentary: Recommend means to present.
Jiǎng refers to the surname,
a family name.
Wǎn and Chè are personal names.
These two worthies' origins are unknown,
details are unclear.
The ruler of Lǔ,
the Marquis of Lǔ,
descendant of Bó Qín,
unsure which specific duke.
The Duke of Lǔ met Wǎn,
requesting methods of governance,
and though he tried to decline, he could not refuse the ruler's command,
so he advised the Duke on the way of governance.
At that time, following his teacher,
he feared it might not be balanced,
so he dared to present what he had advised,
testing it before this worthy.
If it is unsuitable,
he hopes for correction.
I said to the ruler of Lǔ:
"You must practice reverence and frugality,
promote those who are public-spirited and loyal without favoritism,
then who among the people would dare not be harmonious?"
Subcommentary:
Jí is pronounced like "gather."
Ā means biased.
Shú means who.
Jí means harmony.
The way of governance
first requires personal practice of respect,
frugality, simplicity, and purity,
then promoting fair and loyal individuals,
selecting honest and selfless scholars,
advocating the good and rejecting the bad,
governing the people together,
then the borders will be secure,
the realm peaceful,
the people singing the "Striking the Earth" song,
who would dare not be harmonious?
Jì Chè chuckled and said:
"As for your words,
in terms of the virtue of emperors and kings,
they are like a mantis angrily raising its arms to stop a chariot's tracks,
certainly incapable of succeeding.
Note:
'Must practice reverence and frugality'
is not forgetting frugality while being frugal;
'promote those public-spirited and loyal'
is not forgetting loyalty while being loyal.
Thus, even without favoritism,
it is insufficient to overcome the task of dealing with hypocrisy and deceit.
Subcommentary:
Jú jú means laughing while bending over.
To insist on being reverent and frugal,
promoting public loyalty,
these are all artificial sentiments,
not forgetting simplicity.
Thus, using these words for the virtue of facing south as ruler,
how different is it from a mantis angrily using its arms against a chariot's ruts?
Using the small to compare to the great,
thus it cannot succeed.
Moreover, if so,
then he places himself in danger,
his observation tower
Note:
These all mean positioning oneself high and prominent,
like a tower that can be seen.
Subcommentary:
Public frugality and public loyalty,
not able to forget simplicity,
only serve to show off and dazzle the crowd.
Once people are high and perilous,
they are bound to meet collapse,
like a tall observation tower,
precariously situated,
though travelers may come to see it,
its collapse is not long in coming.
Many,
things will come to it,
Note:
It will cause things not to remain within their innate nature,
but to strain and show off to attach themselves.
Subcommentary:
The observation tower is high and distant,
people compete to see it,
establishing conduct and showing off greatly,
Things contend to gather and flock.
Many follow in their footsteps.
Note:
Lifting feet and tracing steps,
They are unsettled in their original pace.
Explanation:
To dazzle and move creatures,
Creatures become unsettled in their roles,
Hence those lifting feet and tracing steps,
And standing on tiptoe are numerous.
Jiǎng Lǘ Miǎn looked startled and said:
"Miǎn is utterly bewildered by the master's words."
Explanation:
"Startled,"
Means a surprised appearance.
"Bewildered" means seeing nothing.
Suddenly hearing lofty discourse,
He was hastily alarmed,
Reflecting without understanding,
Hence he was bewildered.
Even so,
I wish the master would speak of its influence.
Explanation:
"Influence" means teaching.
What I stated earlier
Was deeply contrary to reason;
I wish for a single word,
Hoping it may serve as a guiding teaching.
Jì Chè said:
"When the great sage governs the world,
He stirs and sways the people's hearts,
Making them form teachings and change customs,
Eradicating all their thieving hearts and advancing their unique wills,
As if by nature's own doing,
And the people do not know how it comes about."
Note:
Great wills each have their own inclinations,
They cannot imitate each other.
Thus, following their self-stirring, he stirs them,
So though stirred, it is not forced;
Following their self-swaying, he sways them,
So though swayed, it is not agitated.
Hence their thieving hearts vanish on their own,
Their unique wills advance naturally,
Teachings form and customs transform,
Vastly without trace,
Treading their nature, they act spontaneously, unknowing of the cause,
All saying, 'It is our own nature.'
"All" means everyone.
Explanation:
When the sage governs the world,
He greatly harmonizes with all beings,
Riding their self-stirring to establish methods,
Using their self-swaying to form teachings;
Thus teachings form without visible traces,
Customs change without things knowing,
All eliminating their harmful hearts,
And cultivating their uniquely transforming wills.
Unmoved by external things,
Hence as if by nature's own doing;
Following nature in action,
Thus unaware of how it comes about.
"All" means everyone.
If so,
Would one still regard Yáo and Shùn as elder brothers in teaching the people,
And reverently treat them as younger brothers?
Note:
"Reverently" means holding in high esteem.
Unwilling to overly thank Yáo and Shùn or elevate them as elders.
Explanation:
"Reverently" means holding in high esteem.
If using the earlier method
To teach the common people,
Then governance would be pure and ancient,
All things would attain their nature,
Why must one uniquely esteem Yáo and Shùn and elevate them as elders!
This implies the ethos of yielding,
Without deferring to Táng and Yú.
Wishing to align with virtue and settle the heart.
Note:
"Settle" means
Not chasing after externals;
If the heart is unsettled, virtue cannot align.
Explanation:
"Settle" means being stable.
If the heart races beyond its bounds,
It encounters things unevenly;
If empty, calm, and still,
Then myriad realms become one.
The differences or similarities among realms
Lie in the calm or turmoil of the heart.
Thus, to wish to align virtue with Yáo and Shùn,
One must first settle the heart.
Zǐgòng traveled south to Chǔ,
Returned to Jìn,
Passed by the south bank of the Hàn River,
Saw an old man preparing a garden plot,
Digging a tunnel to enter the well,
Holding a jar to draw water for irrigation,
Laboring strenuously with much effort but little result.
Explanation:
South of the river is called "yīn,"
Growing vegetables is called a "garden,"
Enclosed plots are called "beds."
"Tunnel" means an underground passage.
"Laboring" describes the effortful appearance.
"Old man" is a term for an elder.
Zǐgòng traveled south to the land of Jīng Chǔ,
Passed by the south bank of the Hàn River,
And thus engaged in dialogue with the old man.
The ebb and flow of their discourse
Is fully in the text.
Zhuāngzǐ recorded these two worthies to illustrate the praise of simplicity.
Zǐgòng said:
"There is a tool here
That can irrigate a hundred beds in one day,
Using little effort but achieving much;
Wouldn't you, master, desire it?"
Explanation:
"Tool" means a machine.
Zǐgòng, seeing the old man's great effort with little gain,
Thus taught him about the tool,
Hoping for less effort and more result.
He offered his simple sincerity,
Uncertain if it was desired.
The gardener looked up and said:
"How?"
Explanation:
"How"
Means "in what way,"
Asking about the method.
He said:
"Carve wood into a machine,
Heavy in back, light in front,
Lifting water as if drawing it,
Rapid like boiling water overflowing,
Its name is the shadoof."
Explanation:
"Machine" means a mechanism.
Lifting the water,
Irrigating as if drawing it,
To speak of its speed,
It resembles boiling water bubbling over,
Light in front, heavy in back,
It is what we now call the well-sweep.
The gardener, angered, changed expression and laughed:
"I have heard from my teacher:
Those with machinery inevitably have mechanical affairs,
Those with mechanical affairs inevitably have mechanical hearts.
If a mechanical heart resides in the breast,
Then pure whiteness is not preserved;
If pure whiteness is not preserved,
Then the spirit becomes unsettled;
If the spirit is unsettled,
It is not supported by the Dào.
It's not that I don't know,
But I am ashamed to do it."
Note:
Using what is timely and useful
Leads to pure preparedness.
This person wishes to cultivate pure preparedness
By clinging to one and guarding the past,
Missing the essential meaning.
Explanation:
Those with contrived tools
Inevitably have mechanical tasks;
Those with mechanical tasks
Inevitably have scheming hearts.
With scheming in the heart,
Pure, simple whiteness is incomplete.
If pure, simple whiteness is incomplete,
The spirit hangs in uncertainty,
Rising and falling unsteadily.
If unsteady,
The ultimate Dào does not support it,
Hence ashamed and unwilling to do it.
This shows he has not yet embodied true cultivation,
Thus clinging to one and guarding whiteness.
Zǐgòng looked ashamed,
Bowed and did not reply.
Explanation:
"Ashamed" describes a embarrassed appearance.
Having misspoken,
He did not know how to respond.
