After a while,
The gardener said:
"Who are you?"
Note:
"After a while"
Means a short time.
"Who" means what.
Asking Zǐgòng:
"Under whose disciple are you?
What study do you pursue?"
He said:
"A follower of Kǒng Qiū."
Explanation:
Answer: A disciple of Confucius.
The gardener said:
"Aren't you the one who, with broad learning, aspires to be a sage,
Do you use flattery and sycophancy to cover up the masses,
strumming a lone string and singing mournful songs to sell your reputation throughout the world?
Subcommentary:
"Yú yú" refers to being obsequious and fawning.
It means that with your broad learning and extensive knowledge,
you imitate the sages,
flattering and currying favor,
to overshadow all things;
sitting alone, playing strings and singing,
modulating mournful sighs,
holding onto these traces of sageliness,
peddling that reputation of yours,
traveling to various states on invitations,
roaming all over the world.
You should forget your spirit and energy,
let go of your physical form,
and then you might come close!
Commentary:
If you do not forget and do not let go,
then there is no way to come close.
Subcommentary:
"Jī" means near.
You should forget and discard your spirit and energy,
break down your physical body,
once both mind and body are forgotten,
then you may come near to the Way.
If you cannot govern your own self,
what leisure do you have to govern the world!
You may go now,
do not hinder my affairs!
Subcommentary:
"Ér" means you.
"Fá" means to lack or hinder.
When all things govern themselves,
then the world is in order;
to impose order on things from oneself,
then great chaos ensues.
With the virtue of someone like Zǐgòng,
it is insufficient to govern oneself,
how could one respond to invitations throughout the world!
It is fitting to go quickly,
and not abandon my endeavors.
Zǐgòng looked ashamed and changed countenance,
disconcerted and ill at ease,
and only after walking thirty li did he recover.
Subcommentary:
"Bēi zōu" describes an appearance of shame.
"Xū xū" describes a look of self-loss.
Having been rebuked and criticized,
his countenance showed loss,
after walking thirty li,
he finally returned to normal.
His disciples said:
What kind of person was that one we met?
Why did you, Master, upon seeing him, change expression and lose composure,
all day long not returning to yourself?
Subcommentary:
"Fǎn" means to return or recover.
Zǐgòng's disciples refer to Cì (Zǐgòng) as "Master."
That person we met earlier,
what practice did he cultivate,
that upon seeing him, sir,
your expression and composure became abnormal,
all day long,
your spirit and energy did not recover?
The disciples found it strange,
hence they asked.
He said:
Initially, I thought there was only one person in the world,
Commentary:
Referring to Confucius.
I did not know there was another such man.
Subcommentary:
In the past, I received learning,
thinking within the world there was only the Master (Confucius);
now I have met this elder,
whose Dào and virtue are even more profound and far-reaching,
hence I felt ashamed and could not be at ease.
Not having fully grasped the true and the false,
I truly thought he was more worthy than Zhòngní (Confucius).
I have heard from my Master that
in affairs, one seeks what is acceptable,
in achievements, one seeks success.
Using little effort,
yet seeing much achievement—
that is the Way of the sage.
Commentary:
The Way of the sage
is simply to use the hearts of the common people.
Subcommentary:
Affairs are considered acceptable if they suit the times,
achievements are considered successful if they can be accomplished.
Thus, using little effort and seeing much achievement
means fitting the opportunity for accomplishment.
Zǐgòng recounted what he had heard in the past,
considering it the Way of the sage.
But now it is not so.
One who holds fast to the Dào has virtue complete,
one whose virtue is complete has form complete,
one whose form is complete has spirit complete.
One whose spirit is complete—
that is the Way of the sage.
Entrusted with life, he walks alongside the people without knowing where he is going,
vast and profound, pure and complete indeed!
Personal gain, profit, schemes, and cleverness must be forgotten in such a person's heart.
Commentary:
This is the Way of the sage king,
not that of an ordinary man.
Zǐgòng heard his talk of artificial cultivation and was convinced by it.
He did not know that one of pure whiteness is in harmony with the world.
Subcommentary:
Now this elder's words to me
are not like that.
It means that one who holds fast to the Dào has virtue without deficiency,
one whose virtue is complete has form undamaged,
one whose form is complete has spirit concentrated and unified.
One whose spirit is complete entrusts his traces to the human world,
lives among the same generation,
though walking alongside all things,
does not know where he is going,
obscure and profound,
immeasurable.
Therefore, his conduct is pure and harmonious,
his Dào and virtue are perfectly complete,
one cannot speak to his heart of personal gain, profit, schemes, and cleverness.
This is the Way of the sage,
not the method of artificial cultivation.
Zǐgòng, not yet awakened,
spoke recklessly.
As for such a man (the elder),
if it is not his intention, he does not go,
if it is not his heart's desire, he does not act.
Even if the whole world praises him,
and he receives what is said of him,
he remains aloof and pays no heed;
if the whole world criticizes him,
and he loses what is said of him,
he remains untroubled and does not accept it.
The world's criticism or praise
brings him no benefit or harm,
this is what is called a person of complete virtue!
I am what is called a person of wind and waves.
Commentary:
These are the followers of Sòng Róngzǐ,
not sufficient to be considered of complete virtue.
Zǐgòng's delusion and immersion in this man
is like Lièzǐ's heart being intoxicated by Jì Xián.
Subcommentary:
"Áo" describes a contemptuous and negligent demeanor,
"tǎng" is an appearance of nonchalance.
The elder's will and energy are pure and simple,
he does not engage in schemes and cleverness,
his heart harbors few desires,
he does not strive to be active.
Even if the entire world praised him,
calling it this virtue,
knowing it brings no benefit,
he would not even glance back;
if the entire world criticized and slandered him,
causing him to lose his reputation,
understanding that it does no harm,
he would completely not accept it;
since neither slander nor praise moves him,
he can be called a person of complete virtue.
Now, though water's nature is clear,
when it meets wind, waves arise;
my mind is not settled,
resembling those waves,
therefore I am called a person of wind and waves.
Guǒ Xiàng's commentary says,
these are the followers of Sòng Róngzǐ,
not sufficient to be considered of complete virtue.
Zǐgòng's delusion and immersion in this man
is like Lièzǐ's heart being intoxicated by Jì Xián.
He returned to Lǔ,
and reported it to Confucius.
Confucius said:
He is one who artificially cultivates the art of the Hùndùn clan;
Commentary:
Because he turns his back on the present and faces the ancient,
ashamed to engage in worldly affairs,
we know he is not truly of Hùndùn.
Subcommentary:
Zǐgòng went from Lǔ to Chǔ,
and returned to Lǔ,
reporting the circumstances
to consult and inform Confucius.
Now, Hùndùn means without distinction.
Since he turns his back on the present and faces the ancient,
it is said he is not a true one.
He knows the one,
but does not know the two;
Commentary:
He only knows the simplicity of cultivating antiquity and holding to irrigation (past ways),
and does not know the ease of following the times and responding to things.
Subcommentary:
"Knowing the one"
means being fixed on antiquity and unwilling to change.
"Not knowing the two"
It is said that they cannot adapt to the present and adjust to change.
They govern their inner selves,
but do not govern the external world.
Commentary:
The truly undifferentiated and chaotic,
do not govern at all—
how could they distinguish between inner and outer and partially govern one aspect?
Subcommentary:
Holding to the Way and preserving simplicity—
this is governing the inner;
being unable to respond to the times and adapt to changes—
this is not governing the external.
Those who are clear and pure, entering simplicity,
acting through non-action and returning to the unhewn,
embodying their nature and embracing the spirit,
to wander among the世俗—
would you really be startled?
Commentary:
This is true undifferentiated chaos,
thus flowing with the world without losing oneself;
even while wandering in the世俗, they vanish without a trace—
how could they necessarily startle you?
Subcommentary:
With a mind clear and bright,
they unite with the root of质朴;
through non-action and emptiness,
they return to the origin of淳朴.
Awakened to their true nature and embracing essence and purity,
blending with the clamor and dust while wandering in the世俗—
they naturally align with the rivers and seas of living beings,
the forests and marshes of all things;
birds and beasts do not flee—
how could humans be startled?
Saying "you would really be startled"
clarifies that they certainly will not be.
Moreover, the methods of the undifferentiated and chaotic,
how could you and I fully comprehend them?
Commentary:
There, it is that;
here, it is this;
undifferentiated and mysteriously one—
who can comprehend it?
What is comprehended is often just its traces.
Subcommentary:
The undifferentiated has no mind,
transcending thought and wisdom;
even if sages and worthies appear in time,
how could they fully comprehend it?
It is elusive and profoundly mysterious,
thus pushing it beyond the realm of emotion and intention.
Zhūnmáng was going east to the great abyss,
and happened to meet Yuànfēng on the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Subcommentary:
Zhūn means pure.
Yuàn
means a gentle wind,
also said to be a great whirlwind.
Shores, the edge;
great abyss, the sea.
Zhūnmáng and Yuànfēng
are both allegorical figures.
Zhuāngzǐ uses these two characters
to illuminate the Great Way,
thus employing host and guest
meeting by the sea's edge.
Yuànfēng said:
Where are you going?
Subcommentary:
Xī means what.
Zhī means to go.
Asking Zhūnmáng
where he is traveling to.
He said:
I am going to the great abyss.
Subcommentary:
Intending to go to the Eastern Sea.
He said:
What will you do there?
Subcommentary:
Again asking what he seeks there.
He said:
The great abyss as an entity,
pours into it but it does not fill,
draws from it but it does not exhaust;
I will wander there.
Subcommentary:
The vastness of the great sea,
deep and far, hard to fathom;
a hundred rivers flow into it without overflowing,
the尾闾 drains it without drying up.
Using it as a metaphor for the ultimate principle,
its meaning is likewise.
Thus, though he journeys to the azure depths,
he is truly wandering in mind along the Great Way.
Yuànfēng said:
Do you, sir, have no concern for the横目 people?
I wish to hear about sage governance.
Subcommentary:
Within the five elements,
only humans have横目,
thus they are called横目 people.
Moreover, Zhūnmáng travels east,
arriving at the great abyss,
observing its depth and vastness,
to formulate methods of governance.
Yuànfēng, perceiving this intent,
thus poses this question:
Do you, sir, have no regard for the common people?
I wish to hear the methods of sage transformation.
Zhūnmáng said:
Sage governance?
Appoint officials without missing what is fitting,
promote and recommend without overlooking ability.
Subcommentary:
Issuing decrees and establishing offices,
ensuring they are appropriate and suitable;
selecting and recommending,
without missing talent.
Knowing this leads to great peace under heaven,
the natural order properly arranged;
the method of sage governance
lies herein.
Fully perceive the circumstances and act accordingly.
Commentary:
All follow and rely on it.
Subcommentary:
Where there are deviations and conflicts,
affairs and tasks are manifold;
thus, steps differ with the times,
simplicity and complexity vary with the age.
Hence, those who govern must first rely on things,
necessarily observing the circumstances and examining their actions,
then following things and acting accordingly—
then nothing will be amiss.
Actions and words arise from themselves, and the world is transformed.
Commentary:
If things are made to act,
they will not transform.
Subcommentary:
All actions undertaken,
all teachings and decrees spoken,
entirely let things act of themselves,
without making things follow oneself.
In this way,
all living beings under heaven naturally follow and transform.
A wave of the hand or a glance,
and the people from all directions all come—
this is called sage governance.
Commentary:
It means that with a gesture or a look, the people each fulfill their nature,
because they are allowed to act of themselves.
Subcommentary:
Rǎo means to move.
It means moving a finger to direct,
raising the eyes to glance,
and all directions submit sincerely,
myriad states come to pay homage.
The efficacy of sage governance
is thus described.
Some texts have the word "manifest,"
meaning to use manifest direction,
and all directions submit.
Here, there are three types of persons:
first, the sage,
second, the virtuous,
third, the spiritual;
above is sage governance,
below follow in order the virtuous and the spiritual.
I wish to hear about the virtuous person.
Subcommentary:
The previous sage governance
has been explained;
the meaning of the virtuous person
I deeply wish to hear.
He said:
The virtuous person
dwells without thought,
acts without deliberation.
Commentary:
Simply follow nature.
Subcommentary:
Marvelously united with the realm of the Way,
attaining what is without attainment—
thus called the virtuous person.
The virtuous person concentrates spirit and sits upright,
serene and without thought; even when responding to things and acting in transformation, there is no deliberation.
They do not harbor right and wrong, beauty and ugliness.
Commentary:
No right or wrong in the breast, but entrust it to the world.
Subcommentary:
Embracing the Way and upholding virtue,
both self and others are forgotten—
how could they harbor right and wrong,
or store up good and evil?
Within the four seas, sharing benefits brings joy,
sharing provisions brings peace.
Commentary:
There is no heart of selfishness.
Subcommentary:
The virtuous person's grace is broad and extensive,
It universally extends to all beings,
thus wealth and benefits are shared across the four seas,
resources are distributed without distinction among the myriad people,
this is the celebration and joy under heaven,
peace and tranquility throughout the land.
As disconsolate as an infant losing its mother,
as bewildered as a traveler losing the way.
Explanation:
When an infant loses its mother,
the heart is disconsolate and without reliance;
when a traveler loses the path,
the spirit is bewildered and without foundation.
Using these two analogies,
to illustrate the virtuous person.
Having ample wealth without knowing its source,
taking sufficient food and drink without knowing its origin,
this describes the demeanor of the virtuous person.
Annotation:
Virtue is,
the trace of the spiritual person,
hence called demeanor.
Explanation:
Few desires and knowing contentment,
thus wealth is ample;
not craving flavors,
thus food and drink are sufficient;
making no demands on life and nature,
thus not knowing where they come from.
Summarizing the previous meaning,
thus it says the demeanor of the virtuous person.
I wish to hear about the spiritual person.
Annotation:
Wishing to hear about the source of the traces.
Explanation:
Virtue is,
merely the trace of the spiritual person,
wishing to hear about the source of the traces.
It is said:
The highest spiritual person rides light,
and with form perishes,
Annotation:
Riding light means having no light.
Explanation:
Riding means using.
Light means wisdom.
The highest spiritual person,
uses wisdom to illuminate things,
although the light is like the sun and moon,
it illuminates and then vanishes,
abandoning body and dismissing hearing,
both mind and form are relinquished,
thus one perishes with form.
This is called illuminating vastness.
Annotation:
No self and following things,
empty and without attachments,
not darkness or obstruction.
Explanation:
Wisdom encompassing all things,
brightness surpassing the three luminaries,
no darkness unilluminated,
is this not vast and far-reaching!
Fulfilling destiny and exhausting emotions,
heaven and earth rejoice and all affairs vanish,
Annotation:
When emotions are exhausted and destiny fulfilled,
heaven and earth rejoice.
Affairs do not hinder joy,
thus there are no affairs.
Explanation:
Reaching the ultimate of life and nature,
exhausting the emotions of life and transformation,
thus dwelling between heaven and earth, yet always free and joyful.
Having realized the illusoriness of self and things,
thus all affairs vanish.
All things return to their true emotions,
this is called chaotic darkness.
Annotation:
Emotions return and chaotic darkness leaves no trace.
Explanation:
Forgetting illumination yet illuminating,
illumination equals the three luminaries in height and brightness;
forgetting life yet living,
life brings joy together with the two modes.
Thus able to observe the return of all things to their origin,
witness the return to destiny of the four kinds of birth,
therefore chaotic and undifferentiated, darkly united in the one Way.
Mén Wúguǐ and Chìzhāng Mǎnjī observed King Wǔ's army.
Explanation:
Mén and Chìzhāng are surnames.
Wúguǐ, Mǎnjī are personal names.
Two thousand five hundred men form an army,
army means,
multitude.
King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu,
the troops crossed the Mèngjīn River,
at that time these two men observed together.
Chìzhāng Mǎnjī said:
Not equal to Yǒuyúshì!
Thus they encountered this disaster.
Explanation:
Encounter means suffer.
Yú Shùn used abdication to rule his time,
King Wǔ used warfare to save the world.
But abdication and warfare,
are vastly different in quality.
Judging by this,
there are mutual words of inadequacy.
And weapons are instruments of ill omen,
thus they suffered the disaster of slaughter.
Mén Wúguǐ said:
Was the world orderly and Yǒuyúshì governed it?
Or was it in chaos and then he brought order?
Annotation:
Meaning both sages brought order because of chaos,
thus abdication and using armies,
merely differ in timing,
with no superiority between them.
Explanation:
Orderly means peaceful.
If the world was peaceful,
and all things were in order,
why would Yú Shùn need to establish laws to govern!
Truly because Yáo's time was declining,
his virtue daily waning,
thus he yielded to Chónghuá,
to have him restore order.
Chìzhāng Mǎnjī said:
The wish for the world to be orderly,
why then consider Yǒuyúshì!
Annotation:
If orderly, then wishes are each fulfilled,
why calculate Yǒuyúshì's virtue and promote him as ruler!
Mén Wúguǐ's words are correct.
Explanation:
When the world is clear and peaceful,
wishes and aspirations are each fulfilled,
why need to calculate Yǒuyúshì's virtue and promote him as ruler!
This understands Mén Wúguǐ's words,
acknowledging their reason.
Yǒuyúshì's treatment of sores,
Annotation:
The world all suffers from wounds and chaos,
thus seeking Yǒuyúshì's medicine.
Explanation:
Sore means head ulcer.
When the body has sores,
one seeks medical treatment,
just as when the world encounters turmoil,
it requires a sage to govern it.
Thus without illness, no physician is needed,
without chaos, no sage is needed.
Baldness then wearing a wig,
illness then seeking a doctor.
Explanation:
Hair thick as clouds,
no need to wear a wig;
fortunately without illness,
why borrow a physician!
Thus knowing when the world is clear and peaceful,
no need for a great sage.
These two lines,
summarize the previous two matters.
A filial son prepares medicine for his kind father,
his countenance haggard,
the sage is ashamed of this.
Annotation:
Illustrating that governing the world,
is not for glory.
Explanation:
Prepare means hold.
Manage means arrange.
Haggard means worn-out appearance.
The filial son caring for his kind father,
does not boast of his achievements;
the sage saving from disaster and chaos,
how could he boast for glory and prominence!
Acting out of necessity,
thus ashamed of it.
In the age of ultimate virtue,
the worthy are not exalted,
Annotation:
The worthy fit their positions,
not exalted above.
Explanation:
The unworthy and the worthy,
each fit their lot,
not exalted to distinguish the worthy.
The able are not employed;
Annotation:
The able act on their own,
not employed by others.
Explanation:
Those above are simple by nature,
not competing or aspiring,
not exalted and employed.
Those above are like high branches,
Annotation:
Above things yet not self-exalting.
Explanation:
The ruler resides above the people,
serene and free from desires,
like the branches of a tall tree,
with no intention for glory or nobility.
The people are like wild deer;
Note:
Roaming freely and content in their nature.
Explanation:
Since the ruler above practices non-action,
those below remain pure and simple,
akin to wild deer,
untouched by the rituals of kings and lords.
They are upright yet unaware it is righteousness,
love one another yet unaware it is benevolence,
Explanation:
Their hearts are straightforward,
free from wickedness and evil,
how would they recognize the principle of rectifying wrongs?
Following the natural order,
they draw closer to one another,
how could they know of partial, affectionate benevolence?
They are sincere yet unaware it is loyalty,
appropriate yet unaware it is trustworthiness,
Note:
They follow their innate nature spontaneously,
not out of conscious knowledge.
Explanation:
By nature, they are genuine,
unaware that this genuineness is loyalty;
acting according to reason,
how would they consider this appropriateness as trustworthiness?
They move instinctively and assist one another,
without considering it a favor.
Note:
They act by their own impulse,
hence they act without gratitude.
Explanation:
Favor means receiving kindness.
Creatures that move instinctively,
being sentient beings,
drive each other forward,
as it is naturally reasonable.
Like one's limbs,
or one's eyes and ears,
they have no intention in their making,
how could they feel grateful for relying on them?
Governing things through non-action,
the principle is the same.
Thus, actions leave no traces,
Note:
The ruler lets them act on their own,
hence no traces are left.
Explanation:
The ruler and people are pure and simple,
harmony prevails above and below,
acting according to their nature,
so there are no traces to record.
Events are not passed down.
Note:
Each remains within their own role,
thus no teachings are transmitted to others.
Explanation:
Just as the head and feet,
each has its own duties,
staying within their bounds,
without exchanging or learning from each other.
Since traces are obscure,
events too vanish.
A filial son does not flatter his parents,
a loyal minister does not fawn on his ruler,
this is the pinnacle of being a subject or child.
Explanation:
Serving one's parents well is filial piety.
Flattery means falsity.
Fawning means deception.
Not seeking through upright means is called fawning.
As a subject or child,
serving father or ruler,
without fawning or flattery,
fulfilling loyalty and filial duty,
this is the supreme virtue of subjects and children.
If one agrees with everything the parent says,
and praises all they do,
then the world calls them an unworthy child;
if one agrees with everything the ruler says,
and praises all they do,
then the world calls them an unworthy minister.
But is this necessarily so?
Note:
This is merely opposing custom to follow parent or ruler,
so the world calls them unworthy,
not knowing where true correctness lies.
Explanation:
Unworthy means not resembling.
The words and actions of ruler or parent,
regardless of good or evil,
one simply follows along,
without any mind to admonish or dispute,
thus in the eyes of the world,
they are indeed unworthy,
not knowing where the true principle may be affirmed.
If what the world deems right, one deems right,
what the world deems good, one deems good,
then one is not called a flatterer.
Does this mean the world is stricter than parents and more revered than the ruler?
Note:
It says the world does not revere parents or rulers more,
yet following the world,
one is not called a flatterer,
showing that reverence alone does not convince people,
rather, convincing lies in conforming to custom.
Thus, the sage never stands alone against the world,
but always aligns with the times,
so in the era of Huáng, they are like Huáng,
in the era of Wáng, they are like Wáng,
how could they oppose custom and act solely on their own?
Explanation:
Strict means teaching.
This clarifies the uncertainty of opposition or conformity.
If the world approves and praises,
then admonishing and disputing are right.
Opposing custom to follow parents,
is called flattery,
while opposing parents to follow custom,
is that not sycophancy?
Moreover, there is opposition and compliance,
hence views of right and wrong,
but since both opposition and compliance are empty,
where does true correctness lie?
Also, opposing parents to follow custom,
how can that be called revering parents and rulers?
If told they mislead others,
they flare up in anger;
if told they flatter others,
they scowl in displeasure.
Note:
The world takes widespread agreement as correctness,
so if called misleading or flattering,
they show anger and refuse the label.
Yet they mislead others all their lives,
flatter others all their lives,
Note:
Without questioning principles,
only aiming to get along.
Explanation:
Flare,
scowl,
both are expressions of anger.
Misleading means guiding,
directing,
referring to using sycophancy to curry favor with rulers or parents.
When worldly people
are told they are sycophants,
they react with anger,
refusing the title,
yet they mislead and flatter throughout their lives,
and the whole world is like this.
Using analogies and ornate speech to gather crowds,
this is how beginning and end, root and branch, avoid blame.
Note:
Employing analogies and ornate speech
should incur the charge of misleading and flattering,
yet the world gains followers and gathers crowds this way,
and those who conform are never held accountable.
Explanation:
Being able to use fitting analogies,
adorn with flowery words,
attracting people to rush forward,
thus gathering a crowd,
ensuring consistency from start to finish,
aligning root and branch;
since the crowd follows them,
they are not held accountable.
Analogy,
some texts use the character for 'jade disc',
meaning assembling jade discs.
Draping robes and skirts,
displaying colors,
altering expressions,
to charm an entire age,
yet not considering it misleading or flattering,
associating with such people,
sharing their views of right and wrong,
yet not considering themselves part of the crowd,
this is the height of foolishness.
Note:
The world is utterly foolish,
so one must conform all the more.
Explanation:
Huángdì draped robes and skirts to bring order to the world,
upper garment and lower skirt,
symbolizing heaven and earth,
red and purple hues,
interwoven to create splendor,
using such adornments,
changing expressions,
to charm an age,
superficial and false people,
do not call it misleading or flattering,
instead, they follow the ruler in sycophancy.
This is to associate with those vulgar people and their factions,
mutually taking sides,
interchangeably judging right and wrong,
considering themselves superior to the masses,
which can be said to be the height of foolishness and ignorance.
Those who know their own foolishness
are not the most foolish;
those who know their own confusion
are not the most confused.
The most confused
remain bewildered their entire lives;
the most foolish
remain unintelligent their entire lives.
Note:
The way of the sage is the same, yet the traces of emperors and kings differ,
truly because the confusion of the world cannot be resolved,
thus they follow and let it be.
Explanation:
To resolve means to understand.
Intelligent means wise.
Those who know their own foolishness and confusion
are sages.
Following and letting it be,
thus foolishness is not confusion.
The most foolish and confused
are ordinary people,
their minds dark and base,
confused upon encountering situations,
hence they remain unawakened throughout their lives.
If three people travel and one is confused,
the destination can still be reached,
because the confused are few;
if two are confused, they toil but do not arrive,
because the confused outnumber the clear.
But now the whole world is confused,
even if I have aspirations and directions,
they cannot be attained.
Is this not lamentable!
Note:
The whole world is confused,
even if I have the desire to seek the ultimate way, it ultimately cannot be attained.
Thus, Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ
merely adapted to their times.
Explanation:
To go means to proceed.
To attain means to reach.
Confused means lost.
To aspire means to seek.
When three people travel together,
if one loses the way,
the intended destination
can still be reached,
because the clear outnumber the confused;
if two are lost, they labor in vain and do not arrive,
because the lost outnumber the clear.
Now the entire world is lost,
even if Zhuāngzǐ has the desire to seek the ultimate way,
there is no means to attain it,
thus it is lamentable.
Grand music does not enter the ears of the village
Note: It is not valued in the narrow alleys.
But play "Zhé Yáng" or "Huáng Huā" and they laugh heartily

Note: When vulgar people hear sentimental tunes, they laugh together. Explanation: Grand music refers to melodies like Xiánchí and Dàsháo, not heard in the villages and alleys. "Zhé Yáng" and "Huáng Huá" are likely ancient popular ditties. Their playful and rustic nature makes people laugh heartily together. In the past, Marquis Wén of Wèi listened to ancient music and drowsily fell asleep, but upon hearing the new tunes of Zhèng and Wèi, he was delighted—this illustrates the point.
Therefore, lofty words do not linger in the hearts of the masses

Note: They do not hold them in mind. Explanation: The most profound discourse transcends vulgarity, hence called lofty words. They are fit to be stored in the spiritual treasury of sages—how could they linger in the minds of the masses? Just as grand music does not enter village ears, lofty words certainly do not linger in common hearts.
The ultimate words do not prevail; vulgar words triumph.

Note: This is why the world never employs sages but always relies on itself. Explanation: To prevail means to be prominent. The words of the ultimate way are plain and flavorless, not entering the ears of the alleyways, let alone lingering in the hearts of the masses. Yet vulgar words, adorned and false, are like the tune "Zhé Yáng," pleasing to many listeners. Since vulgar talk dominates, the ultimate words remain hidden. Thus, in "The Equality of Things," it is said: "Words are hidden by flowery rhetoric."
If two people stand confused, the destination cannot be reached.

Note: Each relies on their own view, thus not knowing where to go. Explanation: To stand means to plant one's feet. Those who lose direction, pointing north as south—once two are confused, neither can move forward, and one alone cannot advance either. How could they reach the intended destination? This further explains the earlier point about confusion.
But now the whole world is confused; even if I have aspirations, how could they be attained?

Explanation: If two standing confused find it hard to reach their destination, how much more when the whole world is lost—how can it be set right? Thus, even with the desire to seek direction, it surely cannot be attained. This explains the earlier "Is this not lamentable!" The depth of sorrow warrants this emphasis.
Knowing it cannot be attained yet forcing it is another confusion. Thus, it is better to let it go and not push.

Note: Accept and align with it. Explanation: To let go means to release. Since confusion is deep and hard to resolve quickly, forcing correction is another folly. It is better to release and not push, thus both self and others are at peace.
Not pushing—with whom then would one share worries?

Note: Allow them to find timely comfort without forcing resolution; thus, all can be worry-free for a lifetime. Explanation: To share means to be with. If one lets things be, abandons confusion without pushing, then all wander freely—with whom would worries be shared?
An ugly person, giving birth at midnight, quickly brings a light to look, anxiously fearing the child resembles herself.

Note: "Ugly" means a bad person. This says all under heaven do not wish to be evil; some are forced by harsh labor, some are misled and lose their nature. However, the confused think of returning, and the ugly think of goodness, thus I do nothing and the world transforms itself. Explanation: "Ugly" means disfigured or ill. "Quickly" means hastily. "Anxiously" describes a rushed manner. The ugly person, giving birth at midnight, hastily brings a light to see, worried the child might resemble her ugliness. Even the severely ugly hope to change from ugly to fair—this illustrates that the foolish and confused surely detest their迷失 and think of awakening. Letting go without pushing naturally brings no worries.

A hundred-year-old tree is cut to make a sacrificial vessel, adorned with blue and yellow patterns, while the discarded part lies in a ditch. Comparing the vessel to the ditch fragment, there is a difference in beauty and ugliness, but in losing their nature, they are the same.

Explanation: The vessel is carved in the shape of a sacrificial ox for rituals, called a "xī zūn." "Difference" means distinction. Once carved into an ox and decorated with blue and yellow patterns, one part is discarded in a ditch, unused. Comparing the two fragments, beauty and ugliness differ, but in losing their original nature, they are identical. This is an analogy.
Between Zhí and Zēng Shǐ, there is a difference in conduct and righteousness, but in losing their nature, they are equal.
Explanation: This is the conclusion. The tyranny of Jié and Zhí, and the benevolence of Zēng Shǐ—though their good and evil deeds differ, in losing their true nature, they are truly the same.
Moreover, there are five ways to lose one's nature:
Explanation: Losing one's nature through delusion has many aspects, but in summary, there are five.
First, the five colors confuse the eyes, making them unclear.
Explanation: The five colors are green, yellow, red, white, and black. The vulgar indulge greedily, confusing the eyes so they cannot see truth, hence "unclear."
Second, the five sounds confuse the ears, making them unhearing.
Explanation: The five sounds are gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, yǔ. Indulging in vulgar sounds prevents hearing the way, hence "unhearing."
Third, the five odors assail the nose, causing congestion and pain in the forehead.

Explanation: The five odors are rank, fragrant, fishy, rotten, and putrid. "Congestion" means blocked and impassable. The nose, indulging in the five odors, becomes blocked and hurts the forehead. External texts call them "odors," as in the Yì Jīng: "Its odor is like orchids." Daoist scriptures refer to them as "five fragrances," hence the Xī Shēng Jīng says: "Fragrance and taste are grievances."
Fourth, the five flavors foul the mouth, causing it to become diseased and impaired.

Explanation: The five flavors are sour, pungent, sweet, bitter, and salty. "Diseased" means ill; "impaired" means losing function. Indulging in the five flavors fouls the mouth's root, leading to ailments from salt and bitterness, and the tongue loses its taste, hence "diseased and impaired."
Fifth, preferences and aversions扰乱 the heart, causing the nature to become flighty.

Explanation: "Preferences" mean to take; "扰乱" means to disturb. Following the heart means taking, opposing feelings means rejecting—this扰乱s the heart, making the natural nature restless and frivolously agitated, hence "flighty."
These five are all harms to life.
Explanation: Summarizing the previous five, all are like blades that cut life, axes that harm it—great harms to the people.
Yet Yáng and Mò began to strive forcefully, considering it attainment—but this is not what I call attainment.

Explanation: "Strive forcefully" describes exerting effort. Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí each boasted their own abilities, losing nature and harming life, considering this attainment. Since it violates natural principle, it is not what Zhuāngzǐ calls attainment.
If those who are trapped can be considered to have attained, then turtledoves and owls in cages can also be considered to have attained.

Explanation: Benevolence, righteousness, rites, and laws that bind the heart are not true nature. Once nature is falsified, it suffers hardship. If such entrapment is considered attainment, how is it different from turtledoves and owls in cages claiming self-attainment?
Moreover, preferences and aversions, sounds and colors, barricade the inside; leather caps and kingfisher crowns, tablets and sashes, constrain the outside.

Explanation: "Leather caps" are hats made of leather. "Kingfisher" is a bird name, resembling a teal, azure, from Yùlín—its feathers used to adorn hats, hence "kingfisher crowns." This bird knows astronomy, so its feathers are used for crowns. "Tablets" mean to insert; "tablets" are the tablets held. "Sashes" are large belts; "long skirts" are robes. These all adorn court attire. The浮伪之徒 make preferences their trade, so sounds and colors barricade their inner storehouse, while clothing and tablets constrain their outer form. Turning from the way of non-action and violating natural nature—calling this attainment is no different from turtledoves and owls.

Inside, limbs are filled with barricades; outside, bound with multiple ropes—staring blankly within the ropes yet considering it attainment. Then criminals with bound arms and fingers, or tigers and leopards in bags and cages, could also be considered to have attained.

Explanation: "Limbs" mean blocked; "filled" means full; "barricades" are fences; "ropes" are cords; "staring blankly" describes the gaze. With preferences barricading the inner storehouse, and officials constraining the outer form, it is like being bound by ropes. So trapped and yet considering it attainment—how is it different from criminals with arms bound and fingers restrained by ropes? Or like tigers and leopards trapped in bags and cages—no distress greater than this. Considering it attainment—how does it differ?
Nán Huá Zhēn Jīng Annotation and Explanation, Volume 14.
The Nanhua Zhenjing Commentary, Scroll Fifteen, Part One
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá in the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters: The Way of Heaven, Chapter Thirteen
The Way of Heaven operates without accumulation, thus all things are accomplished.

Subcommentary: "Operates" means movement and transformation; "accumulation" means stagnation or hoarding. This says the Way of Heaven revolves and operates, nurturing all living beings, illuminating them with the sun and moon, moistening them with rain and dew, stirring and molding them, never stagnating or accumulating. Therefore, the four seasons revolve, and all things are generated and completed.
The Way of the Emperor operates without accumulation, thus all under heaven submit.

Subcommentary: The king models himself on heaven and earth, operating and governing all beings, dispersing without accumulation, transforming without fixed methods. Thus, the six directions unite in submission, and the eight regions sincerely adhere.
The Way of the Sage operates without accumulation, thus all within the seas submit.

Commentary: These three all follow the nature of things without any obstruction. Subcommentary: The Way of the Sage is the way of the mysterious sage and uncrowned king. Responding accordingly, leaving traces, establishing laws and teachings, like a boat ferrying the conscious, saving and aiding endlessly. Their way aligns with heaven, their virtue matches the emperor's. Their positions differ, hence there are the two ways of Emperor and Sage. Operating with wisdom to save the age, also without stagnation or hoarding, their compassion and creation are vast and broad, thus all within the seas submit.
One who understands heaven, comprehends the sage, and is thoroughly versed in the virtue of emperors and kings, acts spontaneously, silently and entirely tranquil.

Commentary: Letting them act spontaneously, thus even though thoroughly versed, it does not harm tranquility. Subcommentary: "Thoroughly versed" refers to the four directions, above and below. "Versed in the four" refers to spring, autumn, winter, and summer. Only by illuminating the non-action of the Way of Heaven, penetrating the sage's absence of concern, comprehending the six directions for transformation and generation, following the four seasons in actions—with this to rule over ten thousand chariots, one can be said to possess the virtue of emperors and kings. Letting things move spontaneously is called spontaneous action. Concealing traces and hiding light is like darkness. Movement does not harm stillness, thus it is entirely tranquil.
The sage's tranquility is not called tranquility because it is good, hence tranquil.

Commentary: If it is tranquil because it is good, then there are times when it moves. Subcommentary: The reason the sage is empty and tranquil is directly like the body resembling a withered tree, the mind like dead ashes, also not knowing why it is tranquil, hence tranquil. If one considers tranquility as good and beautiful and has attachment to being tranquil, then there will be times when one moves.
When nothing in the myriad things can disturb the mind, then it is tranquil.

Commentary: This is self-attainment. Subcommentary: Marvelously embodying the two principles (heaven and earth) as non-existent, all realms are empty. Thus, participating in change, identical with the dust, without clamor or disturbance, it is not attained through forced effort.
When water is tranquil, it clearly reflects beards and eyebrows; level and centered, it serves as a standard for great craftsmen to take as measure.

Subcommentary: When water moves, it flows in waves; when still, it becomes clear and tranquil, hanging like a mirror, illuminating thoroughly, impartial to things. Thus, it can clearly reflect beards and eyebrows, pure and centered, correcting all curves and deviations, serving as a standard. Even with the skill of craftsman Chuí, one must still use water to level. Therefore, the Laozi says: "The highest good is like water." This raises a metaphor for the meaning above.
Water tranquil still reflects clearly, how much more the spirit! The sage's mind tranquil is the mirror of heaven and earth, the reflector of the myriad things.

Commentary: Having the means and letting it act spontaneously, thus what it illuminates is thoroughly clear. Subcommentary: The sage's virtue aligns with the two principles, wisdom pervades the myriad things—how can they be discussed on the same day as insentient water? Water tranquil still clearly reflects hair and eyebrows, how much more the spirit! The sage's mind tranquil thus reflects the subtleties of heaven and earth, mirrors the profound mysteries of the myriad things—this is indeed fitting. This combines the metaphors.
Emptiness, tranquility, simplicity, detachment, solitude, and non-action are the level of heaven and earth and the pinnacle of the Way and its virtue.

Commentary: All that is not level or not pinnacle arises from deliberate action. Subcommentary: Emptiness, tranquility, simplicity, detachment, solitude, and non-action—these four have different names but the same reality. Praising their beauty, thus possessing these four names, heaven and earth take this as level, the Way and its virtue use this as pinnacle.
Therefore, emperors, kings, and sages rest herein.
Commentary: They have never moved. Subcommentary: They rest their thoughts in tranquility.
Resting leads to emptiness, emptiness leads to fullness, fullness leads to order.

Commentary: Order means principle. Subcommentary: Once thoughts are rested and stilled, one naturally unites with emptiness and void; uniting with emptiness and void, one meets with true reality; meeting with the way of true reality is the principle of spontaneity.
Emptiness leads to tranquility, tranquility leads to movement, movement leads to attainment.
Commentary: Not losing that by which it moves. Subcommentary: Principle is empty and tranquil, stillness can move—this is attainment.
Tranquility leads to non-action; non-action means those tasked with affairs bear responsibility.

Commentary: With non-action, the multitude of talents and varieties each undertake their affairs and naturally bear their responsibilities. Thus it is said: "How majestic! Shùn and Yǔ possessed all under heaven and did not interfere." This means that. Subcommentary: "Those tasked with affairs" are the ministers, meaning the subordinates each have duties to perform. When the emperor or king employs wisdom, resting in tranquility and non-action, then the ministers and subordinates each hold their offices and bear their worries and responsibilities. Thus, the ruler is non-active, while the ministers have affairs. Hence, the ruler lowers the beads before his eyes and does not interfere.
Non-action leads to contentment; contentment means worry and distress cannot dwell, and years and longevity are prolonged.

Commentary: Contentment is the appearance of ease and self-attainment. Subcommentary: Contentment is the appearance of ease, harmony, and joy. Deliberate action stagnates in realms, dust and burdens disturb the mind; non-action is self-attainment, worry and distress cannot dwell in one's thoughts. Contentment, harmony, and joy thus prolong years and longevity.
Emptiness, tranquility, simplicity, detachment, solitude, and non-action are the root of the myriad things.
Commentary: Seeking their root, all come from non-action. Subcommentary: These four phrases are the root origin of the myriad things, hence the previous words are repeated to conclude their beauty.
Understanding this, facing south, Yáo acted as ruler; understanding this, facing north, Shùn acted as minister.

Subcommentary: The beauty of yielding and abdication is unsurpassed by Táng and Yú; the flourishing of ruler and minister is none prior to Yáo and Shùn. Thus, these two rulers are cited to clarify the four virtues. Although again facing south and north respectively, their level and pinnacle are one.
Using this above, it is the virtue of the emperor, the son of heaven; using this below, it is the way of the mysterious sage, the uncrowned king.

Commentary: These are both the pinnacle of non-action. Having the way, being revered by all under heaven, but without the rank—this is called the uncrowned king, self-honored. Subcommentary: Using this non-action to reside above things is the virtue of the son of heaven, Emperor Yáo. Using this emptiness and detachment to reside below as minister is the way of the mysterious sage, the uncrowned king. Having the way but not the rank—this is called the mysterious sage, uncrowned king, self-honored—namely, Lǎojūn and Master Ní (Confucius) are such.
Using this to retire and wander leisurely by rivers and seas, the scholars of mountains and forests submit.

Subcommentary: "Retire" means concealing traces and dwelling in seclusion. Using this way to retire, thus able to wander and play in mountains and waters, leisurely and joyfully at ease. Therefore, all recluses under heaven submit—such as Cháo Fǔ and others.
Using this to advance and soothe the world, then achievements are great, fame is illustrious, and all under heaven are unified.

Commentary: This is again next in order. Thus, retiring, they are like Cháo Fǔ's kind; advancing, they are like Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng's peers. The substance of non-action is great! What under heaven is not done by it? Therefore, if the ruler does not take on the responsibilities of the prime minister, then Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng are tranquil and manage the offices. If the prime minister does not handle the duties of the hundred officials, then the hundred officials are tranquil and handle affairs. If the hundred officials do not attend to the tasks of the myriad people, then the myriad people are tranquil and secure in their occupations. If the myriad people do not exchange what they and others can do, then all under heaven, self and others, are tranquil and self-attained. Thus, from the son of heaven down to the common people, and even insects, who can achieve through deliberate action? Therefore, the more non-action, the more honored. Subcommentary: "Advance" means revealing traces and taking office. Marvelously embodying non-action while mingling with the dust, descending with traces—thus able to soothe the common people with benevolence and longevity, spread ultimate virtue in sagely deeds, establish unfathomable achievements and fame, illustrate the merits of the prime minister. Therefore, all under heaven are greatly unified, chariots and scripts share tracks, perfect goodness and beauty—only peers like Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng are such.
Tranquil, one is a sage; active, one is a king.
Commentary: When the time calls for action, act; when it calls for stopping, stop.
Through non-action, one is honored.

Commentary: Spontaneously, one is revered and supported by things. Subcommentary: When responding in tranquility, it is the honor of the mysterious sage, uncrowned king; when responding in action, it is the nobility of the ninth-five position, ruler of ten thousand chariots. Through non-action, one is honored; emerging, one is the son of heaven; dwelling, one is the uncrowned king. Thus, knowing where the way resides, who dares not to honor it?
Simplicity, and all under heaven cannot compete with it in beauty.

Commentary: What matches heaven in beauty is only simplicity. Subcommentary: Pure simplicity, plain quality, non-action, emptiness, and tranquility—these are indeed the root of the myriad things. Thus, what is honored, who can compete with it in beauty?
One who clearly understands the virtue of heaven and earth—this is called the great root, the great ancestor, harmonizing with heaven.

Commentary: Heaven and earth take non-action as virtue; thus, understanding their ancestral root, one does not oppose heaven and earth. Subcommentary: One whose spiritual mansion is clear and tranquil, divine illumination pure and white, and virtue aligns with the two principles—certainly can be the ancestral craftsman of living beings, the root foundation of all existence, mysteriously united with the way of spontaneity, harmonizing with heaven.
Thereby harmonizing and adjusting all under heaven, harmonizing with people.

Commentary: Following heaven is how one responds to people. Thus, when heaven's harmony arrives, human harmony is complete. Subcommentary: "Harmonizing" means equalizing; "adjusting" means following smoothly. Moreover, responding and sensing without mind, like shadow and echo, equalizing the myriad beings, greatly following the nature of things, mingling traces and uniting with dust—thus harmonizing with people.
Harmonizing with people is called human joy; harmonizing with heaven is called heavenly joy.

Commentary: When heavenly joy is suitable, human joy is sufficient. Subcommentary: Bending to share the common customs, temporarily fitting the joys of the human world; looking up to unite with spontaneity, just then delighting in the joy of the way of heaven.
Zhuāngzǐ said: "My teacher! My teacher! It blends the myriad things without being cruel,

Commentary: Changing and intermixing, thus called blending. It blends itself, not my teacher's violence. Subcommentary: "Blend" means to mix or grind; "cruel" means violent. Zhuāngzǐ takes the spontaneous ultimate way as teacher, saying it twice to praise its virtue. It says: "The great way I take as teacher nurtures living beings; even if it blends the myriad things, it has no mind for violent anger. Thus, in plain autumn, when leaves fall and wither, they do not complain." This clarifies that even though cutting and severing occur, it is not out of righteousness.
Its grace extends to ten thousand generations without being benevolent.

Commentary: Benevolence is the name for universal love; without love, there is nothing to call benevolent. Subcommentary: Benevolence is the trace of partial love. This says the great way opens and closes, heaven and earth create and transform the common people, its compassionate grace is endless but not partial love, thus it is not benevolent.
Older than high antiquity, yet not considered long-lived.

Commentary: Longevity means a distant limit; without a limit, there is nothing to call long-lived. Subcommentary: Not only older than high antiquity, but even prior to the primordial ancestor. Since it neither perishes nor is born, how can there be夭 (premature death) or寿 (longevity)? Guǒ's note says: "Longevity means a distant limit."
It covers and carries heaven and earth, carves and sculpts all forms, yet is not considered skillful.

Commentary: Skillfulness is the marvel of doing; all are spontaneous, thus nothing to call skillful. Subcommentary: Riding the two principles to cover and carry, taking the myriad things to carve and sculpt—yet the two principles use transformation and generation as function, the myriad things use spontaneity as application. Transformation and generation already do not borrow things; carving and sculpting, how could they borrow others? Therefore, things each employ their abilities, people all follow their nature—then the names of skillful and clumsy are extinguished here. Guǒ's note says: "Skillfulness is the marvel of doing."
This is called heavenly joy.
Commentary: Forgetting joy, yet joy is sufficient. Subcommentary: Wherever it is, it fits, concluding heavenly joy.
Therefore, it is said: "Those who know heavenly joy, their life is a heavenly movement, their death is a transformation of things."

Subcommentary: Knowing heavenly joy is not sorrow or joy, then knowing life and death are without life and death. Thus, their life is the same as the movement of the way of heaven; their death merges with the transformation of the myriad things.
Tranquil, they share virtue with yīn; active, they share waves with yáng.

Subcommentary: Marvelously rooted in emptiness and congealing, they equal the utmost yīn in stillness and rest; responding with traces, identical with the world, they unite with the great yáng in its flowing waves.
Therefore, those who know heavenly joy have no complaint against heaven, no blame from people, no burden from things, no reproach from ghosts.

Subcommentary: Virtue aligns with heaven, thus no complaint against heaven; conduct follows the world, thus no blame from people; I am hidden from things, thus things do not burden me; I do not betray the hidden and manifest, thus what ghost reproach is there?
Therefore, it is said: "Their movement is heaven, their stillness is earth."
Commentary: Movement and stillness, though different, are of one mind without mind. Subcommentary: "Heaven" and "earth" conclude the meaning of movement and stillness without mind.
When the one mind is settled, one rules all under heaven; then ghosts do not cause harm, the spirit does not tire.

Commentary: Constantly without mind, thus ruling all under heaven without tiring or ailment. Subcommentary: When realm and wisdom darkly unite, it is called one; when things cannot disturb, it is called settled. Precisely because settled in one mind, one can rule over ten thousand states. Since there is no ghost reproach, what calamity or harm? Moving yet constantly still, thus the spirit does not tire or toil.
When the one mind is settled, the myriad things submit.
Subcommentary: One whose mind is concentrated and still resembles dead ashes and is tranquil, becoming the master of agitation; thus, the myriad things return and submit.
This means extending emptiness and tranquility to heaven and earth, penetrating the myriad things—this is called heavenly joy.

Commentary: If my mind is constantly tranquil, then the minds of the myriad things penetrate. Penetrating, they submit; not penetrating, they rebel. Subcommentary: The reason the one mind settled and the myriad things submit is precisely using the wisdom of emptiness and tranquility to trace the principles of the two principles, penetrating the nature of the myriad things, following the transformation of things without ever not fitting—thus called heavenly joy.
Heavenly joy is the sage's mind with which to nurture all under heaven.
The sage's mind with which to nurture all under heaven—what does it do? Heavenly joy alone.
The virtue of emperors and kings takes heaven and earth as ancestor, the Way and its virtue as master, and non-action as constant.

Subcommentary: The king takes heaven and earth as fundamental ancestor, thus covering and carrying without mind; as ruler, takes the Way and its virtue as master, thus generating without possessing. Although again a thousand changes,
Yáo said: "How vexatious and tumultuous!"

Note: Self-reproach for having affairs. Explanation: "Vexatious and tumultuous" describes a state of chaos. Gaining insight from these words, he daily disliked having many affairs and further stirring things up, thus modestly yielding.
You are in harmony with Heaven, I am in harmony with humanity.

Explanation: Yáo humbly effaced his own brilliance and yielded to Shùn, hence saying: your abundant virtue aligns distantly with Heaven above, while my intentions align closely with human affairs. The virtue of the two rulers Yáo and Shùn was without superiority or inferiority, so these two sages are used here to illustrate the methods of governance.
Now Heaven and Earth are what the ancients considered great.

Explanation: From here onward are the words of Zhuāngzǐ. Heaven covers and Earth supports, giving birth to and nurturing all things; among the four greats in the realm, these two are included. Thus, citing antiquity to prove the present, he praises their attainment.
And they were jointly admired by Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn.
Explanation: Only Heaven is great, only Yáo emulated it. Thus, it is known that Xuānyuán, Zhuānxū, Táng, and Yú all considered virtue aligning with Heaven and Earth as their excellence.
Therefore, what did the ancient kings who ruled the world do? They simply followed Heaven and Earth, that is all.

Explanation: It means, what did the ancient emperors who embodied the Dào do? They merely acted without conscious intent, conforming to things, and their virtue aligned with the two realms (Heaven and Earth), that is all.

Confucius, wishing to deposit his books with the Zhōu royal house, was advised by Zǐlù: "I have heard that the Keeper of the Archives of Zhōu is Lǎo Dān, who has retired and returned home. If you, Master, wish to deposit your books, why not try going to consult him?"

Explanation: His surname was Zhòng, name Yóu, courtesy name Zǐlù, a disciple of Confucius. Confucius, seeing the virtue of Zhōu had declined and could not be rectified or assisted, intended to deposit the books he had compiled in the Zhōu treasury, hoping they might serve future rulers as methods for governance and transformation. Thus, he discussed with his disciples to deliberate its feasibility. Lǎo Jūn, surname Lǐ, name Dān, was the Keeper of the Archives for Zhōu, akin to today's secretarial official in charge of ancient texts. Seeing the Zhōu house in turmoil, he resigned from his post and returned home to rest in quiet. Therefore, Zǐlù advised Confucius, suggesting he try visiting and inquiring.
Confucius said: "Excellent." He went to see Lǎo Dān, but Lǎo Dān did not consent.

Explanation: Lǎozi knew that the books intended for deposit were like straw dogs used by former sages—they could not be preserved long, fearing they would confuse later people. Hence, he said he did not consent.
Thereupon, Confucius expounded the Twelve Classics to explain.

Explanation: Confucius edited the Shī and Shū, established the Lǐ and Yuè, commented on the Yì, and compiled the Chūnqiū—these are the Six Classics. Adding the Six Weft-texts, together they form the teachings of the Twelve Classics. He elaborated and expounded in detail, thus thoroughly explaining them.
Lǎo Dān interrupted his discourse, saying: "Too verbose. I wish to hear the essence."

Explanation: "Interrupted his discourse" means acknowledging there was reason in it. "Too verbose" expresses dissatisfaction with the excessive complexity and verbosity, requesting the essential method.
Confucius said: "The essence lies in benevolence and righteousness."
Explanation: Though there are twelve classics, resulting in abundant complexity, discussing the crucial point, nothing precedes benevolence and righteousness.
Lǎo Dān said: "May I ask, are benevolence and righteousness part of human nature?"
Explanation: Asking if this benevolence follows nature or not.
Confucius said: "Yes. If the gentleman is not benevolent, he cannot be established; if not righteous, he cannot live. Benevolence and righteousness are truly human nature. What else would they be?"

Explanation: "Yes" means it is so. It is said that benevolence and righteousness are the great nature of humans. If worthy gentlemen are not benevolent, their reputation and conduct cannot be established; if not righteous, their way of life cannot be sustained. Thus, it is known that benevolence and righteousness are the true nature of humans. "What else would they be?" expresses doubt about this.
Lǎo Dān said: "May I ask, what is called benevolence and righteousness?"
Explanation: Previously, it was said that benevolence and righteousness are the true nature of humans. Now asking again, requesting an explanation of their origin.
Confucius said: "A central heart that is kind to things, universal love without selfishness—this is the essence of benevolence and righteousness."

Note: This is what ordinary people call benevolence and righteousness, hence using Confucius and Lǎozi to correct it. Explanation: "Kind" means joyful. A loyal and sincere heart wishing things peace and joy, compassionate love equally, universally aiding without selfishness, truly conforms to human feelings and can serve as worldly teaching.
Lǎo Dān said: "Alas! Nearly so, these later words. Universal love, is it not迂 (yū, far-fetched/impractical)?"

Note: The one with perfect benevolence has no [conscious] love but goes straight forward. Explanation: "Alas" is a sound of dissatisfaction. "Nearly" means almost. "迂" means crooked. Later-developed words are nearly false and artificial, hence he sighs "alas" to express his discontent. The perfect person reasons and goes straight forward without conscious thought or worry, yet you harbor feelings of universal love—is that not partial and crooked?
Where there is no selfishness, that is selfishness.

Note: What the world calls 'without selfishness' means abandoning oneself to love others. But loving others entails desiring others to love oneself—this is extreme selfishness, not forgetting the public to achieve public good. Explanation: Universally loving others and wanting others to love oneself—this is extreme selfishness, how can there be public good?
Do you, Master, wish to make the world not lose its herding?

Explanation: "Herding" means nurturing. If you wish all living beings under heaven to fully attain their inherent nature, nothing is better than each, high and low, keeping to their own roles, self-sufficient and tranquilly nourished—then there is great order. Some texts have "放" (fàng, let go/release) instead of "牧" (mù, herd), meaning if the ruler simply lets the natures of the masses follow their course, then the world will be peaceful.
Then Heaven and Earth certainly have their constancy, the sun and moon certainly have their brightness, the stars certainly have their ranks.

This is the principle of spontaneity, not related to human affairs. Not only these three, all things are so. Just let them be, and none will lack sufficiency. Why labor with intentional effort, acting presumptuously and artificially?
Birds and beasts certainly have their herds, trees certainly have their standing.

Note: All are already self-sufficient. Explanation: Sentient birds and beasts, insentient grasses and trees, each attains its life and standing, each has its herds and divisions. How could they rely on benevolence and righteousness to achieve this?
You, Master, should also follow your inherent virtue in action, proceed along the Dào, and you will have arrived.

Explanation: "Follow" means accord with. Let your inherent virtue roam free and act in the world, accord with the Heavenly Dào and walk among humans. The ultimate wondrous practice is nothing beyond this.
Why then so vehemently uphold benevolence and righteousness, as if beating a drum to seek a runaway child?

Note: There is no way to attain it thus. Explanation: "Vehemently" describes striving with effort. "Uphold" means shoulder/carry. "Runaway child" means an escaped person. It means Confucius strenuously exerts body and mind, shouldering benevolence and righteousness, forcing them upon the world to teach the people—how is this different from beating a great drum to search for a runaway? Thus, the louder the drum, the farther the runaway flees; the more benevolence and righteousness are displayed, the farther the peaceful Dào recedes. Hence, there is no way to attain it.
I fear, Master, you are扰乱 (luàn, disturbing) human nature.

Note: When affairs come, love appropriately; when righteousness demands, stop. This is forgetting benevolence and righteousness. Constantly dwelling on them disrupts the true [nature]. Explanation: Not catching the runaway child, the fault lies in beating the drum; the true nature not being clear, the error arises from benevolence and righteousness. Hence, he sighs "alas" to conclude.

Shì Chéngqǐ went to see Lǎozi and asked: "I have heard you, Master, are a sage. I did not decline the long journey and have come wishing to see you. I have traveled a hundred stages, with repeated calluses on my feet, and dared not rest."

Explanation: Surname Shì, courtesy name Chéngqǐ, unknown where he was from. "Stages" means inns. "Calluses" means blisters on feet. Chéngqǐ had long heard Lǎozi possessed divine and sagely virtue, so without declining hardship, he came from afar admiring righteousness, passing through a hundred inns, not daring to rest once. The road being distant, his feet developed repeated calluses.
"Now I observe you, sir, are not a sage. In the rat's den there are leftover vegetables."

Note: It means he does not cherish things. Explanation: Previously, based on reputation, he thought he was a perfect person; today, seeing personally, he knows he lacks sagely virtue. Seeing leftover vegetables in the rat's hole in the earth, he dislikes their filthiness, hence utters this criticism.
"And you abandon the ignorant—this is not benevolent."

Note: Lacking closeness and kindness, hence called abandoning. Explanation: "Ignorant" means the benighted. Those who are dark and ignorant should be guided and advanced; abandoning them without teaching—can that be called benevolent and kind?
"Raw and cooked foods are not fully distributed before you."

Note: Being supremely sufficient, thus always having surplus. Explanation: "Raw" means grain and silk; "cooked" means food and drink. Beyond sufficiency, he does not concern himself with distribution, hence food, drink, and resources lie scattered before him. Moreover, the great sage is broad and tolerant, not拘 (jū, constrained) by small matters. Shì Chéngqǐ, being petty and trivial, considers this wrong. Measuring a true sage by such minutiae is like using a conch to measure the sea—how can one fathom its depth?
"Yet you accumulate and amass without limit."

Note: All things return to his bosom; those who come receive, he does not set small boundaries. Explanation: Since he has sagely virtue, things return to him. Thus, provisions and gatherings for collection have no limit or shore; vast and without conscious mind, accumulation and dispersal are left to things.
Lǎozi remained indifferent and did not respond.
Note: Not letting his words affect his mind. Explanation: Words of dust and grime—how could they ever enter his ears? Indifferent and empty, why should they be harbored?
The next day, Shì Chéngqǐ came again and said: "Yesterday I criticized you. Today my mind feels empty about it. Why is this?"

Note: Wondering why his critical and mocking mind has subsided. Explanation: "Empty" means void, ceased. Yesterday upon first coming, he falsely produced criticism; today upon reflection, he realizes his own error. Thus, admitting fault and blaming himself, deeply feeling ashamed and awed, his mind is empty. He doesn't know why.
Lǎozi said: "As for the one with clever knowledge and divine sageliness, I consider myself to have transcended that."

Note: "Transcended" means passed beyond. Explanation: The one with clever knowledge and divine sageliness—this is the trace, not the source of the trace. You say I aspire to be a sage? I have long transcended that. Why do you say I am sage or not sage? Lǎo Jūn wished to suppress Chéngqǐ's critical mind, thus showing him the cessation of traces and return to the root. Guō Xiàng's note says: "Transcended means passed beyond," meaning I have already passed beyond and left sageliness.
"Formerly, you called me 'ox' and I accepted being called 'ox'; you called me 'horse' and I accepted being called 'horse'."
Note: Following what things name him.
If there is the reality, and people give the name, if one does not accept it,
Note: Having the reality, thus not taking slander or praise to heart.
One receives double calamity.

Note: One slander, one praise—if accepted in the mind, then both name and reality become burdens. This is the reason for receiving double calamity. Explanation: Yesterday you called me ox, I immediately followed and called myself ox; called me horse, I also followed and called myself horse. I ultimately did not resist, and moreover had the reality of ox and horse—this is one name. If people give the name and one avoids and does not accept it, that is double calamity. Critical words are not even as significant as ox and horse—if I do not avoid those, how much more so what is not?
My compliance is constant compliance.

Note: "Compliance" refers to the capacity for action. Not bringing calamity upon oneself through slander or praise, thus able to remain unchanged in capacity. Explanation: Guō Xiàng's note says: "Compliance refers to the capacity for action." Lǎo Jūn embodied the Dào as a great sage, thus able to subdue body and mind, act and contain, accepting being called ox or horse, solely following things. This is constant, not due to deliberate intention.
I do not comply with conscious intention to have compliance.

Note: If done with conscious action, then one cannot constantly comply. Explanation: It means I follow my nature, trust the genuine, and naturally contain and accept. It is not related to having a conscious mind and using intention to achieve it. If one must use the mind, it becomes forced nature. Since it involves deliberate action, how can it be called non-action?
Shì Chéngqǐ walked obliquely like a goose, avoiding [Lǎozi's] shadow, stepping forward, then advanced and asked: "How does one cultivate the self?"

Explanation: Chéngqǐ, knowing he had spoken wrongly, felt ashamed in body and mind. Thereupon, he walked obliquely like a goose, stepping sideways, turning his body to avoid the shadow, following behind Lǎozi, not daring to tread on his footsteps. Then slowly advancing, he asked to request the method of cultivating the self.
Lǎozi said: "Your appearance is stiff and imposing,"
Note: The manner of advancing restlessly. Explanation: "Your" means you. It says you adorn your appearance to startle others, making yourself steep and imposing, unable to be at ease.
"Your eyes are staring sharply,"
Note: The manner of protruding. Explanation: Since the mind is uneasy, the eyes also dart about—thus looking left and right, gazing wildly and boastfully.
"Your forehead is broad and prominent,"
Note: The manner of high, exposed, and displaying beauty. Explanation: The forehead is high, elevated, exposed, and adorned. Holding this demeanor, you are arrogant and haughty towards things.
"Your mouth is gaping open,"

Note: The manner of being fierce and wide-open. Explanation: Guō Xiàng's note says: the manner of being fierce and wide-open. It means the will is strong and forceful, speech is bold and fierce, exaggerated and intimidating, making people fearful.
"And your posture is rigidly upright."

Note: The manner of standing on tiptoe, self-possessed. Explanation: "Upright" means declared/displayed. Standing on tiptoe, proud and bold, truly contrary to the detailed rites, yet adorning and cultivating one's appearance, naturally seeming fitting.
"You are like a horse tethered and stopped."
Note: The will is set on galloping. Explanation: Though the form is stern and dignified, the mind and nature are clamorous and agitated, like a runaway horse tied up, its intention set on running.
"Moving, yet held back,"
Note: Unable to relax and let go oneself. Explanation: The emotions gallop pursuing objects, stirred upon encountering things, unable to let go and be at ease, constrained in every action.
"When active, it is like a trigger,"
"Observing, yet scrutinizing,"
Note: Discerning right and wrong. Explanation: Unable to dismiss and forget, attain smoothness and forget both, but clearly examines right and wrong, fixating the mind on determining what is correct.
"Knowledgeable and clever, yet seeing the excessive,"

Note: "Excessive" means going beyond one's inherent nature. Being clever at seeing excess means being clumsy at embracing simplicity. Explanation: "Excessive" means too much. Unable to forget cleverness and forget knowledge, he observes the single principle of non-action yet uses fraudulent knowledge and cunning to see the many affairs of conscious action.
"All these are considered not genuine."

Note: All these ten matters are considered not genuine to innate nature and destiny, but rather a dissipation of praise and slander—all are not the way of cultivating the self. Explanation: "Genuine" means real. It means these ten matters are all actions of falsity and deceit, not
The Authentic Scripture of Nanhua with Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Sixteen, Part Two
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá of the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters, Chapter Fourteen: The Operation of Heaven
Does Heaven operate?

Commentary: It operates without being made to operate; it moves by itself. Subcommentary: This means Heaven receives the pure, floating yang energy above, and without intention to operate, it moves automatically.
Does Earth remain still?

Commentary: It remains still without being made to; it stops by itself. Subcommentary: Earth receives the turbid, sinking yin energy below, and also without intention to be tranquil, it stops by itself.
Do the sun and moon contend for their positions?

Commentary: They do not contend for positions; they alternate naturally. Subcommentary: Shining upon day and night, appearing and disappearing, coming and going, they are naturally so. Since they are without emotion regarding alternation, how could they have intention to contend for positions?
Who is it that directs this?

Subcommentary: "Who" means "who." "This" refers to the preceding text. It means the four seasons and eight nodes, clouds moving and rain falling, nurturing the common people and fostering all beings—who acts as the master and arranges this? This sentence explains "Heaven's operation."
Who is it that maintains the order?

Commentary: All are so of themselves. Subcommentary: Mountains and peaks produce and nurture; rivers and streams flow and pour forth, containing all things and bearing them endlessly. Spring growth and summer growth certainly occur without error. Who maintains the order so that it is like this? This sentence explains "Earth's stillness."
Who, residing without affairs, pushes and makes them proceed?

Commentary: If there is nothing, then there is nothing to push; if there are things, then each has its own affairs. So then, who is it that, without affairs, pushes and makes them proceed? Each moves by itself. Subcommentary: The alternation of sun and moon, the bright shining of stars and constellations, each has its measures and numbers, all following nature. Who, residing without affairs, calculates and makes them proceed? This sentence explains "the sun and moon contending for positions." The preceding three questions are all hypothetical inquiries to reveal the subtle and obscure. Thus, we know all are so of themselves; no thing makes them so.
Is it that there is some mechanism and constraint, making it unavoidable?

Subcommentary: "Mechanism" means a device; "constraint" means closure. The profound winter's stern killing, the night's darkness and obscurity—if one speculates with intention, one might say there is a master controlling, closing affairs, making it unavoidable, causing it to be so. But reasoning it through, all are so of themselves. The principle of Earth's stillness is likewise.
Is it that they operate and revolve, unable to stop themselves?

Commentary: Being so of themselves, they cannot be known. Subcommentary: For instance, when spring's energy arises, all things are born; when day and night open bright, the whole world is illuminated. The sequence of energies operates and revolves, leading to this growth and nurturing. Examining its principle and tendency, no thing makes it so. The circular Heaven's operation, its meaning is also thus.
Do the clouds make the rain? Does the rain make the clouds?

Commentary: The two cannot act for each other; each is so of itself. Subcommentary: Energy rises upward to become clouds; clouds disperse and descend, moistening to become rain. But tracing the beginning and end, there is no originator. Thus, we know the two cannot act for each other.
Who promotes and relaxes this?
Subcommentary: "Promote" means to raise; "relax" means to abandon. It means who raises the clouds and rain to pour down abundantly? Who abandons the sweet moisture, causing such drought?
Who, residing without affairs, indulges in pleasure and encourages this?
Subcommentary: Who, residing without affairs, encourages himself and urges that to create this excessive rain and enjoy it? The Sīmǎ version has the character for "weary."
The wind arises from the north, now west, now east; it rises and wanders about. Who exhales and inhales it? Who, residing without affairs, fans and stirs it?

Subcommentary: "Wanders about" describes its circling and turning. "Exhales and inhales" is like breathing out and in. "Fans and stirs" is like wafting. The north is where yin energy arises, the place of wind, hence "from the north." The wind blows without intention, going east and west as it fits. Sometimes it wanders and resides in the empty sky; sometimes it exhales and inhales within the mountains. Fanning and stirring, rising and falling, it has no fixed standard. Who, residing without affairs, does this? It is simply natural.
May I ask the reason?
