Commentary: Poses the question of the reason for being so of themselves. Subcommentary: This sentence generally asks the reason for the preceding.
Wūxián Tiǎo said: Come, I will tell you. Heaven has the six poles and five constants.

Commentary: For things and affairs near at hand, one might know their reason. But tracing their origin to the ultimate, then without reason, they are so of themselves. Being so of themselves, there is nothing to ask about the reason; one should simply follow them. Subcommentary: Wūxián is a spirit shaman. Tiǎo is his name. The six poles are the six directions: the four directions, up and down. The five constants are the five phases: metal, wood, water, fire, earth—the constant nature of human relations. It means natural principle has these six poles and five constants. As for the sun, moon, wind, and clouds, all are likewise. One should simply let them be, naturally complete. Why place intention among them?
If emperors and kings follow it, there is order; if they oppose it, there is calamity.

Commentary: What is learned can be changed, but inborn nature cannot be opposed. Subcommentary: Emperors and kings, above conforming to the Way of Heaven, below following the common people, ruling effortlessly and without action, following and relying on things, then the world is ordered. But opposing the joy of all states, violating the harmony of the two modes, acting with calamitous perversity, then disaster and chaos arise.
The affairs of the nine Luò are ordered, virtue is complete, shining down upon the earth below.

Subcommentary: "The affairs of the nine Luò" means the affairs of the nine regions' settlements. It means the king responds to Heaven and follows things, guiding without intention, thus causing the world to be greatly peaceful. People sing, striking earthen drums. In the lands of the nine regions' settlements, order is settled and merit achieved. In the countries of the eight wilds and the barbarians, the Way is perfect and virtue complete. Already in accord with the two modes covering and bearing all things, and also aligning with the three lights shining down upon the earth below.
The world upholds him; this is called the Supreme Sovereign.

Commentary: Because he follows their being so of themselves. Subcommentary: His Way matches nature; his virtue equals creation. Thus, the multitude gladly推举 him without weariness; the common people bear and support him without refusal. This can be called returning to simplicity and purity—the governance of the Supreme Sovereign.
The Grand Steward Dàng of Shāng asked Zhuāngzǐ about benevolence.

Subcommentary: Sòng inherited from Yīn, so Shāng here means the state of Sòng. Grand Steward is an official title. His given name was Yíng, courtesy name Dàng. Wishing to resolve his own doubts, he asked Zhuāngzǐ about benevolence.
Zhuāngzǐ said: Tigers and wolves are benevolent.

Subcommentary: Benevolence is the trace of affection. Tigers and wolves are fierce beasts, yet they still understand mutual affection, sufficiently showing that all categories have a benevolent nature.
He said: What do you mean?
Subcommentary: The Grand Steward, not yet understanding the deep meaning, asked again what was meant.
Zhuāngzǐ said: Father and son are affectionate with each other; why is that not benevolent?
Subcommentary: The affection between father and son comes from natural endowment. This is true benevolence; why trouble to ask again?
He said: May I ask about perfect benevolence?
Subcommentary: The affection of tigers and wolves, its meaning is not yet broad. So he asked about perfect benevolence, hoping to hear the profound meaning.
Zhuāngzǐ said: Perfect benevolence has no affection.

Commentary: "Has no affection" does not mean belittling or disliking. In the human body, there is no affection, yet the head is naturally above, the feet naturally below; the organs reside inside, the skin and hair outside. Outside and inside, above and below, noble and base, within the body each fulfills its ultimate role, yet there is no affection among them. But perfect benevolence is sufficient. Thus, the five relationships and six clans, the wise and foolish, the distant and near, do not lose their proper place in the world—this is principle's natural state. Why then seek to have affection? Subcommentary: The perfectly benevolent forget thoughts and eliminate concerns, uniting with the great void as one body, blending all things into one. How can affection and distance be discussed? Serenely without intention, they follow the world's affections and distances.
The Grand Steward said: Dàng has heard that without affection there is no love; without love there is no filial piety. To say perfect benevolence is unfilial—is that acceptable?

Subcommentary: No love, no affection, then it is unfilial. To say perfect benevolence is unfilial—is that acceptable in principle? Shāng Dàng, not understanding the deep meaning, thus produced shallow confusion. Zhuāngzǐ, to clearly refute it, set forth the meaning below.
Zhuāngzǐ said: Not so. Perfect benevolence is supreme; filial piety is indeed insufficient to describe it.

Commentary: One must speak of it in the realm where benevolence and filial piety are forgotten, then one reaches it. Subcommentary: Perfect benevolence forgets righteousness and forgets benevolence; it is precious and supreme. How can one use the near traces of love and respect to speak of its mind? It is indeed insufficient to describe it.
This is not a statement that exceeds filial piety; it is a statement that falls short of filial piety.

Commentary: All names arise from what falls short. Thus, passing beyond the names of benevolence and filial piety, and entering the realm of no-name, then one reaches it. Subcommentary: Shāng Dàng's question was near, stuck within boundaries; Zhuāngzǐ's answer far surpassed the external. Thus, we know the meaning of affection and love is not a statement exceeding filial piety; clinging to names and teachings is a statement falling short of filial piety.
One who travels south reaches Yǐng, but facing north, he does not see Míng Mountain. Why is this? Because he is far from it.

Commentary: Míng Mountain lies in the north pole, but traveling south to view it; perfect benevolence lies in having no affection, but speaking of it with benevolence and love. Thus, though Yǐng is seen, one is farther from Míng Mountain; though benevolence and filial piety are manifest, one is farther from the ultimate principle. Subcommentary: Yǐng lies in the south, Míng Mountain in the north, so Guǒ's commentary says: Míng Mountain lies in the north pole; traveling south to view it; perfect benevolence lies in having no affection, but speaking of it with benevolence and love. Thus, though Yǐng is seen, one is farther from Míng Mountain; though benevolence and filial piety are manifest, one is farther from the ultimate Way. This commentary is very clear; no need for further explanation.
Therefore it is said: To be filial through respect is easy; to be filial through love is difficult.
Subcommentary: Respect lies in outward form; love follows the original mind. The mind comes from inborn nature, hence difficult; traces involve human emotions, hence easy.
To be filial through love is easy, but to forget one's parents is difficult.

Subcommentary: Though filial love is difficult, it still remains within boundaries, not equal to forgetting one's parents, which is serene and unattached. When the will surpasses love, and again falls short of non-being—using this standard to measure difficulty and ease makes it clear.
To forget one's parents is easy; to make one's parents forget me is difficult.

Subcommentary: The gibbon leaping breaks its intestines; the old cow licks its calf—kindness and compassion flow downward, the constant nature of creatures. Thus, for a child to forget parents is easy; for parents to forget a child is difficult. Unless one has attained the Way, who can practice this?
To make one's parents forget me is easy; to simultaneously forget the world is difficult. To simultaneously forget the world is easy; to make the world simultaneously forget me is difficult.

Commentary: The perfectly benevolent find all joints fitting, so all day they do not recognize themselves. The sage is above, not acting purposefully; he lets them each attain their own self. When each attains their own being, then all affairs are naturally fitting, all lives naturally content. How can the world not each forget me? When each forgets, where does the ruler reside? This is called simultaneous forgetting. Subcommentary: "To simultaneously forget the world" means abandoning the ten-thousand chariots like discarding sandals. "To make the world simultaneously forget me" means the common people use it daily without knowing it. Ruling effortlessly from Fényáng, yet wandering mind in Gūyě; the beauty of yielding and courtesy lies in empty forgetting—this is comparable to simultaneously forgetting the world. Compared to the former it is difficult; compared to the latter it is easy. Not equal to forgetting all, reaching the ultimate Way, ceasing knowledge, being natural, unifying with creation in achievement, joining with Heaven and Earth in virtue. Thus, one can let the natures of all things be, follow the actions of the common people, great and small all attain, flying and sinking not lost, benefits and grace silently bestowed, all things natural. Above, like the topmost branch; the people, like wild deer. At that time, where does the ruler reside? This is "to make the world simultaneously forget me." It can be said to be like the rulers of ancient simplicity before Xuānyuán and Zhūanxū. Their virtue unseen, thus the world forgets them. This is from inferior to superior, from coarse to subtle, dismissing again, mysterious upon mysterious.
Virtue abandons Yáo and Shùn and does not act.

Commentary: Abandoning Yáo and Shùn, then the virtue of Yáo and Shùn is complete. If tied in the heart, then it is not self-attained. Subcommentary: "Abandon" means to forget and discard. It means the two rulers Yáo and Shùn had profound and far-reaching great virtue, and yet they forgot their virtue, relying on things without acting. This explains "to simultaneously forget the world is difficult."
Benefits and grace extend for ten thousand generations, but the world does not know it.

Commentary: Obliterated, constantly fitting. Subcommentary: Having beneficial grace, kindly moistening all lives, even after ten thousand generations, their virtue does not cease, and the ultimate virtue silently bestowed, used daily without knowing. This explains "to make the world simultaneously forget me is difficult."
How could one merely sigh and speak of benevolence and filial piety?

Commentary: Having lost the rivers and lakes, one then thinks of the mouthful of foam. Subcommentary: "Sigh" means to lament. One whose great virtue equals Yáo and Shùn can still forget and not display himself—how again would he sigh and speak of benevolence and filial piety, lamenting over old traces?

Filial piety, fraternal duty, benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, trustworthiness, chastity, and integrity—these are all things by which one urges oneself and enslaves one's virtue; they are not worth prizing.

Subcommentary: "Fraternal duty" means obedience. "Virtue" is the true nature. These eight matters above all force nature and fake emotion, urging oneself with effort, imitating others, laboring and enslaving one's nature. Hence, they are not worth prizing.
Therefore it is said: The most noble discards the ranks of the state.

Commentary: "Discards" means to remove and abandon. Nobility lies in the self. If even the self is forgotten, how much more the ranks of the state? This is the ultimate nobility. Subcommentary: "Discards" means to remove and abandon. Those who value ranks and emoluments originally do so for the self. If even the self is forgotten, how much more ranks and emoluments? This is the ultimate nobility.
The most wealthy discards the wealth of the state.

Commentary: The most wealthy are self-sufficient, hence they remove the wealth of the world. Subcommentary: The most wealthy are those who know sufficiency. Those who know sufficiency take non-covetousness as treasure. Even if the wealth of the state were offered, they would discard it and not use it. Hence, the Lǎojīng says: "He who knows sufficiency is rich." This means that.
The most desired discards fame and reputation.

Commentary: What is most desired is fittingness. Having attained fittingness, the names of benevolence and filial piety are all gone. Subcommentary: The most desired is nothing more than fitting one's nature. Once praise and blame are unified, honor and disgrace forgotten, things and self obliterated, right and wrong erased, then renowned fame is
Alas! How my Master is in straits!
The details of his straits are fully recorded in the chapters that follow, which conclude with this theme.
When Confucius reached the age of fifty-one and had still not heard of the Way, he went south to Peì to see Lǎo Dān.

Although Confucius led three thousand disciples and was called the Unrowned King, and widely practiced the five virtues, he had not yet heard of the Great Way. Therefore, he went from Lǔ to Peì, traveling from north to south to see Lǎo Jūn in order to inquire about the ultimate mystery.
Lǎo Dān said, "You have come, sir? I have heard that you are a worthy man of the north. Have you attained the Way?" Confucius said, "I have not yet attained it."

He asked whether Confucius, being a worthy and capable man of his time, had perhaps attained the ultimate Way. The reply was that he had not. Since he looked from Chǔ toward Lǔ, it was called the north.
Lǎo Zǐ said, "How did you seek it?"
He asked where he had sought the ultimate Way.
He said, "I sought it through measures and calculations for five years, but did not attain it."

Measures refer to calculations and methods. There is a minor completion of the heavenly pattern every three years with an intercalary month, and a major completion every five years with two intercalary months, hence the mention of five years. But the Way is not a matter of calculations and methods, so he did not attain it.
Lǎo Zǐ said, "How else did you seek it?"
He further asked by what method he sought the Way.
He said, "I sought it through yīn and yáng for twelve years, but did not attain it."

This all uses Confucius and Lǎo Zǐ to illustrate the meaning of transcending learning. Twelve years represent one cycle of yīn and yáng. Not attaining it clarifies that seeking the Way through yīn and yáng means the Way is not yīn and yáng, hence it is said below that in the central states there are people who are neither yīn nor yáng.

Lǎo Zǐ said, "So. If the Way could be presented, then no one would fail to present it to their ruler. If the Way could be offered, then no one would fail to offer it to their parents. If the Way could be told to others, then no one would fail to tell it to their brothers. If the Way could be given to others, then no one would fail to give it to their children and grandchildren. Yet it cannot be so—for no other reason"

than that the ultimate Way is profoundly mysterious, transcending words and images; it is neither non-existent nor existent, neither self-originated nor other-originated. Therefore, it cannot be offered to rulers or parents, nor told to younger generations. The reason for this is none other, hence the record of Confucius and Lǎo Zǐ, sages who illuminate the mystery within mystery.
"If there is no host within, it will not stay."

If the mind lacks the substance to receive the Way, then even upon hearing it, it will pass by. If there is no host within to receive the Way, even if one hears the sage's words, they cannot dwell in the heart. Thus, it is known there is no other reason.
"If there is no correspondence without, it will not proceed."

If there is no host within, then external things also lack that which rectifies oneself, hence it never penetrates. Since the mind within lacks the capacity to receive the Way, there is nothing external that can rectify oneself, so it cannot proceed.
"What comes from within is not received externally—the sage does not bring it forth."

What comes from within is the Way of the sage; it only comes forth when there is someone externally capable of receiving it. "Comes from" means follows. What follows from within is the sage manifesting traces and teachings. It is precisely because beings can sense the sage that the sage responds. If external beings cannot receive it, the sage ultimately does not bring forth teachings.
"What enters from without finds no host within—the sage does not conceal it."

What enters from without refers to those who achieve their nature through artificial learning. Although nature can be cultivated, it is essential to have the substance within. If there is no host within, then there is nothing to store the sagely Way. "Conceal" means to hide. What enters from without is nature formed through study and practice. When one externally receives the sagely teaching and it sinks into the heart, if there was originally no mind to receive it, then the sagely Way cannot be stored.
"Fame is a public instrument."

Fame is something shared by all under heaven. "Fame" means reputation; "public" means common; "instrument" means tool. There are two kinds of fame: one is naming things, the other is praise and blame. What is referred to here is the fame of praise and blame.
"One should not take much of it."

Those who take much are those who affect and exceed reality. Taking much leads to disorder under heaven. Good reputation and fame are shared by all under heaven. If one takes too much, it leads to affectation beyond reality, and contention arises.
"Benevolence and righteousness are the temporary lodge of the former kings."
It is like a relay station.
"They may be used for a single night's stay but not for prolonged dwelling. To encounter them often brings blame."

Benevolence and righteousness are human nature, but human nature changes, differing between ancient and modern times. Thus, when wandering, one lodges temporarily and moves on, becoming obscure as if unhindered. But if attached to one side, it becomes visible; visibility gives rise to artifice; artifice gives rise to much blame. The temporary lodge is an inn for travelers, where one cannot stay long. Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom should be discarded after use. Staying long as a guest gives rise to flaws; leaving traces of sageliness invites excessive blame.
"The ultimate men of old borrowed the path of benevolence and lodged in righteousness"
to adapt to the times and change, leaving no constant traces.
"in order to wander in the realm of carefree freedom."

The true men of old, harmonizing their light and descending their traces, acted in accordance with opportunity. They responded to beings with broad love and served the multitude. How different is this from borrowing a road, lodging temporarily, wandering briefly? It is not real, yet action does not harm stillness, response does not leave truth. Thus, they always wandered carefree in the field of self-attainment, roaming in the realm of non-action.
"They fed in the fields of simplicity and stood in the gardens of non-giving."

"Simple" means plain and brief; "non-giving" means not bestowing or giving. Knowing when to stop and being content, they fed in the fields of simplicity without depleting their own substance, and stood in the gardens of non-giving. Speaking of fields and gardens clarifies that these are the places where the sage nourishes life.
"Carefree and non-acting,"
for acting intentionally is not benevolence or righteousness.
"Simple and easy to nourish,"

completely following simplicity, hence easy to nourish. Only when carefree and burdens are exhausted can one be non-acting, tranquil, and plain. Simple means plain and frugal, self-sufficient, hence easy to nourish.
"Non-giving, without output,"
meaning not depleting oneself for the sake of others. Not harming oneself to benefit others, hence no output. These three sentences reiterate and explain the previous meaning.
"The ancients called this the wandering of gathering the true."

Wandering and letting things be—this is truly gathering. Gathering the true means colors are not false. The ancient sages practiced methods like simplicity and called it the wandering of gathering the genuine and real without falsity, carefree and following transformation in roaming.
"Those who consider wealth right cannot yield emolument; those who consider prominence right cannot yield fame; those who cling to power cannot give others the handle."

Under heaven, none are burdened by what they disapprove, but each exhausts their life for what they approve. Those who exhaust their lives for what they approve are not standing in the garden of non-giving. Those who approve wealth and disapprove poverty, greedy for goods, how can they yield wealth and emolument to others? Those who approve prominence and disapprove obscurity, stuck in glory and position, how can they yield fame to others? Those who cherish power and boast of things, how can they give the handle to others? The handle is power. Only those who detest the dusty world and the stench of glory and profit can discard them as if lost.
"Grasping it, they tremble; letting it go, they grieve."

Those who grieve at letting it go tremble because they cannot help grasping it. Holding the handle of power, they fear losing it, hence tremble; relinquishing mighty force, they mourn its loss, hence grieve.
"And having no insight whatsoever to see what they never cease pursuing—they are the condemned of heaven."

This means they know how to advance but not how to stop, so they lose their innate nature and life—this is why they are condemned. Those who love wealth and power have dull, dark minds, stuck only in fame and profit, utterly lacking insight. How can they hear of profound principles and rest their minds, ceasing thought? Such people, even if not yet punished by execution, are already constrained in their innate nature, hence they are the naturally condemned.
"Resentment, favor, taking, giving, admonition, teaching, life, and death—these eight are instruments of correction."

Enemies must be killed; favors must be repaid; what is within one's lot is taken; what is beyond is given to others. Ministers admonish superiors; rulers teach inferiors. Respond to spring with growth and life; follow autumn with execution and punishment. These eight are instruments of governing correctly; they cannot but be used.
"Only those who follow great change and are unblocked can use them. Hence it is said, 'To correct means to rectify.' Those whose minds think otherwise find the gate of heaven closed."

Holding to the old without change leads to loss of correctness. "Follow" means comply; "blocked" means obstructed. Only by complying with the great principle, following transformation, penetrating the nature of things without obstruction, can one use these eight things to govern and rectify affairs, conforming to correct principle. Hence, "to correct means to rectify." Those whose minds cannot be thus find the gate of heavenly mechanism blocked and unopened. The gate of heaven is the mind.

Confucius saw Lǎo Dān and spoke of benevolence and righteousness. Lǎo Dān said, "When winnowing chaff gets in the eyes, heaven and earth and the four directions shift positions. When mosquitoes and gadflies sting the skin, one stays awake all night."

External things like these, though small, injure innate nature greatly. Confucius, stuck in sagely traces, thus spoke of benevolence and righteousness. When winnowing chaff gets in the eyes, the eyes are dimmed and cannot distinguish east from west. When mosquitoes and gadflies sting the skin, the pain keeps one awake all night. Thus, though external things are tiny, their harm is great. How much more so when benevolence is not heavenly principle, righteousness not following nature, abandoning oneself to imitate others, losing one's innate nature—its harm is surely greater than chaff in the eyes or stings on the skin. "Sting" means to bite.
"Benevolence and righteousness, so poisonous, disturb my mind—there is no greater disorder."

Esteeming them adds to innate nature, hence disorder. The poison of benevolence and righteousness is worse than mosquitoes and gadflies; it disturbs my mind, causing vexation and confusion. Nothing disrupts the nature of things more than this. Some texts also use the character for "disturb."
"If you, sir, would cause the world not to lose its simplicity,"
then innate substance remains whole and benevolence and righteousness appear.
"then you, too, could follow the wind and move, uphold virtue and stand firm."

The wind moves of itself and one relies on it; virtue stands of itself and one holds it—this is the Way easy to maintain and practice. "Follow" means let go, allow. To make the common people lose their simple and honest nature, nothing is better than abolishing benevolence and righteousness, then returning to the mystery of my ultimate. Confucius should also let go of non-acting wind and teaching, respond to things according to opportunity and duty, uphold the ultimate virtue of emptiness and non-reality, and establish unfathomable divine merit. Some texts interpret "follow" as "rely on" or "comply with."
"Why then so vigorously, as if carrying a great drum to seek a runaway child?"

To raise benevolence and righteousness and hurry to the land of the Way and virtue is like beating a drum to seek an escapee—there is no way to find him. "Vigorously" means with effort. To raise benevolence and righteousness and hurry to the land of the Way and virtue—how different is it from beating a great drum to seek a runaway child? Thus, the drum's sound is loud and the runaway child flees quickly; benevolence and righteousness are evident and the Way and virtue are abandoned.
"The swan is white without daily bathing; the crow is black without daily dyeing."
Each is naturally sufficient.
"The simplicity of black and white is not fit for dispute."

Both are natural, with no partiality. "Bathe" means wash; dyeing black is called "dyeing." "Dispute" means distinguishing victory and defeat. The swan is white, the crow black—this is endowed by nature. Must they bathe or dye daily to become so? This illustrates that the nature of things is thus. But the simplicity of black and white is each sufficient in its portion; encountering what is suitable, it is content. Hence, it is insufficient to use portions to argue victory and defeat. Also, "dispute" can mean change; the distinction of black and white is fixed—one cannot change white to black.
"The spectacle of fame and reputation is not fit for broadening."

The fully sufficient forget fame and reputation; forgetting fame and reputation is true breadth. Cultivating fame and establishing reputation attract the observation of things—this is narrow and inferior, not worthy of self-aggrandizement. Only by discarding fame and reputation can one be called great.
"When the springs dry up, the fish are left on the land, gasping for moisture and wetting each other with spit,"
showing that the reputation of benevolence and righteousness arises from insufficiency.
"better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes."

This is forgetting benevolence and yet being benevolent. This summarizes the previous text, criticizing the flaws of benevolence and righteousness. When the spring source dries up, fish pass spit to moisten each other; when simplicity disperses and honesty departs, one practices benevolence and righteousness to aid beings. But when rivers and lakes are vast and full, each is sufficient, so they forget each other; when the Way and virtue are profound and mysterious, one attains nature, hence empty and tranquil. Here, rivers and lakes compare to the Way and virtue; moistening with spit compares to benevolence and righteousness. Using this standard, they cannot be mentioned in the same day.
Confucius saw Lǎo Dān and returned without speaking for three days.
Lǎo Zǐ, a great sage beyond the world, changes unpredictably, immeasurable, hence there was nothing to speak of.
His disciples asked, "Master, when you saw Lǎo Dān, what advice did you offer him?"

The names are not specified, simply "disciples"—likely those who had entered his hall, sharing this doubt. Having seen Lǎo Zǐ, he should have offered some admonition; what did he hear that he did not speak for three days?
Confucius said, "Now at last I have seen the dragon! The dragon coils to form a body, spreads to form patterns,"

meaning Lǎo Dān could transform. The virtue of the dragon changes constantly, illustrating the ultimate person who hides and appears without fixed form. Thus, fundamentally coiling to form a wondrous body, mysterious and obscure; traces spreading to rise, patterns brilliant and splendid.
"Riding on clouds and mist, nourished by yīn and yáng."
This means he follows no fixed method, naturally sufficient. The ultimate person rides clouds and mist without mind, follows yīn and yáng to nourish beings.
"My mouth fell open and would not close; what advice could I offer Lǎo Dān?"
"Close" means shut. His heart was fearful and unsettled, his mouth open and not closing; how could he have leisure to hear words of admonition?
Zǐ Gòng said, "So, can there indeed be a man who dwells like a corpse yet appears like a dragon, whose thunderous voice is yet a deep silence, whose movements are like heaven and earth?"

The ultimate person, when dwelling, is like a dead corpse at rest; when emerging, resembles the transformations of a dragon spirit; when speaking, is like the vibration of thunder; when silent, resembles the soundlessness of profound principle. Thus, he stirs and moves the mechanism, akin to the two modes (heaven and earth) generating beings. Then, whether dwelling or emerging, speaking or silent, how can one differentiate based on differences in dwelling, emerging, speaking, or silence? Yet the ultimate person must have the ability of dwelling, emerging, speaking, and silence beyond words. Therefore, when Confucius saw him, his mouth
remained open and would not close.
"May I too go and observe him?" Thereupon, using Confucius's name, he went to see Lǎo Dān.
Cì is Zǐ Gòng's name. Zǐ Gòng wished to go observe the appearance of the ultimate person's dragon virtue, so he went to see him using Confucius's reputation and teaching.
Lǎo Dān was just then sitting upright in his hall and responded faintly, "My years have passed by; what will you use to admonish me?"

"Upright" means erect; "passed" means time. Lǎo Zǐ, self-possessed and composed, sat erect in his hall, lofty and expansive. Things moved him, he responded, faintly speaking: "Your years are declining; you may
The Nanhua Zhenjing Commentary, Scroll Seventeen, Part Three
Annotated by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Sub-commentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Xīhuá in the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters: On Cultivating the Mind, Fifteenth

Those who cultivate their will, exalt their conduct, withdraw from the world, and differ from customs, who discourse loftily and lament resentfully—they merely seek to be aloof. These are the preferences of those who dwell in mountain valleys, despise the world, and are devoted to austerity or drowning themselves.

Sub-commentary: "Cultivate" means to carve and shape; "will" refers to intention. "Aloof" means to be isolated. It speaks of biased and stagnant individuals who fail to comprehend principle, who harshly discipline their bodies and minds, exalt their conduct, separate from worldly customs, stand alone and unyielding, engage in pure discussions of the ways of the Five Emperors, and discourse loftily on the teachings of the Three Sovereigns. They resent having talent but not meeting opportunity; they lament the absence of the Way and rampant indulgence. They harbor lofty aspirations in the forests and echoes, and erase their traces beneath cliffs and crags. These are the scholars who dwell in mountain valleys, those who criticize and despise their era. The austere include those like Bào Jiāo and Jiè Tuī; those who drown themselves include Shēn Dí and Biàn Suí. They are but one-sided scholars—how can they be spoken to of the ultimate Way? "Merely" means to stop; their methods stop here.

Those who speak of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, trust, respect, frugality, deference, and humility—they merely seek self-cultivation. These are the preferences of those who bring peace to the world, teach and instruct others, and traveling or residing scholars.

Sub-commentary: In their speech and expression, they speak of benevolence and righteousness, using such methods as the foundation for self-cultivation. These are the scholars of peaceful and well-governed times, those who teach and instruct others. These include Zǐxià west of the Hé River, and Xuānní residing between the Zhū and Sì Rivers—some travel and debate, others dwell peacefully and lecture. They are what learned men prefer, but certainly not what those devoted to the Way prioritize.

Those who speak of great achievements, establish great fame, ritualize the roles of ruler and minister, and rectify the distinctions between high and low—they merely seek governance. These are the preferences of court scholars, those who honor the ruler and strengthen the state, and those who strive for merit and territorial expansion.

Sub-commentary: They establish achievements within the seas, set great names through the ages, bring about the grand rituals between ruler and minister, and uphold the great righteousness of ruling all under heaven, thereby pacifying the altars of soil and grain and illuminating the constant Way. Thus, they honor the sovereign and subdue distant lands, strengthen their own state and annex rival states. Are these not the court scholars and temple ministers? Such are Gāo Yáo, Yī Yǐn, Lǚ Wàng, and their like.

Those who seek marshes and wetlands, dwell in open wilderness, fish leisurely, and reside in idleness—they merely seek non-action. These are the preferences of those by rivers and lakes, recluses who avoid the world, and those who cherish leisure.

Sub-commentary: They perch in hidden mountains and marshes, roam freely in open wetlands, dwell leisurely engaged in fishing, avoid the world and abide in non-action. The Son of Heaven cannot make them ministers; feudal lords cannot befriend them. These are the carefree and leisurely individuals, such as Cháofù, Xǔ Yóu, Gōng Yuè Xiū, and their kind.

Those who exhale and inhale, breathe out the old and take in the new, imitate the bear's stretch and the bird's extension—they merely seek longevity. These are the preferences of those who practice guiding and pulling, nurture their forms, and those like Péng Zǔ who live to great age.

Commentary: These several types of people have different preferences, indulging in what they like, each going to their own direction—this too is a way to be carefree. Yet each finds their own fulfillment; how could they establish everything? As for enabling all things to attain their share without losing themselves, one should indeed entrust it to non-grasping action. Sub-commentary: Exhaling cool to expel the old, inhaling warm to take in the new; like a bear climbing a tree to stretch, or a bird flying in the sky extending its feet—these are all methods to guide the spirit and breath to nurture the body and soul, the way to prolong years and the art of preserving the form. Thus Péng Zǔ lived eight hundred years, Báishí three thousand years—long-lived people belong to this category. The previously mentioned several types have different aspirations and adhere to one side; this is not comprehensive excellence. Only by not cultivating the will can one later meet the profound mystery's subtle attainment.

As for those who do not cultivate their will yet are lofty, lack benevolence and righteousness yet are cultivated, lack merit and fame yet govern, are not by rivers and lakes yet are leisurely, do not practice guiding and pulling yet are long-lived—
Commentary: This is what is called spontaneity.
They forget everything yet possess everything.

Commentary: Forgetting enables possession; if one possesses, one cannot save it from being forgotten. Thus, possession is not having by holding, but having by forgetting. Sub-commentary: Those who mysteriously penetrate and unite with change, who darkly accord with principle—they do not cultivate their will, yet their Way is even loftier; they lack benevolence and righteousness, yet constantly cultivate themselves; they forget merit and fame, yet the world is greatly governed; they leave rivers and lakes, yet are tranquil and leisurely; they do not practice guiding and pulling, yet their lifespan is boundless. Thus, they can forget both things and self completely, and all things return to them, so they possess everything. This is having by forgetting, not having by holding.
Serenely boundless, and all beauties follow them.

Commentary: If one forces oneself to do it, one cannot be boundless, and all evils arise. Sub-commentary: The mind does not stagnate in one direction; traces darkly accord with the five phases. Thus, serene and empty, their Way is boundless; all virtues' beauties follow them.
This is the Way of Heaven and Earth, the virtue of the sage.

Commentary: Not acting for the myriad things, yet the myriad things spontaneously arise—this is Heaven and Earth. Not acting for the hundred conducts, yet the hundred conducts spontaneously complete—this is the sage. Sub-commentary: Heaven and Earth have no mind in nurturing, yet the myriad things are born; the sage has no mind in transforming and nurturing, yet the hundred conducts are accomplished. Thus, Heaven and Earth take non-birth as birth to be the Way; the sage takes non-action as action to complete virtue. Therefore, the Lǎojīng says: "Heaven and Earth are not benevolent; the sage is not benevolent."
Therefore it is said: Composed and tranquil, solitary and still, empty and nonexistent, non-active—this is the level of Heaven and Earth, the substance of the Way and virtue.

Commentary: If not solitary, still, and non-active, one endangers one's level and loses one's substance. Sub-commentary: Composed and tranquil, solitary and still—this is a concentrated and deep mind. Empty and nonexistent, non-active—this is the wisdom of silent functioning. Heaven and Earth take this method as the source of equilibrium; the Way and virtue take this method as the substance of genuineness.
Therefore it is said: The sage rests in rest, and thus is even and easy.

Commentary: Resting in composure and tranquility, solitary and still; ceasing in emptiness and nonexistence, non-action—then even when encountering dangerous changes, one remains even and easy without difficulty. Sub-commentary: Resting the mind in the land of composure and tranquility, ceasing cognition in the realm of emptiness and nonexistence—then one treads difficulties with simplicity, traverses dangers with ease.
Even and easy, then composed and tranquil.

Commentary: Worry and difficulty arise from having action; having action also arises from worry and difficulty. Thus, even ease and composure mutually complete each other. Sub-commentary: Not only does resting the mind in composure lead to even ease, but even ease also leads to composure. Thus it is known that even ease and composure mutually complete each other.
Even, easy, composed, and tranquil—then worry and distress cannot enter, perverse energies cannot assail.

Commentary: Extinguished, one goes together with the correct principle. Sub-commentary: The mind is already composed and tranquil; traces are also even and easy. Though mind and traces are one kind of non-action, thus deep worries and burdens cannot enter their spiritual tower; perverse and sinister energies cannot assail their internal organs. "Assail" means to enter; the text alternates the terms.
Thus their virtue is whole and their spirit is not impaired.

Commentary: Those who are not even and not tranquil—do they only harm their form? Spirit and virtue are both lost within. Sub-commentary: Those who are composed, tranquil, and non-active—do they only have an unharmed outer form? Their inner virtue is also perfectly whole. When form and virtue are both peaceful, then spirit and essence are unimpaired.
Therefore it is said: The sage's life is the operation of Heaven.
Commentary: He entrusts movement to spontaneity.
His death is the transformation of things.

Commentary: Shedding off without any attachment. Sub-commentary: The sage embodies the non-duality of toil and rest, penetrates the oneness of coming and going. Thus, his life is like the operation of Heaven's Way; his death is like the transformation of the myriad things. He entrusts himself to the furnace's casting, without the slightest concern in his breast.
In stillness, he shares the virtue of Yin; in movement, he shares the waves of Yang.

Commentary: Movement and stillness are without mind and are entrusted to Yin and Yang. Sub-commentary: Concentrating spirit and stilling thought, he shares the abundant virtue of the Great Yin; responding to stimuli and moving, he shares the waves of Yang energy. Movement and stillness follow the times—he is without mind.
He does not initiate fortune, does not begin misfortune; he responds only after being stimulated.

Commentary: He does not initiate anything. Sub-commentary: Good initiates fortune; evil begins misfortune. Since both good and evil are dismissed, fortune and misfortune are both forgotten. He responds only after being stimulated—how could he initiate or begin?
He acts only after being pressed.
Commentary: He moves only when meeting the utmost. Sub-commentary: "Pressed" means reached, compelled. "Acts" means responding in harmony, not initiating, meeting the opportunity and responding.
He arises only after it is unavoidable.

Commentary: He arises according to principle; it is unavoidable for me. Sub-commentary: "Avoidable" means to stop. When the opportunity and stimulus penetrate to the utmost, affairs cannot be stopped, and only then does he arise to respond—it is not premeditated.
He discards knowledge and artifice, follows the principle of Heaven.

Commentary: Heaven's principle is spontaneous; knowledge and artifice have no place in between. Sub-commentary: "Follows" means to accord with. Internally, he discards mental knowledge; externally, he forgets deliberate affairs. Like the primordial chaos's non-action, he accords with spontaneity's subtle principle.
Thus there is no heavenly disaster.
Commentary: Disaster arises from opposing Heaven. Sub-commentary: Accordance with Heaven, thus no disaster.
No burden from things.
Commentary: Burdens arise from opposing things. Sub-commentary: Accordance with things, thus no burden.
No blame from others.
No reproach from ghosts.
Commentary: Same as self-attainment, thus no reproach.
His life is like floating, his death is like resting.

Commentary: Floating without any attachment. Sub-commentary: The sage's movement and stillness are without mind; life and death are one thread. Thus, his life is like a bubble temporarily rising, changing in an instant; his death is like resting from fatigue, without any attachment.
He does not think or ponder.
Commentary: He entrusts it to Heaven's principle. Sub-commentary: His mind is like dead ashes, cut off from conditional thoughts.
He does not premeditate.
Commentary: He responds when principle arrives. Sub-commentary: Like a mirror hung high in the hall, it reflects when things come—it never premeditates or awaits affairs beforehand.
He is bright but does not dazzle.

Commentary: He uses the world's own brightness; it is not I who dazzle. Sub-commentary: His wisdom's illumination is brighter than the sun and moon, yet he conceals his light and hides his traces, thus not dazzling things.
He is trustworthy but does not anticipate.

Commentary: He uses the world's own trust; it is not I who anticipate. Sub-commentary: Pressed by opportunity and responding to stimuli, like a shadow following the form, his trustworthiness is like the four seasons, never erring. He responds only when the opportunity comes, without anticipation.
He sleeps without dreaming, awakes without worry.
Sub-commentary: Accordance with truth leads to concentrated stillness and no dreams; burdens exhausted lead to constant ease and no worry.
His spirit is pure and unadulterated.

Commentary: Entirely without any desires. Sub-commentary: "Pure and unadulterated" means unmixed. Since there are no dreams and no worries, and he accords with truth and unites with the Way, thus his mind and spirit are pure and unadulterated without mixture.
His soul does not tire.
Commentary: Having desires leads to fatigue. Sub-commentary: Composed, tranquil, and non-active, mind and spirit are leisurely and at ease. Thus, his essential soul functions without ever tiring.
Emptiness, nonexistence, composure, and tranquility—then he accords with Heaven's virtue.
Commentary: Then he shares Heaven and Earth's virtue of composure and tranquility. Sub-commentary: Praising this emptiness and nonexistence that shares virtue with Heaven and Earth.
Therefore it is said: Sorrow and joy are deviations of virtue.
Sub-commentary: Going against the mind brings sorrow; following the intention brings joy. Not penetrating opposition and compliance is the deviation of virtue.
Joy and anger are excesses of the Way.
Liking and disliking are failures of virtue.
Sub-commentary: Having no liking as liking, no disliking as disliking—this deluded mind is the fault of virtue.
Thus, the mind without sorrow or joy is the height of virtue.

Commentary: The highest virtue is constantly at ease; thus, feelings have nothing to measure. Sub-commentary: Without joy or anger, without worry or pleasure, serene and empty—this is the person of highest virtue.
One and unchanging—the height of stillness.

Commentary: Still and one—it cannot be changed. Sub-commentary: Embracing the mysterious Way of pure oneness, mixing with clamor and dust yet unchanging—unless one is supremely still, who could be like this?
Without any opposition—the height of emptiness.

Commentary: His mind is open and thoroughly clear, without the slightest violation. Sub-commentary: "Opposition" means to go against. Greatly accordant with all living beings, without any conflict—unless one is empty and open to the extreme, who could be so?
Not interacting with things—the height of blandness.

Commentary: Things come of themselves; the supremely bland have no intention to interact with things. Sub-commentary: Guarding purity and clarity, not interacting with things, having no needs or expectations—the height of composure and tranquility.
Without any conflict—the height of purity.

Commentary: If mixed with turbid desires, then there is something not accordant. Sub-commentary: Wisdom's illumination is bright and clear, supremely pure without mixture. Thus, he can blend with the myriad things and greatly accord with all living beings. Regarding "opposition" and "conflict," their principle is not different; to clarify the two meanings of emptiness and purity, it is stated again.

Therefore it is said: If the form toils without rest, it becomes exhausted; if the essence is used without cease, it labors, and labor leads to depletion. Commentary: All things have their proper place; they must not be lost.

Sub-commentary: The body and spirit are endowed with limits, yet their use is without bounds—this must lead to the place of death. Thus, toiling the form beyond its share without knowing rest gives rise to exhaustion and ruin. The spirit chasing after things without knowing stop must lead to labor and damage; damage leads to the drying up of essential energy.
The nature of water: if not mixed, it is clear; if not moved, it is level. If blocked and not flowing, it cannot be clear—this is the image of Heaven's virtue.

Commentary: Those who image Heaven's virtue have no mind and yet meet. Sub-commentary: "Image" means to emulate. It says water's nature is clear and level, good at reflecting things. If mixed and adulterated, blocked and obstructed, then it goes against its constant nature. It can neither flow smoothly nor reflect things. Only when not moved or blocked is it clear and level, penetratingly illuminating without bias, serving as the standard for things—this is the image of Heaven's virtue. It illustrates the sage's mind, empty and bright, illuminating without bias, emulating spontaneity, sharing
The Southern Florescence True Classic: Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll 18, Part Four
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters: Mending the Nature, Sixteenth
Mending the nature through vulgar learning, seeking to return to one's original state.

Commentary: Having already governed one's nature with vulgarity, yet wishing to use vulgar learning to return to the root of one's innate destiny—the method of seeking increasingly misses the proper path. Subcommentary: To mend means to govern; nature means innate character; vulgar means habitual; original means the root. It means people receive their nature naturally, each abiding by their innate lot; following and acting accordingly, they naturally accord with principle. But now, using artificial wisdom to govern the true nature, they strain and force it, already exhausting and impairing it. Then, further practicing the learning of humaneness, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom—Confucian vulgar studies—to seek to return and recover the original nature, thus the more one gains in vulgarity, the more one loses in nature; the closer the learning, the farther the Way.
Confusing desires through vulgar thoughts, seeking to attain clarity.

Commentary: Having already disordered the mind with desires, yet now again employing thought to seek clarity—the more refined the thought, the farther one strays. Subcommentary: To confuse means to disorder; to attain means to obtain. Desires refer to things that can be coveted, like fame, profit, sounds, and appearances. It means the reason people's spiritual minds become dim and disordered is because they covet desires within the dusty vulgar world. Now, to dispatch and employ discriminating thoughts, pondering and seeking through study, hoping to obtain the way of clear illumination—it is certainly impossible. Only by learning through non-learning can one return to the root; by thinking through non-thinking can one attain clarity. Some versions also read "confusing desires through desires."
These are called obscured and benighted people.

Commentary: As for those who would dispel benightedness, they must depart from vulgarity and remove desires, and only then come close. Subcommentary: Obscured means blocked; benighted means dim. This concludes the previous: using vulgar learning to return to the root, using thought and consideration to seek clarity—such types can be called obscured, benighted, and dim people.
The ancients who governed the Way used tranquility to nurture knowledge.

Commentary: Only after being tranquil can knowledge not be agitated; knowledge not agitated, then nature is not lost. Subcommentary: Tranquil means quiet. The ancient sages, using the Way to govern themselves and the state, necessarily used the method of tranquility to nurture genuine, essential knowledge, preventing it from being agitated outwardly.
To live without using knowledge for action is called using knowledge to nurture tranquility.

Commentary: Not using knowledge for action but entrusting it to its own knowing—then even if knowledge encompasses the myriad things, one is tranquil and self-content. Subcommentary: Following nature to illuminate, knowledge arises spontaneously. Without deliberate mind and yet knowing, it is not using knowledge for action. Entrusting knowledge to proceed, there is no use of forced action. This is knowing without knowing, knowing yet without deliberate knowing; it is not knowing through deliberate knowing. Thus, all day knowing yet never having known, yet also never not knowing; all day acting yet never having acted, yet also never not acting. Still using this true knowledge to nurture tranquility—if not like this, how could one be tranquil?
Knowledge and tranquility mutually nurture each other, and harmony and principle emerge from one's nature.

Commentary: If knowledge is not used for action, then it does not harm tranquility; if tranquility acts spontaneously, then it does not injure knowledge. This can be called mutual nurturing. When the two mutually nurture, then the distinction of harmony and principle—how could it emerge from elsewhere? Subcommentary: If one cannot be tranquil, how can that true knowledge arise? Without true knowledge, how can one achieve such tranquility? Therefore, tranquility comes from knowledge, hence one can be still; knowledge relies on stillness, hence it attains genuineness. Thus, knowledge and tranquility mutually nurture each other. This is the way of central harmony existing within the inch-heart, natural principle emerging from innate nature—within oneself only, how could it concern others?
Now, virtue is harmony; the Way is principle.

Commentary: Because harmonious, thus there is nothing not attained; because the Way, thus there is nothing not ordered. Subcommentary: Virtue extends to others, hence it takes central harmony as its meaning; principle penetrates things, hence it takes the great Way as its name.
Virtue that excludes nothing is humaneness.

Commentary: That which excludes nothing is not for the sake of humaneness, yet the traces of humaneness proceed. Subcommentary: The mysterious virtue is profound and far-reaching, excluding nothing, embracing all; compassionate love vast and broad, the traces of humaneness appear here.
The Way that orders everything is righteousness.

Commentary: That which orders everything is not for the sake of righteousness, yet the merit of righteousness becomes evident. Subcommentary: The Way can penetrate things; each thing attains its proper principle. Since principle is already appropriate, the merit of righteousness becomes evident.
Righteousness clear and things draw near—this is loyalty.

Commentary: If righteousness is clear but not from loyalty, then things become increasingly distant. Subcommentary: Righteous principles are clear and evident, feelings follow from within; since there is no arrogance, thus things come to draw near and adhere.
Centered, pure, and sincere, returning to one's feelings—this is joy.

Commentary: Humaneness and righteousness issue from within, and following one's original heart without coercion, then the will is satisfied. The will satisfied, its trace is joy. Subcommentary: Since humaneness and righteousness come from within, the will and nature are pure and sincere. Although again involved with material realms, constantly returning to true feelings, what is created is harmonious and fitting, hence called joy.
Sincere conduct, accommodating form, and conforming to pattern—this is propriety.

Commentary: Sincere conduct, accommodating form, and conforming to natural moderation and pattern—its trace is propriety. Subcommentary: Sincere conduct is evident, demeanor and appearance model things and do not conflict with moderated pattern—its trace is propriety.
When propriety and music are universally practiced, then the world falls into disorder.

Commentary: Taking what one body practices and what one will enjoys, applying it to the world, then one region attains it but ten thousand regions lose it. Subcommentary: Those who cannot empty their minds to respond to things but cling to traces to rule the world will inevitably stagnate in ornate, flowery propriety and drown in wanton, excessive music. Thus, when straw dogs are displayed again, the world falls into disorder.
If they are correct and obscure their own virtue, then virtue does not impose. If it imposes, then things must lose their nature.

Commentary: Each correct in its innate destiny and obscuring its own virtue, then one does not use this to impose on that. If one uses this to impose on that, how can things not lose their nature? Subcommentary: To obscure means to be dark; to impose means to disturb. "They" refers to the sage who treads the correct path. It means people and others; if imposing and disturbing, then self and others lose their nature.
The people of antiquity, in the midst of primal chaos, together with the whole age attained calm indifference.

Subcommentary: This refers to the sovereigns before the Three Sovereigns, in the mysterious antiquity without names or titles. At that time, simple customs were not yet dispersed, thus they dwelt in the midst of primal, chaotic obscurity, becoming one with the age and world, darkly without traces. Ruler and minister, above and below, did not interact; all attained the Way of calm indifference, solitude, and non-action.

At that time, yīn and yáng were harmonious and quiet; ghosts and spirits did not disturb; the four seasons followed their rhythms; the myriad things were unharmed; all living beings did not die young. Though people had knowledge, they had no use for it.

Commentary: They simply entrusted themselves to spontaneity. Subcommentary: At that time of primal chaos, the simple and plain age, the whole world was calm and indifferent, embodying non-action. Consequently, yīn rose and yáng descended, the two energies harmonious and peacefully quiet; ghosts hidden, humans manifest, each abiding by their lot without disturbance. Heat and cold followed in sequence, the four seasons attained their rhythms, thus no disasters or calamities; the myriad things unharmed, all living beings each fulfilled their natural lifespan, ultimately without premature death. Though people had the techniques of mind and knowledge, due to non-action, they had no use for them.
This is called perfect unity. At that time, there was no deliberate action, but constant spontaneity.

Commentary: Things were all spontaneous, hence perfect unity. Subcommentary: Equalizing self and other in non-action, blending right and wrong in calm indifference; self and things not two, hence called perfect unity. "Mò" means without. Not acting yet acting spontaneously—non-action. Not knowing why it is so, yet it is so—spontaneity. Therefore, at that time, people embraced the virtue of non-action, things conformed to the Way of spontaneity.
When virtue subsequently declined,

Commentary: The reason virtue subsequently declined is because sages did not succeed the age; thus, those above could not practice non-action but admired the traces of non-action, hence leading to this flaw.
and Suìrén and Fúxī began to govern the world, therefore there was compliance but not unity.

Commentary: The age had already lost unity; perhaps it could not be unraveled, hence they released it and did not push, simply complying with it. Subcommentary: "Dǎi" means reaching to. The ancients ate hair and drank blood, grouping with deer and elk. When it reached Suìrén, he began to change raw to cooked; Fúxī then yoked oxen and rode horses, established kitchens, drew the eight trigrams to create writing, imitated spiders to make fine nets. Thereafter, cunning and artifice sprouted, cravings and desires gradually grew. The simple, plain heart was eroded, the non-active virtue dispersed; virtue declined and they began to govern the world—this is what it means. It is complying with the hearts of the multitude but unable to blend into perfect unity.
Virtue further declined, and when Shénnóng and Huángdì began to govern the world, therefore there was stability but not compliance.

Commentary: They stabilized it according to what was stable for it. Subcommentary: Virtuous transformation further declined, flaws and harms increased. Thus, Shénnóng had the campaign against Gònggōng, Huángdì led to the war with Chīyóu; baleful energies did not cease, weapons and armor repeatedly arose. Therefore, punishing the violent, removing the cruel, comforting the people, condemning offenses—they merely sought to stabilize the world, but could not greatly comply with all living beings. This is it.
Virtue further declined, and when Táng (Yáo) and Yú (Shùn) began to govern the world, they initiated the stream of governance and transformation, eroding simplicity and dispersing plainness.

Commentary: The sage has no deliberate mind, entrusting the age to form itself. What forms, whether simple or thin, is not due to the sage. The sage can entrust the age to attain by itself; how could he make the age attain sagehood? Therefore, the traces of the august kings shift with the age, but the Way of the sage has never not been complete. Subcommentary: Now, Táng Yáo and Yú Shùn dwelt at the end of the Five Sovereigns but initiated governance and conducted transformation, heading the beginning of the Three Kings. Thus, they established the five regulations to order the five conducts, set up the hundred officials to distinguish and clarify the hundred clans. The hundred clans thereby became eroded and deceitful; the five conducts from this became neglected and endangered. Branch streams divided, reaching to the present—is it not destroying simplicity and plainness to create erosion and deceit, dispersing plain substance to become flowery artifice?
They departed from the Way to practice goodness,

Commentary: Goodness is a name for exceeding appropriateness; hence, having goodness, the Way is not complete. Subcommentary: The vacuous, penetrating Way forgets both good and evil. Now, they abandoned themselves to imitate others, boasted of reputation and strived for goodness—already perverse to principle, hence called departing.
and endangered virtue to conduct themselves.

Commentary: Conduct means acting contrary to nature; hence, when conduct is established, virtue is not level. Subcommentary: To endanger means to hazard, to obstruct. Unable to follow nature and entrust genuineness, obscuring their tracks, they instead forced their feelings to establish conduct to seek fame and reputation. Truly, because external conduct and reputation are floating and artificial, thus causing internal virtue to be hazardous and endangered—what levelness and ease could there be?
Thereafter, they abandoned their nature and followed their mind.

Commentary: Using the mind to驱使 itself, then nature is abandoned. Subcommentary: Departing from the vacuous, penetrating Way, abandoning the simple, harmonious virtue, thereafter they abandoned their spontaneous nature and followed the discriminating mind.
Mind and mind recognized,

Commentary: One's own and others' minds competed to be foreknowing, no longer entrusting nature. Subcommentary: One's own and others' minds further schemed and considered; right and wrong, praise and blame, competed to be foreknowledge.
and knowledge was insufficient to stabilize the world.

Commentary: Forgetting knowledge and entrusting nature—this then stabilizes it. Subcommentary: Now, the mind climbs and grasps at realms of existence, knowledge discriminates in the limitless. The six directions become smoke and dust for it, the eight wilds boil and seethe; the four seasons thereby err in sequence, the three lights thereby comet and portend. This is the source of calamity and disorder—how could it suffice to stabilize the world?
Thereafter, they attached ornamentation to it and added erudition. Ornamentation extinguishes substance; erudition drowns the mind.

Commentary: Ornamentation and erudition are adornments of the mind's substance. Subcommentary: Previously, having made the mind operate with knowledge, it was insufficient to stabilize the world. Therefore, later they attached documents and writings to rectify the times, increased broad learning to aid the age. They did not know that substance is the root of ornament, and flowery ornament then obscurely extinguishes the plain substance; that erudition is the branch of the mind, and broad learning then drowns and sinks in the spiritual mind. Only by ending learning and removing ornament can one meet the beauty of non-action.
Thereafter, the people began to be deluded and chaotic, unable to return to their innate feelings and nature and recover their original state.

Commentary: "Original" means the root of innate destiny. Subcommentary: Ornamental flourish having already extinguished the plain substance, broad learning again drowning the spiritual mind, thereupon the people began to become foolish and chaotic. Wishing to return to their calm, indifferent feelings and nature, recover their spontaneous original root—how could it be possible? Alas! The fault of mental knowledge, ornamental writing, and broad learning.
From this perspective, the age lost the Way, and the Way lost the age. The age and the Way mutually lost each other.

Commentary: The Way, by not being valued, can thus be preserved in the age. However, if the age exists then it values it; valuing it, the Way thereby is lost. The Way cannot make the age not value it, and the age also cannot but value the Way; hence, they mutually lose each other. Subcommentary: To lose means to abandon. Observing from these events and traces, thus we know the times and age became eroded and floating, abandoning the Way of non-action. Also, because the Way of non-action was abandoned, it transformed the simple, harmonious age. Thus we know the age and the Way mutually lost each other.
How could a person of the Way arise in the age? How could the age arise through the Way?

Commentary: If not valued, then they would mutually arise. Subcommentary: Therefore, the sage who embraces the Way strides high above the dusty vulgar, unwilling to arise and expand to rule the age. And the eroded, artificial age—how could it arise and be moved by the sagely Way?
The Way has no means to arise in the age; the age has no means to arise through the Way. Even if sages do not dwell in mountain forests, their virtue is hidden.

Commentary: Now, the reason they are not hidden is because they have feelings that cause them to arise. How do they arise? Because there is no valuing. Subcommentary: In the eroded end-times, the Way cannot be used; the non-active Way does not again practice in the age. Suppose a sage who embodies the Way descends his traces into the dusty vulgar, blending with the mass of commoners, unknown to anyone—concealing his sagely virtue, unable to be seen and used. Though dwelling in court and market, how is it different from mountain forests?
Hidden, yet they do not hide themselves.

Commentary: If they hid themselves and yet used things, then the Way and the age would mutually arise. What hiddenness would there be? Subcommentary: The times encounter darkness and disorder, hence the sagely Way does not proceed—how could it be concealing their light, hiding their own virtue?

What the ancients called reclusive scholars were not those who concealed their bodies and did not appear, nor those who closed their words and did not speak out, nor those who hid their knowledge and did not express it. The times and fate were greatly perverse.

Commentary: Not knowing to return to unity to cease traces, but pursuing traces to seek unity—the more one attains traces, the more one loses unity. This is greatly perverse. Even if they again raise their bodies to make it clear, open their words to utter it, display their knowledge to express it, how could they and the age mutually arise? It only leads to mutual loss. Subcommentary: Perverse means false
The Nanhua True Classic: Commentary and Subcommentary, Volume 19, Part Five
Commentary by Guō Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huà in the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters: Autumn Floods, Seventeenth
When the autumn floods arrived, the hundred rivers poured into the Yellow River. The flow was so vast that between the two banks and the islets, one could not distinguish an ox from a horse.

Commentary: This speaks of its breadth. Subcommentary: The Yellow River at Mèngjīn; "flow" means passage; "banks" are the shores; "edges" are the boundaries; "islets" are sandbars—places in the water where one can dwell are called islets. Great floods arise in spring and peak in autumn; in plain autumn, yin energy is fierce and strong, often bringing continuous rain, hence the autumn floods arrive. Then all hundred river valleys pour into the Yellow River, filling it to overflowing, its waters immense, shores broad and distant, islets far and wide, making it impossible to distinguish oxen from horses when viewing from across the water.
Thereupon, the River Earl was overjoyed, thinking all the beauty under heaven was gathered in himself.

Subcommentary: The River Earl is the river deity, surname Féng, name Yí, a man from Tóngdī Village in Huàyīn, who attained the Way of water immortals. The river being so vast, he was joyfully pleased, believing all the glorious splendor and beauty under heaven resided in himself.

Following the current eastward, he reached the Northern Sea. Looking eastward, he could not see the water's end. Thereupon, the River Earl began to turn his face, gazing out at the ocean and sighing to Ruò: "There is a saying: 'Having heard a hundred parts of the Way, one thinks no one is equal to oneself.' It refers to me.

Subcommentary: The Northern Sea is present-day Láizhōu. "Gazing out at the ocean" means indistinct; water and sun reflect each other, hence gazing out at the ocean. Ruò is the sea deity. The River Earl followed the flow east to the great sea, glanced around but could not see the water's edge, then turned his face, looked up at Hǎi Ruò, and sighed deeply, citing a rustic saying: "a hundred" is one ten-thousandth, truly not enough to boast about, yet thinking no one equals oneself—that refers to the River Earl. This is but village talk, not a comprehensive discourse.

Moreover, I have heard of those who belittle Zhòngní's learning and disparage Bóyí's righteousness—at first I did not believe it. Now I see your boundlessness; had I not come to your gate, I would be in peril, forever laughed at by those of great understanding."

Commentary: Knowing one's smallness and unable to inflate oneself, then principles are inherently plain, and aspirations have no place therein. Subcommentary: "Understanding" means the Way. People all consider Zhòngní's editing of the Six Classics as vast learning and broad knowledge, and Bóyí's yielding the state as pure and righteous, worthy of respect. Yet there are penetrating, accomplished scholars who debate loftily, regarding Bóyí's righteousness as light and Zhòngní's learning as meager. The River Earl had heard this but secretly disbelieved. Now seeing the vastness and boundlessness of the great sea, hard to exhaust, he realizes past hearsay was indeed not false. Had the River Earl not come to Hǎi Ruò's gate, it would have been greatly perilous. With such narrow, inferior views, he would long be ridiculed by those of the great Way.

Hǎi Ruò said: "One cannot speak of the sea to a well frog—it is confined by its abode. One cannot speak of ice to a summer insect—it is fixed in its season. One cannot speak of the Way to a narrow scholar—it is bound by its teachings."

Commentary: Where living beings are born and at ease, their inclinations each have extremes. Subcommentary: Hǎi Ruò, knowing the River Earl's narrow inferiority, cites three things as analogies: a frog in a pit well, hearing the sea has waves a hundred feet high without wind, would refuse belief, confined by its domain. A summer-born insect, dying by autumn, hearing that in deep winter water freezes to ice and rain forms sleet, would refuse belief, its heart set on summer. Narrow-viewed scholars, biased and stubborn, hearing of the void-penetrating ultimate Way that rejects sages and discards wisdom, making the tiny great and the great small, considering a short-lived child long-lived and Péngzǔ early-dead, would refuse belief, bound by name and teaching. The River Earl, not reaching the great river, not meeting Hǎi Ruò, boasted of his own greatness—the principle is the same.
"Now you have come out from between your banks, beheld the great sea, and recognized your own ugliness. Now I can speak with you of the great principles."

Commentary: Because he knows his measure, he can be spoken to of principles. Subcommentary: The River Earl, riding the water's flow, went beyond the banks, met Hǎi Ruò, and within the vast sea carefully observed the endless great abyss, then despised the meanness of his small river. Realizing the limits of his dwelling, he can now be spoken to of the void-penetrating great principles.

"Under heaven, no water is greater than the sea. All rivers return to it, never ceasing, yet it never fills; the Wěilǘ drains it, never stopping, yet it never empties. Spring and autumn bring no change; flood and drought it never knows. This surpasses the streams of the Jiāng and Hé beyond measure.

Subcommentary: Wěilǘ is where the sea drains, east of the Blue Sea, with a stone forty thousand lǐ wide, forty thousand lǐ thick, below all rivers, at the tail as a drain, hence Wěilǘ. Seawater pouring there scorches it, also named Scorching Pour. The Classic of Mountains and Seas says: Yì shot nine suns, which fell as Scorching Pour—this tale is far-fetched, not detailed here. Spring rain is scant, autumn rain plentiful; Yáo faced floods, Tāng faced drought. Yet the sea, as a thing, receives all rivers without filling, Scorching Pour drains it without emptying, unchanging in spring and autumn, unaware of flood or drought. In greatness, it far surpasses the Jiāng and Hé streams, the disparity vast—how can one speak of its measure?

"Yet I have never prided myself on this. I compare my form to heaven and earth, and my received breath to yin and yang. I am between heaven and earth like a small stone or tree on a great mountain. Just aware of my smallness, how could I pride myself?

Commentary: Exhausting the measure of all rivers, suspended in the Hé; the Hé suspended in the sea; the sea suspended between heaven and earth—each has its measure. This phrasing seems to observe the great to clarify the small, but its meaning is otherwise. What the world worries about is unevenness. Thus, the large complacently call the small lacking substance; the small obstinately call the large supremely full. Hence, superiors and inferiors boast and aspire, looking up and down, losing themselves—this is the delusion of the people. The deluded seek correction; to correct them, nothing is better than first exhausting their disparities and following their terms. What they call large is supremely full; thus, the autumn down burdens not heaven and earth. What they call small is lacking nothing; thus, heaven and earth surpass not the autumn down. Then the deluded have means to return, each knowing their extreme, things secure in their lot; the carefree use their innate steps to wander in self-attained fields. This is why Zhuāngzǐ utters virtuous words. If like the deluded, turning to pit small and large against each other, then such opposition is endless. To see the great and not rest in one's small, view the small and pride oneself in abundance—this rushes into realms of victory and defeat, aiding people's boastfulness—how could it reach Zhuāngzǐ's intent? Subcommentary: "Aware" means presence; "how" means why. Nothing surpasses heaven and earth in covering and bearing all things; nothing surpasses yin and yang in spreading breath and generating transformation. Thus, Hǎi Ruò compares his form to heaven and earth—no hierarchy for words; receives breath from yin and yang—thus one thing among yin and yang's images. So, using things as analogy, like a small tree or stone on Tài Mountain. Yet Hǎi Ruò, in heavenly principle, is in scant presence; each thing has its measure—how can it be enough for self-pride?
"Consider the four seas between heaven and earth—are they not like a hollow in a great marsh? Consider the Middle Kingdom within the seas—is it not like a grain in a great granary?

Subcommentary: "Hollow" means an ant hole; "grain" is grass like barnyard grass with very fine seeds; the Middle Kingdom is the nine provinces. The four seas between heaven and earth, the nine provinces within the four seas—are they not like ant holes in a great marsh, grains in a great granary? Their size and superiority-inferiority disparity is like this.

"The number of things is called ten thousand; humans are one among them. Humans crowd the nine provinces, where grain grows and boats and carts travel—humans are one among them. Compared to the ten thousand things, is this not like the tip of a hair on a horse's body?

Commentary: The distinction of small and large has its gradations; they cannot aspire to each other. Subcommentary: "Number" means name and designation; "crowd" means multitude. The number of things exceeds ten thousand, but worldly speech conveniently calls them ten thousand things; humans are one among ten thousand things. The multitude of humans in the Middle Kingdom's nine provinces, where hundred grains grow and boats and carts come and go—among ten thousand, also one. Yet comparing humans to the ten thousand things, the nine provinces to the cosmos, it is no different from a single hair on a horse's body—how could it warrant concern?
"What the Five Emperors connected, the Three Kings contested, the humane worried over, the capable labored for—all ends here.

Commentary: Not beyond one realm. Subcommentary: The Five Emperors connected through abdication; the Three Kings raised armies to contend; the humane deeply worried for the altars of soil and grain; the capable toiled in their duties—though these four endeavors differ, all principles end in the tip of a hair.
"Bóyí declined it for fame; Zhòngní discoursed on it for breadth. Their self-praise—is it not like your earlier self-praise over the water?"

Commentary: Things have fixed realms; even the wisest cannot go beyond. Thus, raising the disparity of small and large will clarify that the ultimate principle has no distinction. Subcommentary: Bóyí yielded the five ranks to gain fame; Zhòngní discussed the Six Classics to show breadth. Using this to belittle things, holding this for self-praise—how different from the River Earl's earlier self-praise over water? This connects with the previous analogy and further explains belittling Zhòngní's learning and disparaging Bóyí's righteousness.
The River Earl said: "Then, may I consider heaven and earth great and the tip of a hair small?"

Subcommentary: In form, nothing surpasses heaven and earth in greatness; in substance, nothing precedes the tip of a hair in smallness. Thus, citing the extreme great and small to show inherent differences, the River Earl presents his understanding to inquire of Hǎi Ruò. Also, if self-sufficiency is greatness, I can be greater than the two realms (heaven and earth); if lacking nothing is smallness, I can be smaller than the tip of a hair. The River Earl, having grasped this, equalizes things and self, thus expressing his resolved mind to ask if it is permissible.
Hǎi Ruò said: "No. The measures of things are endless.

Commentary: Each thing has its measure. Subcommentary: Having understood the doubt, he replies: Not permissible. The vessels and measures of things, their inherent lots differ; each, according to its reception, attains fittingness. With thousands of differences and myriad distinctions, categories are endless.
