And without insisting on fixed actions.

Subcommentary: This means that having subtly relinquished the middle one and far transcended the four propositions, how could one still flatter feelings of defamation and praise, or be deluded by thoughts of dragons and snakes? Therefore, they float and sink with the age, evolving together with the times. How could they insist on biased stagnation and commit to being one fixed thing?
Now ascending, now descending, using harmony as the measure.
Subcommentary: This means the ultimate person can ascend and descend according to the times, using harmony as the uniform measure.
Floating freely in the ancestral source of the myriad things.
Subcommentary: Using great harmony to equalize and balance, roaming to the ancestral source of creation.
To treat things as things but not be treated as a thing by things—how could there be any entanglements?
Subcommentary: If things do not treat each other as things, then there are no worries or calamities.
These are the laws of Shénnóng and Huángdì.
Commentary: Therefore, Zhuangzi also positions himself here. Subcommentary: Guǒ's commentary says: Therefore, Zhuangzi also positions himself here.
But as for the conditions of the myriad things and the transmissions of human relations, it is not so.
Subcommentary: Lún means principles. The common customs, things, transmissions, and practices are not like the former.
What joins will separate, what is complete will be destroyed, what is sharp will be blunted, what is honored will be criticized.

Subcommentary: What joins will necessarily separate; what is complete will necessarily be destroyed. The pure and incorruptible will be thwarted and injured; the honored and noble will again encounter doubt and criticism. The sentiments of the world are treacherous and skewed; how can anything be fixed? Also, being sharp wounds things; things cannot endure transformation and instead react with thwarting. Valuing one's own wealth and goods; things cannot endure disgrace and instead harbor doubt and criticism.
Having purposeful action brings loss; being worthy brings scheming against.
Subcommentary: Kuī means loss. Having purposeful action causes loss. Being worthy, due to high ambitions, becomes a target for others' schemes.
Being unworthy brings deception. How can one insist on anything?

Subcommentary: This means that regarding the above matters like worthiness and unworthiness, etc., why must one insist? Insistence means biased attachment; naming the middle is why there is completion and loss.
Alas! Disciples, remember this.
Subcommentary: "Alas!" is an exclamation of sighing. "Remember" means to record.
Is it not only in the realm of Dào and Dé?

Commentary: Because nothing can be insisted upon, one must await it and cannot use one fixed method. Only those who evolve together with the times can traverse changes and always penetrate. Subcommentary: This means that those who can use central and balanced principles reside only in the realm of Dào and Dé.
Shìnán Yìliáo visited the Marquis of Lǔ.
Subcommentary: His surname was Xióng, name Yìliáo, who lived in the southern market, hence the name.

The Marquis of Lǔ had a worried expression. Shìnánzǐ said, "Why do you have a worried expression?" The Marquis of Lǔ said, "I study the way of the former kings, cultivate the enterprise of my ancestors. I revere ghosts and honor the worthy."
Subcommentary: The former kings refer to Wáng Jì and King Wén. The ancestors refer to the Dukes of Zhōu and Bó Qín.
I am personally practicing it, without a moment's departure from dwelling in it.
Subcommentary: "Departure" means to scatter. "Dwelling" means peaceful abiding.
"Yet I cannot avoid calamities. Therefore, I worry." Shìnánzǐ said, "Your method for removing calamities is shallow."

Commentary: Having a self and being proud of your state, thus although you worry with countless concerns, honor the worthy and esteem conduct, your anxieties and thoughts deepen even more. Subcommentary: This means the methods of revering ghosts and honoring the worthy, these methods have not been removed.
"The sleek fox and the patterned leopard,"
Subcommentary: "Sleek" means large. Because their patterned, beautiful fur is pleasing and glossy, they are sought for profit by humans.

"Dwell in the mountain forests, hide in rocky caves—this is their stillness. They travel by night, rest by day—this is their caution. Though hungry and thirsty, they still carefully move about over the rivers and lakes to seek food."

Subcommentary: "Caution" means carefulness. "Carefully" still means deliberating. "Dàn" means dawn. "Xū" means all. This means though hungry and thirsty, they still deliberate and at dawn, when there are no people, call to each other over the rivers and lakes, pushing through sparse grass to seek food.
"Truly settled. Yet they cannot avoid the calamity of nets, traps, and snares. What crime have they committed? Their fur is their disaster."

Subcommentary: "Traps and snares" refer to nets and traps. This means that even with such deliberate and settled plans, they still cannot avoid the disaster of traps—there is no other crime; it is simply the disaster of their skin and color.
"Now, is the state of Lǔ not your fur? I wish you would hollow out your form, shed your skin, wash your heart, remove desires, and roam in the wilds where there are no people."

Commentary: He wants you to have no self, forget your state, and let things transform spontaneously. Subcommentary: "Hollow out your form" means forget the self. "Shed your skin" means forget the state. "Wash your heart" means forget wisdom. "Remove desires" means cease greed. "The wilds where there are no people" refers to the realm of Dào and Dé. Guǒ's commentary says: He wants you to have no self, forget your state, and let things transform spontaneously.
"In Nányuè there is a settlement called the Land of Established Dé."
Commentary: Placing it in Nányuè takes it as being far from Lǔ. Subcommentary: This means since it is far from Lǔ, it is named for establishing the way of non-action.
"Its people are simple and guileless, with few selfish desires. They know how to produce but not how to store."
Subcommentary: "Produce" means farming and work. "Store" means storing and hoarding. Since the ruler embraces the Dào, the people also return to simplicity.
"They give without seeking repayment. They do not know where righteousness should go, nor where ritual should lead."
Subcommentary: "Righteousness" means what is fitting. "Lead" means to conduct.
"They are recklessly unrestrained in their actions,"
Subcommentary: "Recklessly unrestrained" means without a calculating mind. "In their actions" means mixing with the traces.
"Yet they tread the great square."

Commentary: Each follows their own fundamental step, and everyone treads their own square; thus, the ten thousand squares are attained—is that not great? Subcommentary: "Square" means the Dào. Recklessly unrestrained, following their nature, mixing traces and unrestrained actions, they can tread the great square of the Dào.
"Their life is joyful, their death is a burial."
Commentary: This means one can abide in it from beginning to end. Subcommentary: Guǒ's commentary says: This means one can abide in it from beginning to end.
"I wish you to leave your state, abandon customs, and walk alongside the Dào."

Commentary: The so-called leaving the state and abandoning customs means to sweep clean what is in your chest. Subcommentary: "Abandon" means to discard. This means to discard customs and walk alongside the ultimate Dào of non-action, mutually guiding.
The Marquis said, "That Dào is distant and perilous, and there are rivers and mountains. I have no boat or carriage—what can I do?"
Commentary: He truly thinks he wants him to go to Nányuè. Subcommentary: Delusion and enlightenment have different natures, hence the separation between Lǔ and Yuè.
Shìnánzǐ said, "Do not be arrogantly rigid in form,"
Commentary: "Arrogantly rigid in form" means obstructions and hindrances. Subcommentary: Do not rely on high rank and honor, with an arrogantly rigid demeanor.
"Do not滞留 in dwelling,"
Commentary: "滞留 in dwelling" means stagnant clinging. Subcommentary: Follow things and accept their course, without stagnating in glorious views.
"And use this as your carriage."
Commentary: Form level with things, heart transforming with things—this is relying on things to carry oneself.
The Marquis said, "That Dào is dark and distant, with no people. With whom will you be neighbors? I have no provisions, I have no food—how can I get there?"
Subcommentary: He has not yet embodied solitary transformation and cannot forget things.
Shìnánzǐ said, "Reduce your expenses, lessen your desires. Then, though you have no provisions, you will have enough."

Commentary: The so-called knowing contentment means there is nothing not sufficient. Subcommentary: This means the Dào is not completed by relying on things, but only through tranquility and simplicity.
"Then cross the river and float on the sea."
Subcommentary: "River" means wisdom. "Sea" means the Dào. Cross the river of supreme goodness, roam the sea of the great Dào.
"Look, and you cannot see its shore; the further you go, the more you do not know where it ends."
Commentary: This cuts off the distance of emotional desires. Subcommentary: How can one know its ultimate limit?
"Those who see you off all turn back from the shore."

Commentary: If you wish to cut off ties, then the people each return to guarding their own roles. Subcommentary: Those who send you off on your journey to the realm of Dào and Dé, the people return to guarding their inherent simple roles. "Shore" means boundary.
"And you, from here, go far away."
Commentary: Transcendent and independent above the myriad things. Subcommentary: "From" means following. You, from here, follow the purity and height of Dào and Dé, mysteriously distant.
"Therefore, to possess people is an entanglement."

Commentary: "To possess people" means to have them as one's own private possession. Subcommentary: Ruling over the state of Lǔ, enriching and possessing people and things as one's own—this deeply becomes a sickness and entanglement.
"To be possessed by people is a worry."

Commentary: "To be possessed by people" means to be used and employed by others. Subcommentary: This means being unable to forget Lǔ, being possessed by others—thus revering ghosts, honoring the worthy, pitying people, caring for the multitude—is this not worry and calamity from being employed and toiled?
"Therefore, Yáo did not possess people, nor was he possessed by people."

Commentary: Although he possessed the world, he entrusted it all to the hundred officials, delegated it to the myriad things, and did not involve himself—this is not possessing people. Following the people and employing things without toiling himself—this is not being possessed by people. Subcommentary: Guǒ's commentary says: Although he possessed the world, he entrusted it all to the hundred officials, delegated it to the myriad things, and did not involve himself—this is not possessing people. Following the people and employing things without toiling himself—this is not being possessed by people.
"I wish to remove your entanglements and eliminate your worries, and alone roam with the Dào in the Land of Great Nothingness."
Commentary: He wants you to be cleansed and without any thought of the state. Subcommentary: "Great Nothingness" is like great non-being. This means nothing in the world can adulterate it.
"Using a double boat to cross the river,"
Subcommentary: Two boats side by side are called a double boat.
"An empty boat comes and collides with it. Even a narrow-minded person would not get angry."
Subcommentary: "Narrow-minded" means petty and quick-tempered. The reason for not getting angry is that the boat is empty.

"If there is one person in it, then he calls out to him to draw in or push away. One call, and he doesn't hear; a second call, and he doesn't hear; then at the third call, he will surely follow it with angry shouts."
Subcommentary: "Angry shouts" mean cursing and insults.
"Before, he was not angry, but now he is angry. Before, it was empty; now, it is full. If a person can empty himself and roam the world, who can harm him?"
Commentary: Although the world changes, in emptying oneself to avoid harm, it is the same. Subcommentary: "Emptying oneself" means having no calculating mind.
Běigōng Shē
Subcommentary: Surname Běigōng, name Shē. He lived in the northern palace, hence the surname. A minister of Wèi.
Collected taxes for Duke Líng of Wèi to make bells, and built an altar outside the outer city gate.
Subcommentary: This means that to make bells, one must first set up a sacrifice, hence the altar.
In three months, he completed the upper and lower sets of bells.
Subcommentary: The upper and lower sets harmonize the eight tones, fully prepared, hence called "sets."
Prince Qìngjì saw him and asked, "What method did you employ?"
Subcommentary: Prince Qìngjì of the Zhōu king, a minister of Zhōu. This means he saw the bell altar was extremely exquisite and, finding it strange, asked about it.
Shē said, "In the unity, I dared not employ any method."

Commentary: Serenely embracing unity—I dared not artificially set up methods to enhance affairs. Subcommentary: Guǒ's commentary says: Serenely embracing unity—I dared not artificially set up methods to enhance affairs.
"I have heard: 'After carving and polishing, return to the unhewn wood.'"
Commentary: Returning to use its original nature. Subcommentary: Guǒ's commentary says: Returning to use the original nature.
"Childlike, as if without knowledge,"
Commentary: Simply following its pure simplicity. Subcommentary: "Childlike" describes the appearance of no artificial feelings. Simply following its淳朴 simplicity.
"Absent-minded, as if indolent and doubtful,"
Commentary: Having no direction. Subcommentary: "Absent-minded" means without scheming. "Indolent" means withdrawing. This means that matters of doubt and scheming

Zhuāngzǐ said, "It is poverty, not exhaustion. A scholar who possesses the Way and virtue but cannot practice them is exhausted. Worn clothes and tattered shoes signify poverty, not exhaustion. This is what is called not encountering the right time. Have you, King, not seen the leaping monkeys? When they get hold of nán, zǐ, or yùzhāng trees, they cling to the branches and reign supreme among them. Even Yì or Péng Méng could not glance askance at them.

Note: When encountering the right time and obtaining the right place, they extend their long branches. Thus, even ancient skilled archers could not harm them. Explanation: Nán, zǐ, and yùzhāng are all upright and fine trees. 'Clinging' means grasping. 'Reigning supreme' means being self-satisfied. Yì was a skilled archer in ancient times; Péng Méng was his disciple. 'Glancing askance' means looking sideways. Some texts use the character '聒', read similarly, meaning that a worthy scholar or virtuous man, when encountering the right time and place, is like a monkey finding straight trees—leaping and jumping freely. Even if there are skilled archers, they dare not lift their eyes to look sideways, let alone bend their bows.

When they find themselves among zhè, jí, zhǐ, or gǒu trees, they move cautiously, glance sideways, and tremble with fear. This is not because their sinews and bones have become tighter and less flexible,

but because the situation is inconvenient and insufficient to display their abilities. Explanation: Zhè, jí, gǒu, and zhǐ are all thorny, undesirable trees. When monkeys are among thorny trees, they cannot display their agility and cleverness, so they feel sorrowful and tremble inwardly, moving cautiously and glancing sideways. It is not that their sinews and bones have changed from before, but that the circumstances are inconvenient. Scholars encountering a chaotic age must also be like this.
Now, dwelling between foolish rulers and chaotic ministers, how can one avoid exhaustion? This is the evidence of Bǐ Gān having his heart cut out.

Note: If one forces action when the situation is inconvenient, one will suffer harm. Explanation: This is a comprehensive discussion. At that time, the Zhōu court was weak, and the six states were flourishing. Thus, with foolish rulers above and chaotic ministers below, Zhuāngzǐ, embracing the Way and virtue, could not be employed. He concealed his traces to avoid harm, hence these words. In the past, when King Zhòu of Yīn was unprincipled, Bǐ Gān remonstrated loyally and had his heart cut out—was that not evidence? Citing the past to prove the present is like a clear mirror for another day.

Confucius was trapped between Chén and Cài, with no cooked food for seven days. He leaned left on a withered tree and beat a withered branch with a stone, singing the air of Biāo's era. He had the instruments but not the rhythm, the sound but not the melody. The sound of the wood and the human voice were distinctly fitting to the human heart.

Explanation: Biāo refers to Shénnóng. Confucius, being a sage, was content with poverty and success. Though trapped between Chén and Cài, he did not abandon non-action. Thus, beating a withered branch with his left hand and leaning on a dry branch with his right, he was serene and self-satisfied, singing the pure air of Biāo's era. Wood is one of the eight musical materials; though he beat it, there was no melody, no pitch—merely striking wood, how could there be scales? Yet the song and the wood sound were clear and light, pleasing and rectifying the heart, thus fitting to the human heart.
Yán Huí stood upright with hands clasped, turning his eyes to gaze. Confucius feared that he was exaggerating himself to achieve greatness or loving himself to create sorrow.

Explanation: Yán Huí, having seen Confucius beating wood and singing, straightened his body and turned his eyes to look. Confucius feared he had not understood and was wildly speculating, thinking that the Master was exaggerating his own virtue to aspire to greatness or loving himself to lament his poverty. Worrying he might think thus, Confucius called him to instruct him.
He said, "Huí, it is easy not to accept Heaven's diminishment,
Note: Only by accepting it is it easy.
but difficult not to accept human increase."

Note: Things that come by chance cannot be resisted. Explanation: The principle of nature includes the diminishment of poverty and obstruction; understanding fate and accepting it is easy. Human relations include the increase of emolument; when it comes by chance, pushing it away is difficult. This clarifies that Confucius, though beating wood and singing, had no sorrow or resentment in his heart.
"There is no beginning that is not an end.

Note: What is a beginning today was an end yesterday. Thus, the so-called beginning is the end, indicating the boundlessness of change. Explanation: 'End' means conclusion. What is a beginning today was an end yesterday. To clarify that there is no beginning, no end, no birth, no death—since there is no death or birth, how can there be poverty or obstruction to sorrow over?
Humanity and Heaven are one."
Note: Both are natural. Explanation: The so-called Heaven's diminishment and human increase are still teachings of traces. When reaching the principle of doubt, all is natural, hence not dual.
"Now, who is the one singing?"

Note: Let it be spontaneous, then the singer is not me. Explanation: The great sage empties and forgets, losing both self and others. Since I am not I, who is the one singing? I have no self; where then can the song reside?

Huí said, "May I ask about 'not accepting Heaven's diminishment is easy'?" Confucius said, "Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, poverty, and obstruction are the movements of Heaven and Earth, the flow and discharge of things.

Note: They cannot be escaped. Explanation: Previously, names were briefly indicated; here, the meaning is explained. 'Obstruction' means blockage. Fate's ultimate poverty and obstruction, the inability to practice the Way and virtue—this is like the emptiness and fullness of Heaven and Earth, the turning of the four seasons, the movement and discharge of all things and climates.
This means to go along with them.

Note: This is the so-called 'unknowing and unlearning, yet following the rule of the Emperor.' Explanation: 'Along' means together; 'go' means to proceed. Since one embodies the inconstancy of moving things, one goes along with changes without joy or aversion therein.
As a minister, one dares not leave this. If the way of a minister is like this, how much more so for how one should await Heaven?

Note: Being at peace wherever one is, not considering diminishment as diminishment—this is awaiting Heaven without accepting its diminishment. Explanation: As a minister, one dares not escape the ruler's command; upholding the way of a minister is thus natural. How much more for the changes of poverty and success—one must await the principle of nature; how can one oppose it?
"What does 'not accepting human increase is difficult' mean?" Confucius said, "When first employed, one reaches out in all directions,
Note: Responding and connecting widely is reaching out in all directions.
ranks and emoluments come together without end,
Note: Connecting widely thus allows one to驾驭 the high and great.
but the benefits of things are not one's own.

Note: They are not sought and taken by oneself. Explanation: 'First' means origin; 'should' means fitting. The wondrous origin is empty and still; traces respond to opportunities, connecting widely in all directions, concentrating illumination across the nine realms. Once bound by fine ranks, wealth and virtue are endless; seeking benefit from all things is fitting.
My fate lies externally.

Note: Human life must externally encounter the fate of interacting with things, not like tiles or stones limited to form and substance. Explanation: Confucius, a sage, upheld Heaven's mandate, operating with external virtue to save the common people, not like the form and substance of tiles or stones.
A gentleman does not rob, a worthy does not steal—if I were to take them, what would that be?

Note: 'Robbing' and 'stealing' mean taking privately. Now, the ranks and emoluments of worthies and gentlemen are not taken privately but accepted as they come. Explanation: Worthies and gentlemen do not even rob or steal, let alone Confucius, a great sage—would he violate Heaven and principle to privately take ranks and emoluments? When they come by chance, accept them—that is all, for there is no mind involved.
Thus it is said, 'No bird is wiser than the yìér; where its eyes deem unsuitable, it does not linger to look. Even if it drops its food, it abandons it and flees.'

Note: Avoiding harm swiftly. Explanation: Yìér is a swallow. 'Food' means sustenance. Intelligent enough to avoid harm and preserve the body, no bird surpasses the swallow. Flying into human dwellings to build nests, if its eyes briefly see an unsuitable place, it does not wait to look thoroughly but flies far away. Even if it drops food it carried, it quickly abandons it and flees, never retrieving it—such is its speed in avoiding harm.
It fears humans yet nests among them,

Note: None who distance themselves from others are preserved by them. Fearing humans yet entering human dwellings—this is why this bird is called wise. Explanation: 'Nest' means to enter. The swallow fears humans yet依附 on them, entering human houses to build nests. Thus, people love and befriend it, allowing it to avoid harm. Similarly, the sage harmonizes light in the world, blending traces among humans, cautious of disasters and dangers, not drowning in dusty realms. The common people gladly support without tiring, thus achieving long life and enduring vision.
The state is preserved therein.

Note: Compared to the ultimate person, who mysteriously unites with the world, the world gladly supports without tiring, jointly establishing altars and millet—this is why not accepting human increase is difficult. Explanation: The sage's virtue extends far, the multitude gladly supports—the preservation of the state is thus fitting. The so-called human increase refers to this.
"What does 'there is no beginning that is not an end' mean?" Confucius said, "It transforms all things without knowing what succeeds them,

Note: None perceive their change. Explanation: 'Succeed' means to replace. The Way generates all things, transforms the multitude, operates unceasingly, renewing and changing daily without awareness, thus none perceive their succession. Since there is daily renewal and change, how can there be beginning and end?
How can one know their end? How can one know their beginning? Simply uphold correctness and await it, that is all."

Note: Day and night alternate without beginning or end, so uphold correctness and await it, without any personal concerns. Explanation: The end is the beginning, the beginning is the end—how can one fix beginning and end? Since there is no end and beginning, there is no death and life. Thus, follow change and accept transformation, meeting all with adaptability. Hold fast to true correctness and await the Creator, that is all.
"What does 'humanity and Heaven are one' mean?" Confucius said, "What is of humanity is Heaven; what is of Heaven is also Heaven.

Note: All so-called Heaven clarifies spontaneity without action. Explanation: Human relations and all things are all spontaneous; love and spontaneity are included. Thus, humanity and Heaven are not dual; all things are blended and unified.
Humanity cannot possess the nature of Heaven.

Note: Speaking of spontaneity, it is spontaneous; how can humans deliberately have this spontaneity? It is spontaneous, hence called nature. Explanation: Spontaneity means not knowing why it is so, yet it is so—spontaneous, not acted upon. How can it be possessed? If it were possessed, it would not be spontaneous. Thus, know that spontaneity is nature, not something humans possess. This explains the earlier meaning of 'having Heaven.'
The sage is tranquil, embodying passage until the end."

Note: Tranquil without pride, embodying and changing together. Explanation: 'Tranquil' means peaceful; 'passage' means going. The sage penetrates the non-duality of beginning and end, comprehends the oneness of life and death, thus able to peacefully dissolve the body, follow transformation and go, floating without beginning, accepting change until the end.

Zhuāng Zhou was wandering in the fenced area of Diāolíng when he saw a strange magpie coming from the south, with wings seven feet wide and eyes an inch in diameter. It brushed against Zhuāng Zhou's forehead and perched in a chestnut grove.

Explanation: Diāolíng is the name of a chestnut garden. 'Fenced area' means a hedge. He was wandering inside the hedge of the chestnut garden. 'Diameter' means round. 'Brushed' means touched. 'Forehead' means brow. An unusual magpie came from the south, wings seven feet long, eyes round an inch, striking Zhuāngzǐ's forehead and then perching in the chestnut grove.
Zhuāng Zhou said, "What bird is this? Wings large yet not flying away, eyes big yet not seeing." He hitched his robe and strode quickly, holding a catapult to await it.

Explanation: 'Large' means big. 'Fly away' means to go. 'Striding quickly' means walking rapidly. 'Await' means to watch for. Wings large but unable to fly far, eyes big but unable to see far—Zhuāngzǐ found it strange and immediately formed an intention to seek it. Then he stepped quickly, holding a catapult to watch.
He saw a cicada that had just found a fine shade and forgotten itself. A mantis, hiding behind a cover, seized it, seeing gain and forgetting its form.
Note: Hiding behind a leaf to stalk the cicada, forgetting that its form was seen by the strange magpie.
The strange magpie followed to profit from it, seeing gain and forgetting its true self.

Note: Eyes can see, wings can fly—this is the bird's true nature. Now, seeing gain, it forgets it. Explanation: 'Seize' means to catch. 'True self' means essential nature. Zhuāngzǐ, holding the catapult unused, suddenly saw a cicada hiding under leaves, enjoying the shade, unaware of its own body. A mantis, hiding behind a leaf, intended to catch the cicada, unaware its form was seen by the magpie. The magpie, following behind the mantis, sought profit from catching the cicada, intending to gain benefit, unaware of the danger to its life—this is called forgetting its true self.
Zhuāng Zhou was startled and said, "Ah! Things indeed entangle each other.

Note: Those who mutually seek profit often entangle each other. Explanation: Having seen the cicada and magpie pursuing profit and forgetting themselves, he was startled and alarmed, then said 'ah!' in sigh. Thus, he knew that things seeking mutual profit must have entanglements and worries.
Two kinds attract each other."

Note: Those who desire things are also desired by things. Explanation: Those who desire things are also desired by things. Thus, cicada and magpie are both worldly beings; profit and harm attract each other—this is inevitable.
He discarded the catapult and turned to leave, but the park keeper pursued and questioned him.

Note: 'Questioned' means to interrogate. Explanation: 'Discarded' means abandoned. The park keeper is the guardian of the chestnut garden. 'Questioned' means to ask. Realizing profit and harm follow each other, he abandoned the catapult and turned to leave. The park keeper, suspecting theft of chestnuts, pursued and questioned him.
Zhuāng Zhou returned home and did not enter the courtyard for three months. Lìn Jū followed and asked, "Master, why have you not entered the courtyard lately?"

Explanation: Zhuāng Zhou, seeing the magpie forget himself, was suspected of stealing chestnuts. Returning home ashamed, he did not go out into the courtyard. Lìn Jū, a disciple of Zhuāngzǐ, wondered why his master had lately secluded himself, thus following to ask.
Zhuāng Zhou said, "I guarded form and forgot myself,
Note: Being in the human world, there are dangers and safeties. If one applies a safe form to this world without gauging what suits this world, this is guarding form and forgetting oneself.
gazed at turbid water and was confused by the clear abyss.

Note: Seeing others without clarity, one relies on them to see oneself, almost forgetting the way of reflection. Explanation: I saw profit and pursued things, guarding form while profit and harm attracted each other, forgetting myself. Having seen the magpie and cicada, returning home and not entering the courtyard, I also blamed myself. Thus, quietly gazing at turbid water, I was confused by the clear spring. Though not my original nature, fitting intentions still remained—the way of reflection.
Moreover, I have heard the Master say, 'Enter a custom, follow its rules.'

Note: Do not violate its prohibitions and orders. Explanation: Zhuāng Zhou studied under Lǎo Dān, thus calling the latter 'Master.' The enlightened blend with dust and enter customs; where customs have prohibitions, follow and practice them. Now, having wandered in Diāolíng, suspected of stealing chestnuts, I lightly violated the law—words of regret and self-blame.

Now I wandered in Diāolíng and forgot myself; the strange magpie brushed my forehead. Wandering in the chestnut grove, I forgot my true self; the park keeper took me for a offender. This is why I have not entered the courtyard."

Note: Considering the questioning as an offense. Zhuāngzǐ promoted equality under heaven, thus often used words to convey meaning, hence slandering Confucius, belittling Lǎo Dān, attacking the Three Sovereigns above, and paining his own body below. Explanation: Intending towards the strange magpie, I forgot the chestnut grove's prohibitions—this is forgetting myself. Some texts use 'true self'; read accordingly. The park keeper
The Southern Florescence True Classic Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Twenty-Three, Part Two
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Outer Chapters, Tián Zǐfāng, Number Twenty-One
Tián Zǐfāng was attending upon Wèi Wénhóu seated and repeatedly praised Xī Gōng.

Subcommentary: His surname was Tián, his personal name was Wú Zé, his courtesy name was Zǐfāng. He was a worthy man of Wèi and a teacher to Wèi Wénhóu. Wèi Wénhóu was the seventh-generation descendant of Bì Wàn and the father of Wǔhóu. Xī Gōng, surname Xī, personal name Gōng, was also a worthy man of Wèi.
Wèi Wénhóu said: "Is Xī Gōng your teacher, Master?" Zǐfāng said: "He is not. He is a man from my village. His explanations of the Way are frequently apt, therefore I, Wú Zé, praise him."
Subcommentary: Xī Gōng was a man from Zǐfāng's village. His explanations and discourses on the Way were frequently in accordance with principle, therefore Wú Zé praised him. He was not his teacher.

Wèi Wénhóu said: "Then do you have no teacher, Master?" Zǐfāng said: "I have." [Wèi Wénhóu] said: "Who is your teacher, Master?" Zǐfāng said: "It is Dōngguō Shùnzǐ." Wèi Wénhóu said: "Then why has the Master never praised him?"

Subcommentary: He lived east of the outer city wall, hence he took Dōngguō as his surname. His name was Shùnzǐ, and he was Zǐfāng's teacher. Since he is your teacher, Sir, why do you not praise or speak of him?
Zǐfāng said: "His person is authentic."
Commentary: Without falsity. Subcommentary: What is called an authentic person of the Way.
"He has the appearance of a man but is of Heaven."

Commentary: Although his appearance is the same as a man's, he uniquely relies on spontaneity. Subcommentary: Although his appearance again conforms to human principles, his mind is in accord with spontaneity.
"Empty, compliant, and preserving authenticity."

Commentary: Empty and compliant with things, therefore he does not lose authenticity. Subcommentary: 'Yuán' means compliance. His mind is empty and compliant with things, constantly guarding the authentic source. Active yet constantly tranquil.
"Pure and accommodating of things."

Commentary: Purity is troubled by being overly clean. Now, being pure yet accommodating things is identical with Heaven. Subcommentary: Guǒ's commentary says: Purity is troubled by being overly clean. Now, being pure yet accommodating things is identical with Heaven.
"When things lack the Way, he rectifies his countenance to enlighten them, causing people's intentions to dissipate."

Commentary: Vastly empty and clear, he merely rectifies himself, and the perversity of things naturally dissipates. Subcommentary: For things in the world that lack the Way and people who are perverse and unorthodox, Dōngguō rectifies his own demeanor and appearance, causing them to awaken and understand, making their deluded and confused intentions naturally dissolve and vanish.
"How could Wú Zé be sufficient to praise him?"
Subcommentary: My teacher's abundant virtue is so profound and mysterious; someone as庸鄙 as Wú Zé, how could he be sufficient to praise and extol him?
Zǐfāng went out. Wèi Wénhóu looked lost and did not speak the entire day. He summoned the ministers standing before him and said to them: "Far-reaching indeed! The noble man of complete virtue."

Subcommentary: 'Tǎngrán' is the appearance of being lost. Hearing the discussion of Shùnzǐ's virtue, he was lost and ungrounded, naturally bereft of what he had called his own. Therefore, he did not speak the entire day. Thereupon, he summoned the ministers standing in attendance before him and spoke with them, sighing that the Way of Dōngguō Zǐ was profound and far-reaching, difficult to know. Truly, a person of complete virtue can be a nobleman to the myriad things.

"Initially, I considered the words of sages and wise men and the conduct of humaneness and righteousness to be the ultimate. Having heard of Master Zǐfāng's teacher, my body felt dissolved and I did not wish to move; my mouth felt clamped shut and I did not wish to speak."
Commentary: He spontaneously felt his own nearness.
"What I have learned is truly but a clod of earth!"

Commentary: It is not an authentic thing. Subcommentary: I, in my earlier studies, used the words of the former kings, the sages and wise men, and the conduct of the Zhōu and Kǒng, humaneness and righteousness, considering them the ultimate in exhausting principle. Now, hearing the description of Zǐfāng's teacher, whose Way is vast and broad, consequently caused my body to dissolve and disperse, unable to move or stop; my tongue clamped and trapped, with no words to speak. I spontaneously realized that what I had learned was merely a 'man of earth'—when it encounters rain, it crumbles—it is not an authentic thing. A 'clod of earth' is a figurine made of earth.
"And this state of Wèi is truly a burden to me!"

Commentary: One who knows the ultimate nobility considers human ranks a burden. Subcommentary: Having already heard the authentic Way, his body collapsed and he sat in forgetfulness. Therefore, he knew that ranks and positions, altars and earth, are precisely burdens of worry.

Wēn Bó Xuězǐ was going to Qí and lodged in Lǔ. A man of Lǔ requested to see him. Wēn Bó Xuězǐ said: "It cannot be. I have heard that the noble men of the Central States are clear about ritual and righteousness but clumsy in knowing the human heart. I do not wish to see him."

Subcommentary: Surname Wēn, personal name Bó, courtesy name Xuězǐ, a man of Chǔ who embraced the Way. The 'Central States' refers to the state of Lǔ. 'Clumsy' means awkward. Traveling from Chǔ to Qí, he passed through Lǔ and stopped at a host's lodging. The man of Lǔ was a disciple of Confucius. Hearing that Wēn Bó Xuězǐ was a worthy man, he requested an audience. Wēn Bó did not consent, saying: "I have heard that the people of the Central States are clear about the traces of sages, ritual and righteousness, but clumsy in knowing the human heart. Therefore, I do not wish to see him."
When he reached Qí and returned, lodging again in Lǔ, this same man again requested to see him.
Subcommentary: Wēn Bó reached Qí and, upon returning, lodged again in Lǔ. The man from before again wished to request an audience.
Wēn Bó Xuězǐ said: "When I was going, he sought to see me; now, again, he seeks to see me. This must mean he has some way to stir me up."

Subcommentary: 'Qí' means to seek. 'Zhèn' means to stir or move. Previously, when I was going to Qí, he sought to see me. Now that I have returned to Lǔ, he again comes seeking an audience. He must certainly have some other reason, wishing thereby to move and stir me.

He went out and saw the guest; upon entering, he sighed. The next day, he saw the guest and again, upon entering, sighed. His servant said: "Every time you see this guest, you invariably enter and sigh. Why is that?"
Subcommentary: Seeing the guest repeatedly, he sighed to himself frequently. Wēn Bó's servant found it strange and asked him about it.

He said: "I had already told you: The people of the Central States are clear about ritual and righteousness but clumsy in knowing the human heart. The one who came to see me—his advances and withdrawals were entirely by the compass, entirely by the square; his demeanor was now like a dragon, now like a tiger."

Commentary: Pivoting his steps, winding his path. Subcommentary: Bowing, kneeling, making salutations and deferrals, advancing and withdrawing in perfect squares and circles, winding like a coiling dragon, pivoting like a tiger.
"In admonishing me, he was like a son; in guiding me, he was like a father."
Commentary: Such are the flaws of ritual and righteousness.
"This is why I sighed."

Subcommentary: In correcting and admonishing me, he was like a son serving his father; in instructing and guiding me, he was like a father teaching his son. Now, distance and closeness, honor and humility, inherently possess their own natural affection and duty. Since this is not his innate nature, why such earnestness? This shows the flaw of sage traces, leading to such artifice. This is why I sighed.
Zhòngní saw him but did not speak.
Commentary: He already knew his mind.
Zǐlù said: "My Master, you have long wished to see Wēn Bó Xuězǐ. Having seen him, why did you not speak?"
Subcommentary: The two men had grasped the meaning, therefore they forgot words. Zhòng Yóu found it strange, hence he raised the question.
Zhòngní said: "As for that man, with a glance the Way is present. There is no room for speech."

Commentary: As soon as the eyes move, the meaning is already conveyed; there is no place for his virtuous words. Subcommentary: 'Jī' means to move. A person who embodies understanding, forgetting words and grasping principle—as soon as his eyes move, the mysterious Way is present. There is no need to further trouble with words and expend speech allowing for verbal explanations.

Yán Yuān asked Zhòngní, saying: "When you, Master, walk, I also walk; when you hurry, I also hurry; when you run, I also run; but when you dash away, leaving the dust behind, I can only stare blankly from behind!" The Master said: "Huí, what do you mean?" He said: "When you, Master, walk, I also walk—that is, when you speak, I also speak. When you hurry, I also hurry—that is, when you debate, I also debate. When you run, I also run—that is, when you speak of the Way, I also speak of the Way. But when you dash away, leaving the dust behind, and I stare blankly from behind—that is, when you, Master, do not speak yet are trusted, do not associate closely yet are comprehensive, hold no rank yet the people gather before you—and I do not know how it is so. That is all."

Subcommentary: 'Dashing away, leaving the dust behind' means running swiftly. 'Staring blankly' is the appearance of staring straight ahead. Vanishing dust, rapid and swift, impossible to catch up to, hence staring straight ahead while left behind. 'Rank' means noble position. The Master does not speak yet is trusted by others; he has never been personally intimate yet circulates with things; he truly holds no ruler's position, yet the people fully gather before him, and the multitude assembles. I do not know how it is so, yet it is so—it is simply so, that is all. This is what is called 'dashing away, leaving the dust behind.'
Zhòngní said: "How can you not examine this! There is no sorrow greater than the death of the heart, while the death of the person is next."

Commentary: If the heart considers death as death, then it further hastens its death. The speed of its death arises from sorrow leading to the loss of itself. If there is no sorrow, that is all; if there is sorrow, then the heart that considers death as death is the greatest sorrow. Subcommentary: Not associating closely yet being comprehensive, not speaking yet being trusted—this surely stems from an empty heart complying with things; how could it be for no reason? How can you not forget your reflections, shine your mirror, and carefully examine your mind? Now, among the burdens of emotions, none surpass the changes and transformations of the heart. Changes, transformations, production, and extinction are deeply sorrowful and grievous. Yet to sorrow over life and death is secondary.
"The sun emerges in the east and enters at the western extreme; the myriad things all take it as their measure."

Commentary: All are visible. Subcommentary: The night is dark, the day bright; it emerges east, enters west. This is also like people entering obscurity and emerging into clarity, dying and being born. Therefore, know that human death and life are analogous to the day and night of heaven. Using this as a metaphor, why regret anything?
"Those with eyes and feet depend on this to achieve success."

Commentary: Eyes achieve the work of seeing; feet achieve the work of walking. Subcommentary: 'Zhǐ' means feet. All the hundred parts of a person receive from Yīn and Yáng; eyes see, feet walk, relying on creation and transformation. If they did not depend on this, how could they achieve success? Therefore, know that death and life do not depend on man.
"When this emerges, there is existence; when this enters, there is demise."

Commentary: Simply because it is not seen, it is called demise; ultimately, it does not perish. Subcommentary: Seeing the sun emerge is called existence; observing the sun enter is called demise. This is merely the reckless attachment of ordinary feelings, not the penetrating perspective of the sage.
"The myriad things are likewise: they depend on it for death; they depend on it for life."

Commentary: Depending on concealment is called death; depending on manifestation is called life; ultimately, there is no death or life. Subcommentary: The concealment and manifestation of things all depend on creation and transformation. Concealment is called death; manifestation is called life. Since the sun's emergence and entrance have no existence or demise, how can the concealment and manifestation of things have death and life?
"Once I received this formed body, I do not transform but await its end."

Commentary: What exists cannot change into non-existence; therefore, once it receives its form, its transformations are endless. Subcommentary: My form and nature are received from creation and transformation; brightness and darkness, beauty and ugliness, the limits and boundaries are already fixed. After this, there are no further changes. I merely sit upright awaiting the end, spending my years thus. Since beauty and ugliness are not of my own freedom, surely life and death should also be entrusted [to fate].
"I imitate things and move."

Commentary: Spontaneously without a heart. Subcommentary: The ultimate sage is empty and concentrated; when stimulated, he responds accordingly. Things move and he moves, spontaneously without a heart.
"Day and night without interval"
Commentary: Constantly transforming, ever new. Subcommentary: Transforming and changing, daily renewed, vanishing without a gap.
"And I do not know its final end."
Commentary: He does not consider death as death. Subcommentary: Following it, one does not see its rear.
"Vapor-like, it forms the body."

Commentary: Vapor-like, it spontaneously forms; what, then, is it doing? Subcommentary: 'Vapor-like' describes the appearance of spontaneous movement. Vapor-like, it receives the vital breath and forms the body; no thing causes it to be so.
"Knowing fate, one cannot plan ahead of it; I, Qiū, therefore daily proceed."

Commentary: Not tied to what is ahead, he goes along with the changes. Therefore, he daily proceeds. Subcommentary: 'Cú' means to go. Penetrating the changes of the times, he cannot pre-establish plans and models. Embodying daily renewal, therefore he goes along with the transformations.
"All my life I have been with you, and in the crossing of our arms I lost you—is this not sorrowful?"

Commentary: Change and transformation cannot be grasped and retained. Therefore, even if you hold arms and guard each other, you cannot make it stop. If one sorrows over the dead, then this too can be sorrowed over. Now, if you have never considered this sorrowful, why sorrow over death alone? Subcommentary: Confucius and Yánzǐ, two worthy sages, cultivated together in one body. Each was like crossing arms, yet changing and transforming daily anew, flowing and shifting rapidly. Rarely holding fast and guarding firmly, unable to pause even briefly—between the clasping of arms, suddenly it has already passed. The new is already in motion, therefore it is lost. If you grieve because of this loss, this is deeply sorrowful.
"You are nearly attached to what I am attached to. That has already vanished, yet you seek it as if it exists—this is like seeking a horse in a market road."

Commentary: A market road is not a place where horses stop. This means seeking what was there before cannot be regained. Human life is like a horse passing through a marketplace; it never stays for a moment. The new and old succeed each other without ceasing, day and night. 'Attached' means to perceive. This means you nearly see what I see. What I see is daily renewal. Therefore, what has passed has already vanished; how can you possess it? Subcommentary: 'Dài' means nearly. 'Zhù' means to perceive. 'Táng' means road; 'sì' means market. What I perceive is changing events, daily renewed. Yán Huí and Confucius were talking face to face; the words spoken a moment ago are not far off, hence he says 'nearly'. Those past events have already vanished by now. You still seek the existence of that earlier time, thinking
Bó Hūn Wú Rén said, "This is shooting with the intention to shoot, not shooting without the intention to shoot."
Commentary: It means although you are skillful, it is still shooting with a conscious mind, not the shooting that forgets and is without intention.
I shall try climbing a high mountain with you, treading on precarious rocks, facing an abyss a hundred rèn deep—would you be able to shoot then?
Commentary: Seven chǐ make one rèn, so it is seven hundred chǐ deep. "If" refers to you. This is the shooting without shooting.

Thereupon, Wú Rén then climbed the high mountain, trod on the precarious rocks, faced the abyss a hundred rèn deep, stepped backward until two-tenths of his feet hung over the edge, bowed to Yù Kòu, and invited him forward. Yù Kòu lay prostrate on the ground, sweat streaming down to his heels.

Commentary: Earlier, he briefly described the idea of shooting; here, he directly intended to draw the bow. "Stepping backward" means retreating. "Invite" means to yield. He climbed the towering high mountain, trod on the dangerously hanging rocks, faced the extremely perilous abyss, still turned his back to the abyss and stepped back, with two-tenths of his feet hanging outside in the void, drawing the bow as calmly as ever. He bowed to Yù Kòu and yielded to him. Yù Kòu, terrified and unable to lift his head, closed his eyes, lay prostrate on the ground, sweat streaming down to his feet.
Bó Hūn Wú Rén said, "The ultimate person gazes up to the blue sky above and dives into the yellow springs below, roaming freely to the eight extremes, his spirit and energy unchanged."

Note: "Roaming freely" means to let go and wander. When virtue fills the inside, the spirit overflows outward; there is no distance, darkness, or depth that is not illuminated. Thus, he discerns the moment of safety and danger and remains calm and self-possessed.
Now you are frightened and have the look of terror in your eyes; your chances of hitting the target are almost gone."

Note: Unable to understand the ultimate distinction, thus there is fear. With fear, much is lost—how could it be only in archery? Commentary: "Roaming freely" means to let go and wander. "Terror" means fear. The person of ultimate virtue is equal in measure to the vast emptiness, hence able to gaze up to the blue sky above and hide in the yellow springs below, like a divine dragon, rising and sinking without fixed pattern, roaming freely in all directions, spirit unchanged. Facing a ten-thousand rèn abyss, what is there to mind? Now I see you have a fearful heart, eyes dazzled and confused, harboring a terrified intent. Your shooting is in peril indeed.

Jiān Wú asked Sūn Shū Áo, saying, "You have been prime minister three times without feeling glorious, and three times removed without showing worry. At first, I doubted you, but now I see the expression between your nose and brow is serene and content. How alone do you manage your mind?"

Commentary: Jiān Wú is a recluse. Shū Áo is a worthy of Chǔ. "Serene and content" describes a joyful appearance. The enlightened remain unmoved by praise or blame, unshaken by honor or disgrace. Thus, Sūn Shū Áo held office three times without feeling glorious and was dismissed three times without worry. Jiān Wú, upon first hearing his words, still harbored doubts, but upon observing his demeanor, found him serene and self-content. How alone did he manage his mind to achieve this?

Sūn Shū Áo said, "How am I superior to others? I consider that what comes cannot be pushed away, and what goes cannot be stopped. I regard gain and loss as not pertaining to me, and thus have no worried expression. How am I superior to others?"

Commentary: High positions and glory are but things that come by chance; thus, their coming cannot be refused, their going cannot be stopped. Success and failure, gain and loss—do they depend on me? Understanding this coming and going, hence no worried expression. What art or skill could make one superior?
Moreover, I do not know whether it lies in others or in myself. If it lies in others, then it is lost in me; if in myself, then it is lost in others.

Note: Vast and unbound, mysteriously uniting others and self, then in others it is not solely lost, in self it is not solely preserved. Commentary: "Lost" means to disappear. Moreover, not knowing whether glory lies in others or in myself: if in others, then it is a loss to me; if in myself, then it is a loss to others. But since others and self are mysteriously united, gain and loss naturally vanish.
Just when I am wandering at ease, just when I am looking all around, what leisure have I to care about others honoring or dishonoring me?"

Note: "Wandering at ease, looking all around" means there is no must or must not. Commentary: "Wandering at ease" is to be content and self-satisfied; "looking all around" is to gaze broadly in all directions. Just when embracing all things, roaming freely through the universe, how could there be any leisure to mind the honors and disgraces among humans? Thus, he was removed without a worried expression.
Zhòng Ní heard this and said, "The true person of old could not be persuaded by the wise, seduced by the beautiful, robbed by thieves, or befriended by Fú Xī and Huáng Dì."

Note: Fú Xī and Huáng Dì are titles of achievement, not the means of achievement. Thus, comparing achievement titles to the means of achievement is far apart, so their names are insufficient to befriend such a person. Commentary: Zhòng Ní, hearing Sūn Shū Áo's words, admired his virtue and thus cited ancient times to attest to this man. The true person of old, profoundly subtle and wondrous, even with wise speakers could not be debated, with beautiful forms could not be seduced, with thieves and robbers could not be plundered, and even the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors were not worthy to be friends.
Life and death are also great matters, yet they do not change him—how much less could titles and emoluments?"
Commentary: Though humans renew daily, life and death are great matters, yet they do not change him; how much less would titles and emoluments occupy his mind?

Such a one, his spirit passes through great mountains without hindrance, enters deep springs without getting wet, dwells in lowly places without distress, fills heaven and earth; the more he gives to others, the more he himself possesses."

Note: Those who cut their flesh and skin for the world lose both self and others. Those who enable everyone to attain self-possession give to others without loss to self. His divine intelligence fills heaven and earth, thus wherever he is, it is acceptable. Because wherever is acceptable, he does not harm himself for things but rests in the land of self-possession. Commentary: "Hindrance" means obstruction. "Fills" means to complete. The true person enters fire without heat, enters water without wetness, passes through great mountains with spirit unobstructed, humbles himself in lowly stations without his Way being diminished. His virtue unites with the two realms (heaven and earth), thus filling heaven and earth. Not harming himself for things, thus he possesses more.
The king of Chǔ was sitting with the lord of Fán when, shortly after, the king's attendants said three times, 'Fán is doomed.'"

Note: It means there are three signs of doom. Commentary: King Wén of Chǔ and Lord Xī of Fán were sitting together discussing matters of alliance and covenant. Fán is a state name, descendants of the Duke of Zhōu, located in the region of Jí Commandery; what is now called Fánjiàn. The three refer to not revering ghosts, honoring worthies, and nurturing the people. Chǔ was large, Fán small; Chǔ had intentions to annex, thus the attendants used words to provoke.
The lord of Fán said, "The doom of Fán is not enough to destroy my existence."
Commentary: He transcends Fán, hence so. Commentary: Self-possessed by creation, joyful and unafraid, it can be said that the descendants of the Duke of Zhōu do not lack worthies.
"If the doom of Fán is not enough to destroy my existence, then the existence of Chǔ is not enough to make existence exist."
Note: If transcending it means not considering doom as doom, then existence is also not considered as existence. Vast and without pride, that is constant existence.
From this perspective, Fán has never perished, and Chǔ has never existed."

Note: Existence and perish alternate based on where the mind places them; in the end, the world has no fixed existence or perish. Commentary: Existence and perish lie in the gain and loss of the mind. Since transcending gain and loss, the perished may not necessarily perish, and the perished may further exist; the existing may not solely exist, and the existing may further perish.
Nán Huá Zhēn Jīng Annotation and Commentary, Scroll Twenty-Three.
Nanhua Zhenjing Zhushu, Scroll Twenty-Four, Part Three
Annotated by Guō Xiàng of Hénán Sub-commentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá Outer Chapters: Wandering North of the Northern Dipper, Twenty-Second
Zhī wandered north above the Mysterious Waters, ascended the hidden Fèn hill, and by chance encountered Wúwèi Wèi.

Sub-commentary: This chapter entirely fabricates names and uses allegory to clarify principle. North is the realm of darkness and obscurity; water is also a direction of obscurity and murkiness. "Hidden" means profound and distant, difficult to know; "Fèn" means luxuriant and visible. Wishing to clarify that the ultimate Dào is mysteriously transcendent, with manifestation and concealment being inconstant, it therefore entrusts these words to make its meaning clear.
Zhī said to Wúwèi Wèi: "I wish to ask you a question.
Sub-commentary: "Ru" means "you." This clarifies employing knowledge and exhausting the mind to inquire about the Dào, setting up guest and host, calling him "Wúwèi" (Non-Action).
What thinking, what pondering, then knows the Dào? Where dwelling, what practice, then is at peace with the Dào? What following, what path, then attains the Dào?

Sub-commentary: These are hypothetical words, just employing knowledge to inquire about the Dào. If one seeks through thought, what pondering and considering then knows the ultimate Dào? If one practices diligence, in what place and practice then pacifies the mind and unites with the Dào? What reliance and following, what path and explanation, then attains the Dào?
Three times he asked, and Wúwèi Wèi did not answer. It was not that he did not answer, but that he did not know how to answer.

Sub-commentary: Zhī is analytical. Having posed these three questions, ultimately there was not a single answer. It was not that Wúwèi Wèi was sparing of feeling and did not answer; simply, principle is without analysis, therefore he did not know how to answer.
Zhī, failing to get an answer, returned south of the White Waters, ascended atop Hú Què, and saw Kuáng Qū. Zhī, with his words, asked Kuáng Qū.

Sub-commentary: White is the color of purity and simplicity; south is the direction of clarity and brightness. "Hú" implies doubt and hesitation; "Què" means empty, tranquil, and without things. Failing to get a resolution to his question, he turned his reflection south of the White Waters, abandoning being and returning to non-being. Hesitant and unable to exhaust principle, then acting wildly and recklessly, withered like a dried-up tree—wishing to express this meaning, it is therefore called "Kuáng Qū" (Wildly Bent).
Kuáng Qū said: "Ah! I know it. I will tell you—in the middle of wishing to speak, I forgot what I wished to say."
Sub-commentary: "Āi" is a sound of response. Initially wishing to speak, midway he forgot it. This technique of forgetting is the way of turning reflection inward.

Zhī, failing to get an answer, returned to the imperial palace, saw Huángdì and asked him. Huángdì said: "No thinking, no pondering, then begin to know the Dào. No dwelling, no practice, then begin to be at peace with the Dào. No following, no path, then begin to attain the Dào."
Sub-commentary: Xuānyuán embodied the Dào and profoundly understood mysterious words, therefore used a single "no" to negate the three questions.

Zhī asked Huángdì: "I and you know it; those others do not know it. So who is right?" Huángdì said: "That Wúwèi Wèi is truly right; Kuáng Qū is close to it; I and you are ultimately not near it. Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know. Therefore the sage practices the teaching without words."

Commentary: Letting it act by itself—this is the teaching without words. Sub-commentary: "Truly right" is because of not knowing. "Close to it" is because of forgetting in the middle. "Not near it" is because of their knowing. "Practices the teaching without words" cites the Lǎozǐ as proof.
The Dào cannot be attained.

Commentary: The Dào is in spontaneity; it is not something that can be attained through words. Sub-commentary: "Attained" means "gotten." The mysterious Dào cannot be gotten by words; what is gotten by words is not the Dào.
Virtue cannot be reached.
Commentary: Not losing virtue is called virtue; called virtue but not reaching it. Sub-commentary: The highest virtue is without virtue; if one acts with virtue, it is not the ultimate virtue.
Benevolence can be practiced.
Sub-commentary: The ultimate benevolence is without partiality, but now practicing biased, affectionate benevolence is merely something that can be done, that is all.
Righteousness can be compromised.
Sub-commentary: Judging right and wrong, cutting and dividing, can only compromise and damage; it is not the complete whole. The complete whole simply lets things live, that is all.
Ritual is mutual pretense.
Sub-commentary: Ritual emphasizes mutual interaction, increasingly mutual superficiality and pretense; flowery adornment disrupts virtue; it is not genuine reality.

Therefore it is said: "Lose the Dào, and then virtue remains; lose virtue, and then benevolence remains; lose benevolence, and then righteousness remains; lose righteousness, and then ritual remains. Ritual is the flower of the Dào and the beginning of disorder."

Commentary: Ritual has constant rules, therefore it is the source from which affectation and imitation arise. Sub-commentary: Abandoning the root and pursuing the branches, scattering the uncarved block into superficiality, the Dào is lost and simplicity diluted, reaching the point of practicing ritual. Therefore, it cites the Lǎozǐ to prove and complete its meaning.
Therefore it is said: "Those who cultivate the Dào diminish daily.
Commentary: Diminish the flowery and false.
Diminish it and again diminish it, until reaching non-action. Non-action, and yet nothing is left undone."

Commentary: The flowery removed and the uncarved preserved whole, then even when acting, it is not acting. Sub-commentary: Those who cultivate the Dào diminish the flowery and false daily. Then, first diminishing being, later diminishing non-being, both being and non-being are simultaneously dismissed, until reaching the non-action of neither being nor non-being. Quiescent and unmoving, through non-action, therefore nothing is left undone. This cites the Lǎozǐ, reiterating to clarify its meaning.
Now it has already become a thing.
Commentary: Things lose their proper place, therefore there are acting things.
To wish to return to the root, is it not difficult? If it is easy, is it only for the great man?

Commentary: Those for whom returning to the root is easy are only the great man. The great man embodies and unites with transformation, therefore transforming things is not difficult. Sub-commentary: The category of inversion, with superficial falsity dwelling in the heart, pursuing the branches and forgetting the root, taking the Dào as a thing—even if they wish to return to the root and revert to their destiny, can it be obtained? Now, considering returning to the origin is not difficult, it lies only in the great sage.
Life is the companion of death.
Commentary: Those who know the way of transformation do not consider it strange.
Death is the beginning of life. Who knows their ordering?

Commentary: Mutually being each other's beginning, then one does not know which is death and which is life. Sub-commentary: Qì gathers and there is life, yet it is still of the same category as death. Qì disperses and there is death, yet it is still the fundamental beginning of life. Life, death, end, beginning—who knows their guiding principle? Gathering, dispersing, coming, going, transformation and change are indefinite.
Human life is the gathering of qì. Gathering then is life; dispersing then is death.
Commentary: All are gathering; all are dispersing.
If death and life are companions, what have I to worry about?

Commentary: Worry arises from differentiation. Sub-commentary: Qì gathering is life; qì dispersing is death. Though gathering and dispersing are different, as qì they are the same. Thus, death, life, gathering, dispersing can be companions. Since there is no distinction, what cause for sorrow?
Therefore the myriad things are one.
Sub-commentary: Since life and death are not two, the myriad things in principle should return to one.

What they deem beautiful is magical and marvelous; what they deem foul is putrid and rotten. The putrid and rotten again transforms into the magical and marvelous; the magical and marvelous again transforms into the putrid and rotten. Therefore it is said: "The whole world is but a single qì."

Commentary: Each takes what it deems beautiful as magical and marvelous, and what it deems foul as putrid and rotten. However, what they deem beautiful, I may deem foul; what I deem beautiful, they may deem foul. Therefore, the magical and marvelous is shared, the putrid and rotten is shared. Death and life, them and me—how are they different? Sub-commentary: Things have no inherent beauty or ugliness, but feelings have preferences and aversions. Therefore, what feelings deem beautiful is then called magical, marvelous, and extraordinary; what feelings deem foul is then called stinking, putrid, and rotten. To invert root and branch reaches this extent! However, the nature of things differs; what each likes varies. What they deem beautiful, this one deems foul; what this one deems foul, that one again deems beautiful. Therefore, Máoqiáng and Lìjī, whom people deem beautiful—fish see them and dive deep, birds see them and fly high. Thus, putrid and rotten, magical and marvelous; magical and marvelous, putrid and rotten. And right/wrong, beautiful/foul—how can they be fixed? From this we know that the myriad things of the world are all the same single harmonious qì.
Therefore the sage values the one.
Sub-commentary: The sage who embodies the Dào, his wisdom is one with the myriad things, therefore he values this true one and darkly unites with the ten thousand realms.

Zhī said to Huángdì: "I asked Wúwèi Wèi; Wúwèi Wèi did not respond to me. It was not that he did not respond to me, but that he did not know how to respond to me. I asked Kuáng Qū; Kuáng Qū, in the middle of wishing to tell me, did not tell me. It was not that he did not tell me, but that in the middle of wishing to tell, he forgot it. Now I ask you, and you know it—why are you ultimately not near it?" Huángdì said: "That one is truly right because of his not knowing; this one is close to it because of his forgetting; you and I are ultimately not near it because of our knowing." Kuáng Qū, hearing this, considered Huángdì's words to be knowing.

Commentary: Clarifying that spontaneity is not what verbal knowledge can obtain; therefore one should be obscure in the realm of no words. Thus, first raising the standard of not speaking, and afterwards entrusting clarity to Huángdì—then that dark unity of spontaneity with things is roughly seen as something obtained. Sub-commentary: That Wúwèi Wèi wonderfully embodied non-knowing, therefore is truly the Dào. This Kuáng Qū, turning reflection inward, dismissing words, forgetting his answer in the middle, is close to the Dào but not truly it. Zhī and Huángdì, these two men employed wisdom to explain principle, therefore were not near the true Dào. Kuáng Qū, hearing from afar this evaluation, considered that Huángdì, though not near the true, was just able to know mysterious words, that is all.
Heaven and Earth have great beauty but do not speak; the four seasons have clear laws but do not debate; the myriad things have complete principles but do not explain.

Commentary: This is why Confucius said, "I wish to not speak." Sub-commentary: The two spheres (Heaven and Earth) cover and support; their achievement is most beautiful. The four seasons proceed in sequence; each has clear laws. The myriad things are generated and completed; all rely on principle. Ultimately, they do not speak or explain, and never engage in debate.
The sage takes the beauty of Heaven and Earth as his origin and penetrates the principles of the myriad things. Therefore, the ultimate person practices non-action.

Commentary: Simply let each act by itself, that is all. Sub-commentary: The sage unites with the covering and supporting of the two spheres, is one with the generation and completion of the myriad things. Therefore, his mouth speaks nothing, his mind acts on nothing.
The great sage does not act.
Commentary: Only follows along.
This is called observing Heaven and Earth.

Commentary: Observe their forms and appearances, emulate their appropriate adaptations—no different from Heaven and Earth. Sub-commentary: The great sage, the ultimate person, practices non-action and non-creation, observes the covering and supporting of Heaven and Earth, models himself on the generation and completion of the ultimate Dào—non-action, non-speaking, this is what is meant.
Now, that spirit-like intelligence, most essential, and that hundredfold transformation—

Commentary: The hundred transformations transform by themselves, and the spirit-like intelligence is not usurped. Sub-commentary: That spirit-like, sagely, intelligent, essential, ultimate, subtle, mingles with things and blends, follows the flow of transformation, sometimes gathering, sometimes dispersing, without joy or sorrow. Now speaking of "hundred, thousand, myriads" is just citing the general numbers.
Things already die and are born, square and round; none know their root.

Commentary: The dead have already died by themselves, and the living have already lived by themselves; the round have already become round by themselves, and the square have already become square by themselves. None have a maker as their root, therefore none know. Sub-commentary: Things sometimes live, sometimes die, suddenly square, suddenly round—transformation and change are spontaneous; none know their root or sequence.
Abundantly, the myriad things have existed firmly since antiquity.

Commentary: How could they wait for making and only then exist? Sub-commentary: "Abundantly" describes the appearance of universal generation. It means the myriad things flutteringly, following the times, generate and nurture; from antiquity onward, they must have existed firmly by themselves—how could it be that only after deliberate intention do they exist?
The six directions are immense, yet not beyond its interior.
Commentary: To calculate the six directions as within the limitless—then they are small!
The autumn down is small, yet it depends on it to form its substance.

Commentary: The autumn down, though small, is not non-existent, yet also there is nothing that can contain its substance. Sub-commentary: The six directions are Heaven, Earth, and the four directions. Animals, encountering autumn, grow down on the tips of their hair. The down is extremely minute, called "autumn down." "Immense" means huge. The six directions, though immense, still reside within the ultimate Dào. The autumn down, though small, relies on the Dào to form its substance.
Under Heaven, none do not sink and float, lifelong not old.

Commentary: Daily renewal. Sub-commentary: The common things of the world, none do not float and sink, rise and fall, live and die, come and go, not dwelling, moving without cease, continuously renewed, never holding to the old.
Yīn and Yáng, the four seasons, operate, each attaining its proper sequence.

Commentary: Do not wait for acting. Sub-commentary: The two qì blend and intertwine; the four seasons revolve and operate; spring, autumn, cold, heat follow their sequence naturally—how could they wait for acting and only then proceed?
Dimly, as if non-existent, yet existing.
Commentary: If clearly apparent as if existing, then it is non-existent. Sub-commentary: Dimly, as if obscure, seeming without, yet with.
Fluidly, without form, yet spirit-like.

Commentary: If distinctly having form, then it is not spirit-like. Sub-commentary: "Spirit-like" refers to that which subtly acts through the myriad things. Fluidly, without attachment, not seen as form and appearance, yet its spirit-like function is without fixed method.
The myriad things are nurtured by it yet do not know it—this is called the root.

Commentary: Nurturing them but not getting to the root of their nature, therefore they do not know that by which they are nurtured. Sub-commentary: It brings things to fruition and nurtures the myriad beings, rears and nourishes the myriad things, and its mysterious achievement covertly covers them, used daily yet unknown. This true power is the one root of the ultimate Dào.
One can thereby observe Heaven.

Commentary: Observe together with Heaven. Sub-commentary: "Observe" means "see." Heaven is spontaneity. Those who can penetrate principle and understand the mysterious, recognize the root and know the origin, can be said to observe the ultimate Dào of spontaneity.
Niè Quē asked about the Dào from Bèi Yī. Bèi Yī said: "Correct your form, unify your vision, and heavenly harmony will arrive.
Dōngguōzǐ said, "Only after specifying it can it be acceptable."
Note: He wanted Zhuangzǐ to indicate where it is. Sub-commentary: Guō Xiàng's annotation states, "He wanted Zhuangzǐ to indicate where it is."

Zhuangzǐ said, "It is in the ant." He said, "How lowly is that?" He said, "It is in the panic grass." He said, "How even lower is that?" He said, "It is in the tiles and bricks." He said, "How even more so is that?" He said, "It is in the excrement and urine." Dōngguōzǐ did not respond.

Sub-commentary: The Great Way is omnipresent, yet where it exists, it is all nonexistent; thus, it is present everywhere without excluding the filthy and lowly. Dōngguōzǐ had not comprehended this meaning, thinking the Way was lofty and pure. Already considering tiles and bricks too base, upon hearing about excrement and urine, he became angry and did not respond.
Zhuangzǐ said, "Your question, sir, fundamentally does not reach the essence."

Note: Pointing to its superficial qualities, saying it is omnipresent, yet you still find this strange—this is not reaching the essence. Sub-commentary: Essence means reality. The Way is omnipresent; how could it only be in the panic grass? My answer to your question indeed has not yet attained the truth.
Just as Zhèng Huò inquired of the market inspector about treading on pigs, the lower one goes, the more evident it becomes.

Note: "Xī" means a large pig. The market inspector treads on the pig to know its fatness or leanness; the more he treads on the harder-to-fatten parts, the more he understands the key to the pig's fatness. Now, asking where the Way is and comparing it to lower and baser things makes it clear that the Way does not escape things; it must be so. Sub-commentary: "Zhèng" is an official title, like today's market director. "Huò" is a name. The market inspector is the head, like today's butcher. "Xī" means pig. Generally, asking a butcher about buying pigs involves treading between the pig's legs and thighs, the harder-to-fatten parts, to better understand the pig's fatness or leanness—this is comparison. Why? If the lower, harder-to-fatten parts have flesh, one knows the easier-to-fatten parts have ample fat. Similarly, if there is the Way in the lowly places like excrement and urine, then it is clear that even in pure and empty places, it is everywhere.
If only you would not insist, then nothing escapes things.

Note: If you insist that nothing escapes things, then the Way is not all-encompassing. If the Way is not all-encompassing, then it is not worthy of being called the Way. Sub-commentary: "Nothing" means the Way is non-action. The Great Way is vast and boundless, encompassing everything without exception. If only you would not say that the ultimate Way abandons things, if it truly escaped things, how could it be all-pervading?
The ultimate Way is like this, and great words are likewise.

Note: Clarifying that the Way does not escape things. Sub-commentary: The ultimate principle is the Way; great words are teachings. Since the principle does not escape things, the teachings are also universally pervasive without bias.
"Universal," "all-pervading," and "all-inclusive"—these three are different names but the same reality; their meaning is one.

Sub-commentary: Universal, all-pervading, and all-inclusive all possess the Way. This reiterates that the ultimate Way does not escape things. Although there are three different names, their actual principle and direction return to the same one.
Let us try to wander together in the palace of non-existence, unite and discuss without end or limit.

Note: If one wanders in existence, one cannot be universal, all-pervading, and all-inclusive. Therefore, uniting and discussing it, one then knows the Way is omnipresent. Knowing the Way is omnipresent, one can then be open-minded and carefree, wandering in that boundlessness. Sub-commentary: The palace of non-existence refers to the abode of the profound Way. There is not a single thing that can be had, hence it is called non-existence. And universal, all-pervading, and all-inclusive—wandering together in the land of the ultimate Way, the essence being one, uniting and discussing, silently conforming to the profound principle, thus there is no end, beginning, or limit.
Let us try to be non-active together: tranquil and quiet, vast and clear, harmonious and leisurely.

Note: This is all due to non-action. Sub-commentary: This summarizes the praise of the three functions of universal, all-pervading, and all-inclusive, their virtuous power abundant. Having wandered to the land of the ultimate Way and dwelling in the realm of non-action, one can be placid and quiet, serene and clear, gentle and harmonious, relaxed and at ease.
Vast and empty is my will.
Note: Vast and empty. Sub-commentary: The attained sage of the Way, in accord with principle and merging with truth, has a will that is silent and vast.
Not going anywhere, yet not knowing where it arrives.

Note: If the will is truly vast, then there is nowhere to go. Not going anywhere, thus going without knowing where it arrives. If there is going, then the principle has not moved, but the will has already arrived.
Leaving and coming, yet not knowing where it stops.
