Note: This is following it. Sub-commentary: Since the speech is silent and vast, it neither comes nor goes. Even if it goes without going, comes without coming, ultimately there is no place of arrival, nor any dwelling.
I have come and gone, yet not knowing its end.

Note: Only coming and going is not through knowing; it is not that there is no coming and going. Coming and going is the constant principle of nature. Does it have an end? Sub-commentary: Even if coming and returning to creation, going and coming to life and death, following change and accepting transformation, one also does not know the end or beginning.
Wandering in the vast emptiness, great knowledge enters it yet does not know its limits.

Note: "Vast emptiness" means void and expansive. Great knowledge arises from the vastness, freely changing according to what it knows, hence it does not know. Sub-commentary: Wandering is the name for letting go; vast emptiness is the appearance of void and expansiveness. It means entering and uniting. The person of great sage knowledge can unite with the principle of silence and vast emptiness, thus being free and self-attained, letting go without limit.
That which makes things things has no boundary with things.

Note: Clarifying that the thing-maker is not a thing, and things are things themselves. Since things are things themselves, they are merged. Sub-commentary: Boundary means brink. One who can make things into things is a sage. The sage silently unites with all realms, thus having no boundary of self and other with things.
But if things have boundaries, it is what is called the boundary of things.

Note: Things have boundaries, hence often cannot merge with each other; this is truly what is called a boundary. Sub-commentary: The discrimination and selection of things' emotions are myriad, hence there are boundaries between things and self.
The boundary of no-boundary, the no-boundary of boundary.

Note: No-boundary means although there is the name "thing-maker," it directly clarifies that things are things themselves. The thing-maker ultimately is not a thing. Where then is the boundary? Sub-commentary: The no-boundary of boundary is the sage's penetrating view. The boundary of no-boundary is the stagnant sentiment of the ordinary and vulgar.

Speaking of fullness and emptiness, decline and extinction: that which is fullness and emptiness is not fullness and emptiness; that which is decline and extinction is not decline and extinction; that which is root and tip is not root and tip; that which is accumulation and dispersion is not accumulation and dispersion.

Note: Having clarified that the thing-maker is not a thing, and further that things cannot be things themselves, then who is it that makes them? All are suddenly so of themselves. Sub-commentary: Wealth and honor are fullness; poverty and lowliness are emptiness; old age and sickness are decline and extinction; beginning and end are root and tip; birth is accumulation; death is dispersion. That which makes things things is not a thing; then who produces things? This clarifies that both the maker and the made are not things. Since things are not things, how can one speak of fullness and emptiness, decline and extinction? Thus it is known that what is called fullness and emptiness are not fullness and emptiness. Therefore, the "Western Ascension Scripture" says, "If one can clarify it, what is affirmed is actually denied."
Ē Hégān and Shénnóng studied together under Lǎo Lóngjí.
Sub-commentary: Surname Ē, courtesy name Hégān. Shénnóng here is not the Shénnóng of the Three Sovereigns, but a later figure. The two studied together under Lǎo Lóngjí; Lǎo Lóngjí is also a title.
Shénnóng leaned on his desk and closed his door, dozing during the day. Ē Hégān pushed the door open at noon and entered, saying, "Lǎo Lóng is dead!"

Sub-commentary: "Leaned" means relying. "Closed" means shut. "Pushed" means opened, also forced open. A student of the Way, mind and spirit concentrated and still, closed the door, leaned on the desk, kept silent and dozed. Hégān, hearing of his teacher's death, pushed the door open to inform.
Shénnóng, leaning on his desk and holding his staff, rose up, then with a crash dropped his staff and laughed.

Note: Rising and realizing that death is not worth startling over, thus he dropped his staff and laughed. Sub-commentary: "Crash" is the sound of dropping the staff. Shénnóng, hearing of Jí's death, was startled and held his staff; upon further thought, death is not worth mourning, so he dropped his staff and laughed.
He said, "Heaven knew I was narrow-minded and negligent, so he abandoned me and died. Finished! My master had no mad words to inspire me, and he died!"

Note: From Jiānwú onward, all considered the ultimate words mad and did not believe them. Hence, without Lǎo Lóng, Lián Shū, and their like, there is no one to speak with. Sub-commentary: "My master" is Lǎo Lóngjí. Saying he had the virtue of nature, he called him "Heaven." "Mad words" are like ultimate words, not understood by worldly people, hence the ultimate words are called mad. And the teacher knew I was biased and vulgar, negligent and unfocused, so he abandoned us, ceased and died. The wise man is gone; the ultimate words are cut off. No more discussing the profound and imparting teachings to enlighten my mind.
Yǎn Gāngdiào heard of it and said, "Those who embody the Way are what the gentlemen of the world rely upon."
Note: Those who embody the Way are the masters of people.
Now, regarding the Way, he had not attained even one ten-thousandth of the tip of an autumn hair.

Note: The tip of an autumn hair is minute, and he had not even obtained one ten-thousandth of it, yet he knew to conceal his mad words and die. How much more so for those who embody the Way? Note: Clarifying that the ultimate Way is not obtained through words; it is only in self-attainment. Sub-commentary: Surname Yǎn, name Gāng, a recluse. "Rely upon" means belong to. Hearing of Lǎo Lóng's death, he discussed aside: Those who embody the Way are universally valued in the world; wise men and gentlemen rely upon and return to them. Now, Lǎo Lóng, regarding the profound Way, had not even one ten-thousandth of the tip of a hair, yet he knew to conceal his mad simplicity, abide in compliance and die. How much more so for those who profoundly comprehend? Who would be willing to expose their words? Thus it is known that those who embody the Way deeply and profoundly, forget words and unite with principle, are extremely rare.
Looking at it, it has no form; listening to it, it has no sound. Among human discussions, it is called obscure; thus, what is discussed as the Way is not the Way.

Note: Obscure and yet still not the Way, clarifying that the Way is nameless. Sub-commentary: The profound Way is empty and vague, its subtle substance rare and imperceptible, not form, not sound, beyond sight and hearing. Thus, among learners' discussions, they discuss and call it obscure, but calling it obscure is still not the true Way.
Thereupon, Tàiqīng asked Wúqióng, "Do you know the Way?" Wúqióng said, "I do not know."

Sub-commentary: "Tài" means great. The ultimate Way is vast and expansive, placid and clear, empty, encompassing without limit, hence named Tàiqīng and Wúqióng. Then Tàiqīng used knowing to ask about the Way; Wúqióng answered with not knowing, wanting to clarify that the Way transcends form and sound, and cannot be sought through verbal knowing.
He又问 asked Wúwéi. Wúwéi said, "I know the Way." He said, "Your knowing the Way, does it have a number?" He said, "Yes." He said, "What is its number?"
Sub-commentary: Since you know the Way, does it somewhat have names and numbers? What is its number? Please briefly describe it.
Wúwéi said, "I know the Way can be noble, can be base, can be gathered, can be dispersed. This is how I know the number of the Way."

Sub-commentary: Noble as emperor, base as servant; gathered as life, dispersed as death; the number is without limit. This is said briefly, wanting to clarify that it is not names yet names, not numbers yet numbers.
Tàiqīng, with these words, asked Wúshǐ, "If so, then Wúqióng's not knowing and Wúwéi's knowing—which is right and which is wrong?"

Sub-commentary: The ultimate Way is mysteriously penetrating, silent and non-active, unfathomable in response, without end or beginning, hence entrusting Wúqióng and Wúshǐ as their names. Wúqióng's not knowing and Wúwéi's knowing—who is right and who is wrong? Please determine good and bad.
Wúshǐ said, "Not knowing is deep; knowing is shallow. Not knowing is internal; knowing is external."
Sub-commentary: Not knowing accords with principle, hence profound and mysterious, dwelling internally; knowing violates the Way, hence crude and shallow, estranged externally.
Thereupon, Tàiqīng sighed from within and said, "Not knowing is then knowing? Knowing is then not knowing? Who knows the knowing of not knowing?"

Note: All attainment not through knowing is merging. Sub-commentary: Tàiqīng attained the middle way and sighed, realizing that not knowing is true knowing. Who knows the knowing of not knowing? Clarifying that true knowing is extremely rare.
Wúshǐ said, "The Way cannot be heard; what is heard is not it. The Way cannot be seen; what is seen is not it. The Way cannot be spoken; what is spoken is not it."

Note: Therefore, silently accomplish in the realm of not hearing and not seeing, and then reach it. Sub-commentary: The Way has no sound, cannot be heard with ears; what is heard with ears is not the Way. The Way has no form, cannot be seen with eyes; what is seen with eyes is not the Way. The Way has no name, cannot be spoken with words; what is spoken with words is not the Way.
Do you know that which forms forms is formless?

Note: Forms are forms themselves; that which forms forms ultimately is not a thing. Sub-commentary: That which can form and color the myriad things is certainly not form and color; thus it is said, "That which forms forms is formless."
The Way does not correspond to names.

Note: There is the name "Way," but ultimately no thing; hence, naming cannot correspond to it. Sub-commentary: Names have no power to attain the Way; the Way has no reality corresponding to names. Therefore, naming the Way is not it.
Wúshǐ said, "If one is asked about the Way and responds, he does not know the Way. Even the one asking about the Way has not heard the Way."

Note: Not knowing, hence asking. If asked and responds, then it is not the Way. Not responding is not what the questioner obtains; hence, even if asked, he ultimately does not hear. Sub-commentary: The Way transcends names and words, cannot be asked or answered; hence, asking about the Way or responding to the Way, all do not know.
The Way has no question; questioning has no response.

Note: Cease learning and discard teaching, returning to the meaning of nature. Sub-commentary: Embodying the Way, transcending words—what question and response? All words here reiterate the previous text.
Asking where there is no question is questioning emptiness.
Note: So-called valuing emptiness. Sub-commentary: Emptiness is exhausted. Principle has nothing to ask, yet forcing a question is valuing emptiness. [
The Southern Florescence True Classic Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll 25 of 29
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Florescence of the Táng Dynasty Miscellaneous Chapters, Gēngsāng Chǔ, Chapter 23
Among Lǎo Dān's disciples, there was one called Gěngsāng Chǔ, who uniquely grasped Lǎo Dān's Dào.

Subcommentary: His surname was Gěngsāng, his personal name was Chǔ, a disciple of the Old Lord (Lǎo Dān), likely a recluse. "Disciple" (yì) is a term for followers. In ancient times, those who served a teacher shared in his labors, not shirking hardship or danger, hence the term "disciple." The Old Lord was a great sage with many disciples. Among his followers, Gěngsāng Chǔ was the most outstanding, hence it is said he "uniquely grasped" it.
He dwelt north in the Wèilěi mountains. His ministers who were ostentatiously knowing, he dismissed; his concubines who were fastidiously benevolent, he distanced.

Commentary: "Ostentatiously" means adorned with knowledge; "fastidiously" means boasting of benevolence. Subcommentary: Wèilěi is a mountain name in the state of Lǔ. "Ministers" and "concubines" refer to associates. It means people who use benevolence and knowledge as ministers and concubines. Gěngsāng Zǐ entirely rejected benevolence and knowledge in his dealings with the noble man. Chǔ, being a recluse, resided in the mountain wilderness, his disposition sincere and simple, his mind despising superficiality. The men and women near the mountain vied to be his ministers and concubines. Thus, those who ostentatiously displayed their knowledge and showed off their brilliance, When affairs enter and do not depart,

Note: Affairs are matters not residing within one's portion. Subcommentary: Affairs of the world, entangling and disturbing, constantly enter the heart-mind without understanding avoidance or compliance, hence they cannot be stopped and let go.
Each change becomes a loss.

Note: If initiated from one's own sincerity, then it is attainment. Subcommentary: Each time the mind deludedly arises, chasing after former states, claiming it as attainment, it instead further loses the genuine.
Those who do evil in the bright and open, people can punish them; those who do evil in the dark and secluded, ghosts can punish them.

Subcommentary: Humans and ghosts, dark and bright, are said to be different paths; but when it comes to extending sincerity and practicing trustworthiness, the principle is without separation. If one deviates from their portion and loses the genuine, they will inevitably attract retribution; resentment and enmity mutually affect each other, hence they suffer punishment—examples are like Cái Bó and Péng Shēng.
One who is clear about humans, clear about ghosts, can then act alone.

Note: Without shame in the heart-mind towards the dark and bright, then one can act alone without fear. Subcommentary: The two paths of dark and bright are distinct without condemnation, not offending against things, hence acting alone without fear.
Those bound internally act without name.

Note: Bound means portion. Those who wander within their portion act not through name. Subcommentary: Bound means portion. Without name is the Dào. Treading the Dào and acting within one's portion, though acting, leaves no trace of name.
Those bound externally aim at expected expenditure.

Note: Beneficial or not, expecting to diminish oneself for the sake of things. Subcommentary: Expecting means final. Establishing intent with arrogance and affectation, wandering mind externally, ultimately without accomplishment or benefit, finally having expenditure and loss.
Those who act without name, only their usefulness has light.
Note: Originally having this light, thus using it. Subcommentary: Usefulness means application. Wandering mind in the nameless Dào, the wisdom they use daily has brightness.
Those who aim at expected expenditure are only merchants.

Note: Even if one lacks it oneself, still borrows from others to buy and sell. Subcommentary: Aiming sought externally, demanding expected fame and greed that diminishes spirit and wisdom—their intent is only for name and profit, like high-priced merchants.
People see them on tiptoe, yet they consider themselves secure.

Note: Those who expect expenditure, people already see them on tiptoe, yet they still consider themselves safe. Subcommentary: On tiptoe means precarious; secure means安稳. Intensely passionate, greedily taking externally, seeking on tiptoe, others see their peril, yet they consider themselves hidden and safe—the utmost folly.
Those who exhaust things with things, things enter them.

Note: Exhaust means beginning and end. Subcommentary: It means dwelling. Those with whom things and self darkly tally, exhausting principle and fulfilling nature, thus external things rely on and adhere to them.
Those who barely manage things with things, their own selves cannot contain them, how can they contain others?

Note: Barely means those bound externally and on tiptoe. Those on tiptoe do not stand, how can they contain themselves? Unable to contain themselves, how can they contain others? If others are not accommodated, they leave. Subcommentary: Briefly associating with people, careless in superficiality, greedy for profit and seeking fame, their selves still arrogantly aspire, their minds and spirits agitated and competitive, unable to contain themselves, how can they contain things?
Those who cannot accommodate others have no intimacy; those without intimacy are all others.

Note: If one's self cannot be contained, then even oneself is not oneself, how much less can there be intimacy? Hence all are others. Subcommentary: Narrow and intolerant, then no intimacy or affection; since no intimacy or affection, then all are others. Opposition and transgression many, enemies and foes not few—seeking peace and security, how can it be obtained?
No weapon is more cruel than the will; Mò Yé is inferior.

Note: That which the will entangles, scorches fire and freezes water, hence it as a weapon is worse than swords and halberds. Subcommentary: Weapons like blades and edges, Mò Yé is a fine sword. Cruel poison and harm, nothing exceeds the heart-mind; what the will follows, not swift yet fast, hence its damage is worse than Mò Yé; compared and measured, swords and halberds are inferior.
No brigand is greater than Yīn and Yáng; there is no escape between heaven and earth.

Subcommentary: Brigand means enemy. Gains and losses in the realm of the heart, joy and anger battle in the chest—its cold freezes water, its heat scorches fire—this is the brigand of Yīn and Yáng. Powerful enemies and great brigands can still be escaped, but when weapons arise within the heart, how to avoid them?
It is not that Yīn and Yáng harm people; the heart makes it so.

Note: If the heart commands the qì, then Yīn and Yáng accumulate and knot in the five viscera, and wherever they are, it is all Yīn and Yáng, hence inescapable. Subcommentary: It is not that Yīn and Yáng can harm people, only because the heart has agitation and competition, thus making it so.
The Dào connects their portions; their completion is destruction.

Note: Completion and destruction are inconstant; portions, yet the Dào connects all. Subcommentary: Things receiving qì each have their limits; beauty, ugliness, good, evil, endowed portions, destruction and completion—this calls it completion, that calls it destruction; the Dào connects them, none not fully sufficient.
What is disliked about portions is that the portion is already complete.

Note: Not guarding one's portion but seeking completeness, hence disliking the portion. Subcommentary: Honor, disgrace, longevity, premature death, endowed from nature, within plain portion, turning within already fully sufficient; those galloping externally seeking completeness, wandering mind in the realm of right and wrong, dislike the portion they receive.
The reason for disliking completeness is that there is already completeness.

Note: The original portion is not complete, yet seeking completeness, hence disliking completeness. If the original portion was always complete, how would one dislike it? Subcommentary: The creator has already made complete, yet disliking and hating it—how could they know nature had already prepared it first?
Hence, going out and not returning, one sees their ghost.

Note: Not returning to guard within one's portion, then their death is not long. Subcommentary: Those going out foolishly and deludedly chasing realms of right and wrong, unable to return to the root and revert to the origin, move towards the land of death, hence appear as ghosts.
Going out and attaining this is called attaining death.

Note: Not going out and having no attainment is attaining life. Subcommentary: Their heart going out chasing things, following their desires and emotions, and having some gain—this can be called attaining the root of death and extinction.
Extinguished yet having substance, one among ghosts.

Note: Already extinguished their nature, though having this life, how different from a ghost? Subcommentary: Deludedly extinguishing the original nature, claiming the body truly exists, no different from losing death, hence one with ghosts. Having form resembles without form, and thus is settled. Note: Though having this form, if able to be vast and without care, then life is whole and form settled. Subcommentary: Resembles means similar. Though having this form, similar to having none, because form is non-existent. Vast and forgetting self, hence the heart-mind spirit harmonizes light and settles.
Emerging has no root.
Note: Suddenly self-generated, not having a root.
Entering has no aperture.

Note: Suddenly self-dying, not having a root. Subcommentary: Emerging is birth; entering is death. From non-being emerging into being, being has no root or origin; from being returning to non-being, non-being has no aperture or hole.
Having substance but no place; having duration but no beginning or end.

Subcommentary: End means tip, also origin. Beginning also written as biāo; now following the character reading: saying from non-being emerges being, truly having this body, tracing causes, meaning no place; from ancient times to now, very long and far, seeking now ultimately no beginning or end.
Having emergence but no aperture, has substance.

Note: Saying the emergent inherently has substance; that from which it emerges has no root or aperture to emerge from. Subcommentary: Having emergence but no aperture—from a common view, claims it has substance, but actually it does not have.
Having substance but no place is space.

Note: Space has four directions, up and down, and four directions, up and down have no exhausted place. Subcommentary: Space is four directions, up and down. The birth of all things, claiming they have substance, seeking responsibility in space, ultimately no place of origin; space is already not, how could there be a place?
Having duration but no beginning or end is time.

Note: Time has the duration of ancient and modern, and the duration of ancient and modern is limitless. Subcommentary: Time is past ancient, coming modern. Seasons and eras long, called ancient and modern; tracing succession, ultimately no beginning or end; time is already not, how could there be a beginning?
There is birth, there is death, there is emergence, there is entrance; entrance and emergence without seeing their form.

Note: Death, life, emergence, entrance are all suddenly self-so, without any cause, hence nothing to see their form. Subcommentary: Emergence and entrance come from death and life. Claiming their emergence and entrance, death and life, hence have names of emergence and entrance; tracing exhaustively nature and principle, ultimately no form of place of emergence and entrance to be seen.
This is called the gate of heaven.

Note: Gate of heaven is the collective name of the myriad things. Calling it the gate of heaven is like saying the gate of all wonders. Subcommentary: Heaven means what is called natural. Natural means taking having no cause as the meaning. Saying the myriad existences all have no whence, cannot fathom the reason, natural is the gate of the creator.
The gate of heaven is non-existence; the myriad things emerge from non-existence.

Note: Death, life, emergence, entrance are all suddenly self-so, none having a doer. Yet there is gathering, scattering, hidden, visible, hence having names of emergence and entrance. Only having names, ultimately no gate of emergence and entrance—where is its peace? Hence taking non-action as the gate; taking non-action as the gate, then there is no gate. Subcommentary: The natural principle, the gate of creation, only has its name, ultimately no its reality, and all myriad things are born from this gate, hence Guō Xiàng's note says: taking non-action as the gate; taking non-action as the gate, then there is no gate.
Being cannot use being to have being.

Note: Before being is born, from what is it born? Hence necessarily from itself being, how could being be able to have being? Subcommentary: Being already is, how can it have being? Before being is born, who gives birth to its being? Tracing gradually being, ultimately no being.
Necessarily emerges from non-existence.

Note: This clarifies that being cannot create being, but is from itself being; not saying non-being can create being. If non-being can create being, what is called non-being? Subcommentary: Already born, not yet born, both are without being; this being emerges from non-existence, not saying this non-being can give birth to being; if non-being gives birth to being, what is called non-being?
And non-existence, one non-existence.

Note: One non-existence then consequently non-existence; non-being consequently non-existence, then being suddenly self-generates, clearly. Subcommentary: Not questioning hundred negations, four propositions, all at once are non-existent, hence called one non-existence.
The sage hides in this.
Note: Let it self-generate without generating life. Subcommentary: The mysterious virtue sage, darkly genuine, tallying principle, hiding spirit, concealing wisdom—is it not here?
The people of old, their knowledge had something reached.
Subcommentary: The dark ancient sage, attained Dào person, knowledge and realm unite, hence called reaching.
What is reached?
Subcommentary: What is reached from? What is the reason for reaching?
Having considered that there has never been any thing, is reaching the ultimate, cannot be added to.

Subcommentary: This reveals the substance of reaching. Knowledge already reaches the extreme, observation within all empty, hence can use all existent dharmas as never having a single thing. Can be called subtle and minute, reaching the extreme, exhausting principle and fulfilling nature, empty and wondrous exceedingly, cannot be added to further.
Next, considering that there are things.
Subcommentary: Next below, not reaching true emptiness, and all myriad realms are used as having things.
Will consider life as loss.
Note: Loss means its scattering goes towards gathering.
Consider death as return.

Note: Returning, melting and dissolving. Subcommentary: Loss means losing. Common people consider life as gain, death as loss. Now wanting to reverse deluded feelings, hence consider life as loss because it is non-existent; consider death as return, returning to emptiness and stillness. Though not exhausting the ultimate wonder, still equalizing life and death.
Thus, already divided.
Note: Though wanting to equalize, already divided. Subcommentary: Though equalizing life and death, still seeing the difference of life and death, hence from non-existence arising discrimination.

Next says: Beginning with non-existence, then having life, life momentarily then death; taking non-existence as the head, life as the body, death as the buttocks. Who knows non-existence, existence, death, life as one guard? I would be friends with them.

Subcommentary: Next below, mind knowledge slightly dim, and beginning originally non-existent, from non-existence life, momentarily between, this born that extinguished, hence use non-action as its head, life as its body form, death as its buttocks. Who can know non-existence and existence, death and life as non-dual, and with this cultivate guard? Zhuāng Zǐ would associate and befriend such a person, yet difficult to obtain.
These three, though different, are a ducal clan.

Note: Some have yet treat as non-existent, some have yet treat as one, some divide yet equalize, hence called three. These three, though having exhaustion and non-exhaustion, yet all can have no right and wrong in the chest, hence called a ducal clan. Subcommentary: Three means taking non-existence as head, life as body, death as buttocks. Within one body arising these three differences, like the Chǔ family, within one surname divided into three clans.
Zhāo, Jǐng, are distinguished by wearing; Jiǎ shì, are distinguished by fief; not one.

Note: These four, though ducal clan, already not one, then the former three already again differ. Subcommentary: Zhāo, Qū, Jǐng, the ducal clan of Chǔ, three surnames. Formerly Qū Yuán was the Sān Lǘ grand master, in charge of the three clans, three surnames, namely these. Here text is brief, hence directly says Zhāo, Jǐng. Royal grandsons, duke's sons, grown up capped, hence wearing clothes and wearing caps. Each have rank and precedence, all assume office and official, because of office granted surname, hence Jiǎ rank, clan lineage. Merits and achievements already distinguished, enfeoffed with land, branches and offshoots divide and flow, hence not one. Like within one Dào, divided into non-existence, existence, life, death, kinds and categories not same, names and realities each have differences, hence citing the clan as internal analogy.
Life is a blemish.
Note: Merely gathered qì. Subcommentary: Blemish means flaw. Not having this form and substance yet calling it life, merely gathered qì becoming a flaw, all not valued.
Disperately said: shifting this.

Note: Already desperately having division, then each considers their own as right; this right is not constant, hence called shifting. Subcommentary: Disperately means scattered. Heavenly Dào has no self and other, yet things have right and wrong; right and wrong not fixed, hence scattered, shifting and moving, not constant. The state of shifting this is listed below again.
Once spoke shifting right and wrong, is spoken.
Note: The shifted right already manifested in speech before. Subcommentary: Principle forms right and wrong, hence sometimes spoken. Yet shifting right and wrong is not constant speech.
Though so, cannot be known.

Note: Not speaking its shift, then its shift cannot be known, hence trying speech. Subcommentary: Though again right and wrong not due to speech, yet without speech nothing to know right and wrong, hence trying speech right and wrong. Once dismissed right and wrong, names not lodged in speech, then not knowing right and wrong as without right and wrong.
The ox tripe and hoofs in the year-end sacrifice can be dispersed yet cannot be dispersed.

Note: Things each have use. Subcommentary: Year-end sacrifice means great sacrifice. Tripe means the hundred leaves (reticulum); hoof means preparation, also said to be ox hooves. During the year-end sacrifice, sacrificial animals very complete, even to the four limbs and five viscera all displayed. After the sacrifice is completed, then again dispersed, then taking dispersal as right; if the sacrifice not finished, then should not disperse, then taking dispersal as not right. Thus knowing right and not right, shifting right is inconstant.
Viewing the chamber, circulate through the sleeping and ancestral temples, then go to the resting place.
Note: Resting means screen toilet. Subcommentary:
When anger emerges without being angry, then anger arises from non-anger; when action emerges without acting, then action arises from non-action.

Comment: This indeed conveys the idea that non-being cannot generate being, and being cannot be produced from nothing. Explanation: Those capable of manifesting anger or action are not those who refrain from anger or action. Therefore, since they emerge from non-anger and non-action, we know action fundamentally stems from non-action, and anger fundamentally stems from non-anger. One who can embody this principle remains unangered even when insulted.

To desire tranquility, harmonize the qi; to desire spiritual power, follow the heart's inclinations—this is purposeful action. To desire appropriateness, base it on inevitability. What arises from inevitability constitutes the Way of the Sage.

Comment: Harmonizing qi brings sufficient tranquility; following the heart achieves ultimate spiritual efficacy. Basing actions on inevitability makes all deeds appropriate—thus the Sage takes this as the Way, never seeking non-action in realms of obscurity. Explanation: "Basing" means aligning. To desire tranquility amid attachments, one must regulate will and qi. For spiritual transformations, nothing precedes surrendering to the heart's innate harmony. To make purposeful actions align with principle, one must further comply with inevitability. Inevitability means responding only after being stirred—matters within one's natural capacity. Such examples illustrate what the Sage employs as the true Path.
Nánhuá Zhēnjīng Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Twenty-Five
Nanhua Zhenjing Zhushu, Scroll Twenty-Six, Qing Five
Annotated by Guō Xiàng of Hénán Sub-commentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Xīhuá in the Táng Dynasty Miscellaneous Chapters, Xú Wúguǐ Chapter Twenty-Four
Xú Wúguǐ, through Nǚ Shāng, had an audience with Marquis Wǔ of Wèi.

Sub-commentary: His surname was Xú, courtesy name Wúguǐ, a recluse. Nǚ Shāng's surname was Nǚ, given name Shāng, a minister of Wèi. Marquis Wǔ was the son of Marquis Wén and an eighth-generation descendant of Bì Wàn. Wúguǐ wished to admonish Marquis Wǔ, so he relied on the minister to gain an audience.
Marquis Wǔ consoled him, saying: "You are suffering, Sir. Weary from the toils of the mountains and forests, thus you have consented to see me."

Sub-commentary: Having long dwelt in the mountains and forests, enduring hardship, poverty, and illness, he suddenly lowered his aspirations to mix among the common folk. His heart was joyful, hence the consolation.

Xú Wúguǐ said: "It is I who should console you, my lord. What need have you to console me? If you, my lord, are to fill your desires and prolong your likes and dislikes, then the essence of your nature and destiny will ail. If you, my lord, are to suppress your desires and restrain your likes and dislikes, then your ears and eyes will ail."

Annotation: Desires, likes, and dislikes have no distinction between internal and external. Sub-commentary: To suppress is to abolish and retreat; to restrain is to pull back and remove. If you, my lord, fill your desires to the full and advance your likes and dislikes, then the essence of your nature and spirit will be afflicted. If you, my lord, dismiss and eliminate desires and restrain your likes and dislikes, since they are not suited, your ears and eyes will ail. Therefore, I shall console you, my lord. What leisure have you to console me?
"I shall console you, my lord. What need have you to console me?"
Sub-commentary: This reiterates the previous meaning.
Marquis Wǔ was taken aback and did not reply.
Annotation: Unpleased with his words. Sub-commentary: "Taken aback" means resentful. Since it did not match his feelings, he was distant and did not answer.
After a short while, Xú Wúguǐ said: "Let me tell you, my lord, of my skill in judging dogs."
Sub-commentary: Sensing Marquis Wǔ's displeasure, he tried speaking of dogs and horses, hoping to please his heart.
"The lowest quality is satisfied with fullness alone—this is the virtue of a fox."
Sub-commentary: Holding fast to their nature, they only crave to eat their fill. Such physical form has virtue comparable to a fox—a low-grade dog.
"The medium quality is like gazing at the sun."
Sub-commentary: Their spirit and ambition are lofty and far-reaching, their gaze like looking at the sun. Their physique is thus that of a medium-grade dog.
"The highest quality is as if it has lost itself."
Sub-commentary: "Itself" means its body. Its spirit and energy are settled and attentive, as if it has lost its body—a high-grade dog.
"My judgment of dogs is not as good as my judgment of horses."

Sub-commentary: Dogs have three grades, horses have several levels, yet the ability to judge dogs is not as good as judging horses. Marquis Wǔ was mediocre and vulgar, so he used this to engage his interest, hoping to delight him and perhaps guide him back to correctness.
"In judging horses, the straight ones match the line."
Sub-commentary: Refers to the horse's front teeth.
"The curved ones match the hook."
Sub-commentary: Refers to the horse's neck.
"The square ones match the square."
Sub-commentary: Refers to the horse's head.
"The round ones match the compass."
Sub-commentary: Refers to the horse's eyes.
"These are state horses."
Sub-commentary: Matching the above judgments, these are called the high-grade horses of the feudal lords' states.
"But they are not like the horses of the empire. The horses of the empire have innate talent."
Sub-commentary: Their talent and virtue are inherently complete, not relying on training. These are the superior horses within the realm, ridden by the Son of Heaven.
"They appear anxious, as if lost, as if they have forgotten themselves."

Sub-commentary: Their eyes glance about as if worried; their hooves move slowly yet seem to dash away. Observing their divine brilliance, it is as if they have forgotten their own bodies. Such talent belongs to the Son of Heaven's horse.
"Such horses transcend and outstrip, leaving dust behind, and one knows not where they go."
Sub-commentary: "Transcend" means to surpass. They run swiftly, exceeding the herd, fast as a sudden wind, dust left far behind. Since they are not trained, one knows not whence they come.
Marquis Wǔ was greatly pleased and laughed.
Annotation: The words of a true man—why be humble? Only what things delight in can be so. Sub-commentary: His words hit the mark, hence he laughed with joy.
Xú Wúguǐ went out. Nǚ Shāng said: "How alone did you, Sir, please my lord?"
Sub-commentary: The discussion ended, he took leave and departed. Nǚ Shāng, surprised at the lord's joy, thus inquired of Wúguǐ.
"What I use to please my lord: speaking broadly, it is the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music; speaking narrowly, it is the Golden Plates and Six Bows."

Sub-commentary: The Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music are the Six Classics. The Golden Plates and Six Bows are chapter names in the Zhou Documents, or perhaps secret prophecies. Some texts have "Tāo" instead, read accordingly, said to be the Military Methods of Tàigōng, referring to the civil, martial, tiger, leopard, dragon, and dog stratagems. "Broadly" means widely; "narrowly" means closely. Marquis Wǔ favored military matters and disliked culture, so he considered military methods as narrow and the Six Classics as broad.
"Those who serve and achieve great merit are too numerous to count, yet my lord has never shown a smile."
Annotation: This is merely delighting a quail with bells and drums, hence sorrow. Sub-commentary: (Implied from context)
"Now, how did you, Sir, please my lord, making him so joyful?"

Sub-commentary: Serving Marquis Wǔ with utmost loyalty and integrity, offering advice on what to adopt or reject, achieving clear merits—such individuals are beyond count, yet my lord never opened his mouth to smile slightly. Now, what method did you use to make my lord so delighted?
Xú Wúguǐ said: "I merely told him of my judgment of dogs and horses."
Sub-commentary: Medicine has no nobility or baseness; what cures the illness is good. Thus, I merely spoke of dogs and horses, with no other discourse.
Nǚ Shāng said: "Is it so?"
Sub-commentary: Merely setting it forth thus, speaking of dogs and horses? Surprised at the simplicity of his method, hence this question.
He said: "Have you not heard of the exiles of Yuè? After leaving their state for a few days, they rejoice upon seeing those they know."

Annotation: Each thinks of what their innate nature delights in. Sub-commentary: Leaving the state, distant are the exiled ones—some violated laws, some suffered under harsh governance. Just departed from their homeland, having been gone only a few days, suddenly meeting an acquaintance—doubtless they are joyful and comforted. This begins a parable.
"After leaving their state for ten days or a month, they rejoice upon seeing what they once saw in the state."
Sub-commentary: As days and months pass, longing for home gradually deepens. Though not acquaintances, having seen them in the state, thus upon seeing such a person, they rejoice.
"When a full year has passed, they rejoice upon seeing someone who resembles a human. Is it not that the longer they are away from people, the deeper they long for them?"

Annotation: When each obtains what they delight in, there is no longing; without longing, they forget what made them rejoice. Sub-commentary: After a year away from the state, the place they've gone to is gradually distant, so upon seeing someone resembling a fellow villager, they rejoice. Is it not that the farther they are from home, the deeper their longing? This compares to Marquis Wǔ's innate delight in dogs and horses, long unexposed to governance, like one away from home suddenly hearing familiar talk and laughter.

"Those who flee to desolate places, with weeds blocking the paths of weasels, stumbling in the emptiness, hear the sound of human footsteps and rejoice. How much more so for the laughter and talk of brothers and relatives by their side?"

Annotation: Obtaining what brings utmost joy leads to great delight. Sub-commentary: "Blocking" means obstructing; "stumbling" means treading; "sound of footsteps" is the noise of walking. In times of turmoil and famine, fleeing and scattering to deserted dwellings, only wild weeds block the courtyards, and the paths of monkeys and weasels are there. If in the hall, the human position is empty and vast, in such circumstances, longing for home grows strong. Suddenly hearing another's footsteps, they are still joyful—how much more the laughter and talk of brothers and close kin by their side? This reiterates the parable.
"It has been long indeed since any with the words of a true man laughed and talked by my lord's side!"

Annotation: This is why he never showed a smile. The words of a true man are what match my lord's nature. Initially obtaining them, he rejoices; after long obtaining them, he forgets. Sub-commentary: Marquis Wǔ longed to hear of dogs and horses for a long time, like the exile or the fleeing guest, long stranded, truly harboring homesickness. Now, with the words of true men—the discourses of the Six Classics and Tàigōng's military methods—laughing and talking by his side, it is inappropriate. This connects to the previous discussion.

Xú Wúguǐ had an audience with Marquis Wǔ. Marquis Wǔ said: "You, Sir, have dwelt in the mountains and forests, eaten acorns and chestnuts, and been content with leeks and chives, avoiding me for so long. Now you are old—is it that you desire the taste of wine and meat, or that I might have the blessing of the state?"

Sub-commentary: "Desire" means to seek. Long dwelling in the mountains and forests, consuming vegetables and fruits, aged and toil-weary, is it not that you wish to seek flavors to nourish your declining years? Perhaps to receive virtue and secure the ancestral temple.
Xú Wúguǐ said: "Wúguǐ was born in poverty and lowliness, and has never dared to drink your wine or eat your meat. I have come to console you, my lord."
Sub-commentary: Living in poverty and lowliness, content in the mountains and marshes, how could I crave food and drink to nourish myself? It is not so; I have come to console you, my lord.
The lord said: "What do you mean? How do you console me?"
Sub-commentary: "How" means what; asking the reason.
He said: "I console your spirit and form."
Sub-commentary: Desires for food are insatiable, the form toils and the spirit wearies, hence I console you.
Marquis Wǔ said: "What does that mean?"
Sub-commentary: Asking what his words intend.
Xú Wúguǐ said: "The nourishment of Heaven and Earth is one."

Annotation: Not acting as lord and indulging without limit. Sub-commentary: Heaven and Earth, the two modes, nurture all beings. Things rely on nourishment, universally without bias, not acting as lord to indulge in extravagance. These are all Wúguǐ's words consoling the lord.

"Being on high cannot be considered long; being below cannot be considered short. You alone, as the lord of ten thousand chariots, torment the people of the state to nourish your ears, eyes, nose, and mouth."

Annotation: Thus violating the balance of Heaven and Earth. Sub-commentary: Ascending to high position as a nobleman, one cannot delight in it as long; dwelling low as the common people, one cannot suffer it as short. Yet you alone boast the might of ten thousand chariots, tormenting the masses of this state, coveting colors, sounds, scents, and flavors to indulge your ears, eyes, nose, and mouth. Since this violates the intent of Heaven and Earth, I privately consider it unacceptable.
"The spirit does not approve of itself."
Annotation: Things give to it. Sub-commentary: "Approve" means to give. The sage lord is divine and humane, treating self and others equally, surely not greedily seeking flavors to give to himself.
"The spirit loves harmony and hates cunning."
Annotation: Harmonizing with things is harmony; selfish approval is cunning. Sub-commentary: The divine sage loves to harmonize with things and hates cunning and selfishness.
"Cunning is a sickness; thus, I console you. Only you, my lord, are sick with it—why is that?"
Sub-commentary: Cunning is privately violating principle, which is sickness. You alone are sick and troubled—how so?
Marquis Wǔ said: "I have long wished to see you, Sir. I wish to love the people and act righteously, to lay down arms. Can this be done?"
Sub-commentary: Wishing to practice benevolent care and righteous judgment, cultivating civil education and ceasing warfare—governing thus, I wonder if it can be done.
Xú Wúguǐ said: "It cannot. Loving the people is the beginning of harming them."
Annotation: The traces of loving the people are esteemed by the people; esteeming them becomes love, and love is already artificial.
"Acting righteously and laying down arms is the root of creating arms."

Annotation: Acting righteously makes fame manifest; manifest fame stirs competition; competition arising loses genuineness. Father and son, ruler and minister, harbor feelings and deceive each other. Though wishing to lay down arms, how can it be achieved? Sub-commentary: Partial benevolent love, righteous judgment, achievements in disarming, efforts in civil cultivation—once these traces are manifest, things follow them. Harming the people and creating arms begin here.
"If you, my lord, proceed thus, it will nearly fail."

Annotation: Only by following non-action can it succeed. Sub-commentary: "Proceed" means to follow; "nearly" means close. Following this path will surely lead to near failure, ruining the root of non-action.
"All achieved beauty is a vessel of ugliness."

Annotation: Beauty achieved before gives birth to artificiality after; thus, achieved beauty is a vessel of ugliness. Sub-commentary: The affair of esteeming goodness, achieved before—once beautiful traces are manifest, things rush to compete, hence it becomes a vessel of ugliness.
"Though you, my lord, practice humaneness and righteousness, it is nearly artificial!"

Annotation: The people will judge it as artificial, unwilling to be genuine. Sub-commentary: "Nearly" means close. The traces of humaneness and righteousness are evident, things all lose genuineness, hence close to artificiality at the root.
"Form surely creates form."

Annotation: Humaneness and righteousness have form, surely artificial form must arise. Sub-commentary: The two paths of humaneness and righteousness both have traces; thus, prior traces being established, later forms must be created.
"Achievement surely brings contention."
Annotation: Achievement makes it manifest. Sub-commentary: Those who achieve merit and fame inevitably invite rivalry, hence there is contention.
"Change surely leads to external war."
Annotation: Losing its constant nature. Sub-commentary: Creating laws and changing constants—things will surely harm it, leading to external enemies and much conflict.
"You, my lord, must also not array crane formations between ornate towers."
Annotation: Crane formations are troop arrays; ornate towers are tall buildings.
"Nor assemble foot and chariot in the Zītán Palace."

Annotation: Foot soldiers are called "foot." Only do not act righteously or love the people; also do not amass troops or run horses. Sub-commentary: Crane formations are troop arrays, meaning deploying troops like cranes in rows. Ornate towers are tall buildings, meaning华丽 and lofty. Zītán is a palace name. You, my lord, need only not set your mind on disarming and righteousness, nor labor to array troops below tall towers or assemble foot and horse within palace gardens.
"Do not harbor rebellion in gain."
Annotation: Gain contains rebellion, then loss occurs. Sub-commentary: Do not conceal rebellious intent and be content with gain.
"Do not use cleverness to surpass others."

Annotation: Guard their simplicity, and each simplicity has its capability, then there is equality. Sub-commentary: Great cleverness seems clumsy; each should uphold simplicity, not use cunning minds to compete and surpass others.
"Do not use schemes to surpass others."

Annotation: Follow their genuine knowledge, and each knowledge has its strengths, then there is balance. Sub-commentary: Forget mind and dismiss thoughts, follow straightforward knowledge; do not use plots to surpass and defeat others.
"Do not use warfare to surpass others."
Annotation: Using the Way to respond to things, things submit without the name of victory. Sub-commentary: First engage
Huìzǐ said it was acceptable.
His scattered words each affirmed their own truths, claiming all under heaven were Yáo-like. While this principle exists, Huì Shī's stagnant arguments had words without substance.
Zhuāngzǐ said, "If so, then the Confucians, Mohists, Yángzǐ, and Bǐng—making four—with you, sir, as the fifth, which one is truly correct?"

The commentary notes: If all were Yáo, why would these five still dispute each other? The subcommentary explains: The Confucian refers to Zhèng Huǎn, the Mohist to Mò Dí, Yáng to Yáng Zhū, and Bǐng is Gōngsūn Lǒng's courtesy name. These four were all exceptionally intelligent and world-renowned debaters. Adding Huì Shī makes five, each disputing the others' correctness, with no certainty on who is right. If all under heaven were Yáo, why would these five still oppose each other?
Perhaps it is like Lǔ Jù? His disciple said, "I have attained my master's Dào; I can cook with a cauldron in winter and make ice in summer."

The subcommentary explains: Surname Lǔ, name Jù, a figure from the early Zhōu. In winter, he took dry thousand-year-old ashes to bank a fire, quickly producing flames to cook with a cauldron. In midsummer, he placed a clay pot of water in hot water, then suspended it in a well, swiftly forming ice. Yet deluded commoners, each affirming their own views, are no different from Lǔ.
Lǔ Jù said, "This merely uses yáng to summon yáng, yīn to summon yīn—not what I call the Dào."

The subcommentary explains: Thousand-year-old ashes are yáng, fire is also yáng—this is using yáng to summon yáng. The well's interior is yīn, water is also yīn—this is using yīn to summon yīn. Lǔ Jù said this to criticize his disciple.

"Let me show you my Dào." Thereupon, he tuned two se zithers, leaving one in the hall, one in the room. Plucking the gōng note in the hall, the gōng string in the room vibrated; plucking the jué note, the jué string moved—their pitch standards aligned.

The commentary notes: Both also used yáng to summon yáng, yet he arrogantly considered himself correct. The subcommentary explains: "Left" means placed. Placing one se in the hall, one in the room, plucking the hall's gōng or jué, the corresponding strings inside responded—this is because the five notes and six pitch standards matched, still using yáng to summon yáng.
If one alters a single string's tuning, making it dissonant with the five notes,
the commentary notes: Changing with the tuning. The subcommentary explains: Altering one string's tuning in the hall, the room's strings no longer respond, as their pitch standards differ.
plucking it causes all twenty-five strings to vibrate.

The commentary notes: Without sound, nothing stirs; with sound, if not in harmony, no response. Now changing this one string, all twenty-five change their tuning to match its urgency or slackness. The subcommentary explains: Previously, only gōng and jué responded; subtly, all twenty-five strings vibrate—those with matching pitch standards all respond.
Never differing from the sound, yet it becomes the ruler of tones.

The commentary notes: Lǔ Jù boasted of this to his disciple, but it still relies on like responding to like, not a unique skill. The subcommentary explains: Beyond sound and pitch, was there any extraordinary technique? Though responses varied, all ultimately followed the five notes as their sovereign. Without other arts, how could he boast?
"And is it like this?"

The commentary notes: The five each privately uphold their views, affirming their own correctness, no different from Lǔ Jù boasting to his disciple—none can surpass the others. The subcommentary explains: Huìzǐ's words, each privately correct, striving to boast and surpass others, are no different from Lǔ Jù—hence "like this."
Huìzǐ said, "Now the Confucians, Mohists, Yángzǐ, and Bǐng are disputing with me, clashing with arguments, suppressing with rhetoric, using sound, yet none have proven me wrong—so what about that?"
The commentary notes: "None have proven me wrong" means each considers themselves correct. Huìzǐ then wishes to see this as ultimate.
Zhuāngzǐ said, "There was a man from Qí who abandoned his son in Sòng, making him a gatekeeper, not intact."

The commentary notes: Casting him to a foreign land, having a gatekeeper guard him—once out, his hands are harmed, not kept whole. This Qí man was unkind, yet also considered himself right, hence did it. The subcommentary explains: A gatekeeper guards the gate. The Qí man discarded his son in Sòng, still commanding this—is that not his 'I am right'?
"He sought a xíng bell, binding it up,"
the commentary notes: Instead, he considered loving the bell correct, binding it lest it break.
"seeking his lost son, yet never leaving the region—he has lost his kind."

The commentary notes: "Táng" means lost. Losing his son but not searching afar, he forsakes his own kind, yet never faults himself—people's self-rightness has such absurdity. The subcommentary explains: Xíng is a small bell. Táng means lost. Seeking the lost son, not beyond the border, binding the xíng bell fearing damage—cherishing the vessel, despising the son, is unkind. Forsaking his kind also speaks of "I am right."
"The Chǔ man, lodging and offending the gatekeeper,"
the commentary notes: Both dwell but cannot elevate themselves to higher ground.
"in the dead of night when none are about, fights with the boatman—never having left the bank, yet enough to create enmity."

The commentary notes: "Cén" is the bank. At midnight, boarding a boat alone, not yet left shore, already fighting—the Qí and Chǔ two act thus, yet never consider themselves wrong. Now the five's self-rightness—how differs from this? The subcommentary explains: A man from Chǔ Yǐng, his son lodged near the river, entrusted to a gatekeeper's house, at midnight when none are around, enters another's boat, and before the boat leaves shore, fights with the boatman—showing no gratitude, creating grievances. Such folly, yet also saying "I am right"—Hùizǐ's followers are like this. Cén is the bank.

Zhuāngzǐ, seeing off a funeral, passed Hùizǐ's grave. Turning to his followers, he said, "A Yǐng man had plaster speckling his nose tip, like a fly's wing, had Craftsman Shí chop it. Craftsman Shí swung his axe like wind, chopping by sound."

The commentary notes: Closing eyes, free hand. The subcommentary explains: Yǐng, capital of Chǔ. In Yáng Xióng's Hànshū biography, written as Yǐng, referring to the plaster-splattered man. "È" is white clay. "Màn" means to smear. Zhuāngzǐ, escorting a close friend's funeral, passed Hùizǐ's grave, reminiscing the past, raised this analogy. Closing eyes, free hand, chopping by sound—the axe-swinging skill created a wind-like sound. "Like a fly's wing" describes its divine marvel.
"The plaster was entirely removed, the nose unharmed. The Yǐng man stood without losing composure. Sòng Yuánjūn heard of it, summoned Craftsman Shí, saying, 'Try it for me.'"
The subcommentary explains: Removing the plaster smear, the nose undamaged; the Yǐng man stood by, demeanor unchanged. Yuánjūn, hearing of its wonder, tried summoning him to perform it.
"Craftsman Shí said, 'I indeed once could chop it. However, my counterpart has long been dead. Since my master's death, I have no one to act as counterpart; I have no one to speak with.'"

The commentary notes: Without an unmoving counterpart and wordless dialogue, even the ultimate words and marvelous chops are useless. The subcommentary explains: "Counterpart" means partner. Though Craftsman Shí was skilled, he needed an unmoving counterpart. Though Zhuāngzǐ was wise, he relied on wordless dialogue. Knowing Hùizǐ's death left Zhuāngzǐ bereft, the craftsman ceased his wind-like marvelous sound, Zhuāngzǐ ended his subtle words on the Háo river.
Guǎn Zhòng fell ill. Duke Huán asked him, "Zhòngfù's illness is grave—can it not be said? If it reaches the great illness, to whom should I entrust the state?"

The subcommentary explains: Guǎn Zhòng, surname Guǎn, name Zhòng, courtesy name Yíwú, chancellor of Qí, friend of Bào Shūyá. Duke Huán honored him as Zhòngfù. Duke Huán was Xiǎo Bái, who unified the realm, assembled lords nine times, becoming hegemon—all due to Guǎn Zhòng's efforts. "Illness is grave" means extremely severe. "Great illness" means death. As he neared death, the duke visited, asking after Zhòngfù's death, to whom state affairs should be entrusted.
Guǎn Zhòng said, "Whom does my lord wish to give it to?" The duke said, "Bào Shūyá."
The subcommentary explains: Asked whom to give state affairs, answered: to Bào Shūyá.

He said, "No. His character is clean and honest, a good man, but towards those not as good as himself, he does not associate; also, once hearing others' faults, never forgets them lifelong. Having him govern the state, above he would constrain the lord, below oppose the people. His offenses against the lord would soon be punished."

The subcommentary explains: Bào Shūyá, surname Bào, courtesy name Shūyá, upright, clean, honest, a good man. But with petty people not his equal, he does not associate. Hearing others' faults, never forgets till death. Upright and honest, unfit for ministry. Above, his loyalty would restrain the lord; below, his clarity oppose the commoners. Unable to harmonize, the lord would surely punish him. Guǎn Zhòng, wise, discerning things, feared endangering the state, worried for Shūyá, thus did not recommend him.
The duke said, "Then who is suitable?" He replied, "If unavoidable, then Xí Péng is suitable. His character: above, he forgets; below, does not oppose."

The commentary notes: High but not arrogant. The subcommentary explains: Surname Xí, name Péng, a worthy of Qí. "Oppose" means expectant. Blending high and low, unifying glory and shame, he, as minister, could forget noble honor, below comfort the masses, forgetting lowly station. If unavoidable, he can be used.
"Ashamed not to match Huángdì, and pitying those not as good as himself,"
the commentary notes: Thus none are abandoned. The subcommentary explains: Those not his equal, he only pities. Assisting the Qí lord, aiming for simplicity, his heart ashamed not reaching Xuānyuán.
"Dividing virtue among others is called sage; dividing wealth among others is called worthy."
The subcommentary explains: Sages save beings with virtue; worthies aid people with wealth.

"Using worthiness to oversee others, none have gained people; using worthiness to humble oneself before others, none have failed to gain people. For the state, there are things he does not hear; for the family, things he does not see. If unavoidable, then Xí Péng is suitable."

The subcommentary explains: Using intelligence to oversee the people opposes their nature. With Shūyá governing, he would not overlook minor flaws; managing a family, not see others' faults. If unavoidable, Xí Péng is suitable—summarizing the prior meaning.

The King of Wú floated on the river, ascended the mountain of monkeys. The monkeys saw him, fled in terror into deep thickets. One monkey, leisurely swinging and grabbing, displayed skill before the king. The king shot at it, swiftly.

The commentary notes: "Mǐn" means quick; "gěi" means continuing the arrow's flight. The subcommentary explains: "Jū" are macaques. The mountain had many, hence named Jū mountain. "Xún" means fearful. "Zhēn" is thorny thicket. "Wěi yí" means relaxed. "Jué zǎo" means leaping and grabbing. "Mǐn gěi" means rapid. The King of Wú floated, touring, gazing afar. The monkeys feared, fled to deep thorns. One old monkey, relying on its ease, scorned the king. The king, angered, swiftly shot.
It caught the swift arrow.

The commentary notes: "Jié" means fast. Though the arrow flew swiftly, the monkey still caught it. The subcommentary explains: "Bó" means catch; "jié" means swift; "shǐ" means arrow. Though the arrow sped, the monkey caught it—such was its agility.
The king ordered his aides to rush and shoot it. The monkey held on and died.

The subcommentary explains: "Mìng" means summon; "xiāng" means assistants, the king's attendants. The king, missing his shot, summoned his aides to shoot wildly. Thus, the monkey clung to the tree and died.
The king turned to his friend Yán Bùyí, saying, "This monkey, flaunting its skill, relying on its ease, scorned me—thus it met death. Beware! Alas, do not let your demeanor pride you before others!"

The subcommentary explains: Yán Bùyí, surname Yán, courtesy name Bùyí, the king's friend. "Jí" means death. "Yǔ" means me. The monkey boasted of its skill, relied on its convenience, arrogantly scorned the king, thus met death. Alas, this cunning beast can warn people not to indulge in pride and extravagance in the world.
Yán Bùyí returned and studied under Dǒng Wú to remove his proud demeanor, abandoned music, declined prominence. After three years, the state's people praised him.

The commentary notes: Praising his forgetting skill, discarding demeanor, and embracing simplicity. The subcommentary explains: Dǒng Wú, surname Dǒng, name Wú, a worthy of Wú. "Chú" means remove. Receiving the king's admonition, he returned, repented, renewed himself, studied under a Dào-possessor, removed his fine demeanor, abandoned musical pleasures, emphasized simplicity, declined glory, cultivated virtue. After three years, the state's people praised his goodness.
Nánbó Zǐqí leaned on his armrest, sat, looked up and sighed.
The subcommentary explains: This is the same Nánguō Zǐqí from "Equalizing Things." The leaning, etc., meanings are explained in the inner chapters.
Yánchéng Zǐ entered, saw him, said, "Master, you are the utmost among beings! Can the body truly be made like dry bones, the mind truly like dead ashes?"

The subcommentary explains: Yánchéng Zǐ, a disciple of Zǐqí. "Yóu" means extreme. Often looking up, sighing, the master forgets things profoundly—surely the body like dry bones, mind like dead ashes. Admiring his virtue, earnest, he sighed thus.
He said, "I once dwelt at the mouth of a mountain cave. At that time, Tián Hé once saw me, and the people of Qí congratulated him thrice."

The commentary notes: Considering seeing Zǐqí an honor. The subcommentary explains: The mountain cave in southern Qí mountains. Tián Hé, the Qí king's name. Zǐqí dwelt hidden in the mountain cave, his virtuous fame spread afar. The Qí lord briefly saw him, considered it an honor, so the whole state congratulated him thrice.
"I must have preceded it, thus he knew me; I must have sold it, thus he traded it."
The subcommentary explains: My reputation came first, thus things knew me; I sold myself for fame, thus Tián Hé saw and imitated me.
"If I did not possess it, how could he know it? If I did not sell it, how could he trade it?"

The subcommentary explains: If I concealed my light, hid traces, had no reputation, how could the world know me? If my fame had no price, how could he see and imitate me? Only because I could not erase traces, hide ends, I was traded by things.
"Alas, I grieve for those who lose themselves."
The subcommentary explains: "Sàng" means lose. Zǐqí grieves people abandoning themselves, admiring others, losing the Dào.
"I also grieve for those who grieve for others."
The subcommentary explains: The Dào has no gain or loss, but beings have sorrow and joy. Thus, grieving for those who lose themselves is also grievable.
"I also grieve for those who grieve for the grievers. Thereafter, it daily recedes."

The commentary notes: Zǐqí knew acting could not save them but would harm oneself. Thus, using non-grief to grieve, the grief gradually leaves, becoming placid, heartless, withering the form—thus daily receding. The subcommentary explains: The mysterious Dào is empty, without loss or joy. Thus, grieving for self-losers and grievers, though differing in depth, all miss the Dào, hence grievable. G
Shùn was raised in a barren land; his years and teeth had grown long, his hearing and sight had declined, yet he could not retire and return home — this is what is called being toil-worn and weary.

Note: The sage's form is no different from ordinary people, hence the functions of ears and eyes decline. But as for the spirit, it remains complete from beginning to end. If it were immature in youth and decayed upon growing up, then the sage's sageliness would not last even a morning — is that possible? Explanation: Having ascended to the imperial throne, his authority spanned ten thousand chariots; he pitied the common people, worrying and caring for the ordinary masses. Thus, as his years and teeth grew old, his ears and eyes weakened and failed, with no way to rest — how could he return to peace? Hunched and cramped, his body toiled and spirit wearied — this is what is called being toil-worn and weary.
Therefore, the spiritual person dislikes crowds gathering.
Note: The crowds come of themselves; it is not that he delights in and attracts them. Explanation: He moved three times to distance himself — this is because he disliked it.
When crowds gather, there is no harmony; without harmony, it is not beneficial.

Note: It is clear that Shùn possessed the empire out of inevitability — how could he seek harmony and benefit from it? Explanation: "Bǐ" means harmony. When crowds gather, there is no harmony; without harmony, it is not beneficial to me.
Therefore, he shows no extreme intimacy nor extreme distance; he embraces virtue and warms harmony to comply with the world — this is called the true person.
Explanation: "Yáng" means to warm. The unfathomable spiritual person views intimacy and distance as one, embracing and maintaining warmth and harmony — this may be called true sageliness.
With ants, discard wisdom; with fish, attain their way; with sheep, discard intention.

Note: For the people, there is bestowed favor; for Shùn, there is physical toil. Explanation: Not admiring the benevolence of mutton, thus with ants, discard wisdom. Not practicing alluring conduct to teach others, thus with sheep, discard intention. Having abandoned benevolence and righteousness, conforming to the ultimate way, not clinging to each other like fish in stranded puddles but forgetting each other in rivers and lakes, thus fish attain their way. This criticizes Yú Shùn's alluring conduct, hence these words.
Use eyes to look at eyes, use ears to listen to ears, use heart to return to heart.

Note: These three have not yet reached having no ears, eyes, heart, or intent. Explanation: Looking at what the eyes see, listening to what the ears hear, returning to what the heart knows — not chasing things beyond one's portion but knowing to stop within one's portion — this is the way of the true person.
If so, his evenness is like a plumb line.
Note: Unable to remove the line and be naturally even. Explanation: The line has no mind yet straightens things; the sage forgets concerns and is equal.
His changes follow along.

Note: Unable to erase traces and mysteriously meet. Explanation: "Xún" means to follow. In dealing with the world, harmonizing with the light, undergoing a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, greatly complying with the common people, never opposing the few.
The true persons of antiquity used heaven to treat things.

Note: Residing in non-action to treat affairs — thus affairs are attained. Explanation: As explained above, this is the mysterious ancient true persons using the way of nature to empty their hearts and treat things.
Not using the human to enter the heavenly.
Note: Using action to seek non-action — affairs become more chaotic. Explanation: Not using human affairs, choices and rejections, to disturb natural wisdom.
The true persons of antiquity: gaining it, they lived; losing it, they died; gaining it, they died; losing it, they lived.

Note: Life, death, gain, loss — each follows its dwelling. For life, it is gain; for death, it may again be loss — there has never been constancy. Explanation: Speaking from the standpoint of life, then life is gain; if based on death, then life becomes loss. Since life and death are undetermined, where do gain and loss truly lie? Alas, it cannot be known. Therefore, they mixed life and death, unified gain and loss — hence called true persons.
Medicine — its realities are jǐn, júgěng, jīyōng, shǐlíng — these, in their time, are emperors. How can one fully express it?

Note: When needed, none are lowly; when not their time, none are noble. Nobility and lowliness have their times — who can be constant? Explanation: Jǐn is wūtóu, treating wind paralysis; júgěng treats heart and abdomen ailments; jīyōng is jītóu grass, prolonging life; shǐlíng is zhūlíng root, resembling pig eggs, treating thirst illness. These are all lowly medicines. "Dì" means sovereign. Medicine has no nobility or lowliness — curing illness makes it good. When illness and medicine match, thus it becomes sovereign. Even eyes seeing, ears hearing, hands grasping, heart knowing — functions have their application and retirement, times have their rise and decline. Thus, those worthy in their time become rulers; talents not fitting the age become ministers. This matter is inevitable — how can it be fully expressed?
Gōu Jiàn, with three thousand armored soldiers, dwelt on Kuài Jī.
Explanation: Gōu Jiàn, king of Yuè. Kuài Jī, mountain name. Yuè was devastated by Wú's army, forced to retreat and dwell on Mount Kuài Jī.
Only Zhǒng could know how perishing could lead to survival; only Zhǒng did not know why his own person would face sorrow.

Explanation: Zhǒng, senior official of Yuè. At that time, Gōu Jiàn was greatly defeated, with only three thousand soldiers, fleeing to Mount Kuài Jī. Annihilation was near, yet Zhǒng secretly planned with deep wisdom — the time of perishing could be preserved. At that time, he feigned peace with Wú; after twenty-two years, they destroyed Wú. When the cunning hare dies, the good hound is cooked; when the enemy state perishes, the loyal minister dies — such is the pattern. After pacifying Wú, Fàn Lǐ left Yuè and wandered rivers and seas, changing name and surname, concealing light and hiding traces — that is Táo Zhū Gōng. Senior official Zhǒng did not leave and was executed by Gōu Jiàn. He only knew the state's perishing could be survived, not knowing his own person would surely die. The character is also written as "Zhǒng" — read accordingly.
Therefore it is said: The owl's eyes have their suitability; the crane's legs have their joints — to remove them is sorrow.

Note: Each suits a temporary function; unable to do what cannot be done, then sometimes loss, sometimes sorrow. "Jiě" means to remove. Explanation: The owl's eyes are dim by day, open at night — thus suited to night, not day. The crane's legs, endowed by nature, are long — thus can be long, not short. With branches and joints thus, to remove them is sorrow. Just like Zhǒng, dim in planning for himself, skilled in preserving the state.
Therefore it is said: When wind passes the river, there is diminishment; when sun passes the river, there is diminishment.

Note: What has form naturally accumulates burdens together. Only what is beyond form, grinding it does not thin. Note: Wind and sun are qi; the river has form and substance. All with form and qi cannot be without burdens. Wind blowing and sun burdening necessarily cause damage. Relying on the source to flow, thus unaware. Just like after Wú obtained Yuè, the strategist necessarily relied on his merit, thinking no future worries, yet met execution. Thus knowing things mutually benefiting necessarily mutually harm.
Say, just wind and sun together guard the river, yet the river thinks it has never been disturbed.
Note: Actually already diminished, yet unaware itself.
Relying on the source to flow.

Note: Thus unaware — not that it is not diminished, but relying on the source flowing. Explanation: "Shì" means to rely. "Yīng" means to diminish. Wind and sun together guard the river; the river is diminished yet unknowing, relying on its source flow.
Therefore, water's guarding earth is stable; shadow's guarding person is stable; thing's guarding thing is stable.

Note: Without intent, then stopping within its portion — thus stable. Explanation: "Shěn" means stability. Water without earth is不安; shadow without person is unseen; thing without creator is unestablished. Thus the three guard each other and deem themselves firm, yet the new and old do not remain, existence and cessation do not stop — yesterday's things today already transformed, mountains and boats secretly vanish, the ignorant unaware — this is its meaning.
Therefore, eyes for sharp sight are perilous; ears for keen hearing are perilous; heart for pursuit are perilous.

Note: Having intent, then no limits — thus perilous. Explanation: "Xùn" means to follow. Using eyes to seek Lí Zhū's sight, ears to seek Shī Kuàng's hearing, heart to pursue limitless knowledge — wanting to avoid peril, how can it be obtained?
All abilities from the organs are perilous; when peril forms, there is no time to change.

Note: Thus valuing inability and entrusting to nature. Explanation: Employing discriminating wisdom from the organs, and boasting of ability necessarily leads to peril and ruin. Thus, even with successful achievements, unable to circulate and change in time.
Calamity's growth thus accumulates.

Note: "Cuì" means to gather. If unable to forget knowledge, then calamity's growth has many sources. Explanation: "Zī" means many. "Cuì" means to gather. Servitude to organs, displaying one's ability — thus inauspicious disasters and calamities grow and accumulate.
Its reversal depends on merit.

Note: Returning to guard one's nature, then achievements are made without striving. Explanation: Boasting of one's ability and instead attracting calamity and defeat — depends on not withdrawing after merit is achieved.
Its fruition awaits long.
Note: Wanting speed then no fruition. Explanation: Sincerely intending success, determined to boast — awaiting such mind, its days are indeed long.
And people consider it their treasure — is it not sorrowful?

Note: "Own treasure" means having one's knowledge and ability. Explanation: Wandering people, minds dwelling in foolish darkness, treasuring their own ability, successful and obstinate — thus very sorrowful.
Therefore, there are destroyed states and slain people without end.

Note: All have calamities from having a self. Explanation: Coveting land as one's great treasure, seizing it without way — states broken, families destroyed, common people harmed — countless, endless.
Not knowing to inquire about this.

Note: Not knowing to ask the source of calamity — due to having a mind and cultivating mind to save calamity. Explanation: The world has enlightened people as mirrors; not knowing to ask the source of ruin and defeat, only hating poverty and lowliness — utmost folly.
Therefore, feet regarding the ground tread; though treading, they rely on what is not trodden to then be good for broad movement.

Explanation: "Jiàn" and "niǎn" both mean to tread. Feet able to walk must tread the ground, still relying on untrodden earth to then be able to walk. Without extra ground, no way to safely achieve broad distance. This is an analogy.
People regarding knowledge are few; though few, they rely on what they do not know to then know heaven's meaning.

Note: Forgetting heaven and earth, discarding the myriad things, then the cicada's wings can be known — how much more wanting to know heaven's meaning, can one not empty the mind? Explanation: Knowledge has clarity and darkness, ability has little and much — each stopping at its portion, then things wander freely. Thus earth relies on untrodden to enable walking; mind relies on unknown to enable illumination. Thus dwelling in stillness, nurturing tranquility — nature's principle. Hence the Lǎo Jīng says: Having it is for benefit; not having it is for use. This fits the discussion.
Know the great one, know the great yīn, know the great eye, know the great equality, know the great square, know the great trust, know the great stability — reaching the ultimate.
Explanation: This briefly marks that those who can know the seven greats may be said to reach the extreme. From here below, sequentially explaining meanings.
The great one connects it.
Note: The way. Explanation: One is a yang number; the great one is heaven. Able to connect and generate the myriad things — thus called connecting.
The great yīn resolves it.
Note: Using its internal portion, then the myriad affairs have no obstructions. Explanation: The great yīn is earth. Unintentionally moving and carrying, without dividing, resolves things' forms.
The great eye sees it.
Note: Using the myriad things' self-seeing is also the great eye. Explanation: Each sees what it sees — called the great eye.
The great equality follows it.
The great square embodies it.

Note: Embodying it so each attains its portion, then all directions are attained — thus the great square. Explanation: The myriad things' forms each have their methods — like the spider weaving its web — thus embodying and reaching them.
The great trust verifies it.

Note: What fate expects, not letting it transgress — this is great trust. Explanation: "Xìn" means reality. "Jī" means to reach. Following and entrusting to it, each reaching its reality — this is great trust.
The great stability holds it.
Note: True without disturbance then naturally stable — thus holding it with great stability is not holding. Explanation: Things each trust emptiness; holding and using it, its principle is empty.
Exhaust it, and there is heaven.
Note: Among things, none lack nature. Explanation: The above seven greats — none are not from their nature.

Note: Following it then bright, with no action. Explanation: "Xún" means to follow. Just follow nature, wisdom naturally illuminates. The mysterious has a pivot. Note: The ultimate principle has extremes; just darken it then attain its pivot. Explanation: The principle of mystery naturally has a pivot; using it requires no deliberate effort.
Begin, and there is that.
