Note: Beginning to have it — that is it. Thus I transmit, not create. Explanation: Beginning to have it — that is it. Thus I transmit, not create.
Then its understanding seems like not understanding it.

Note: Understanding entrusts to that, then it understands itself; understanding without merit, thus seems not understanding. Explanation: The body follows that, learns and understands. Guarding against small attainments' nature, thus not like understanding.
Its knowing seems like not knowing it.
Note: Clarifying that knowing. Explanation: Able to forget its knowing, thus seems not knowing.
Not knowing, then afterwards knowing.

Note: I not knowing, then that knowing self-applies; that knowing self-applying, then none under heaven do not know. Explanation: Not knowing yet knowing — thus not knowing then afterwards knowing — this is true knowing.
Its questioning cannot have limits.
Note: Responding to things appropriately, without fixed direction.
Yet cannot have no limits.
Note: Each according to its portion.
Chaos has reality.

Note: The myriad things, though chaotic and slippery differently, each thing itself has reality. Explanation: "Jiéhuá" means different. The myriad things,纷扰 chaotic and slippery different, unifying and governing them, all rely on the reality of the way.
Ancient and modern do not substitute.

Note: Each has its reason, cannot substitute each other. Explanation: Ancient itself exists in ancient, not from ancient generating present; present itself exists in present, not from present generating ancient. Things each have their natures, thus do not substitute.
Yet cannot be diminished.
Note: Should each exhaust their portion. Explanation: Time does not come and go; principles do not shift or trade — how rely on ancient to make present?
Then, can it not be said to have great exposition?

Note: Expounding and elevating it, there is great limit. Explanation: As questioned above, its way is vast and great — can it not be said to manifest and elevate subtle principles, and expound substantively?
Why not also inquire this? Why confusedly act so?

Note: If inquiring its great exposition, then things have ultimate portions; thus the principle of forgetting self and entrusting to things can be known. Why be confused like this? Explanation: "Hé" means why not. "Xī" means why. Those without recognition, like night wanderers — why not inquire of the sage? And why, having lost their roots, be confused, troubled, and suffering so?
Using non-confusion to explain confusion, returning to non-confusion — this esteems great non-confusion.

Note: Confusion cannot be resolved; thus esteeming great non-confusion is utmost folly. Therefore, the sage follows and entrusts to it — thus emperors and kings different traces, following the age as names. Explanation: Non-confusion is sage wisdom; confusion is ordinary feelings. Using sage wisdom's words to discern ordinary confusion, forgetting gain, returning to origin, returning to true root. Yet unable to attain meaning and forget words, clinging to sage traces, valuing bright words, considering non-confusion as great — this is wanting to esteem non-confusion, how can it remove confusion? This again dismisses non-confusion.
Nán Huá Zhēn Jīng Notes and Explanation, Scroll Twenty-Six.
The Nanhua True Classic Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Twenty-Seven, Part One
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá in the Táng Dynasty Miscellaneous Chapters, Zé Yáng, Number Twenty-Five
Zé Yáng traveled to Chǔ.
Subcommentary: His surname was Péng, given name Yáng, courtesy name Zé Yáng; he was from Lǔ. He traveled serving various feudal lords, later entering Chǔ wishing to serve King Wén of Chǔ.
Yí Jié spoke of him to the king, but the king had not yet seen him.

Subcommentary: Surname Yí, given name Jié, a minister of Chǔ. Since Zé Yáng wished to serve in Chǔ, he thus relied on Yí Jié to speak of him to the king. The king, being noble and important, had therefore not yet seen him. Yí Jié's recommendation had not yet succeeded, so he ceased court and returned home.
Yí Jié returned home. Péng Yáng went to see Wáng Guǒ, saying, "Why does my master not speak of me to the king?"

Subcommentary: Wáng Guǒ was a worthy senior official of Chǔ. "Tán" means to praise or speak of. Some versions also have the characters for "speaking" and "discussing." Previously, through Yí Jié, he had not managed to see the king; later, he spoke to Wáng Guǒ, hoping he would talk and recommend him.
Wáng Guǒ said, "I am not as good as Gōng Yuè Xiū."

Subcommentary: "Ruò" means "like." Gōng Yuè Xiū was the name of a recluse. Wáng Guǒ, being a worthy man, disliked Péng Yáng's greed for glory and his hasty emotions, so he greatly praised the recluse to suppress his heart's tendency to advance.
Péng Yáng said, "What does Gōng Yuè Xiū do?"
Subcommentary: "Xī" means "what." Since he mentioned Gōng Yuè Xiū, saying he himself did not know, he asked what he did, hoping to hear the reason.
He said, "In winter, he spears turtles in the river; in summer, he rests in the mountain groves. If someone passes by and asks, he says, 'This is my dwelling.'"

Commentary: Saying this is to suppress Péng Yáng's urge to advance. Subcommentary: "Chù" means to spear. "Fán" means the edge, also dense forests. In deep winter, he spears turtles on the riverbanks to be carefree; in midsummer, he returns to rest, reclining in dense forests to find comfort. Since he has no attachments, he points to the mountain edge as his abode. This briefly describes Gōng Yuè Xiū's deeds.

"Now, Yí Jié already cannot, and how much less can I? Moreover, I am not as good as Yí Jié. As for Yí Jié's character, he has no virtue but has knowledge; he does not restrain himself to spiritualize his interactions. Firmly, he is deluded in the realm of wealth and honor."

Commentary: This says that I am not like Yí Jié's fondness for wealth and honor, his ability to form connections, exhausting his form in the service of knowledge to seek favor from superiors. Subcommentary: "Diān míng" means being lost and submerged. It means Yí Jié's social interactions are firm, his intention set on glory and splendor; he is topsy-turvy and deluded, his emotions greedy for wealth and honor. Truly, he has no genuine virtue but has worldly knowledge; he cannot be empty and tranquil to follow the spirit, but prefers to rely on knowledge to approach superiors. Repeatedly acting like this, he still cannot manage; how much less can I, guarding my simplicity? How could I be worthy of recommendation? This is Wáng Guǒ's humble and deferential words.
"He does not assist with virtue; his assistance destroys."

Commentary: Forcing advancement, thus virtue is thin and reputation is destroyed. Subcommentary: "Xiāo" means to destroy and harm. It means if Zé Yáng relies on me to speak of him to the king, this would only ruin his reputation and conduct; it certainly would not benefit his great virtue.
"Now, the frozen person borrows clothes from spring; the sunstroke victim longs for winter's cold wind."

Commentary: This says that I follow the application of the four seasons and cannot rush to Péng Yáng's urgency. Subcommentary: A person suffering from cold gets warm with clothes; one struck by heat revives upon encountering water. Yet they wait for the warm harmony of spring to thaw the freeze, and need the cold wind to save them from heatstroke. Though contrary to human affairs, it actually follows the timeliness of heaven. One who treads the path and understands people embodies no immediate favors; not advancing Péng Yáng, the principle is the same.
"Now, as for the King of Chǔ's character, his form is尊贵 and severe; regarding offenses, there is no pardon. He is like a tiger; if not a clever man of proper virtue, who can bend him?"

Subcommentary: His bearing has the尊贵 of facing south, his威严 rests on the尊贵 of a thousand chariots. His blazing anger executes poison, like a fierce tiger. Slaughtering and humiliating the common people, he certainly shows no pardon. Unless one is a greatly clever person, one cannot bear the appointment. If one treads uprightness and embraces virtue, who can bend their will and serve him?
"Therefore, when the sage is in poverty, he makes his family forget their poverty."

Commentary: Indifferent and without desire, content with what he encounters, not valuing extravagance and luxury but honoring the Way and virtue; therefore, his family does not recognize poverty as something to suffer. Subcommentary: Liè Yǔkòu resided in Zhèng, Lǎo Lái in Chǔ; their wives and children were poor and destitute, yet joy was within. Worthy scholars are still like this, how much more so the true sage? This is the will regarding poverty.
"When he is successful, he makes kings and dukes forget their ranks and emoluments and transform into humility."

Commentary: He轻视 ranks and emoluments and重视 the Way and virtue; transcendentally sitting in forgetfulness, he does not perceive glory in his person, thus causing kings and dukes to lose that by which they are exalted. Subcommentary: Concealing one's light is poverty; revealing one's traces is success. Duke Āi befriended Confucius in virtue; Xuānyuán knelt and walked before Guǎng Chéng. These all show that where the Way is, there is尊贵, not constrained by status or mandate. Therefore, he can make the king of ten thousand chariots and the lords of the five ranks transform their尊贵 hearts into humble conduct.
"As for things, he amuses himself with them."
Commentary: He does not make things bitter for himself. Subcommentary: Sharing the dust and engaging affairs, he is selfless towards things; all he creates is suitable, therefore he is always joyful.
"As for people, he delights in the connection with things and preserves himself."

Commentary: Connecting with others, he does not lose himself. Subcommentary: Blending traces among people without obstruction; though again connecting with things, he does not lose himself. Action does not harm stillness, and he constantly guards his authenticity.
"Therefore, sometimes without speaking, he lets people drink harmony."
"Standing together with people, he makes them transform."
Commentary: Seeing his influence, they are swayed. Subcommentary: Harmonizing light and sharing dust, this is standing together. Each returns to their authenticity, this is people transforming.
"The proper relation between father and son—they each return to their dwelling."

Commentary: Making those fathers be fathers, sons be sons, each returning to their proper place. Subcommentary: Though again blending noble and lowly, the ethical order is without deficiency. Therefore, fathers and sons, rulers and ministers, each reside in their position without mutual encroachment—is that not proper?
"And uniformly闲暇 in their actions."

Commentary: Their actions are同于 the virtue of heaven and earth, therefore闲暇 and tranquil, not dual. Subcommentary: All bestowed favors harmonize with the sequence of the four seasons; never without闲暇 and从容, movement and stillness are non-dual.
"As for the human heart, it is so far like this."
Subcommentary: The sage's use of the heart is as described above; thus, we know it is pure, lofty, deep, and distant.
"Therefore, it is said, 'Wait for Gōng Yuè Xiū.'"
Commentary: Wanting him to release the King of Chǔ and follow Yuè Xiū, intending to use the wind of tranquil abundance to calm his restless heart. Subcommentary: This is the concluding summary.
"The sage penetrates entanglement."

Commentary: What is called mysterious penetration. Subcommentary: "Chóu móu" means bonds and ties. The sage who penetrates the Way transcends and is mysteriously untied; realizing that the realm of things is empty and illusory, how could he be bound by the dust net? Though Yuè Xiū has not reached the ultimate Way, he is thus relied upon to speak of it.
"He is同 with all, one body."

Commentary: Without outside or inside, all are equally illuminated. Subcommentary: Now, wisdom encompasses all things, exhausting principle and fulfilling nature; things and self are non-dual, therefore blended as one body.
"And does not know how it is so—it is his nature."

Commentary: Not knowing how it is so, yet it is natural—if not nature, what is it? Subcommentary: Ability and object correspond; realm and wisdom darkly merge. Not knowing the reason, unable to discern how it is so; therefore, it accords with true nature.
"Returning to life, moving and acting, he takes heaven as his teacher."

Commentary: The moving ones move themselves, the acting ones act themselves; none do not return to life and take their natural state as teacher. Subcommentary: Returning to the true root, restoring to the original life; though again moving and acting in accordance with things, movement and stillness are without heart, merging with heaven and earth; therefore, he takes the two modes as teacher.
"People then follow and name him."

Commentary: This is not pursuing fame to elevate his traces; teaching from nature and acting, his traces are naturally lofty, therefore people cannot lower his name. Subcommentary: "Mìng" means to name. The sage who conforms to the Way originally has no name; because there is pure dust to admire, people afterward name him.
"Anxious about knowledge, and what he constantly practices is almost never for long; if it has a stop, what can be done?"

Commentary: Relying on knowledge to act, then worry and hardship follow one after another. Subcommentary: Relying on knowledge for things, worry and hardship thus arise; the heart-mind is easily snatched away, what is practiced is almost never for long. Clinging to thoughts and concerns, how could there be a time of abiding? Even the divine Yǔ could do nothing.
"One born beautiful—people give him a mirror; if not told, he does not know he is more beautiful than others."

Commentary: "Jiàn" means mirror. A mirror reflects things selflessly, therefore people find it beautiful. Now, does the mirror know it is mirroring while it mirrors? Born capable of mirroring, then people call it a mirror. If people do not tell each other, then none know it is more beautiful than others—analogous to the sage, people give him a name. Subcommentary: "Jiàn" means mirror. "Gào" means to tell. Now, born bright and illuminating, reflecting things selflessly, people admire it, therefore name it mirror. If people do not tell each other, the bright mirror originally also has no name. This raises the analogy.
"If he knows it, if he doesn't know it; if he hears it, if he doesn't hear it—his being delightful never ends."

Commentary: The mirror's delightfulness lies in its lack of emotion. Regardless of knowing or not knowing, hearing or not hearing, when they come, it mirrors them; therefore, it never ends. If the mirror depended on hearing and knowing, then it would sometimes cease. Subcommentary: "Yǐ" means to stop. Now, the mirror's reflection of things, the principle lies in lack of emotion. Regardless of enemy or kin, its reflection is constantly equal. If it does not hear and does not know, the mirror also does not reflect. Once there is hearing and knowing, the mirror can reflect—this then involves matters of interruption and snatching, sometimes resting and ceasing. How can it reflect long? Only because its concentrated reflection is endless, therefore it is what people like and favor.
"People's fondness for it also never ends—it is their nature."

Commentary: If not liked by nature, how could it reflect long? Subcommentary: The mirror's ability to reflect comes from natural spontaneity; people's fondness follows creation. Since it is not forced nature, it is endless.
"The sage's love for people—people give him a name; if not told, they do not know he loves people."

Commentary: The sage has no love, like a mirror. Yet, since his actions save things, people give him a name. If people do not tell each other, then none know he loves people. Subcommentary: The sage's grace covers all living beings, kindness flows for ten thousand generations; things receive his virtue, people give him a name. Telling each other further, a fine title thus arises. If not so, how could there be a sage's name?
"If he knows it, if he doesn't know it; if he hears it, if he doesn't hear it—his love for people never ends."

Commentary: Vastly, he treats the common people as straw dogs, yet his Way accords with loving people; therefore, he can be endless. If love depended on hearing and knowing, then it would sometimes decline. Subcommentary: Now, the sage's virtue is vast and far-reaching; connecting with things, he is selfless. Nurturing all living beings, treating the common people as straw dogs—how could he wait to know and hear before loving them? Only because his compassionate salvation is unbiased, therefore his virtue is endless. This combines the discussion.
"People's peace with him also never ends—it is their nature."

Commentary: What is peaceful to nature, therefore can last long. Subcommentary: "Ān" means peaceful. Now, tranquil, he shares virtue with yīn; active, he shares waves with yáng. Therefore, he is heartless regarding movement and stillness. Thus, he can have violent thunder split mountains yet remain constant, great winds shake the sea yet not be startled—this is following his true nature. If he forces nature and falsifies emotions, then he would sometimes be agitated. Therefore, Wáng Bì said, "If not making one's emotions natural, how can one long practice what one hopes for?"
"The old state, the old capital—seeing it, one is cheerful."

Commentary: Gaining the old still makes one cheerful, how much more gaining one's nature? Subcommentary: The state and capital metaphorically refer to one's true nature. Now, losing one's native land young, wandering displaced in another city, gazing back at one's hometown, one is cheerfully happy. How much more having lost the Way for a long time, chasing the branches for so long? Now, having returned to the origin and recovered the root, it is said to be cheerful.
"Even if the hills and mounds, plants and trees are overgrown,"
Commentary: "Mín" means merged.
"And those who enter it are ninety percent, still one is cheerful—how much more seeing what one has seen and hearing what one has heard?"

Commentary: Seeing what one has seen, hearing what one has heard, and still cheerful—how much more embodying one's nature? Subcommentary: "Mín" means merged. The old state, old capital, long abandoned and ruined; hills and mounds perilous and rough, plants and trees growing thick. Entering among them to visit, ten people recognize nine. Seeing what one has seen, hearing what one has heard, the emotions of living beings are cheerfully joyful. How much more having lost the Way for a long time, drifting submerged in life and death, suddenly returning to the origin, meeting that true source, returning to that village of profound mystery, seeing that realm of the ultimate Way—the joy of it, how could it be easily expressed?
"It is like a platform of ten rèn hanging among the multitude."

Commentary: What the multitude is accustomed to, even if dangerous, is still familiar; how much more the sage who is without danger? Subcommentary: Seven feet is one rèn. A platform seventy feet high can be called dangerous. Hanging, with many people repeatedly ascending, they become unafraid. Accustomed through nature, still naturally relaxed and leisurely—how much more attaining the true? Where would one not be at peace?
"Rǎn Xiàng Shì attained the center of the circle to follow completion."

Commentary: Rǎn Xiàng Shì was a sage king of antiquity. Dwelling in emptiness to follow things, things completed themselves. Subcommentary: Rǎn Xiàng Shì was an无为 emperor before the Three Sovereigns. The center of the circle is emptiness. It means the ancient sage king attained the true empty Way, embodying the mystery of the circle's center; therefore, the Way followed all living beings, blending into completion the myriad beings.
"With things, there is no end, no beginning, almost no time."
Commentary: Suddenly, he goes
Zhuāngzǐ heard this and said: "Modern people's cultivation of their physical form and ordering of their minds often resemble what the border official described."

Explanation: People of this modern age are frivolous and shallow, chasing after desires and sensory pleasures, weary yet never resting. As for ordering their minds and forms, it's as the border official said. Zhuāng Zhōu heard this and thus commented on it.
They evade their Heaven, depart from their nature, extinguish their emotions, and lose their spirit - all because they follow the crowd.

Commentary: Evading, departing, extinguishing, and losing are all consequences of following the crowd. If each reaches its ultimate, then what worries remain? Explanation: Those who escape natural principles, scatter their pure harmonious nature, destroy their genuine emotions, and lose the Way of nurturing their spirit - all do so because they pursue what lies beyond their lot and stagnate in deliberate action.
Thus, those who are crude and hasty with their nature find that the evils of desires and aversions become like reeds choking their nature.

Commentary: Reeds harm millet and grain; desires and aversions injure the true nature. Explanation: Reeds are rushes. Desires and aversions mostly create calamities. Just as reeds harm millet and grain, desires and aversions injure the true nature - all arise from crude and hasty superficiality, hence leading to such outcomes.
When reeds first sprout, they seem to support our form.

Commentary: When supported and sparse, then spirit and energy flow freely. Explanation: Reeds are also rushes. When filthy grass first sprouts, it's still easy to remove. But when it grows dense and abundant, it inevitably harms the millet and grain. Similarly, when desires first emerge, they're still easy to stop. But when one becomes deluded and immersed in them, prevention lies in subtlety. Therefore Lǎozǐ said: "Its end is not easily planned for."
They gradually pull out our nature.

Commentary: Using desires and aversions to lead the nature, not stopping at what is proper. Explanation: "Xún" means to lead; "zhuó" means to pull out. Using matters of desire and aversion to lure and draw the mind, thus causing the true nature to be pulled out, not stopping at what is proper.
Together they erupt like leaking sores, discharging without choosing where, producing floating ulcers, scabies, carbuncles, internal heat, and turbid urine -

this is it. Commentary: This is the retribution for being crude and hasty. Therefore, can those who cultivate their nature not align with their ultimate allotment? Explanation: "Kuìlòu" refers to cold sores in people. "Piāojū" are hot toxic swellings. "Yōng" is also a type of ulcer. "Sōugāo" is turbid urine or semen. Indulging in material realms, drowning in sounds and sights, thus leads to confused spirit, depleted physical energy, and various illnesses erupting without choosing their location.
Bǎi Jǔ studied under Lǎo Dān and said: "Please let me travel throughout the world."
Explanation: Surname Bǎi, name Jǔ, a scholar embracing the Way, a disciple of Lǎozǐ. He requested to travel within the cosmos to observe customs and examine the nature of things.
Lǎo Dān said: "Enough! The world is just like this."
Explanation: Lǎozǐ stopped him, not permitting his going, saying the nature of things in the world is no different from here.
He asked again. Lǎo Dān said: "Where will you begin?"
Explanation: Sincere and earnest, his requests unceasing, then asked about his journey, wanting to know which state he would visit first.
He said: "I'll begin with Qí."
Explanation: Bǎi Jǔ was from Lǔ, neighboring Qí. The people of Qí were without the Way, so he wanted to go there first.
When he reached Qí, he saw an executed criminal. He pushed him to make him lie straight, removed his court robes and covered him with them.
Explanation: Traveling to Qí to observe customs, he suddenly saw a criminal punished and executed. Thereupon he pushed him to make him lie straight, removed his court robes and covered him with them.
Weeping to Heaven, he cried: "Oh you, oh you! The world has great calamities, yet you alone were the first to encounter them!" Saying: "Don't be a robber! Don't be a murderer!"

Commentary: Murder is a great disaster. Meaning from here downward are matters of great disaster. Since great disasters already exist, even if warned not to commit them, can it be stopped? Explanation: "Lí" means to encounter. "Zāi" means calamity. Crying out to Heaven, weeping sorrowfully, pitying his wrongful punishment. Hence repeating "oh you!" Robbery and murder are great disasters in the world. What crime did you alone commit to encounter this first? The details of great calamities are listed below. Further explanation: the so-called executed criminal was actually a court official. Meaning they forcefully pushed and yielded to each other while wearing court robes, heavily setting traps to ensnare the common people. Therefore he cried to Heaven, making clear that calamities arise from this. The pre-set nets are listed in the text below.
When honor and disgrace are established, then we see what ails people.

Commentary: When each attains their own fulfillment, then there's no honor, disgrace, gain, or loss in confusion. Thus when honor and disgrace are established, people boast about what's called honor and strive for what's called disgrace. Racing between boasting and striving - how could this not be a sickness? Explanation: High positions are considered honorable, punishment and shame are considered disgraceful. Racing after gains and avoiding losses - how could this not be a sickness?
When goods and wealth accumulate, then we see what people contend for.
Commentary: If one considers contentment as wealth, then what contention remains? Explanation: When treasures accumulate excessively, competition and strife arise.
Now establishing what people consider ailments, gathering what people contend for, exhausting and trapping people's bodies so they have no rest - wanting to avoid reaching this point, is it possible?

Commentary: When superiors have preferences, then inferiors cannot abide in their fundamental lot. Explanation: Rewarding with high positions, amusing with pearls and jades, thus causing the masses to race after them incessantly - wanting each to abide in their fundamental lot, how could it be possible?
The ancient rulers considered achievements as belonging to the people, and failures as belonging to themselves.

Commentary: When the ruler makes no mistakes, then the people naturally achieve. Explanation: Attributing merit to others, thus considering achievements as belonging to the people; accepting the country's misfortunes, thus considering failures as belonging to themselves.
They considered correctness as belonging to the people, and errors as belonging to themselves.

Commentary: When the ruler makes no errors, then the people are naturally correct. Explanation: Acting without deliberate action, entrusting things to others, correctness lies with the people; taking blame upon oneself, errors lie with oneself.
Therefore, if any single form lost its proper form, they would withdraw and blame themselves.

Commentary: Why do the forms and natures of things get lost? All because rulers disturb them, leading to such troubles. Hence self-blame. Explanation: People receive different energies, endowed with varying allotments. If each follows their own abilities, then all things attain self-fulfillment. If any single thing loses its place, damaging its form and nature, then they attribute the fault to themselves, withdraw and blame themselves. Like when Shāng Tāng cut his own hair.
Now it's not like this.
Explanation: Times differ in pace, ages vary in purity. Thus modern people chasing after things no longer act like this.
They conceal matters and consider the ignorant foolish.

Commentary: Returning to one's nature is concealment; using one's nature is manifestation. Thus when manifested through things, all recognize. Explanation: Established laws and regulations all go against the nature of things. Hiding crimes makes the ignorant foolish, hence crimes become numerous.
They make things greatly difficult and punish those who dare not.
Commentary: When things are made easy, then all dare. Explanation: When laws are difficult to establish and hard to implement, they punish those who definitely violate them.
They impose heavy burdens and penalize those who cannot bear them.
Commentary: When burdens are lightened, then all can bear them.
They set distant journeys and execute those who don't arrive.

Commentary: When suited to their foot strength, then all arrive. Explanation: When strength is slight but tasks heavy, blaming them for not bearing it; when roads are long but deadlines short, punishing them for arriving late - both are unacceptable.
When the people's knowledge and strength are exhausted, they resort to falsehood.
Commentary: This is to avoid punishment. Explanation: When knowledge and strength are exhausted, unable to escape punishment, fearing penalty in desperate circumstances, thus resorting to falsehood.
When falsehood emerges daily, how can the scholars and people avoid becoming false?

Commentary: When the king daily promotes falsehood, how can the scholars and people obtain truth? Explanation: The wind of deceit emerges daily. When falsehood multiplies like grass, how can truth be obtained?
When strength is insufficient, they become false; when knowledge is insufficient, they deceive; when wealth is insufficient, they steal. Whom should we blame for these thieving actions?

Commentary: The blame should lie with superiors. Explanation: When knowledge and strength are exhausted, deceit inevitably arises. When taxes become increasingly urgent, greed and theft emerge. All because the ruler lacks virtue and laws proliferate. If one can forget attachments, release selfishness, and not value treasures, the blame should lie with superiors - how can we fault the common people?
Qú Bóyù, at sixty years of age, had transformed sixty times.

Commentary: He could follow the world without being attached to self and others. Explanation: Surname Qú, name Yuàn, style Bóyù, a worthy minister of Wèi. His abundant virtue and brilliant understanding penetrated empty principles, thus he could renew himself daily, transforming with each year.
Never did he not begin by affirming something, yet end by negating it as wrong.

Commentary: Following things and flowing with their changing nature. Explanation: In the initial year of practice, he called it right; when the year ended, he called it wrong. Within a single year, right and wrong constantly shifted. Thus what began as right eventually became negated as wrong.
We don't know whether what we now call right might not be considered wrong at fifty-nine.

Commentary: The changes of things' nature have no ultimate beginning. Explanation: Thus change becomes new, and the new is considered right. The past has passed, so the old is considered wrong. However, last year's wrong becomes this year's right; this year's right becomes next year's wrong. Thus we know that those who cling to right or wrong, stagnate in new or old, are people of inverted views. Therefore Róngchéngshì said: "Without days, there are no years." Qú Yuàn understood this, thus he followed the transformation of things.
All things have their birth, yet none see their root; they have their emergence, yet none see their gate.

Commentary: Without root or gate, suddenly natural, thus none see. Only those without birth and without emergence can see the gate and discern the root. Explanation: Following transformation they are born, yet birth has no root source. Following transformation they emerge, yet emergence has no gate. Since it's said there's no root or gate, we know there's no birth or emergence. Birth and emergence having no gate, principle being thus - how can years be imagined?
People all respect the knowledge of what they know, but don't know to rely on what their knowledge doesn't know before they can know. Can this not be called great confusion?

Commentary: What I don't know, things may know. Thus using things' knowledge, then nothing is unknown. Relying solely on my own knowledge, knowledge becomes very scarce. Now not relying on things for knowledge but self-respecting knowledge - then things don't inform me. How is this not great confusion? Explanation: What is known is conventional knowledge; what is unknown is true knowledge. Ordinary people all respect discriminating knowledge, intensely pursuing preferences, yet cannot rely on their discriminating wisdom to illuminate the true source. They can be called greatly confused people.
Stop, stop! Moreover, there's nowhere to escape.

Commentary: If unable to use that, then there's no place to entrust the body. Explanation: "Yǐ" means stop. Intensely pursuing preferences - better to cease. Surely encountering calamity, with no place to escape bodily.
This is the so-called "this is so" and "is it so?"

Commentary: What calls itself so, the world may not consider so. Explanation: Each considers their own as so, each approves their own as acceptable. Self and others relative - who is right, who is wrong?
Confucius asked Grand Historian Dà Tāo, Bó Cháng Qiān, and Xī Wéi:
Explanation: Grand Historian is an official title. The following three are the historians' names. The matters asked about are listed below.

Saying: "Now Duke Líng of Wèi drank deeply and enjoyed pleasure, not attending to state affairs; hunted with nets and arrows, not responding to feudal lords' meetings. Why then was he called 'Líng' (Numinous)?"

Explanation: "Bì" means large net; "yì" means arrows shot with attached strings. A mediocre and corrupt ruler, indulging in decadent music and alcohol, hunting animals, not attending to state affairs, not attending feudal lords' meetings and interactions - you historians should determine posthumous titles. Being so without the Way, why was he titled "Líng"?
Dà Tāo said: "This is because it was so."

Commentary: "Líng" means the posthumous title for being without the Way. Explanation: According to the Duke of Zhōu's system of posthumous titles, "being chaotic but not damaging is called Líng." "Líng" is the posthumous title for being without the Way. This is because he was without the Way, he was titled "Líng," hence "this is because it was so."
Bó Cháng Qiān said: "Now Duke Líng had three wives with whom he bathed together in the same tub."
Commentary: Men and women bathing together - this is ritualess.
"Shǐ Qiū presented himself for service, whereupon [the Duke] grasped the gifts and supported him."

Commentary: Considering Qiū as worthy and presenting himself for service labor, therefore he grasped the gifts and supported him, preventing him from completing the ritual. This is why he was called "Reverent to Worthies." "Bì" means objects presented for service. Explanation: "Làn" means bathing vessel. Surname Shǐ, style Qiū, a worthy minister of Wèi. "Bì" means silk. Also, according to the system of posthumous titles, "having virtuous essence and brightness is called Líng." Men and women bathing together, making a worthy man present himself - when the Duke saw Shǐ Yú, a good minister, he felt deeply ashamed and alarmed, sent someone to grasp the silks, ordered them to support him by the arms and comfortingly send him off, preventing completion of the ritual. Being so reverent to worthies like this, he was an enlightened ruler. Hence he was titled "Líng." "Líng" then means the posthumous title for having the Way.
"His negligence was so extreme like that, yet when seeing a worthy man he was so reverent like this - this is why he was called Duke Líng."

Commentary: Wanting to use reverence for worthies to compensate for his personal negligence. "Líng" has two meanings, cannot be called good. Hence Confucius asked. Explanation: Men and women bathing together - extreme arrogance and negligence. Suddenly seeing a worthy man, immediately feeling reverent respect. Used as having the Way, hence titled "Líng."

Xī Wéi said: "Now Duke Líng died. Divining burial in the old tomb was inauspicious; divining burial in Shāqiū was auspicious. Digging several ren down, they found a stone outer coffin. Washing and examining it, there was an inscription: 'Not relying on his son, Duke Líng will seize and bury here.' The Duke's being 'Líng' was long determined!"

Commentary: "Zǐ" means Kuǎi Kuì. Meaning: "Not relying on his son, Duke Líng will seize your place." Things all have their predetermined fate, thus future matters can be known. Therefore, all that is done cannot but be done; all that is not done cannot be done. Yet fools think it depends on themselves - is this not deluded?
"How could these two men understand it?"

Commentary: They only recognize apparent events, not knowing apparent events emerge from spontaneity. Explanation: Shāqiū is a place name, north of the Mèngjīn River. "Zǐ" means Kuǎi Kuì. Wanting to clarify that people's names and posthumous titles are all determined before signs appear, not dependent on worldly sentiments with rises and falls. Thus the Shāqiū stone coffin already had its inscription beforehand. How could it rely on Kuǎi Kuì to enable seizure of burial? How could the historians and Cháng Qiān understand?
Shǎozhī asked Tàigōng Diào:

Explanation: "Shǎozhī" means limited knowledge. "Tài" means great; "gōng" means impartial. His virtue greatly impartial and selfless, moreover able to harmonize all things, hence called Tàigōng Diào. Establishing hypothetical persons to discuss principles.
Saying: "What are called village sayings?"
Explanation: In ancient times, ten households formed a "qiū," twenty households formed a "lǐ." Villages and neighborhoods had different customs, hence using question and answer to debate this.
Tàigōng Diào said: "A village combines ten surnames and hundred names to form customs."
Explanation: Adopting ten surnames, taking hundred names, combining and discussing them
The Nanhua True Classic Commentary and Subcommentary, Scroll Twenty-Eight, Part Two
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá of the Táng Dynasty Miscellaneous Chapters: External Things, Chapter Twenty-Six
External things cannot be forced.

Subcommentary: To fix the mind and stubbornly insist on certainty. Human affairs are diverse and intricate; only by embracing great compliance can one be empty and penetrating everywhere. If one opposes things and clings to emotions, calamity is certain to follow.
Thus, Lóng Páng was executed, Bǐ Gàn was slain, Jīzǐ feigned madness, È Lái died, and Jié and Zhòu perished.

Commentary: The outcomes of good and evil cannot be forced. Subcommentary: Lóng Páng and Bǐ Gàn have been explained in the Outer Chapters. Jīzǐ was a paternal uncle of King Zhòu of Yīn. His loyal remonstrance was unheeded; fearing harm from Zhòu, he feigned madness but ultimately could not escape execution. È Lái was a sycophantic minister of Zhòu who devoted himself entirely to following Zhòu, leading to their mutual destruction.

No ruler fails to desire loyalty from his ministers, yet loyalty is not necessarily trusted. Thus, Wǔ Yún was cast into the river, and Cháng Hóng died in Shǔ, his blood stored for three years before transforming into jade.

Commentary: The ultimate of essence and sincerity. Subcommentary: Jade. Zǐxū and Cháng Hóng have been explained in the Outer Chapters. As for "cast into the river," he loyally remonstrated with Fūchāi, who killed him, had a horsehide made into a bag shaped like an owl, placed Wǔ Yún's corpse inside, and floated it on the river—hence "cast into the river." Cháng Hóng, slandered and exiled back to Shǔ, resented his loyalty being maligned and cut open his own intestines to die. The people of Shǔ, moved, stored his blood in a container, and after three years it transformed into jade—this is the ultimate of essence and sincerity.
No parent fails to desire filial piety from their child, yet filial piety is not necessarily loved. Thus, Xiào Jǐ grieved, and Zēng Shēn sorrowed.

Commentary: Therefore, the ultimate person has no fixed mind but responds to things, adapting only to change. Subcommentary: Xiào Jǐ was the son of Emperor Gāozōng of Yīn. He suffered the hardship of a stepmother, dying in sorrow and bitterness. Zēng Shēn was extremely filial, yet his parents hated him, often beating him nearly to death, hence his weeping. The bond between father and son is innate, the duty between ruler and minister is weighty, yet even utmost loyalty and filiality may not be loved or understood—how much more so for the myriad paths of worldly affairs, which can be forced? Only by embracing things and self appropriately can one preserve the whole person and avoid harm. Wood rubbed together produces fire; metal held near fire melts.

Subcommentary: Wood generates fire, fire overcomes metal—this is the natural principle of the five phases' energy. Thus, wood rubbing wood produces fire; fire holding metal melts it. Therefore, those who stubbornly insist with sincere intent on external things face the ruin of dissolution.
When yin and yang err in their course, heaven and earth are greatly disturbed, and thus there is thunder and lightning; fire in water burns the great locust tree.

Commentary: This is what is meant by erring course. Subcommentary: Fire in water is lightning; burning the great locust tree is a thunderclap. When yin and yang are disordered and do not follow the five phases, thunder and lightning strike in fury, startling all things. Similarly, when humans deviate from harmonious energy, they suffer damage and loss.
There are those deeply troubled, trapped on both sides with no escape.

Commentary: If one cannot forget the body, then following what the body encounters, one falls into sorrow and joy, with no proper direction. Subcommentary: Unable to empty the will and forget the body, fixing the mind stubbornly, thus emotions race between the two realms of honor and disgrace, sinking into the two extremes of sorrow and joy, with no place to escape the body.
Anxieties and hesitations lead to no accomplishment.

Commentary: The more one esteems something, the more difficult it becomes, not knowing what to hold onto, thus achieving nothing. Subcommentary: "Anxieties and hesitations" means apprehension. Unable to forget emotions and let go of concerns, though toiling the body and troubling the mind, ultimately nothing is achieved.
The heart seems suspended between heaven and earth.
Commentary: What one aspires to is high and broad. Subcommentary: The heart pursues action, high and far-reaching; emotions chase things, penetrating the cosmos.
Comfort in obscurity, sinking into difficulty.

Commentary: Not emotionally calm and smooth. Subcommentary: Following the heart brings comfort and joy; going against intention brings confusion and distress. Encountering situations leads to sinking; touching things brings stagnation. Since it is not clear and calm, how can it be smooth?
Benefit and harm rubbing together produce much fire.

Commentary: Because of internal heat. Subcommentary: Where there is benefit, there must be harm—as with the cicada and the magpie. Entangled between benefit and harm, the inner mind is constantly heated, thus producing much fire.
The masses burn up harmony.

Commentary: If the masses discard benefit, then there is harmony. If benefit and harm remain in the heart, then harmony is burned up. Subcommentary: "Burn" means to consume. "The masses" refers to common people. Unable to abide in their lot and act through non-action, they constantly race their hearts after benefit and harm, internal heat like fire, thus burning away their harmonious nature.
The moon surely cannot overcome fire.

Commentary: Large and dark, it bears many burdens; small and bright, it knows its portion. Subcommentary: The moon, though large, has round light; fire, though small, shines brightly. This illustrates that great ambition with much greed is不如 knowing one's portion with a small heart.
Thus, there is collapse, and the Way is exhausted.

Commentary: Only by collapsing without pride, forgetting the body and attaining self, is the Way fully realized. Subcommentary: "Collapse" means letting go, without pride. Forgetting emotions of benefit and harm,淡然 without pride, the empty and mysterious principle of the Way is fully realized here.
Zhuāng Zhōu's family was poor, so he went to borrow grain from the Marquis of Jiānhé.
Subcommentary: The Marquis of Jiānhé was Marquis Wén of Wèi. Zhuāngzǐ, lofty and plain, did not engage in purposeful action; his family livelihood being poor, he came to borrow grain.
The Marquis of Jiānhé said, "Yes. I am about to receive the metal from my fief; I will lend you three hundred pieces of metal. Is that acceptable?"

Subcommentary: "Yes" means agreement. Copper and iron types are all called metal; this is not gold. "Wait until the year's end when I receive the common people's租赋 from my fief, then I will lend it to you."

Zhuāng Zhōu, flushing with anger, said, "Yesterday, as I came, there was a call from midway. I looked and saw a crucian carp in the rut of my carriage. I asked it, 'Crucian carp, come here! What are you doing?' It replied, 'I am a wave-official of the Eastern Sea. Do you, sir, have a dou or sheng of water to keep me alive?'"
Subcommentary: A minor official of the waves, trapped in the carriage rut. Do you, sir, have some water to save me?
I said, 'Yes. I am going south to visit the kings of Wú and Yuè; I will stir up the waters of the Western River to welcome you. Is that acceptable?'"
Subcommentary: The Western River is the Shǔ River. Among the many rivers flowing north, only the Shǔ River comes from the west, hence called the Western River.

The crucian carp, flushing with anger, said, 'I have lost my constant companion and have no place to be. If I had a dou or sheng of water, I could live. But you speak like this—better to seek me early in the dried fish market!'"

Commentary: This says that if it accords with principle, nothing is too small; if it does not, even the great is of no benefit. Subcommentary: "Seek" means to look for; "market" is a marketplace. Constantly moving in seawater, the crucian carp lost its constant place; a dou or sheng of water could preserve its life. Stirring the Western River is not appropriate. Since it cannot save me momentarily,不如 seek me in the dried fish market. This says that in affairs, regardless of size, there is a timely opportunity; if not seized, even the great is of no benefit.
Rén Gōngzǐ made a large hook with a giant black line, using fifty oxen as bait.

Subcommentary: Rén is a state name; Gōngzǐ means a noble scion. "Giant" means huge; "black line" is a black rope; "oxen" are castrated bulls; "bait" is the meat on the hook. Since it was a giant hook, he used a large rope with fifty oxen as bait.
He crouched at Kuàijī, casting his rod into the Eastern Sea.
Subcommentary: With such a giant hook, for a whole year he caught no fish. "Crouched" means to squat; he sat on the mountain.

Day after day he fished, for a whole year catching nothing. Then a great fish swallowed it, pulling the giant hook, sinking it down, startlingly rising and shaking its fins, white waves like mountains, seawater shaking and roaring, sound matching ghosts and gods, terrifying for a thousand li.

Subcommentary: After a year, a great fish swallowed the hook, thus pulling the hook, sinking it down, startlingly descending, raising its head and tail, shaking its scales and fins, making white waves like mountains, vast waves reaching the sun.
Rén Gōngzǐ caught this fish, cut it up, and dried it; from the Zhè River east to north of Cāngwú, none failed to be satiated by this fish.

Subcommentary: "This fish" was a sea god. "Zhè" is the Zhèjiāng River; "Cāngwú" is a mountain name south of the ridges, where Shùn was buried. The sea god's flesh was abundant, divided and dried as jerky. From north of the Five Ridges to east of the Three Xiāngs, all were satiated.
Afterward, later generations of petty talents and gossipers were all astonished and told each other.

Subcommentary: In latter ages, those of frivolous talent, reciting and discussing, not profound in the mysterious Way, heard of the great fish and were astonished, telling each other. Some texts have "petty" as "light," meaning lightweight or measuring.
To lift a pole and line, hurry to irrigation ditches, guarding for minnows and crucian carp—for such, catching a great fish is difficult indeed.
Subcommentary: "Line" is a thin cord; "minnows and crucian carp" are small fish. Carrying a thin pole and cord, hurrying to irrigation ditches, might catch minnows but hardly a great fish.
To adorn petty discourse in order to seek high reputation—for great understanding, this is far off indeed.

Subcommentary: "Seek" means to pursue; "high" means elevated. Those who cultivate minor conduct, holding fast to speech to seek high fame and good report, certainly cannot greatly penetrate the ultimate Way. The character for "high" often omits the heart radical in ancient script.
Thus, those who have never heard of the customs of the Rén clan cannot engage with the world—they are far off indeed.

Commentary: This says that aims and interests differ; thus, the appropriate way to manage the world varies in scale, each finding its fit. Subcommentary: The path in the human world, smooth or perilous, is not constant. Unless one embraces openness and empty penetration, one cannot govern chaos. If one prides on reputation and adorns conduct, they are far from it.
Confucians used the Odes and Rites to rob graves. The great Confucian announced: "The east is bright! How goes the affair?"

Subcommentary: "Great Confucian" means a great scholar. Announcing from above to below: "Announce" means to relay. "The east is bright" means dawn is breaking. The Confucian disciple, robbing the grave as a thief, fears daybreak, hence催促 to ask how the task proceeds.
The minor Confucian said, "The skirt and jacket are not yet removed; there is a pearl in the mouth."
Subcommentary: "Minor Confucian" is the disciple. The dead person's skirt and clothes are not yet removed; feeling the mouth, he knows there is a precious pearl.
The Odes indeed have it: 'Green, green the wheat, grows on the mound slopes. In life, you did not give alms; in death, why hold a pearl?'"
Subcommentary: This is a lost ode, long deleted. Generally, the noble buried often have pearls in their mouths; hence, reciting the "Green, Green" ode mocks them.
He grasped the temples, pressed the jaws, and with a metal rod pried open the chin, slowly separating the cheeks without damaging the pearl in the mouth.

Commentary: The Odes and Rites are the stale traces of former kings. If not the right person, the Way does not emptyly act. Thus, Confucians can use them for treachery—traces are not enough to rely on. Subcommentary: "Grasp" means to take hold; "press" means to push; "jaws" means the mouth; "pried" means to strike. Grasping the temples, pressing the mouth, striking with an iron rod, still fearing to damage the pearl, thus carefully separating. Thus, Tián Héng used benevolence and righteousness to steal Qí; Confucians recite the Odes and Rites to rob graves. From this, it is seen that sage traces are not reliable.
The disciples of Lǎo Láizǐ went out for firewood, met Zhòngní, and returned to report.

Subcommentary: Lǎo Láizǐ was a worthy of Chǔ, a recluse. He often hid in Méng Mountain. The King of Chǔ, knowing his worth, sent an envoy to summon him as minister. His wife, gathering firewood, returned to see carriage tracks at the door. She asked the reason; Lǎo Láizǐ said, "The King of Chǔ summoned me as minister." His wife said, "Those who receive from others are inevitably controlled by them; one who cannot control others is controlled." The wife then left, and Lǎo Láizǐ followed her. The husband carried, the wife bore, fleeing to south of the Yangtze; none knew where they went. "Went out for firewood" means gathering fuel. Having seen Confucius, they returned to report to their master.
Said, "There is a man over there, tall above and short below."
Commentary: Long above and short below.
Stooped and with ears set back.
Commentary: Ears receded close to the back and stooped upward.
His gaze seems to encompass the four seas.
Commentary: Looking weary, as if managing others' affairs.

Subcommentary: "Tall" means long; "short" means brief; "stooped" refers to shoulders and back. The seen scholar is short below, long above, shoulders and back hunched, ears receded close to the back, gaze high and far, actions hurried. Observing his demeanor,似乎 managing the world; unknown which clan's son he is. Noting his abnormality, thus the question.
Lǎo Láizǐ said, "That is Qiū. Summon him here."
Subcommentary: A man of Lǔ, Kǒng Qiū. You should call him.
Zhòngní arrived. [Lǎo Láizǐ] said, "Qiū, remove your personal pride and your knowledgeable demeanor—then you may be a noble man."

Commentary: Meaning Zhòngní could discard form and remove knowledge, thus considering him a noble man. Subcommentary: "Personal" refers to the body. Kǒng Qiū having arrived, Lǎo Láizǐ, before speaking: "You should dismiss your body's adornment, forget your appearance and mental knowledge—at such a time, you may be a noble man."
Zhòngní bowed and withdrew.
Commentary: Accepting his words. Subcommentary: Respectfully accepting his words, bowing and withdrawing.
Anxiously changing expression, he asked, "Can my studies be advanced?"

Commentary: Posing the question to let Lǎo Láizǐ clarify that advancement is impossible. Subcommentary: "Anxiously" means alarmed appearance. Asking if the sage traces and conduct of learning can be cultivated and advanced for worldly use.
Lǎo Láizǐ said, "To be unable to bear the injuries of one age and thus alarm the calamities of ten thousand generations—"

Commentary: Acting for one age leaves traces that become troubles for ten thousand generations; thus, it cannot be taken lightly. Subcommentary: Sage wisdom and benevolence-righteousness save the injuries of one time; later, held as treachery, they become disasters for ten thousand generations. Those proud of sage traces, like Chén Héng's followers, are an example. Some
The sage startles the world, yet the spiritual person has never passed by and inquired about it.

Note: The spiritual person is the sage. "Sage" refers to their external aspect, "spiritual" refers to their internal aspect. Explanation: To startle means to shock. "Spiritual" is a title for the unfathomable, "sage" is a name for manifest traces. Because they teach and move people, they do not pass by and inquire.
The worthy person startles the age, yet the sage has never passed by and inquired about it.
Explanation: Understanding emptiness makes one worthy; universal illumination makes one sage. Looking from depth to shallowness, thus they do not inquire.
The gentleman startles the state, yet the worthy person has never passed by and inquired about it.
Explanation: Why does the gentleman startle the feudal states? The worthy person abandons attachments, thus they do not inquire.
The petty person conforms to the times, yet the gentleman has never passed by and inquired about it.

Note: Steps and paces each have their distinctions; high and low each have their ranks. Explanation: Petty persons who follow worldly trends temporarily unite with the times, like Tián Héng and his ilk, not worthy of esteem. Thus, virtuous gentlemen despise and ignore them.
At Yǎn mén, there was one whose parent died; through excelling in emaciation from grief, he was ennobled and made an official commander. Among his partisans, half died from emaciating themselves.

Note: Admiring reward and filial piety are far from genuineness. This is the error of esteeming worthies. Explanation: Yǎn mén is the eastern gate (some texts read "Yín"; follow the character as written). The filial piety from the eastern gate came from within, with external emaciation. Only the ruler of Sòng praised his utmost filiality, thus ennobled him and appointed him as a minister. People in his village, hearing he was honored through filiality, forced weeping and feigned emaciation, distorting their nature and falsifying emotions; consequently, half of them died.
Yáo offered the world to Xǔ Yóu; Xǔ Yóu fled from it. Tāng offered it to Wù Guāng; Wù Guāng was angered by it.

Explanation: Yáo knew Xǔ Yóu was worthy and abdicated the throne to him. Xǔ Yóu washed his ears, declined, and escaped to Jīshān. Tāng offered it to Wù Guāng; Wù Guāng did not accept, scolded in anger, and distanced himself to the forest's sounds. These all followed their innate nature, detesting glory and rank, unrelated to feigning to seek fame.
Jì Tuō heard this, led his disciples, and crouched by Kuǎn water. Feudal lords condoled him for three years. Shēn Tú Dí thereby drowned himself in the river.

Note: Their turmoil harmed their nature, leading to this. Explanation: Surname Shēn Tú, name Dí; surname Jì, name Tuō; both were recluses. Hearing Tāng yielded to Wù Guāng, fearing it would reach them, they crouched by the water with disciples. Feudal lords heard of it, valued their integrity and simplicity, and condoled from time to time, fearing they would drown. Dí heard of this, admired their high reputation, and threw himself into the long river, drowning. Turmoil lost their nature, thus reaching this point.
The fish trap exists for the fish; once you get the fish, you forget the trap. The rabbit snare exists for the rabbit; once you get the rabbit, you forget the snare.

Explanation: The trap is a bamboo fish basket, made from bamboo, hence the character includes bamboo. Some are made from grass—a fragrant grass trap. Fragrant grass can bait fish; placing fragrance among firewood, reeds, to catch fish. The snare is a rabbit net, also a rabbit tether. Tying it to the rabbit's foot, hence called "snare." These two are analogies.
Words exist for the meaning; once you get the meaning, you forget the words.

Explanation: This combines the discussion. Meaning is subtle principle. Catching fish and rabbits originally depends on traps and snares, yet traps and snares are truly different from fish and rabbits. Similarly, profound principle relies on speech, yet speech is truly not profound principle. Get the fish and rabbit, forget the trap and snare; understand profound principle, cease names and words.
How can I find someone who has forgotten words and speak with them?

Note: Reaching where two sages have no intent, then there is nothing said at all. Explanation: Those who forget words and grasp principle, seeing the Way present, are truly rare; hence this difficulty.
Nánhuá Zhēnjīng Commentary and Explanation, Chapter Twenty-Eight
Nánhuá Zhēnjīng Commentary and Explanation, Chapter Twenty-Nine
Commentary by Guō Xiàng of Hénán Explanation by Táng Dynasty Master Chéng Xuányīng of Xīhuá Miscellaneous Chapters, Allegorical Words, Twenty-Seven
Allegorical words are ninety percent.

Note: Entrusting to others, then nine out of ten words are believed. Explanation: Allegory means entrusting. People are foolish and deluded, arbitrarily suspicious; hearing the Way from oneself raises doubts. Entrusting to others, then nine out of ten words are believed. Hence, Hóng Méng, Yún Jiàng, Jiān Wú, Lián Shū, and such are all allegories.
Weighty words are seventy percent.
Note: What the world values, then seven out of ten words are believed. Explanation: Weighty words are from elders respected in villages. Elderly people's words are still seventy percent trusted.
Goblet words daily emerge, harmonizing with the natural divide.

Note: A goblet, full then tips, empty then tilts, not held fixed. Compared to words, they follow things and change, only obeying that. Hence "daily emerge"—daily emergence means daily renewal. Daily renewal then exhausts their natural portion; the natural portion exhausted then harmony. Explanation: Goblet is a wine vessel. Daily emergence means daily renewal. Natural divide is the natural portion. Harmony means blending. A goblet full tips, empty tilts; empty and full follow things, tipping and tilting follow people. Unpremeditated words are goblet words. Thus, speaking without speaking, without attachment, tipping and tilting then match the natural portion. Also interpreted: goblet means branch. Branching their words, words without fixed appropriateness, hence called goblet words.
Allegorical words ninety percent, borrow external discussions.

Note: Words from oneself, many are not accepted; hence borrow external ones. Jiān Wú, Lián Shū, and such are all borrowed. Explanation: Borrow means to rely on. Entrusting to it. Ninety percent of people's words are because they borrow external persons to discuss.
A biological father does not act as matchmaker for his son; a biological father praising him is not like a non-biological father.

Note: A father praising his son, sincerity often not believed, yet sometimes believed, but often suspected due to usual doubts; hence borrow external discussion. Explanation: Matchmaker means to arrange marriage. A father discussing his son, many do not believe; others praising him, many believe.
It is not my fault, but people's fault.

Note: Oneself though sincere but harboring usual doubts, still not accepted; entrusting to others then believed. People's listening has this burden. Explanation: I am the father. Not that the father's talk about the son is untrue, but listeners arbitrarily raise suspicions, causing disbelief's error.
If same as oneself, respond; if not same as oneself, oppose.
Note: Mutually criticizing. Explanation: Common people inverted, arbitrarily judging right and wrong; if same view as oneself, respond and affirm; if different from oneself, oppose and deny.
Same as oneself, affirm it; different from oneself, deny it.

Note: Three differences and similarities in place, and two differences dispute what they take; affirmation must be in the undisputed, both different. Yet solely believe their affirmations and denials; how about borrowing external? Explanation: Deluded attachment to same and different, arbitrary seeing right and wrong. Same and different already empty, right and wrong extinguished.
Weighty words seventy percent, used to stop speech, are for the aged.

Note: Because they are aged, thus commonly valued by custom. Even if words not borrowed externally, still seventy percent trusted. Explanation: Aged is a term for the long-lived. Speaking oneself, not borrowing externally, being elders, thus valued and believed. Common people have this delusion.
Age comes first, but without warp and woof, root and branch, to expect agedness, is not truly prior.

Note: Age precedes in things only; the rest, without root and branch to treat others, is not what precedes. Expect means to await. Explanation: Expect means to await. Vertical is warp, horizontal is woof. Meaning: this person merely placed first due to old age, also without root and branch wisdom; thus treated with elder's rites, unrelated to morality being prior.
A person without what precedes others, lacks the human way. A person without the human way is called a stale person.

Note: Merely a long-stale person, yet custom conveniently believes them. This is why custom rests in old ways and practices routine. Explanation: Without ritual and righteousness to precede others, lacking the way of human relations. Merely a long-stale person, thus valued. Common people without discernment, to this extent.
Goblet words daily emerge, harmonizing with the natural divide, thereby extending, thus exhausting years.

Note: Natural has portions, and right and wrong have no master; no master then extension. Who can fix it? Thus open-minded without concern, thereby following, thus each ends their natural years. Explanation: Extension means unpremeditated. Following daily renewal's changes, turning to match the natural divide, thus able to follow all existence, interact unpremeditated, thus exhaust creation's natural years, extreme life's longevity.
Not speaking then equal.
Explanation: Principle resides in not speaking; speaking then contradicts. Thus directly not speaking, things naturally equal.
Equality and speaking are not equal.
Explanation: Equality is not speaking. Not speaking and speaking are already not one, thus not equal.
Speaking and equality are not equal.
Note: Entrust to things and use their words, then self and other, right and wrong, naturally equal. If cannot thereby establish words to equalize, then self and myriad things again not equal.
Thus say no words.

Note: Speaking what they speak, thus though there are words, I ultimately do not speak. Explanation: Using words to dismiss words, words then endless; even adding hundreds of denials, still not reaching mystery. Only should contemplate sage, wisdom dark to movement and stillness, action and rest, silence and speech, their aim one. Thus able to not speak then speak, speak then not speak. How can there be distinction between speaking and not speaking, difference between equal and not equal? Thus say: speak no words.
Speaking no words, lifelong speaking, never spoken.
Note: Though exit my mouth, all are their words.
Lifelong not speaking, never not spoken.
Note: Based on exiting my mouth. Explanation: This again explains previous "speak no words" meaning.
Have their origin thus affirm; have their origin thus deny; have their origin thus so; have their origin thus not so.
Explanation: Each holds their own view, thus have affirmation and so-ness. Self and other already empty, so-ness and affirmation vanish.
Wherein so? So in so. Wherein not so? Not so in not so. Wherein affirm? Affirm in affirm. Wherein deny? Deny in deny.

Note: From freedom. Due to self and other's biased sentiments, thus have affirmation and denial. Explanation: Wherein means in what. Self and other both empty, things and self both illusory; where is there affirmation and denial? Where is there so and not so? Pushing this to exhaust, so and affirmation naturally cease. This again explains previous "have origin thus so and affirm" meaning.
Things inherently have their so; things inherently have their affirmation.
Note: Each natural, each affirmation.
No thing not so; no thing not affirmable.
Note: Generally speaking, then no affirmation no denial; no affirmation no denial then reach. Explanation: Things in common, inverted ones, in non-so insist so, in non-affirmable insist affirmable.
If not goblet words daily emerge, harmonizing with the natural divide, who can attain longevity?

Note: Only words following things' limits and following their natural portion can avoid premature fall. Explanation: If not following daily renewal's changes, penetrating natural principle, who can verify long life and lasting vision's way? Meaning: those who attain it reach utmost.
Myriad things all are seeds, with different forms succeeding each other.

Note: Though change and transformation replace each other, tracing their vital force is one. Explanation: Succeed means to replace. Things numerous, receive from creation, imbued with one seed, yet forms and substances different; moving and flowing, mutually replacing.
Start and end like a ring.
Note: What is start today, yesterday already was end. Explanation: Things' change and trade, like that cycle; dying and living, ending and restarting—this shows succession's appearance.
None grasp their order.
Note: Principle naturally thus, thus none grasp. Explanation: Order means pattern. Seeking change and transformation's way, ultimately no pattern to reach.
This is called celestial balance; celestial balance is the natural divide.

Note: What balances evenly, how arbitrary? All natural portions. Explanation: Balance means equal. This concludes previous chapter's meaning: called natural equal way. That is, the equalizing way also named natural portion.
Zhuāngzǐ said to Huìzǐ: "Confucius, traveling through sixty years, transformed sixty times."

Note: With time together. Explanation: Moving unceasing, ever new flowing away. Thus traveling sixty years, with years transforming together. Yet Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ met, fond of discussing mystery, thus distantly praising Confucius to show transformation's method.
Initially affirmed, finally denied.
Note: Time changes, common sentiments change; riding things to wander mind, how differ from common?
Do not know today's affirmations are not fifty-nine denials.

Note: Change does not stop; affirmations not constant. Explanation: Human lifespan counts by years; years uncertain, how fixed? Thus last year's affirmations, today denied. Know this year's affirmations still are last year's denials; this year's denials are next year's affirmations. Hence Róng Chéngshì said: "Without days, no years."
Huìzǐ said: "Confucius diligently willed and served knowledge."

Note: Said Confucius diligently willed, embraced, then knew; not able to trust self-transformation. This shows Huìzǐ far from sage's rhythm. Explanation: Serve means use. Huì Shī not comprehending, guessed Confucius, said he encouraged will, diligent practice, used mind to learn way, thus reached this knowledge; not natural, trusting transformation.
Zhuāngzǐ said: "Confucius has shed that, and he never spoke of it."

Note: Shed transformation's natural thus, not knowledge and effort's doing; thus follow time, trust things, not creating words. Explanation: Shed means replace. "He" means you. "Never" means not. Meaning: Confucius regarding diligent serving mind long shed; you should return to spirit, no more reckless words.
Confucius said: "Receiving talent from the great root, returning to spirit to live."

Note: If toil talent and knowledge, not returning to root spirit, then life perishes. Explanation: Humans receive wisdom and ability from great Way, mysterious root; return to spiritual destiny to exhaust life course. How can diligent will, toiling mind, contradict creation? This is Zhuāngzǐ relating Confucius's words, reproving Huì Shī.
"Sounding matches pitch; speaking matches law."

Sounding is what pitch produces; speaking is what law emits. Yet pitch and law are what the multitude creates; the sage uses them. Thus all match, yet never spoke, never acted. Explanation: Sounding means sound. Match means hit. Confucius, sage, united with yīn and yáng, thus wind rhythm hits bell pitch, speech and teaching model standards.
"Benefit and righteousness arrayed before, and likes, dislikes, right, wrong, merely serve people's mouths."

Note: Serve means use. I have no words. My words merely use people's mouths. Likes, dislikes, right, wrong, benefit, righteousness arrayed, never exited my mouth. Explanation: Benevolence, righteousness, benefit, harm, likes, dislikes, right, wrong, meet prior opportunity, respond timely arrayed. Though again words exit mouth, following prior, this is using the multitude's mouths.
"Causing people to thus mind-subdue and not dare oppose, establishing the world's stability."

Note: Mouth thus expresses mind; already use multitude's mouths, then multitude's minds used. I follow multitude's mind, then multitude's mind trusts. Who dares oppose? I follow world's self-stability and stabilize it; why act? Explanation: Follow multitude's appropriateness, use their mind and wisdom. Teaching follows things, things thus follow, like grass following wind, not daring oppose. Following their fundamental stillness, follow nature stabilize, thus stabilize world's stability.
"Enough, enough! How can I reach him?"

Note: Following and riding, thus none not reach. Explanation: Enough means stop. "Him" means Confucius. Repeatedly urge Huìzǐ stop, not speak. We mediocre, shallow, cannot reach. This is Zhuāngzǐ praising Confucius's words.
Zēngzǐ twice held office, and mind twice transformed.
Explanation: Surname Zēng, name Shēn, disciple of Confucius. Twice held office meaning explained below.
Said: "I, when parents alive, held office with three fǔ, mind joyful; later held office with three thousand zhōng, not reaching, mind sorrowful."
Note: Reach means extend to. Explanation: Six dǒ
Nanhua Zhenjing Zhushu Volume Thirty-Four
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá in Táng Dynasty Miscellaneous Chapters: Ràng Wáng - Chapter 28

Yáo offered the empire to Xǔ Yóu. Xǔ Yóu did not accept it. He then offered it to Zǐzhōu Zhīfù. Zǐzhōu Zhīfù said: "To make me the Son of Heaven would still be acceptable. However, I am currently afflicted with a deep, worrisome illness and am just beginning to treat it. I have no leisure to govern the empire."

Subcommentary: The story of Yáo and Xǔ Yóu is fully recorded in the Inner Chapters. His surname was Zǐ, given name Zhōu, courtesy name Zhīfù. He was a man who embraced the Way, a recluse. Yáo, knowing his worthiness, offered him the imperial position. "To make me the emperor is also something I could manage," hence he said "would still be acceptable." Yōu means deep; yōu also means toil and worry. He means, "I am stuck in profound depths, my heart is fixed on toil and worry, and I wish to cultivate my person, hoping to align with the Way. I have no spare time to manage the myriad affairs of state."
The empire is the most important thing, yet he did not let it harm his life—how much less would he care for other things?

Subcommentary: The position of the Nine-Five, whose power spans ten thousand chariots, is the most respected among human relationships. Nothing surpasses this. Yet he did not allow such honor and nobility to damage his livelihood; how much less would he concern himself with external matters?
Only one who does not act for the sake of the empire can be entrusted with the empire.
Subcommentary: One who forgets the empire does not act for the sake of the empire. Only such a person can be entrusted with the empire.
Shùn offered the empire to Zǐzhōu Zhībó. Zǐzhōu Zhībó said: "I am currently afflicted with a deep, worrisome illness and am just beginning to treat it. I have no leisure to govern the empire."
Subcommentary: Shùn's story is fully recorded in the Inner Chapters. Zhībó is the same as Zhīfù.
Therefore, the empire is a great vessel, yet he did not exchange it for his life. This is how those who possess the Way differ from the vulgar.

Subcommentary: The position of the emperor is a vessel of great importance. Yet he did not use this high status to trade for or seize his life. If not one who possesses the Way, who could be like this? Therefore, he differs from the conduct of the common crowd.

Shùn offered the empire to Shàn Juǎn. Shàn Juǎn said: "I stand within the universe. In winter, I wear furs and hides; in summer, I wear hemp cloth. In spring, I plow and sow, my form sufficient for labor; in autumn, I harvest and store, my body sufficient for rest and food. I rise with the sun and rest at sunset. I wander freely between heaven and earth, and my heart finds contentment. Why should I take on the empire?"

Subcommentary: His surname was Shàn, given name Juǎn, a recluse. He dwelt within the six directions, in harmony with the four seasons, content between heaven and earth, wandering freely beyond the dust and grime. The Way was within him, so he had no use for the empire.
Sadly, the ruler does not understand me. Thus, he did not accept and went away into the deep mountains, where none knew his whereabouts.
Subcommentary: The ancients were simple and honest, calling the emperor 'ruler'. He regretted that Shùn did not recognize his rustic purity, hence he sighed in sorrow.
Shùn offered the empire to his friend, the farmer of Shíhù. The farmer of Shíhù said: "How toilsome! The ruler's character is that of a man who preserves his strength."

Subcommentary: The character 'hù' is sometimes written differently; read it accordingly. Shíhù is a place name. The farmer was a common man. In Jiangnan today, people are called farmers. This man was a friend of Shùn. Bǎo means firm and solid. He means that Shùn's will was firm, his efforts diligent and bitter, his back bent with toil, finding no rest. Because of this toil, he instead came to offer abdication, so he did not accept.

He considered Shùn's virtue insufficient. Thereupon, carrying his load on his back, his wife bearing hers on her head, they took their children and went into the sea, never to return for the rest of their lives.

Subcommentary: The ancients often carried loads on their heads, as in Gāolì today, this custom still exists. Because Shùn's virtuous transformation was not yet ultimate, they took their wives and children and did not tread his land.
The Great King Dǎnfù dwelt in Bīn. The Dí people attacked him.
Subcommentary: Dǎnfù was the father of Wáng Jì and grandfather of King Wén. Bīn is a place name. The Dí people were the Xiǎnyǔn. His state bordered the barbarians, so the Dí people attacked him.

He served them with hides and silks, but they did not accept. He served them with dogs and horses, but they did not accept. He served them with pearls and jades, but they did not accept. What the Dí people sought was land. The Great King Dǎnfù said: "To dwell with a man's elder brother and then kill his younger brother, to dwell with a man's father and then kill his son—I cannot bear this. You should all strive to dwell here. To be my subjects or to be subjects of the Dí people—how are they different?"
Subcommentary: Shì means to serve. Miǎn means to encourage. Xī means what. The Dí people were greedy and cruel, their aim was land. "I cannot bear to harm and kill you. Strive to dwell here."

Moreover, I have heard it said: 'Do not harm the nurtured for the sake of what nurtures them.' Thereupon, leaning on his staff, he left. The people linked together and followed him, and so he established a state at the foot of Mount Qí.

Subcommentary: Yòngyǎng means the land (used for nurturing). Suǒyǎng means the people (who are nurtured). Originally, the land is used to nurture people. Now, to kill people to preserve the land is unacceptable. So, leaning on his staff, he left. The people followed in succession, and thus he had a state at Qíyáng.

The Great King Dǎnfù can be said to have known how to honor life. One who knows how to honor life will not, even in wealth and honor, injure his body for the sake of nurture; nor, even in poverty and lowliness, involve his form for the sake of profit. The people of the present age, who hold high office and esteemed rank, all regard their loss heavily. Seeing profit, they lightly lose their lives—is this not delusion?

Subcommentary: In chaotic times, customs are deceitful and human hearts are shallow. They chase after high carriages and official caps, thereby losing their lives; they pursue wealth and profit, thereby destroying their lives. They do not know what is light and what is heavy, deeply falling into confusion.

The people of Yuè murdered three generations of their rulers. Prince Sōu, distressed by this, fled to Dānxué. With Yuè having no ruler, they sought Prince Sōu and finally found him in Dānxué. Prince Sōu refused to come out. The people of Yuè smoked him out with mugwort and made him ride in a jade carriage.

Subcommentary: Sōu was the prince's name. Dānxué is a cave in the southern mountains. The jade carriage is the ruler's chariot. Some texts write 'king' instead of 'jade'; read accordingly. It is the so-called jade carriage. The people of Yuè repeatedly murdered their rulers. The prince, fearful, fled to a cave. Summoned, he would not come out. They smoked him out with mugwort.
