Once requested to be ruler, he was thus made to ride in the jade carriage.

Prince Sōu, taking hold of the carriage strap, mounted the chariot, looked up to heaven, and cried out: "O Sovereign! O Sovereign! Could you not spare me?" Prince Sōu did not detest being ruler; he detested the troubles of being ruler. One like Prince Sōu can be said not to have injured his life for the sake of the state. This was precisely why the people of Yuè wanted him as their ruler.

Subcommentary: Yuán means to take hold. Suí is the strap on the carriage. Unable to decline and escape, he sighed deeply and mounted the chariot. He did not detest being ruler but feared the calamities it brings. Because he valued life and lightly regarded position, he could be compelled to become ruler.
Hán and Wèi were contending over encroached territory. Zǐ Huá Zǐ went to see Marquis Zhāo Xī of Hán. Marquis Zhāo Xī had a worried expression.

Subcommentary: Marquis Xī was the ruler of Hán. Huá Zǐ was a worthy man of Wèi. Hán and Wèi were neighboring states contending over border lands. With weapons already drawn and victory or defeat unknown, he was apprehensive and troubled, hence his worried expression.

Zǐ Huá Zǐ said: "Suppose now the empire were to inscribe a covenant before you, saying: 'If you seize it with your left hand, your right hand will be cut off; if you seize it with your right hand, your left hand will be cut off. Yet, the one who seizes it will surely possess the empire.' Would you seize it?"

Subcommentary: Míng means an inscribed record. Jué means to grab, to seize. Fèi means to cut off. Suppose a covenant inscription were written and cast before you. If you take it with your left hand, your right hand is cut off; if with your right hand, your left is cut off. Yet, the one who takes the inscription will gain the empire. Would you take it? This is a metaphor, a question posed to the Marquis of Hán.
Marquis Zhāo Xī said: "I would not seize it."
Subcommentary: He replied, saying he could not cut off both arms to take possession of the world.
Zǐ Huá Zǐ said: "Very good!"
Subcommentary: He praised the ruler's words as very fitting to principle.
From this perspective, the two arms are heavier than the empire, and the body is also heavier than the two arms. The lightness of Hán compared to the empire is far greater.

Subcommentary: Observing from these words, one's body is heavier than the two arms; the two arms are heavier than the empire; the empire is in turn heavier than Hán. The difference in weight between Hán and the empire is vast.
What is contended for now is far lighter than Hán. Yet you insist on worrying your person, injuring your life, sorrowing and fretting, fearing you will not obtain it.

Subcommentary: What is contended for is a strip of borderland, thus its weight compared to Hán is far less. Yet you must insist on sorrow and worry, injuring your form and damaging your nature, fearing you will not obtain it—is this not delusion?
Marquis Xī said: "Excellent! Many have instructed me, but I have never heard such words. Zǐ Huá Zǐ can be said to know what is light and what is heavy."
Subcommentary: He suddenly understood his words and sighed at their wondrous excellence.
The ruler of Lǔ heard that Yán Hé was a man who had attained the Way. He sent a man with gifts to approach him first.

Subcommentary: The ruler of Lǔ was Duke Āi of Lǔ, or some say Duke Dìng of Lǔ. His surname was Yán, given name Hé, a man of Lǔ, a recluse. Bì means silks and gifts. Hearing that Yán Hé had attained the Way of purity and integrity, he wished to summon him to be prime minister. Therefore, he sent an envoy bearing silks and gifts to first communicate his intent.
Yán Hé guarded his humble alley, wearing clothes of coarse hemp, and himself fed the oxen.

Subcommentary: Jū cloth is cloth made from hemp. Fàn means to feed. He dwelt in a humble alley, wore coarse and poor cloth garments, and personally fed the oxen, sufficient to show his poverty and frugality.

The envoy of the ruler of Lǔ arrived. Yán Hé himself responded to him. The envoy said: "Is this the house of Yán Hé?" Yán Hé replied: "This is Hé's house." The envoy presented the gifts. Yán Hé replied: "I fear the listener was mistaken and has bestowed these upon you, the envoy, wrongly. It would be better to verify it."
Subcommentary: Yí means to bestow. Not wishing to accept the gifts, he offered this dissembling speech to deceive the envoy.

The envoy returned to verify it. When he came again to seek him, he could not be found. Therefore, one like Yán Hé truly detested wealth and honor. Hence it is said: "The genuineness of the Way is used to govern one's person; its remnants are used to govern the state; its dregs are used to govern the empire." From this perspective, the achievements of emperors and kings are the leftover affairs of sages, not the means to perfect the person and nourish life.

Subcommentary: Xù means remnants. Tǔ means dung. Jū means grass. Those who use the genuine Way to maintain their persons necessarily regard the state as a remnant affair, and equate the empire with grass and dirt.

Now, the superior men of the common world often endanger their persons and abandon their lives to pursue things—is this not sad? Whenever sages act, they necessarily examine the reasons for going and the reasons for acting.
Subcommentary: Xùn means to pursue. They examine where the people of the world are going and observe what the common folk are doing; only then do they act and respond accordingly.

Suppose there were a man here who used the pearl of the Marquis of Suí to shoot at a sparrow a thousand ren high—the world would certainly laugh at him. Why? Because what he used was heavy and what he sought was light. Is life not far heavier than the pearl of the Marquis of Suí?

Subcommentary: The state of Suí was near the Pú River. The Pú River produced precious pearls; namely, the pearl the spiritual snake carried in its mouth to repay a kindness, which the Marquis of Suí obtained, hence it is called the pearl of the Marquis of Suí. The sparrow is a thousand ren high; to shoot at it with a pearl—what is sought is light, what is used is heavy. To injure life in pursuit of things is just like this.

Zǐ Lièzǐ was poor, his appearance showed signs of hunger. A guest spoke of him to Zǐyáng of Zhèng, saying: "Liè Yùkòu is a man who possesses the Way. Residing in your lordship's state, he is poor. Is your lordship not then failing to appreciate scholars?"

Subcommentary: Zǐyáng was the prime minister of Zhèng. Yùkòu was a man of Zhèng. He possessed the Way but was poor. Zǐyáng did not favor worthy scholars, so a traveling guest reproached and criticized Zǐyáng.
Zhèng Zǐyáng immediately ordered an official to send him grain. Zǐ Lièzǐ, upon seeing the envoy, bowed twice and declined.
Subcommentary: He ordered the official in charge of the granary to give him grain. Yùkòu, pure and lofty, declined and did not accept.

After the envoy left, Zǐ Lièzǐ went inside. His wife, seeing him, beat her breast and said: "I have heard that the wives and children of those who possess the Way all obtain ease and pleasure. Now we have a hungry appearance. When the ruler sent gifts of food, you, sir, did not accept—is this not fate?"

Subcommentary: Offered grain but not accepting, it is the fate of poverty. Sighing in distress, beating her breast, she blamed her husband for his fault. Thus we know that Yùkòu's wife was far inferior to the wife of Lǎo Lái.

Zǐ Lièzǐ laughed and said to her: "The ruler does not know me himself. On account of another's words, he sent me grain. When it comes to blaming me, he will also do so on account of others' words. This is why I did not accept." In the end, the people indeed rose in revolt and killed Zǐyáng.

Subcommentary: Zǐyáng was harsh and cruel; many resented him. A subordinate mistakenly broke Zǐyáng's bow and, fearing he would certainly be punished, took advantage when the people were chasing a mad dog and killed Zǐyáng.
King Zhāo of Chǔ lost his state. Butcher Yáng Yuè fled and followed King Zhāo.

Subcommentary: King Zhāo, name Zhěn, was the son of King Píng. Wǔ Shē and Wǔ Shàng were executed by King Píng. Wǔ Zǐxū fled to Wú and plowed in the fields. Later, in the time of King Hé Lǘ of Wú, he requested troops to attack Chǔ, then broke through Chǔ and entered Yǐng to avenge his father's enmity. At that time, King Zhāo was in dire straits, abandoned his capital, fled to Suí, then to Zhèng. There was a lowly
Nanhua Zhenjing Commentary Volume Thirty-One, Five Chi
Commentary by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Xīhuá in the Táng Dynasty Miscellaneous Chapters, Robber Zhì, Twenty-Nine

Confucius was friends with Liǔxià Jì. Liǔxià Jì's younger brother was named Robber Zhì. Robber Zhì led nine thousand followers, rampaging across the world, invading and oppressing the feudal lords. He broke into houses, forced open doors, drove away people's oxen and horses, took people's women. Greedy for gain, he forgot his kin, disregarded his parents and brothers, and did not sacrifice to his ancestors. In the cities he passed through, large states guarded their walls, small states retreated into their fortresses, and the myriad people suffered from him.

Subcommentary: His surname was Zhǎn, given name Qín, courtesy name Jì. He was enfeoffed at Liǔxià, hence called Liǔxià Jì. It is also said he lived under a willow tree, hence the name. Zhǎn Qín was from the time of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ. Confucius lived over a hundred years later; calling them friends is likely a fable. Zhì is Qín's younger brother's name. He was often a great robber, hence called Robber Zhì. He pierced through house walls, broke door pivots to take people's oxen and horses. Some texts use "empty" for "pierce" and "drive" for "take." "Bǎo" means a small fortified city. His harm was immense, so the common people suffered from him.

Confucius said to Liǔxià Jì: "As a father, one must be able to instruct his son; as an elder brother, one must be able to teach his younger brother. If a father cannot instruct his son, an elder brother cannot teach his younger brother, then the value of the father-son, brotherly bond is lost. Now you, sir, are a talented scholar of the age, yet your younger brother is Robber Zhì, a scourge to the world, and you cannot teach him. I am ashamed for you, sir. I ask to go and persuade him on your behalf." Liǔxià Jì said: "You say a father must be able to instruct his son, an elder brother must be able to teach his younger brother. If the son does not heed the father's instruction, the younger brother does not accept the elder brother's teaching, even with your eloquence, sir, what can be done? Moreover, Zhì's nature is like a gushing spring for heart, like a whirlwind for will. His strength is enough to resist enemies, his rhetoric enough to gloss over wrongs. Follow his heart and he is pleased; oppose his heart and he is angered, easily insulting people with words. You must not go, sir." Confucius did not listen. With Yán Huí as driver and Zǐ Gòng as attendant, he went to see Robber Zhì. Robber Zhì was then resting his troops south of Tàishān, mincing human livers to eat.
Subcommentary: "Bū" means to eat. Zǐ Gòng served as attendant on the right side of the carriage.

Confucius descended the carriage and approached, saying to the herald: "I, Kǒng Qiū of Lǔ, have heard of the general's high righteousness and respectfully pay homage." The herald entered to announce. Robber Zhì heard this and was greatly angered, eyes like bright stars, hair standing up, lifting his cap. He said: "Isn't this that cunning hypocrite Kǒng Qiū of Lǔ? Tell him for me: 'You invent words and phrases, falsely praising King Wén and King Wǔ,
Subcommentary: Meaning Confucius took King Wén and King Wǔ as models, traced back to Yáo and Shùn, edited and fixed rituals and music, leaving traces for the future.
wearing a cap like branching trees, girded with a dead ox's rib,

Subcommentary: "Xié" means rib. It means the cap Confucius wore was ornate and decorated, with lush leaves and branches, resembling tree branches. Also, he used oxhide for a belt, both broad and hard, like an ox rib.

with many fallacious speeches, not farming yet eating, not weaving yet dressing, wagging your tongue, arbitrarily creating right and wrong to confuse the world's rulers, making the world's scholars not return to their roots, falsely practicing filial piety and fraternal duty to luckily gain enfeoffment and wealth.'

Subcommentary: "Jiǎoxìng" means hoping. Practicing filial piety and ordering human relations aims at wealth and enfeoffment. Hence, he traveled incessantly, receiving Jiē Yú's criticism of "Phoenix, oh phoenix," abandoning the root and stagnating in traces, with Shī Jīn's mockery of the straw dog.
Your crime is extreme and heavy. Leave quickly! Otherwise, I will add your liver to my meal!" Confucius again requested: "I am fortunate to know Jì and wish to pay respects at your tent."

Subcommentary: Meaning I am very fortunate to be friends with your worthy brother, dare not look directly at your demeanor, but wish to step under your tent curtain. Some texts use "qí" for "tent"; "qí" means footprints. "Wishing to follow your footprints" is like saying "at your feet."

The herald announced again. Robber Zhì said: "Bring him forward!" Confucius hurried in, avoided the mat, stepped back, and bowed twice to Robber Zhì. Robber Zhì was greatly angered, stretched out his feet, pressed his sword, glared, voice like a nursing tiger: "Qiū, come forward! If your words follow my will, you live; oppose my heart, you die!"
Subcommentary: "Qū" means walking quickly. "Fǎn zǒu" means stepping back. "Liǎng zhǎn qí zú" means stretching out both feet.

Confucius said: "I have heard that under heaven, there are three virtues: Being born tall and peerlessly handsome, pleasing all regardless of age, status—this is the highest virtue. Wisdom encompassing heaven and earth, able to discern all things—this is the middle virtue. Bravery, fierceness, decisiveness, gathering crowds, leading troops—this is the lower virtue. Anyone with one of these virtues can face south and call themselves lord. Now, General, you possess all three: height eight feet two inches, radiant face, lips like bright cinnabar, teeth like even pearls, voice matching the huángzhōng pitch, yet you are named Robber Zhì. I am ashamed for you and find it unacceptable.
Subcommentary: "Jī" means bright. "Bèi" means pearl. "Huángzhōng" is one of the six pitch standards.

If you, General, are willing to listen, I request to go south to Wú and Yuè, north to Qí and Lǔ, east to Sòng and Wèi, west to Jìn and Chǔ, to build for you a great city hundreds of lǐ wide, establish a fief of hundreds of thousands of households, honor you as a feudal lord, make a new start with the world, cease arms, rest troops, gather and support your brothers, jointly sacrifice to your ancestors. This is the conduct of sages and talented scholars, and the wish of the world." Robber Zhì, greatly angered, said: "Qiū, come forward! Those who can be swayed by profit and advised by words are all called foolish, common people. Now, being tall and handsome, pleasing to others—this is my parents' legacy. Even if you don't praise me, do I not know myself? Moreover, I have heard: those who like to flatter to your face also like to slander behind your back. Now you offer me great cities and masses, wanting to tempt me with profit and treat me as a common man. How can that last?
Subcommentary: Meaning great cities and masses cannot last long.
The greatest city is none other than the world. Yáo and Shùn possessed the world, but their descendants had not a pinpoint of land.
Subcommentary: Yáo yielded to Shùn, not to his son Dānzhū; Shùn yielded to Yǔ, but Shāngjūn did not succeed; hence, no pinpoint of land.
Tāng and Wǔ were established as sons of heaven, but their later generations were cut off—is it not because the profit was too great?
Subcommentary: Yīn Tāng and Zhōu Wǔ governed all affairs, but their descendants all suffered usurpation and regicide—was it not because the profit of the four seas was too heavy, causing this?

Moreover, I have heard: in ancient times, beasts were many, people few, so people nested to avoid them, gathering acorns by day, perching on trees at night—hence called the people of Yǒucháo Shì. In ancient times, people did not know clothing, accumulated firewood in summer, warmed themselves in winter—hence called the people of Zhīshēng Shì. In Shénnóng's time, they slept peacefully, rose contentedly,
Subcommentary: "Jūjū" means a quiet demeanor; "yúyú" means a self-satisfied appearance.

people knew their mothers, not their fathers, lived with deer, plowed to eat, wove to wear, had no mind to harm each other—this was the peak of perfect virtue. Yet Huángdì could not achieve virtue, fought Chīyóu in the wilderness of Zhuōlù, bleeding for a hundred lǐ.

Subcommentary: "Zhì" means to achieve. Chīyóu was a feudal lord. Zhuōlù is a place name, present-day Zhuō County in Yōuzhōu. Chīyóu created the five weapons and fought Huángdì, hence bleeding for a hundred lǐ.
Yáo and Shùn established ministers,
Subcommentary: Set up百官 (hundred officials).
Tāng exiled his ruler,
Subcommentary: Exiled Jié to Náncháo.
King Wǔ killed Zhòu,
Subcommentary: The battle of Zhāogē.
After this, the strong bullied the weak, the many oppressed the few. Since Tāng and Wǔ, all have been troublemakers.
Subcommentary: In campaigns, usurpation, and regicide, Tāng and Wǔ were the worst.
Now you cultivate the way of Wén and Wǔ, control the world's debates to teach later generations,
Subcommentary: Confucius took Wén and Wǔ as models, debated benevolence and righteousness as teachings for later generations.

with stitched collars and shallow belts, false words and hypocritical deeds to confuse the world's rulers and seek wealth and honor. No robber is greater than you! Why does the world not call you Robber Qiū, but call me Robber Zhì?
Subcommentary: Making robes with stitched sleeves, shallow belts, affecting speech and conduct to confuse feudal lords—his harm is worse than Robber Zhì's.
You sweet-talked Zǐ Lù into following you, made him remove his tall hat, unbuckle his long sword, and receive your teaching. The world all says Kǒng Qiū can stop violence and forbid wrongs.
Subcommentary: The tall hat and long sword are attire of the brave. Since he submitted to Confucius, he removed them.
But in the end, Zǐ Lù tried to kill the ruler of Wèi, failed, and was minced at the east gate of Wèi—this shows your teaching is inadequate.
Subcommentary: Zhòng Yóu deeply hated evil, tried to kill Wèi's ruler Kuǎikuì. Failing, he was pickled. Robber Zhì thus mocks him.

You call yourself a talented scholar and sage? Yet you were twice expelled from Lǔ, had your traces erased in Wèi, impoverished in Qí, besieged in Chén and Cài, unable to find a place in the world. Your teaching made Zǐ Lù minced—this trouble leaves you unable to establish yourself above or deal with others below. Is your way worthy of honor? The world's most revered is none other than Huángdì, yet Huángdì could not perfect virtue, fought in Zhuōlù's fields, bleeding for a hundred lǐ. Yáo was not kind,
Subcommentary: Meaning he did not give the world to Dānzhū.
Shùn was not filial,
Subcommentary: Hated by his father.
Yǔ was paralyzed,
Subcommentary: Laboring to control floods, wind-combed and rain-washed, he developed paralysis, half-body immobility.
Tāng exiled his ruler, King Wǔ attacked Zhòu, King Wén was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ,
Subcommentary: Yǒulǐ was a Yīn prison. King Wén suffered under Zhòu's hardship, trapped in prison for seven years before release.
These six are revered by the world, but closely examined, all were deluded by profit, forced against their true nature—their conduct is deeply shameful.
Subcommentary: The six are Huángdì, Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, and King Wén. All sought profit for the myriad chariots, thus deluded from the true way and not returning to spontaneity—hence shameful.

The world's so-called worthy scholars—Bóyí and Shūqí. Bóyí and Shūqí declined the throne of Gūzhú and starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain, bones unburied. Bào Jiāo cultivated conduct, criticized the world, embraced a tree and died.

Subcommentary: The two died poor on Shǒuyáng Mountain, with no descendants to bury them. Surname Bào, name Jiāo, a recluse in Zhōu times. He cultivated conduct, criticized the world, was廉洁 (incorrupt) and self-restrained, carried a shoulder pole, gathered firewood, acorns for food, hence no descendants. Did not serve the son of heaven, not befriend feudal lords. Zǐ Gòng met him, said: "I hear those who criticize a government do not tread its land; those who defile its ruler do not accept its benefits. Now you tread its land, eat its benefits—is that acceptable?" Bào Jiāo said: "I hear the廉洁 (incorrupt) value advancing lightly, retreating heavily; the worthy are easily shamed and light towards death." Then he embraced the tree and stood until dry.
Shēntú Dí remonstrated but was not heeded, carried a stone, threw himself into the river, eaten by fish and turtles.
Subcommentary: Shēntú drowned himself—explained in previous chapter. "Remonstrated but not heeded"—source unclear. Cuī Jiā explained but without specific remonstrance text.
Jièzǐtuī was most loyal, cut flesh from his thigh to feed Lord Wén. Lord Wén later forgot him. Tuī angrily left, embraced a tree, and burned to death.

Subcommentary: Lord Wén of Jìn, Chóng'ěr, suffered under Lì Jī's plot, fled to other states, destitute on the road. Tuī cut thigh meat to feed him. Lord Wén later returned, after three days enfeoffed his followers, forgetting Tuī. Tuī wrote the "Dragon and Snake Song" on his camp gate, angrily left. Lord Wén later regretted, pursued Tuī to Jiè Mountain. Tuī hid; Lord Wén set fire to the mountain hoping he'd flee. The fire reached Tuī, who embraced a tree and burned to death.

Wěishēng met a woman under a bridge; she didn't come, water rose, he didn't leave, embraced the pillar and died. These six are no different from dismembered dogs, floating pigs, or beggars with bowls—all forsake fame, scorn death, not thinking of nurturing life and longevity.

Subcommentary: The six are Bóyí, Shūqí, Bào Jiāo, Shēntú, Jiètuī, Wěishēng. These six did not conform to the mysterious way, affected conduct, oddly differed from custom to gain fame, passed down to later generations—is it not like displaying a dismembered dog, floating in water, or a poor, sick person begging with a bowl? These people are not allowed to be seen or heard. The six's actions are like this: all valued fame lightly, scorned death, not thinking to return to the root, nurture life, and live out heaven's mandate. Some texts use "pig" for "death," "beg" for "walk"—read accordingly. "Pig" means swine.

The world's so-called loyal ministers—none like Prince Bǐgàn and Wǔ Zǐxū. Zǐxū sank in the river, Bǐgàn had his heart cut out. These two are called loyal ministers, yet ultimately laughed at by the world.
Subcommentary: Mocked by those who understand the true way.

From the above view, down to Zǐxū and Bǐgàn, none are worthy of honor. What you, Qiū, tell me—if about ghostly matters, I cannot know; if about human affairs, it's no more than this, all I've heard and known. Now I tell you human nature: eyes desire to see colors, ears to hear sounds, mouth to taste flavors, will and energy desire fullness.
Subcommentary: Eyes seeing, ears hearing, mouth tasting, will full—acting according to nature, endowed by creation—how can it be affected? Within one's lot, the way is therein.

Human longevity: upper 100 years, middle 80, lower 60. Excluding sickness, death, mourning, worries, the days one opens mouth to laugh in a month are no more than four or five. Heaven and earth are endless; human death has its time. Holding this timed vessel in the endless span, fleeting like a steed galloping past a crack.
Sub
Nanhua Zhenjing Commentary Volume Thirty-Two
Henan Guǒ Xiàng notes Tang Dynasty Xīhuá Fǎshī Chéng Xuányīng commentary Miscellaneous Chapters: Discourse on Swords - Chapter Thirty

In the past, King Wén of Zhào loved swords. Swordsmen gathered at his gate, hosting over three thousand retainers. Day and night they dueled before him, with over a hundred casualties yearly. His fondness remained unsated. After three years thus, the state declined, and the feudal lords plotted against him.

Commentary: King Huì of Zhào, named Hé, was the son of King Wǔlíng of Zhào. He delighted in swordsmen, supporting three thousand retainers. His insatiable喜好 led to the state's decline and weakness. Thus, the feudal lords, knowing his lack of virtue, conspired together planning to attack him.

The crown prince Kuī, troubled by this, sought among his attendants, saying: "Who can persuade the king to change his mind and stop the swordsmen? I will reward him with a thousand pieces of gold." His attendants said: "Zhuāngzǐ would surely be able."

Commentary: Kuī was the name of the crown prince of Zhào. Troubled by his father's fondness for weaponry, he wished to offer a thousand gold to recruit a persuader. Zhuāngzǐ, being a great sage, should be able to stop the swordsmen.

The crown prince then sent someone to offer a thousand gold to Zhuāngzǐ. Zhuāngzǐ did not accept it but went with the messenger to see the crown prince, saying: "What instruction does the crown prince have for me, that you bestow a thousand gold upon me?" The crown prince said: "I have heard that you, Master, are wise and sagely. I respectfully offer a thousand gold as gifts for your attendants. Since you, Master, do not accept it, what more dare I say?"

Commentary: "What matter do you wish to instruct me in, that you bestow a thousand gold?" Seeing the large sum, he thus questioned. The crown prince said: "I heard that Zhuāngzǐ is virtuous, wise, and sagely, hence the gift of a thousand gold to serve as silks for the carriages of your retinue."

Zhuāngzǐ said: "I have heard that what the crown prince wishes to use me for is to end the king's喜好. If I go to persuade the great king and oppose his wishes, and below fail to meet the crown prince's expectations, I will suffer corporal punishment and die. What use would I have for gold then? If I go to persuade the great king and below satisfy the crown prince, what in Zhào state could I not obtain?" The crown prince said: "Yes, but what my king sees are only swordsmen." Zhuāngzǐ said: "Fine. I am skilled at handling swords." The crown prince said: "However, the swordsmen my king sees all have disheveled hair, bristling sideburns, drooping caps, thick tassels, short-backed garments, glare with anger and speak with difficulty. Then the king is pleased. Now if you, Master, insist on seeing the king in scholarly robes, the matter will certainly be greatly adverse."

Commentary: Hair disorderly like overgrowth, sideburns protruding. Iron caps drooping, revealing faces. "Thick tassels" means covering the neck and forehead. Short-backed garments are convenient for martial affairs. Glaring angry eyes are the demeanor of the brave. Resentment filling the chest, hence speech is difficult and strained. Such are the appearance and attire of swordsmen.

Zhuāngzǐ said: "Please prepare sword attire." After preparing sword attire for three days, he went to see the crown prince. The crown prince then took him to see the king. The king bared his bright blade, awaiting him. Zhuāngzǐ entered the palace hall without hurrying, saw the king without bowing.
Commentary: One who is self-possessed has no fear within, hence does not rush.
The king said: "What do you wish to instruct me with, that you had the crown prince precede you?"
Commentary: "What technique do you wish to use to admonish me, that you had the crown prince speak to me first?"

He said: "I have heard Your Majesty loves swords, hence I seek an audience with the king regarding swords." The king said: "What can your sword achieve in restraint?" He said: "My sword, within ten steps, one man; a thousand miles, without lingering." The king was greatly pleased, saying: "Invincible under heaven!"
Commentary: His sword kills one man within ten steps, travels a thousand miles without stopping. So sharp and swift, how could there be any match?
Zhuāngzǐ said: "In wielding the sword, show emptiness, open with advantage, follow with release, precede with arrival. I wish to test it."

Commentary: "Wielding the sword" refers to the Dào. Thus, forgetting oneself, emptying the mind, opening and benefiting things, responding only after sensing, illuminating things with时机. Such is Zhuāngzǐ's use of the sword.
The king said: "Master, rest and go to the lodge. Await my command. I will order a contest set up and invite you, Master."
Commentary: His words were clear and far-reaching, moving the king's heart. Hence he was ordered to rest and proceed to the guesthouse, await the setting up of the sword contest, then be invited.

The king then tested his swordsmen for seven days. Over sixty were wounded or killed. Five or six were selected to present their swords below the hall. Then he summoned Zhuāngzǐ. The king said: "Today, let us test and have the men cross swords."
Commentary: "Dūn" means to judge. Test the arrangement of swordsmen, have them examined and judged to determine superiority and inferiority.
Zhuāngzǐ said: "I have been looking forward to this for a long time."
Commentary: "I have been eagerly awaiting for days. Please test it early."
The king said: "What length is the weapon you wield, Master?" He said: "Whatever I wield will do."
Commentary: "Yù" means to use. Asking because Zhuāngzǐ was truly capable of sword fighting.

"However, I have three swords. Only the king may choose which to use. I beg to speak of them first, then test." The king said: "I wish to hear of the three swords." He said: "There is the Son of Heaven's sword, the feudal lords' sword, and the commoner's sword." The king said: "What is the Son of Heaven's sword like?" He said: "The Son of Heaven's sword uses Yānxī and Shíchéng as its tip, Qí and Dài as its edge."

Commentary: "Fēng" is the sword's point. "È" is the blade. Yānxī is in Yān state, Shíchéng beyond the frontier mountains. These northern places serve as the sword's tip. Qí state and Dài mountain in the east serve as the sword's edge.
"Jìn and Wèi as its spine, Zhōu and Sòng as its hilt."
Commentary: "Xín" is the guard. Jìn and Wèi, two states near Zhào, thus serve as the spine. Zhōu and Sòng, two states in the south, thus serve as the guard.
"Hán and Wèi as its grip."
Commentary: "Jiá" is the handle. Hán and Wèi, two states west of Zhào, thus serve as the grip.
"Wrapped by the four barbarians, lined by the four seasons."
Commentary: Embracing the four barbarians with virtue and Dào, aligning with the four seasons for generation and transformation.
"Bound by the Bó Sea, girded by Cháng Mountain."
Commentary: Bó Sea is in Cāngzhōu. Cháng Mountain is the Northern Peak. Within creation, using mountains and seas to stabilize the land.
"Governed by the five phases, discussed by punishment and virtue."

Commentary: The five phases: metal, wood, water, fire, earth. Punishment: penal laws. Virtue: moral transformation. Using these five phases to regulate the realm, discussing punishment and virtue to govern the multitude.
"Opened by yīn and yáng, upheld by spring and summer, enacted by autumn and winter."
Commentary: Yīn and yáng initiate creation, spring and summer sustain, autumn and winter execute with sternness—the natural Dào.

"This sword, thrust forward with nothing before it, raised with nothing above it, pressed down with nothing below it, swung with nothing beside it. Above, it cleaves floating clouds; below, it severs the earth's veins. Once this sword is used, it rectifies the feudal lords, and all under heaven submit."

Commentary: Using the Dào as the sword, it encompasses all. Thus, above, below, and sideways, nothing can obstruct it. Floating clouds and earth's veins—are they even worth mentioning? Since it takes creation as its function, none不服 indeed.
"This is the Son of Heaven's sword." King Wén looked茫然, lost.
Commentary: Small talent hearing grand matters cannot comprehend. Thus茫然 as if crossing the sea and losing direction, similar to King Huì of Wèi hearing the Sháo music.

He said: "What about the feudal lords' sword?" He said: "The feudal lords' sword uses the wise and brave as its tip, the pure and honest as its edge, the worthy and good as its spine, the loyal and sagely as its hilt, the heroic and outstanding as its grip. This sword, thrust forward also with nothing before it, raised also with nothing above it, pressed down also with nothing below it, swung also with nothing beside it. Above, it models the round heaven to follow the three lights; below, it models the square earth to follow the four seasons; in the center, it harmonizes the people's will to pacify the four regions."

Commentary: "Four regions" means the four directions. Being able to model heaven and earth and understand the sentiments of all things—this distinguishes the feudal lords. But if one can wield this sword to govern the state, they too will be invincible within the realm.
"Once this sword is used, it is like the shock of thunder. Within the four borders, none fail to submit and obey their lord's commands. This is the feudal lords' sword."
Commentary: The Yì jīng uses the Zhèn hexagram for feudal lords, hence thunder is the gathering of feudal lords.

The king said: "What about the commoner's sword?" He said: "The commoner's sword: disheveled hair, bristling sideburns, drooping caps, thick tassels, short-backed garments, glaring with anger and speaking with difficulty, dueling before you. Above, severing necks; below, splitting livers and lungs. This commoner's sword is no different from fighting cocks. Once life is ended, it is of no use in state affairs. Now, Your Majesty holds the position of the Son of Heaven but loves the commoner's sword. I私下 consider it unworthy for Your Majesty."
Commentary: Zhuāngzǐ's雄辩 was unparalleled, ancient and modern. Thus he could persuade and transform the King of Zhào to abandon his喜好. The essence concludes here.
The king then led him up to the hall. The steward presented food. The king circled it three times.

Commentary: "Huán" means to circle. The king, realizing his own error, deeply felt shame and remorse. He summoned Zhuāngzǐ to the hall to express his regret. Circling the food three times, he could not sit peacefully. Breathless and heart-oppressed, how could he eat?

Zhuāngzǐ said: "Your Majesty, sit peacefully and calm your breath. The matter of swords is finished and reported." Thereupon, King Wén did not leave his palace for three months. The swordsmen all died服 in their places.
Commentary: No longer receiving rewards, hence they resented and died.
Nanhua Zhenjing Commentary Volume Thirty-Two
Nanhua Zhenjing Commentary Volume Thirty-Three
Guǒ Xiàng notes Xīhuá Fǎshī Chéng Xuányīng commentary Miscellaneous Chapters: The Old Fisherman - Chapter Thirty-One
Confucius was wandering in the Zīwéi Forest, resting seated on the Apricot Altar. His disciples were reading books, Confucius was playing the zither and singing. Before the melody was half done,

Commentary: "Zī" means black. The Venerable Ní traveled about, lecturing on the Shī and Shū. Resting by the riverside, the forest's sounds—its lush foliage遮蔽 the sun, casting deep shade, leaves spreading, branches hanging like curtains, hence called Zīwéi Forest. "Tán" is a high place in the marshes. That place had many apricots, called the Apricot Altar. The zither harmonizes, can harmonize the heart and nurture nature, hence he played it.

An old fisherman came down from his boat, his鬓眉 entirely white, hair loose, sleeves waving, walking up the plain until he reached the high ground and stopped. Leaning on his knee with his left hand, supporting his chin with his right, he listened until the song ended.

Commentary: The old fisherman was Fàn Lǐ, chancellor of Yuè. After assisting King Gōujiàn of Yuè in pacifying Wú, he boarded a small boat, wandered the three rivers and five lakes, changed his name, called himself the Old Fisherman. It was he whom Confucius met there. Later, sailing to Qí, he was called Chīyí Zǐ; in Lǔ, called Báigū Xiānshēng; in Táo, called Zhū Gōng. Concealing his traces, hiding his light, changing with the times, he still left a letter for Minister Wén Zhǒng saying... "Yú" means to wave. "Mèi" means sleeve. "Yuán" is high plain. "Jù" means to reach.鬓眉 entirely white—the appearance of longevity. Loose hair, no cap—the manner of a rustic. Then, gazing afar at the plain, waving his sleeves, he reached the high ground, moored his boat and stopped. Supporting his chin, embracing his knees, he listened to the zither song.
And he beckoned Zǐgòng and Zǐlù. Both responded. The guest pointed at Confucius and said: "What is he doing?"
Commentary: Inquiring what rank or mandate Confucius held.
Zǐlù replied: "A gentleman of Lǔ."
Commentary: Answered: "A worthy gentleman of Lǔ state."
The guest asked about his clan. Zǐlù replied: "The clan is Kǒng."
Commentary: Asked his clan, answered: "Surname Kǒng."
The guest said: "This Kǒng clan, what does he cultivate?"
Commentary: Again asked: "By what method or technique does the Kǒng clan cultivate himself?"

Zǐlù did not respond. Zǐgòng replied: "The Kǒng clan, by nature, practices loyalty and trustworthiness; in person, acts with benevolence and righteousness; adorns ritual and music; selects human relationships. Above, he is loyal to the worldly rulers; below, he transforms the common people. He intends to benefit all under heaven. This is what the Kǒng clan cultivates."

Commentary: Following a nature humble and harmonious, practicing sagely traces, adorning ritual and music, selecting human relationships, loyal and sincere in serving the ruler, transforming things to achieve equality, intending to benefit the multitude—this is the heart of the Kǒng clan.
He asked again: "Is he a ruler with land?" Zǐgòng said: "No." "A helper of marquises and kings?" Zǐgòng said: "No."
Commentary: "Is he a ruler with fiefdom and five ranks? Or a minister assisting kings and marquises?" Both answered: "No."

The guest laughed and turned to leave, saying: "Benevolent, he is benevolent indeed, but I fear he cannot avoid harm to his person. He labors his heart and toils his form, endangering his authenticity. Alas, how far he is! How separated from the Dào!"

Commentary: Those who labor heart and form, endanger and forget their true nature, partially practicing benevolence and love—they depart far from the origin and separate from the mysterious Dào. Hence he laughed mockingly, paced, and sighed "Alas!"

Zǐgòng returned and reported to Confucius. Confucius set aside his zither and rose, saying: "He is a sage, perhaps!" Then he went down to seek him, reaching the marsh's edge. The other was just leaning on his oar and pulling his boat. Turning, he saw Confucius, turned back and stood. Confucius retreated, then stepped forward, bowing twice, and advanced.
Commentary: "Ná" means oar. Retreating then advancing forward is a gesture of reverence.

The guest said: "What do you seek?" Confucius said: "Just now, you, Sir, had some introductory words and left. I, unworthy, did not understand what was meant. I waited respectfully below the wind, hoping to hear the sound of your cough and spit, to finally assist me."

Commentary: "Nǎng" means earlier. "Xù yán" means remaining discourse. "Zú" means finally. "Xiāng" means to assist. Earlier, you, Sir, had clear words and remaining discourse. I, not sharp, did not recognize their origin. I listened respectfully below the wind, hoping to receive your cough and finally use these words to assist my inadequacy.

The guest said: "Ah! How great is your love for learning!" Confucius bowed twice and rose, saying: "Since youth I have cultivated learning until now, sixty-nine years old, yet have never heard the ultimate teaching. Dare I not be虚心?"
Commentary: "Xī" is a sound of laughter. Since youth, Confucius cultivated benevolence and righteousness
Nanhua Zhenjing Zhushu, Scroll Thirty-Four, Chi Seven
Annotated by Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Subcommentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Western Huá in the Táng Dynasty Miscellaneous Chapters, Liè Yùkòu, Number Thirty-Two
Liè Yùkòu was going to Qí but turned back halfway, encountering Bó Hūn Màorén.

Subcommentary: Bó Hūn was a worthy scholar of Chǔ, styled Bó Hūn Màorén, a follower of recluses. Yùkòu, having studied under Húzǐ, also served Bó Hūn. Just as he intended to go to Qí and was traveling on the transformative path, he alarmed himself over his shallow practice and turned back midway. He happened to meet Màorén, who asked him the reason.
Bó Hūn Màorén said: "For what reason have you turned back?"
Subcommentary: "Reason" means the way. "What" means why. "On what path were you traveling, to what place did you intend to go?" He asked the reason for turning back midway.
He said: "I was alarmed."
Subcommentary: He realized his own faults, became alarmed and fearful, and turned back. This briefly answers the previous question's intent.
He said: "What alarmed you?"
Subcommentary: He asks again, from what event or action did Yùkòu's alarm arise?
He said: "I once ate at ten beverage stalls,"
Annotation: Households selling beverages.
"and five of them offered me their浆 first."

Annotation: This means they respected him. Subcommentary: "Offered" means gave. "Ten beverage stalls" means there were ten households selling drinks. Lièzǐ, while traveling and thirsty, went to an inn; ten households sold drinks, and five of them offered theirs first upon seeing his appearance and demeanor. Competing to show alarm arose in him; unable to be darkly merged, he thus became alarmed and fearful.
Bó Hūn Màorén said: "If so, then why were you alarmed?"
Subcommentary: He asks again the reason for the alarm, hoping he will relate his own faults.
He said: "When inner sincerity is unresolved,"

Annotation: Outwardly self-important and adorned. Subcommentary: He realized his inner genuine wisdom was not yet suspended and resolved, yet he was respected by things, thus he was alarmed and returned.
"and one's form, through ingratiating, becomes radiant,"
Annotation: Through fawning movements, one becomes radiant and impressive.
"using this to overawe people's hearts,"

Annotation: His inner reality is insufficient to subdue things. Subcommentary: "Ingratiating" means a fawning appearance. "Overage" means to subdue. One's demeanor and appearance are fawning, movements become radiant splendor; using this external form to subdue and overawe people and things.
"causing them to value one lightly compared to the aged,"
Annotation: If overawing things comes from inner reality, then it makes people's feelings of valuing the aged sincere.
"and this brings disorder to what one fears."

Annotation: This means using a beautiful form to stir things, then the feared disorder arises. Subcommentary: "Disorder" means chaos. Unable to blend with the vulgar and join the dust, but becoming a standard for things, causing people to respect and value oneself and slight the elderly, one rightly fears that calamity and disorder are about to arise.
"Now, the beverage sellers merely deal in the trade of food and soup, their surplus profits are meager, the benefit they seek is thin, and their influence is slight, yet they still acted like this."
Annotation: Their influence slight, profits thin, they could be without seeking from others.
"How much more so for the lord of ten thousand chariots?"

Subcommentary: "Merely" means solely. "Profit" means gain. The beverage sellers solely have soup and food as their goods; the surplus items are probably not many. Since the profit is thin, their influence is also not heavy. Yet they were able to respect him and compete to offer their浆. How much more for a ruler, whose influence is high and profits great, would it not be fitting for them to rush and show respect?
"One's body toils for the state, and knowledge is exhausted in affairs. He will assign me tasks and test me with achievements. This is why I was alarmed."

Subcommentary: A ruler, whose position oversees myriad tasks, whose power spans the four seas, thus personally wearies and tires in the state affairs, his mind exhausts its thoughts in worldly matters. Then he thirsts for the worthy as if parched, to replace his own labors. He will surely assign me duties and test me with accomplishments. Following the external, losing the internal; chasing the false, forgetting the true—this is the source of alarm, fully related as above.
Bó Hūn Màorén said: "Excellent! Your observation!"
Subcommentary: You were able to observe your own person, carefully know gain and loss. Praising his self-awareness, he thus sighs "Excellent!"
"You settle yourself; people will protect you."

Annotation: If one does not shed form, then wherever one is, one will be seen and protected. "Protect" means to gather and guard. Subcommentary: "Protect" means to guard and keep. You settle and place your own person, unable to forget yourself, still displaying form and virtue, thus things will return to you. Disciples seeking improvement will gather and guard you.
Not long after, when he went, the shoes outside the door were full.

Subcommentary: "Not long after" means not much time had passed. In a short while, Bó Hūn went to Yùkòu's place and happened to see shoes discarded outside the door; barefoot, they ascended the hall—those seeking improvement were many.
Bó Hūn Màorén stood facing north, planted his staff, pressed it against his chin, stood among them, and without speaking, went out.
Subcommentary: "Planted" means set upright. Using the staff to prop his chin, he listened to their discussions. Leaning, he stood among them for a long time, then, forgetting words, returned.
A guest informant told Lièzǐ. Lièzǐ, holding his shoes, ran barefoot, reached the gate, and said: "Since you have come, Master, have you not brought medicine?"

Subcommentary: "Guest informant" means one who announces visiting guests. Yùkòu, hearing that his teacher and friend had stood without speaking and returned, then, alarmed and panting, ashamed and fearful, had no time to put on shoes; barefoot he ran, reached the gate, and turned back. "Since the lofty one has come, I hoped to receive acupuncture and moxibustion. Have you not opened and dispensed medicinal stones, abandoning and returning? Sincerely, my heart thirsts; thus I firmly request this."
He said: "Enough! I already told you that people would protect you, and indeed they protect you."

Subcommentary: "Enough" means stop. I already told you beforehand. You could not conceal your light and obscure your traces; you were bound to be relied upon by things. Now indeed I see your disciples fill the room. My earlier words to you were certainly not empty. You should stop your request; no need for further words.
"It is not that you can make people protect you, but that you cannot make people not protect you."

Annotation: If one lets things be level and transforms, then there is no stirring, no seeking. No stirring, no seeking, then there is no mutual protection. Subcommentary: Revealing traces externally, thus one is protected by people. Unable to forget virtue, thus one cannot avoid being guarded.
"And why use this to stir them, prematurely displaying difference?"

Annotation: Bestowing kindness before things, kindness not based on them; acting prematurely is then different. Subcommentary: "And" means you. "Why" means for what reason? When self and things are both forgotten, what need is there for things to come and stir one? There must be a mechanism coming to stir, and only then respond; do not labor to prematurely display difference, bestowing kindness before things.
"Surely there will be stirring that shakes your innate nature, and again, there is no saying."

Annotation: Surely there will be stirring, then it moves with the innate nature. Subcommentary: "Shakes" means stirs. Surely, inherently there is stirring pressure, and only then arises; follow one's innate nature, shake and respond. Erase traces, hide clues—what is there to declare?
"Those who wander with you, again, do not admonish you. Their petty words are entirely poison to people."

Annotation: Subtle, clever words that enter people are petty words. Subcommentary: Those who wander with you share similar understanding; they only engage in superficial debate, subtle and clever words, flattering and fawning on people, entirely like poisoned wine—how could they use the Dao to admonish you?
"No awakening, no enlightenment—how can they mutually know?"
Subcommentary: "Know" means who. Both sides are on confused paths, unable to awaken and enlighten. Who alone understands to mutually admonish?
"The skillful toil, and the knowledgeable worry; the incapable have no seeking. Full-fed, they wander aimlessly, floating like an unmoored boat—they are those who wander empty."

Annotation: Only the sage has no capability. Below this, down to insects, none forget their own capabilities and entrust themselves to the multitude. Subcommentary: Things have never been without useless worries and labors, and necessarily, through knowledge and skill, they are trapped and exhausted. Only the sage floats without ties, anchored nowhere, forgetful of mind, like that empty boat, following fate, carefree and wandering.
A man of Zhèng, named Huǎn, recited and chanted in the region of Qiúshì.
Annotation: "Recited and chanted" means intoning and singing.
Only three years, and Huǎn became a Ruist.

Annotation: "Only" means exactly. Subcommentary: "Recited and chanted" means chanting and reading. "Qiúshì" is a place name. "Only" means exactly. A man of Zhèng named Huǎn studied in the Qiú region; exactly after three years, he achieved the Ruist Way.
He moistened the river for nine lǐ, his beneficence reached three clans, and he made his younger brother a Mohist.
Annotation: "Three clans" means the clans of father, mother, and wife. He was able to make his younger brother accomplished in the Mohist teaching.
The Ruist and Mohist debated each other; his father aided Dí.

Annotation: Dí was the name of Huǎn's younger brother. Subcommentary: Dí was the name of Huǎn's younger brother. The Ruist upheld the statutes of Wén and Wǔ, transmitted Yáo and Shùn, very rigid and opinionated, fond of many words. The Mohist followed the Way of Yǔ, diligent and frugal, fond of giving. Ruist and Mohist paths differed, aims and aspirations unlike; each holding their right and wrong, they debated and contended. The father sided with the younger son, thus aiding Dí.

After ten years, Huǎn killed himself. His father dreamed of him, saying: "It was you who made your son a Mohist. Why not try looking at my excellence? It has already become the fruit of the autumn cypress."

Annotation: Huǎn resented his father's aiding his younger brother, thus, stirred and impassioned, he killed himself. After death, he appeared in a dream, saying: "I was able to transform myself into a Ruist, and also transformed my younger brother, making him a Mohist. My younger brother, transformed by me, could not follow me. I, being an excellent teacher, was thus resented." Sincerity reached the extreme, thus he became the fruit of the autumn cypress. Subcommentary: "Why" means how. "Autumn cypress" is a sturdy tree. The father aided Dí, and Huǎn hated this. After ten years, stirred and impassioned, he killed himself, then appeared in a dream to his father to voice his grievance, saying: "It was my efforts that made your son a Mohist. Why do you not look upon me as a worthy and excellent teacher, but instead befriend and aid my younger brother? My resentment is extreme; I have transformed into a different thing—the autumn cypress fruit grows upon my grave." Some texts have "mound" instead; "mound" means tomb. It says: "Why do you not look at my grave mound, where I have already transformed into an autumn cypress tree and borne fruit?"
Now, the way the Creator repays people is not to repay their person, but to repay their Heaven-given nature.

Annotation: From here down is Zhuāngzǐ's own words. The achievement of accumulated practice is the repayment; it repays their nature, not their doings. Then, the achievement of learning and practice completes the nature, that is all—how could it be for the doing? Subcommentary: The "Creator" is the great furnace of the natural. And the Creator is not a thing. It can create and transform the myriad things, thus it is called the Creator. Now, the knowledge and abilities of things are endowed by the Creator; they are not achieved through following a teacher and learning. Thus, learning is borrowed to assist the Dao naturally; it repays their Heaven-given nature, not their human efforts. Thus, we know Dí had a Mohist nature, not obtained from Huǎn. Huǎn said, "I taught him"—is that not mistaken?
"That one, thus made that one."

Annotation: That one had that one's nature, thus made him practice that. Subcommentary: That Dí originally had a Mohist nature, thus he became a Mohist. If following nature, originally without learning, he would not have achieved it in the end. Not only Mò Dí—all things are like this.
Now, a person considers himself to have what differs from others, and thereby slights his parents.

Annotation: This means Huǎn admired his own Ruism, considered himself able to have the achievement of accumulated learning, not knowing it was his nature's spontaneity. Now, having achievement to slight things, one does not avoid one's parents. Not having one's person to levelly go, then noble and base do not lose their proper order. Subcommentary: This means Huǎn relied on himself having the achievement of learned cultivation, differing from ordinary people, thus he slighted and despised his parents—and you, towards your father! How deluded and stuck can a person be to reach this point?
The man of Qí who had a well: those who drank from it wrestled with him. Therefore it is said: "In the present age, all are like Huǎn."

Annotation: Now, digging a well is to reach the spring; chanting and singing are to penetrate the nature. Without the spring, there is nothing to dig for; without the nature, there is nothing to chant. Yet the age all forgets the spring-nature's spontaneity, only recognizing the minor achievement of digging and chanting, and thereby wishing to boast and possess it—is that not deluded? Subcommentary: Below the earth there is a spring; each person has their nature—this is Heaven. Digging to form a well; learning to form an art—this is man. Alas! How deluded people are! They only know the minor task of digging and learning, not realizing the spontaneity of the spring-nature, and boast of it as their own achievement. Thus, all in the age are of Huǎn's kind. A man of Qí dug and obtained a well; a traveler drew water and drank; the well owner guarded the water and wrestled his head to stop him. Zhuāngzǐ heard of it, thus cited it as an analogy.
From this, the virtuous consider it unknowing, and how much more the one who has the Dao?

Annotation: Observing Huǎn's error, considering learning as the father, thus able to let it be so of itself, and knowing, thus non-action is in between. Subcommentary: Observing Huǎn's delusion, considering himself truly to have virtue—a virtuous person, from this afterwards, forgets knowing and lets things be, no longer boasting of himself. How much more one who embodies the Dao—would he regard his achievement?
The ancients called this "the punishment of fleeing Heaven."

Annotation: Still using the ability of the natural as one's own achievement—this is fleeing Heaven. Thus, punishment and execution reach him. Subcommentary: Not knowing that things' natures are so of themselves, boasting of it as one's own achievement, is fleeing the natural principle. Since it contradicts the Creator, punishment and execution reach him.
The sage finds security in what is secure, not finding security in what is not secure.

Annotation: The sage has no security and no insecurity; he follows the hearts of the hundred clans. Subcommentary: "Finds security" means entrusts. He entrusts to the natures of the multitude, not leading things to follow his own nature. For what is without nature, he does not forcefully secure it. Therefore, he is the sage.
The multitude find security in what is not secure, not finding security in what is secure.

Annotation: What they find secure differs mutually, thus they are the multitude. Subcommentary: They learn what they cannot, finding security in what is not secure. Not secure in their plain lot, they do not find security in what is secure.
Zhuāngzǐ said: "To know the Dao is easy; to not speak of it is difficult."
Subcommentary: The mysterious Dao is dark and deep; words and images are cut off from it. Applying knowledge is easy; forgetting words is truly difficult.
"To know and not speak—this is how one goes to Heaven. To know and speak—this is how one goes to man."
Subcommentary: Marvelously comprehending the mysterious Dao, there is no method to speak of; thus one arrives at the realm of the natural. Although
Those who follow along leaning on things, those who are stiff-necked and cannot bend to tasks, and those who are timid and fearful—these three types, though inferior to others, all achieve success.

Note: "Follow along leaning on things" means relying on objects to move; "stiff-necked" refers to those unable to bend and handle affairs; "timid and fearful" describes the cowardly and weak. Since these three are not entrusted with responsibilities, they are instead assisted and supported, hence they inevitably succeed. Explanation: "Follow along" means compliance; relying on things and complying with others, they cannot stand independently. "Stiff-necked" means holding their heads high, unable to bend and work. "Timid and fearful" means suffering from hardship and timidity. Having these three traits, they are inferior to ordinary people, yet wherever they are, they succeed.
When wisdom reaches outward,
Note: Reaching outward harms the inner self with its boundlessness. Explanation: Holding onto wisdom to illuminate things, they connect outwardly to the dusty world.
Bold actions often breed resentment.
Note: Only by being timid and quiet can one enrich oneself. Explanation: Being vigorous and restless inevitably invites enmity and conflict.
Benevolence and righteousness often attract blame.

Note: The world expects their love, but when they love, it is inevitably incomplete, hence they are often blamed. Explanation: Benevolence and righteousness are incomplete and must attract much blame.
One who understands the essence of life is carefree.
Note: "Carefree" describes a greatly relaxed and liberated appearance.
One who is versed in knowledge is detached.

Note: "Detached" means dissipated and scattered. Explanation: The note says it means to dissolve and scatter. "Carefree" means relaxed and liberated. Understanding the limits of knowledge, with true nature empty and illuminating, one is carefree and unbound, without attachments.
One who comprehends the great destiny follows along.

Note: Merging silently and transforming together. Explanation: The great destiny refers to a long life, like that of Péng Zǔ who lived to an old age; following and顺应ing it, one does not resent its length as toil.
One who comprehends the minor destiny encounters it.

Note: Only when pausing at key moments does one realize it. Explanation: The minor destiny refers to a short life; "encounter" means coming across it. Like a child dying young, meeting it appropriately, without harboring any concern.
A man who had an audience with the King of Sòng was granted ten chariots, and with these ten chariots, he proudly looked down on Zhuāngzǐ.

Explanation: "Granted" means given; "look down on" means to regard as inferior. During the time of King Xiāng of Sòng, there was a mediocre and petty man who traveled to Sòng, deceitfully persuaded the King of Sòng, and was granted ten chariots. Using these to boast and show off, he placed Zhuāngzǐ behind himself, priding himself on being ahead in possessions.

Zhuāngzǐ said, "There was a poor family by the river that made a living by weaving reeds and mugwort. Their son dove into the deep and obtained a pearl worth a thousand pieces of gold. His father said to him, 'Bring a stone and smash it. A pearl worth a thousand gold must lie in the deepest abyss under the chin of the Black Dragon. That you could obtain the pearl was surely because you encountered it while it slept. Had the Black Dragon been awake, how could you have come away with even a fragment?'"

Explanation: Reeds are rush plants; mugwort is artemisia. The poor family wove reeds and artemisia into mats to sell for food. "Smash" means to pound with a mallet. The Black Dragon is a black dragon with a pearl worth a thousand gold under its chin. This is an analogy mocking the man who obtained the chariots.

"Now, the depth of the state of Sòng is no less than the deepest abyss, and the fierceness of the King of Sòng is no less than the Black Dragon. That you could obtain the chariots was surely because you encountered him while he was asleep. Had the King of Sòng been awake, you would have been ground to powder."

Note: To seek wealth and honor, one must align with the people's expectations. Those who rely on strange theories and seize the main road to captivate the ruler's mind are not accepted by enlightened monarchs. Hence, if there is praise, it must be tested among the people without opposition, and when all agree to recommend, it aligns with the hopes of the multitude. This is how the Three Dynasties proceeded with straightforward governance. Explanation: Those who move the ruler with loyalty and integrity will receive extraordinary rewards, while those who use devious means to flatter and deceive the ruler,侥幸 seeking wealth and honor, thus display arrogance and disdain. How is this different from encountering the Black Dragon in its sleep to obtain the pearl? The rest is detailed in the note.
Someone sent a summons to Zhuāngzǐ.
Explanation: The allegory does not specify the family name or clan of the summoner, so it says "someone."
Zhuāngzǐ responded to the messenger, "Have you seen the sacrificial ox?"
Explanation: "Sacrificial" means raised. The king feeds the ox for three days in advance to sacrifice at the ancestral temple, called the sacrificial ox.
"It is clothed in embroidered silk and fed with grass and beans. But when it is led into the great temple, even if it wished to be a lone calf, could it succeed?"

Note: Those who cherish life fear sacrifice and decline summons; the skull frowns upon hearing about life—this shows the difference in the nature of life and death, each fitting its own state. Explanation: Grass is forage; beans are pulses. The sacrificial ox is raised luxuriantly, but on the day of sacrifice, it cannot become a lone calf. How much more so for those who seek official salaries—they often die young, while those who retreat contentedly are sufficient to preserve life. Zhuāngzǐ, pure and lofty, laughs at such fame and profit.

When Zhuāngzǐ was about to die, his disciples wanted to bury him lavishly. Zhuāngzǐ said, "I take heaven and earth as my coffin and outer coffin, the sun and moon as paired jades, the stars and constellations as pearls, and all things as burial offerings. Is my funeral setup not complete? What could be added to this?"

Explanation: Zhuāngzǐ, profoundly understanding the mysterious Way, saw his body as a temporary lodging. Thus, with heaven and earth as coffin and outer coffin, the two modes as furnace and smelter, the stars as pearls, and the three lights as transformations, the provisions for his send-off are complete. His disciples' lavish burial deeply contradicts the creator's intent.

The disciples said, "We fear the crows and kites will eat you, Master." Zhuāngzǐ said, "Above ground, I'll be eaten by crows and kites; below, by ants and crickets. To rob from one to give to the other—how biased is that!"

Explanation: Kites are a type of hawk. The disciples, bearing deep gratitude for their master, wished to bury him lavishly to avoid the crows and kites. Little did they know that a lavish burial would still expose him to ants and crickets. Their affections lead to taking from one to give to another—how partial!
To use the uneven to even things results in unevenness.

Note: Using one family's standard to even all things is not as good as letting all things even themselves. Explanation: Without emotional giving or taking, entrusting and letting things be evenly balanced—this is true evenness. If one applies emotional considerations to even all things, the very intention to do so is already uneven.
To use the unresponsive to respond results in unresponsiveness.

Note: "Respond" means to answer. Not relying on the self-response of all things but trying to respond with one's own views will inevitably lead to mismatch. Explanation: The sage has no mind; when stimulated, he responds—this is true response. If one has a mind to respond to things, one cannot truly respond. "Respond" means to answer.
The clever are only driven by things.

Note: Those who cling to their views are often driven; how can they drive things? Explanation: Flaunting their cleverness, their emotions respond to affairs, being driven by things—how can they command others?
The spiritual are those who respond.

Note: Only by entrusting to the spirit can one achieve perfect compliance, hence responding everywhere without exception. Explanation: The spiritual are mindless, tranquil and unmoving, yet capable of responding to all.
That the clever cannot surpass the spiritual has long been so.

Note: The reach of cleverness does not extend beyond the physical body. Perfect compliance allows both near and far, hidden and deep, to each find its own place. Explanation: The clever have a mind that responds to affairs, driven by things; the spiritual are mindless, responding to stimuli without fixed method. Having a mind is inferior to being mindless; responding is inferior to forgetting response. The difference in measure is clear.
Yet the foolish rely on what they see and impose it on others; their achievements are external—is this not悲哀?

Note: With perfect compliance, function arises from others and is stored in things. If one relies on their views and insists on their own correctness, even if they wish to impose on others, their achievements remain external. Explanation: Those who forget themselves and respond to things act without claiming credit, achieving without dwelling on success. Foolish and confused individuals cling to their own usefulness, appropriating others' accomplishments as their own. Even if they wish to boast of their achievements, they remain external. Such delusion and forgetfulness are profoundly悲哀.
The Thirty-Fourth Scroll of the Annotations and Explanations on the Nánhuá Zhēnjīng.
The Nanhua Zhenjing Commentary, Scroll Thirty-Five, Chi Eight
By Guǒ Xiàng of Hénán Commentary by Chéng Xuányīng, Dharma Master of Xīhuá in the Táng Dynasty Miscellaneous Chapters, Under Heaven, Thirty-Three
Under heaven, those who govern specialized arts are many, all believing that what they possess cannot be surpassed.

Note: To act based on what one possesses is true action. When one acts truly, there is no falsity—what more can be added? Commentary: "Specialized arts" refer to methods. From Xuānyǔ down to Yáo and Shùn, the ways of governance, arts, and techniques were numerous. All followed the nature of things, complied with their inherent tendencies, and allowed the myriad beings to move and grow without imposing external standards. Thus, though they taught, it was as if they did not teach; though they acted, it was as if they did not act.
Where, indeed, did the Way and its arts of antiquity lie?

Commentary: The Way and its arts practiced by the Three Sovereigns of high antiquity followed things and adapted to transformations, embodying simplicity and non-action. Where exactly did such methods reside? This question is posed to elucidate profound principles.
It is said: There is no place where it is not.
Commentary: The answer: The mysterious Way of non-action exists everywhere. From ancient times to the present, there is no place it does not pervade.
It is asked: From where do the spirits descend? From where does intelligence emerge?

Note: Spirits and intelligence descend and emerge in response to events. Commentary: "Spirits" refers to the wondrous essence of things; "intelligence" means comprehensive wisdom. If the sagely Way of emptiness and penetration has existed through all ages, why would there be need for spirits to manifest such intelligence, creating rituals and music to guide things?
Sages have their origin, and kings their fulfillment.

Commentary: The empty and concentrated mysterious Way gives birth to sagely emperors and enlightened kings in response to things; their achievements are the traces they leave—how could this be without reason?
All originate from the One.

Note: Enabling each thing to return to its root, embracing the One without external adornment—this is how sage-kings generate and complete. Commentary: "Originate" means the root. The One, though descending spiritually to interact with things, mingling its traces and harmonizing its light, never leaves true constancy, embracing the One and returning to the source.

Those who do not depart from the Ancestor are called Heaven's people; those who do not depart from the Essence are called Spirit's people; those who do not depart from the True are called Perfect people. Taking Heaven as the ancestor, virtue as the root, the Way as the gate, and perceiving the omens of change—these are called Sages.

Note: These four names refer to one person, differing only in expression. Commentary: Mingling with the ancestor and uniting with the root is called Nature; pure and unadulterated is called Spirit; steadfast and without artifice is called Perfect; taking nature as the ancestor, superior virtue as the root, the mysterious Way as the gate, and observing signs to follow changes in things—these are called Sages. The four above are one, differentiated by function.
Using benevolence for kindness, righteousness for principle, ritual for conduct, and music for harmony—radiating compassionate benevolence, these are called Gentlemen.

Note: These are the coarse traces of the four names, upheld by worthy people and gentlemen. Commentary: Spreading benevolent grace as kindness, applying righteous principles to judge wrongs, practicing refined conduct, and moving with musical harmony to nurture nature—their compassion illuminates the nine regions, their benevolent influence fans the eight directions. Like the fragrance of orchids, their scent pervades far and wide—truly worthy.
Using laws for distinctions, names for standards, comparison for verification, and investigation for decisions—their methods are one, two, three, four.

Commentary: "Investigation" means examination; "decisions" mean holding to standards. Laws fix distinctions, names represent reality, conduct is tested, abilities are assessed—one, two, three, four refer to these methods like names and laws.
Officials use these to order themselves, taking affairs as their constant duty.

Commentary: From Yáo and Shùn downward, officials were established using these four methods to create order, making the handling of affairs between ruler and subject a constant practice—this is the so-called constant principle.
Taking food and clothing as primary, they promote propagation, nurturing, and storage.

Commentary: Farming and weaving cannot be abandoned; food and clothing are indispensable for sages. Thus, the state takes the people as its root, and the people take food as heaven. Promoting growth, nurturing, accumulation, and storage are all methods to support the people.
Showing concern for the old, weak, orphaned, and widowed, ensuring all are cared for—this is the principle of nurturing the people.
Note: Since this is the people's principle, sages and worthies do not oppose it.
The people of antiquity were complete, were they not?

Note: The people of antiquity refer to these four names. Commentary: Caring for the aged, pitying the weak, compassionating orphans, and sympathizing with widows—these have been fully present since the Five Emperors.

Commentary: "Match" means to unite. Sage-emperors, being without mind, followed the myriad things, thus uniting with the subtle principles of the spirits and aligning with the essence of Heaven and Earth, nurturing the people within the cosmos and harmonizing all beings in the realm.
Their beneficence reached the common people; they were clear about fundamental principles and connected to secondary measures.

Note: Clarity about fundamentals ensures secondaries do not stray. Commentary: Fundamental principles are benevolence and righteousness; secondary measures are names and laws. The sage's mind compassionately nurtures, extending grace to the masses, thus clarifying benevolence and righteousness to honor the root and connecting names and laws to save the branches.
Penetrating the six directions and opening to the four seasons, in all things great and small, refined and coarse, their operation is present everywhere.

Note: This is why they were complete. Commentary: "Opening" means modeling. Great as the two realms (Heaven and Earth), small as the myriad things, refined as spiritual wisdom, coarse as forms and images—they roamed through the six directions, modeled on the four seasons, followed opportunities in movement, and were present everywhere.
What is clear and lies in measures and standards—the old methods handed down by historians—still exists in abundance.

Note: What is clear in measures and standards, though abundant, is external. Commentary: Historians refer to ancient records like the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Book of Documents. Measures and standards include benevolence, righteousness, laws, names, etc. What is clearly transmitted from antiquity and manifest in the world still exists abundantly in historical texts and books.
What lies in the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music—the scholars of Zōu and Lǔ, the gentry and先生, mostly understand it.

Note: They understand the traces, not the source of the traces. Commentary: Zōu is a place name; Lǔ is a state. "Gentlemen" refers to Confucian scholars. The benevolence, righteousness, names, and laws spread through the Six Classics are understood by those in Zōu and Lǔ who wear Confucian robes.

The Odes express aspirations; the Documents record affairs; the Rites guide conduct; the Music creates harmony; the Changes illuminate yin and yang; the Spring and Autumn Annals define names and duties.

Commentary: "Express" means to convey and communicate. The Odes convey emotions and wills; the Documents convey worldly affairs; the Rites guide mental conduct; the Music brings harmony and suitability; the Changes clarify hexagrams and omens, communicating yin and yang; the Spring and Autumn Annals praise and blame to fix names and duties.
Their methods scattered under heaven and established in the Central States—the learning of the hundred schools occasionally praises and speaks of them.

Note: All speak of the old traces of ancient people, yet cannot always praise them. Commentary: The traces of the Six Classics are scattered throughout the land, but their influence reaches only the civilized regions. The hundred schools and various masters vaguely resemble the Five Virtues, occasionally speaking of them but unable to achieve great unity.
Under heaven fell into great disorder.
Note: Because the traces were used without unity. Commentary: Clinging to old traces prevented peace.
Sages and worthies were not illustrious.
The Way and its power were not unified.
Note: The hundred schools drilled arbitrarily. Commentary: Doctrines and teachings were numerous and diverse.
Under heaven, many grasped a part.
Note: Each trusted their bias and could not grasp the whole. Commentary: Learners in the world each stuck to their执着, grasping a partial technique—how could they comprehend broadly?
They examined things to suit themselves.

Note: The sage unifies the great feelings of the people and establishes systems accordingly. Thus, the people entrust their feelings to the unified and forget their own likes and dislikes, achieving tranquility with the age. In disorder, it reverses—people indulge their immediate preferences, each family uses its own laws, so states have different governance and families different customs. Commentary: Unable to be tranquil and empty, they constantly used their minds to examine and teach according to their preferences.
For example, ears, eyes, nose, and mouth each have their clarity but cannot interchange.
Commentary: Eyes see colors but cannot hear sounds; the nose smells fragrances but cannot distinguish tastes—each has its function and cannot interchange.
So it is with the hundred schools and various skills—each has its strengths and times of usefulness.

Note: Their strengths differ and are not constantly usable. Commentary: The Six Classics, Five Virtues, and the writings of the hundred schools each have strengths in saving the world. Since they are not centered on the Way, they are sometimes abandoned, like the nose and mouth having blocked functions.
Nevertheless, they are incomplete and not all-encompassing—they are scholars of a single corner.

Note: Hence, they are inadequate for full responsibility. Commentary: Though each has strengths, they are not comprehensive and universal. These are biased scholars,固执于 one aspect, not those who are rounded and adaptable.
They split the beauty of Heaven and Earth and analyzed the principles of the myriad things.

Note: Each used their corner, thus splitting and analyzing. Commentary: Scholars of a single corner, holding biased views, though skilled in methods, cannot unite with the Way. Thus, they disperse the harmonious beauty of the two realms (Heaven and Earth) and analyze the penetrating principles of the myriad things.
Observing the wholeness of the ancients, few can embody the beauty of Heaven and Earth or match the appearance of the spirits.

Note: How much more so for those of a single corner? Commentary: Observing the wholly virtuous people of antiquity, they could embody the nurturing of the two realms and match the appearance of the spirits—how much less can those of a single corner?
Therefore, the Way of the inner sage and outer king became obscured and unillumined, suppressed and unexpressed.

Note: Because complete people are hard to encounter. Commentary: Mysterious sages and plain kings are inner; flying dragons and nine-five positions are outer. With the hundred schools competing, each自私 their views, right and wrong confused, self and other纷纭, the path of engagement and withdrawal became blocked and unillumined, suppressed and unexpressed.
The people of the world each followed their desires, taking them as their method. Alas! The hundred schools go forth without return—they will surely not unite.

Commentary: What the heart desires is held onto as method. Chasing things without returning to the root, seeking to accord with principle—how can it be attained? So contrary to the nature of things, it is deeply lamentable.
Later generations of learners, unfortunately, do not see the purity of Heaven and Earth or the great substance of the ancients.
