Note: The great substance is each returning to the root and embracing the One—this is the purity of Heaven and Earth. Commentary: "Fortunately" means to encounter. The purity of Heaven and Earth is non-action; the great substance of the ancients is simplicity. Later generations belong to this decadent age, not seeing the Way of non-action or encountering the era of simplicity.
The Way and its arts were about to be split under heaven.

Note: "Split" means separation. The Way and its arts, flowing into弊端, each奋 their methods. Some took charge of things, so things departed from their nature to follow them, and their innate nature was lost. Commentary: "Split" means separation. Confucians, Mohists, Logicians, and Legalists each galloped off,各自私 their views, all following their own feelings. The Way and its arts became纷纭, mutually contradictory, causing the common people to have no focus for their hearts, splitting their innate nature—truly due to this.
Not extravagant for later generations, not wasteful with the myriad things, not shining in measures and standards.

Note: Diligence and frugality lead to hardship, so they do not shine. Commentary: "Extravagant" means lavish; "wasteful" means ornate; "shining" means bright. Teaching later generations not to permit luxury, being frugal with self and things, never adorned—this goes against the nature of things, so teachings and methods do not work. Thus, the classical rituals of former kings cannot be clearly manifest in the world.
They used strict standards to discipline themselves.
Note: "Discipline" means to rectify and exert. Commentary: Using benevolence and righteousness as strict standards to encourage and exert their conduct and will.
And prepared for the world's emergencies.

Note: Diligence and frugality make wealth abundant, so emergencies are prepared for. Commentary: "World's emergencies" refer to disasters like floods and fires. Diligence, frugality, and thrift store goods to prepare for the world's calamities and urgent needs.
The ancient Way and its arts existed in this. Mò Dí and Qín Gǔlí heard of this tradition and delighted in it, but they did it excessively and followed it too strictly.

Note: They no longer considered what the masses could bear. Commentary: "Follow" means to comply. The ancient Way and its arts—like Yǔ controlling floods, diligent and frugal, his traces still exist, so it is said to exist in this. Qín Gǔlí was a disciple of Mò Dí. Mò Dí and Gǔlí, fond of diligence and frugality, deeply delighted in Yǔ's tradition and fervently practiced it, toiling excessively. It suited themselves but was too strict to teach others.
They created the "Against Music" and called it "Frugality in Use." The living did not sing; the dead had no mourning clothes.

Commentary: "Against Music" and "Frugality in Use" are titles of two Mohist texts. The living not singing is against music; the dead having no mourning clothes is frugality in use—meaning no burial garments, coffins, etc., reflecting extreme frugality and thrift.
Mòzǐ advocated universal love and mutual benefit and opposed fighting.

Note: When things are insufficient, fighting is considered right. Now Mòzǐ made the people diligent and frugal, each having surplus, so he considered fighting wrong. Commentary: Universal love benefits all beings, enabling each to be sufficient, hence no fighting—he considered fighting wrong.
His Way was not angry.
Note: Only self-restraint. Commentary: Restraining oneself with diligence and frugality, he held no resentment against things.
He also loved learning and was broad, not different.

Note: Since he considered himself right, he wanted all things to be like him. Commentary: Mòzǐ loved learning and was versed in classics. Being diligent and frugal himself, he wanted things to be the same.
He did not agree with the former kings and destroyed the ancient rites and music.

Note: The former kings allowed diverse differences, then unified them, all attaining without knowing how. Commentary: Rites involved elaborate ceremonies; music involved bells, drums, feathers—he disliked their extravagance and luxury, so he destroyed and abandoned them.
Huángdì had the Xiánchí, Yáo had the Dàzhāng, Shùn had the Dàsháo, Yǔ had the Dàxià, Tāng had the Dàhuò, King Wén had the Pìyōng music, King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu created the Wǔ.
Commentary: These are the music names of the Five Emperors and Three Kings.
In ancient funeral rites, noble and humble had their ceremonies, high and low their ranks: the Son of Heaven had seven layers of coffin, feudal lords five, great officers three, scholars two.
Commentary: From the Son of Heaven down to commoners, all had ceremonies and ranks—this is ancient ritual.

Now Mòzǐ alone had the living not sing, the dead not mourn, with coffins of three-inch tong wood and no outer coffin, taking this as the model. Using this to teach others, he恐怕 did not love people; using this for himself, he certainly did not love himself.

Note: All consider acting according to strength and feeling as love. Now taking diligence and frugality as the model and doing it excessively, though intending to enrich the world, is not the way to love. Commentary: Learning from Yǔ's traces, excessively diligent and frugal, he opposed the Three Kings above and went against the masses below. Thus, in life and death, toiling in poverty, he could not support external things; his form emaciated, he could not love his own body.
He did not ruin Mòzǐ's Way.
Note: Only opposed the Way and its power.
Teaching does not reach the ultimate.
Commentary: Only by following one's inherent nature can one attain the ultimate.
The Way leaves nothing behind.
Explanation: All things differ, each with its unique nature; teaching one based on another is far from the ultimate. If guided by the profound Way, all things achieve self-fulfillment without loss.
Thus, Shèn Dào discarded knowledge and self, acting only out of necessity, letting things flow to embody the principle.

Commentary: "Lěngtài" means to let go freely. Explanation: "Lěngtài" is like refining; he abandoned thoughts and knowledge, forgot self and ego, responding only to necessity, refining right and wrong, judging by law. Shèn Dào upheld this as his principle.
He said: "To know what is unknowable is to belittle knowledge and nearly harm it."

Commentary: It means shallow understanding cannot grasp natural spontaneity, so it's belittled and nearly harmed. Explanation: "Neighbor" means near. Knowledge has its limits, so belittling it still falls short of total forgetfulness, thus nearly harming the principle.
Indecisive and uncommitted, he laughed at the world's esteem for worthies.

Commentary: Unwilling to take responsibility, he left it to the masses; if all can do, there's no need to esteem worthies. Explanation: "Xǐkē" means indecisive; following things and顺应ing feelings, without fixed roles, he let each find its own way, thus laughing at esteem for worthies.
Unrestrained and without conduct, he criticized the great sages of the world.
Commentary: He sought to erase traces so things wouldn't be sacrificed. Explanation: Reckless and neglectful, without virtuous deeds, forgetting past traces, he criticized the sages within the realm.
Striking and cutting, he adapted to things with flexibility.

Commentary: Even the subtle Legalists had to strike, so not fully harmonious. Explanation: "Chuí pāi" means beating; "wànduàn" means execution; "wǎnzhuǎn" means change. He could strike and punish yet顺应 the times, thus adapting without固执.
Abandoning right and wrong, he sought only to avoid blame.
Explanation: Not固执 on right and wrong, merely avoiding contemporary troubles.
He did not follow knowledge or forethought, unaware of before and after.

Commentary: Unable to discern right or wrong, past or future, he acted blindly,苟且 avoiding current harms. Explanation: Not adhering to preconceptions, not using knowledge, nor looking ahead or behind, he straightened his nature into emotion, simply upholding broad principles,顺应ing things.
He stood firm and unmoving.
Commentary: Self-reliant and independent. Explanation: "Wèi rán" describes a steadfast, unmoving demeanor; though in the world, he stood alone.
Pushed, he moved; pulled, he went.
Commentary: This is acting out of necessity. Explanation: Pushed and pulled, he responded only to necessity, not initiating.
Like a whirlwind's turn, a feather's spin, or a millstone's roll, he remained whole without fault, moving or still without error, never at fault.

Explanation: "Mó wèi" means grinding; "suì" means turning. Like a whirlwind's return, a falling feather's spin, or a grinding stone's rotation, all mindless, thus achieving wholeness—no right, no wrong, no blame, no error, emotionless in handling things, hence this state.
Why is this so?
Explanation: A hypothetical question to highlight his ability.
Mindless objects have no worry of self-assertion, no burden of knowledge; their movements never stray from principle, thus lifelong without praise.

Commentary: Worry stems from praise, praise from self-assertion. Explanation: Most things cling to self, establishing merit and fame, using knowledge to sink into past states. But grinding stones etc., act through things, mindless in motion, always abiding in wondrous principle, free from worries and burdens, thus ending with nature's decree, without blame or praise.
Thus, it is said: "Be like a mindless object, and there is no need for worthies or sages."

Commentary: Only sages can discard knowledge and artifice, following natural principle, so foolish and wise find their place, noble and lowly their positions, worthies and unworthies embody their nature. To say no need for worthies or sages is to not know the Way.
A clod of earth does not lose the Way.

Commentary: To urge discarding knowledge like a clod; also, ordinary things cannot attain the Way, as the Way is not universal. Explanation: Valuing mindlessness, like tiles or stones, no need for worthies or sages, dark as night wanderers, like clods, called attaining principle—such is Shèn Dào's confusion.
Heroes laughed at him, saying: "Shèn Dào's Way is not for the living but the dead's principle."

Commentary: Discarding knowledge and following nature leads to divine insight, making one a sage. But calling a clod not losing the Way—if humans are like clods, aren't they dead? Hence heroes laugh. Explanation: Sages who attain the Way handle things mindlessly, virtue matching heaven and earth, brightness equaling sun and moon. To equate clods with the Way is no different from death, lacking divine function, not for the living. Thus, learned heroes know its fallacy and ridicule it.
It is indeed strange.
Commentary: Not fitting the ultimate Way, thus peculiar. Explanation: Not conforming to the ultimate Way makes it strange.
Tián Pián was the same, learning from Péng Méng and attaining untaughtness.
Commentary: Attained the principle of self-reliance. Explanation: Tián Pián and Shèn Dào studied under Péng Méng, indulging freely without teaching.
Péng Méng's teacher said: "The ancient Way-followers reached a state of neither affirming nor denying."
Commentary: This is called putting the equality of all things first.
Their influence was swift, how can it be described?

Commentary: The sound of wind against movement. Explanation: "Xù rán" means rapid. Ancient Way-followers emptied themselves, forgot ego, pointed to heaven and earth without right or wrong, their influence swift, passing with the times—how can traces be held and described?
Often opposed people and did not attract attention.
Commentary: Not顺应ing popular expectations. Explanation: Unable to fully顺应 the masses, often忤逆人心, nor could they gain people's admiration.
Yet could not avoid being rounded and blunt.

Commentary: Though establishing laws, they were rounded without edges. Explanation: "Yuán duàn" describes a rounded, edgeless appearance. Though setting laws and teachings, they couldn't fully equalize all things, thus不免于 being rounded.
What they called the Way was not the Way, and their so-called truths were not free from error.
Commentary: "Wěi" means right. Explanation: "Wěi" means correct. What Shèn Dào called the Way is not the true Way; what he claimed right is not, thus不免于 error.
Péng Méng, Tián Pián, and Shèn Dào did not know the Way.

Commentary: The Way is everywhere, yet calling a clod not losing the Way shows ignorance. Explanation: Though崇尚虚忘, taking mindlessness as the Way, they hadn't attained perfect insight, thus not knowing.
Nevertheless, they generally had some acquaintance with it.

Commentary: But not fully. Explanation: Though Péng Méng's kind didn't embody truth, their aspirations knew a rough outline, learning from masters, having transmission—not mere conjecture—so they had heard of it.
Taking the root as essence, things as coarse.
Explanation: The root is non-being, things are being. Using non-action and subtle Way as essence, action and worldly affairs as coarse.
Considering accumulation as insufficiency.
Commentary: Entrusting to the world, then there is surplus.
Serenely alone, dwelling with divine intelligence—ancient Way arts existed in this.

Explanation: Greedy accumulation leaves the heart ever insufficient; knowing sufficiency and staying within bounds leads to purity, emptiness, independence, with spirit and Way omnipresent—this has existed since ancient times.
Guān Yǐn and Lǎo Dān heard of this and delighted in it.

Explanation: Surname Yǐn, name Xǐ, style Gōngdù, commander of Hángǔ Pass during King Píng of Zhōu, hence called Guān Yǐn. Surname Lǐ, name Ěr, style Bóyáng, external style Lǎo Dān, teacher of Yǐn Xǐ, the Old Master. Teacher and student harmonized, corresponding with principle, thus delighting in the wind of non-action.
They established it with constant non-being and being.
Commentary: Non-being cannot establish anything; establishing with constant non-being and being clarifies that things establish themselves.
They took the Great One as master.

Commentary: From heaven and earth to all things, each attains self-fulfillment without added adornment—isn't this taking the Great One as master? Explanation: "Tài" means vast, "yī" means non-dual. The Great Way is boundless, encompassing all, uniting everything as one, hence called the Great One. Establishing teachings, they always took constant non-being as the core, understanding its essence with empty penetration of the Great One as master—this values frugality and laboring the body, not fit to teach others, nor does it toil or fail their Way art.
With gentleness and humility as the exterior, emptiness and non-destruction of things as the substance.
Explanation: Exterior means outward; using softness and harmony as expedient wisdom externally, empty wisdom and clarity as substantial wisdom internally.
Guān Yǐn said: "In oneself, have no fixed abode."

Commentary: When things come, respond; respond without storing, so achievements follow things away. Explanation: Achieve without dwelling, attributing success to things, using this to cultivate oneself.
Forms and things manifest themselves.
Commentary: Not self-asserting but entrusting to all things, so each form reveals itself. Explanation: Entrusting to all things without claiming credit, thus their forms and natures each manifest.
In movement, like water; in stillness, like a mirror; in response, like an echo.
Commentary: Always without emotion. Explanation: Moving like flowing water, still like a hung mirror, responding like an echo to sound—movement and stillness mindless, divine function thus swift.
Vague as if non-existent, silent as if clear; those who agree harmonize, those who gain lose.

Commentary: Those always whole do not know what they gain. Explanation: "Hū" means sudden; "wáng" means non-being. The Way is neither being nor non-being, not clear nor turbid, so dimly sudden like non-existent, yet not non-existent. Silent and clear as if pure. Agreeing with the shallow views of the masses, thus taking this emptiness and non-action as virtue loses the Way.
Never preceding others, always following them.
Explanation: Harmonizing without initiating.
Lǎo Dān said: "Know the male, maintain the female, be the stream for the world; know the white, maintain the disgrace, be the valley for the world."

Commentary: Things each keep their share, then silent and still, without male or white. Male and white are about seeking victory and self-display—doesn't that chase knowledge excessively, endangering life? Thus, the ancients didn't follow boundless knowledge, keeping within their share, so their nature whole, then able to reach the world, and the world returns like to a stream or valley. Explanation: Heroes and talents advance rashly, shortening life; femininity and humility retreat quietly, prolonging it. Thus, discard glorious display, embrace hidden disgrace—this is the pivot of learning the Way, hence the valley within the world. Stream and valley both are waterways, but stream small, valley large, so repeated.
All people take the lead; he alone takes the rear.

Commentary: Not competing with all things, then the world gladly supports without tire, thus putting himself last. Explanation: Commoners all seek victory and precedence; the great sage alone is humble and follows, so the Dàodé Jīng says: "Put himself last, yet comes first."
Said: "Endure the disgrace of the world."
Commentary: Female, disgrace, following—such are what things call disgrace. Explanation: Retreating behind, pushing things forward—this endures disgrace.
All people seek substance.
Commentary: Only know having as benefit, not knowing non-being as function. Explanation: Greed for wealth.
He alone takes emptiness.
Commentary: Maintains emptiness and tranquility to await all substances. Explanation: Maintains empty silence.
Having no storage, thus having surplus.

Commentary: Entrust to all things to each keep, so not worried about lack. Explanation: Storage means accumulation. Knowing sufficiency and keeping within bounds, scattered not accumulated, thus surplus.
Towering and having surplus.
Commentary: Independent and self-sufficient. Explanation: "Kuī rán" means standing alone. Pure and clean, with very little in things, only the sage is mindless.
In conducting himself, leisurely and without waste.

Commentary: Acting according to what benefits the people, achieving with the seasons, always with principle, thus no haste or waste. Explanation: "Fèi" means loss. Those who attain the Way have no immediate favors, eat simple fields, establish non-lending gardens, calm and elegant, never harming self for things—thus acting to nourish life.
Non-action, yet laughing at cleverness.

Commentary: The clever act and damage natural completion; non-action follows self-generation, letting all achieve—each can do, even spiders weave webs, so no need to esteem skilled artisans. Explanation: Acting by nature, simple and non-action, laughing at worldly people's cunning and falseness.
All people seek good fortune; he alone seeks to preserve himself whole.
Commentary: Following ultimate principle, always whole, thus no need to seek fortune—fortune already sufficient.
Said: "Merely avoid blame."

Commentary: Following things, thus things cannot blame. Explanation: "Jiù" means misfortune. Commoners deluded,固执 in seeking fortune without considering misfortune; only the great sage empties mind, yields and follows, preserving life and avoiding disasters.
Taking depth as the root.
Commentary: Principle rooted in the ultimate of the beginning, not shallow.
Taking frugality as the discipline.
Commentary: Removing excess and extravagance. Explanation: Taking profound mystery as the root of virtue, frugality as the discipline of conduct.
Said: "The hard will be destroyed."
Commentary: Ultimate顺应ance, even metal and stone not hard; opposition, even water and air not soft—ultimate顺应ance preserves, opposition destroys, this is correct principle.
The sharp will be blunted.
Commentary: Advancing rashly without limits is sharp. Explanation: Destroying hard and firm conduct, blunting greedy sharpness—thus Dàodé Jīng says: "Blunt its sharpness."
Always tolerant towards things.
Commentary: Each keeping its share, then naturally accommodating with surplus.
Not encroaching upon others.
Commentary: Preserving their nature. Explanation: Retreating and humble, thus tolerant towards things; knowing sufficiency and keeping share, thus not encroaching on others.
Can be called the ultimate—Guān Yǐn and Lǎo Dān, the ancient vast and genuine persons!

Explanation: Guān Yǐn and Lǎo Dān, great sages of old, explored subtleties and wonders, merged with truth and the Way, teaching vast and broad, principle great and profound—Zhuāngzǐ nearly equals, hence this sigh.
Silent and formless, changing without constancy.
Commentary: Following things. Explanation: The subtle origin formless, thus silent; traces follow things, thus without constancy.
Death and life, together with heaven and earth, going with divine intelligence.
Vast, where to go? Sudden, where to head?
Commentary: Without intent or direction. Explanation: Entrusting to natural changes, roaming with vast suddenness—no attachment to going or taking, only following fate to where it goes.
All things encompassed, none sufficient to return to.
Commentary: Thus all entrusted and placed. Explanation: Enveloping all things, containing the world, never leaving the Way—where to return to the root?
Ancient Way arts existed in this; Zhuāng Zhōu heard of it and delighted, with absurd and distant theories, extravagant words, boundless speech, often放任而不偏, not seeing from one angle.

Commentary: Not eager to let things see his intent. Explanation: "Miù" means empty; "yōu" means distant; "huāngtáng" means vast; "zì zòng" means放任; "jī" means uneven. Zhuāngzǐ born to respond to the world,暗合 the mysterious Way, thus capable of虚远深宏 theories, endless talks,放任 with the times without bias, harmonious and blending, never uneven.
Considering the world sunk in turbidity, not fit for solemn discourse.

Commentary: Burdened by forms and names, taking solemn talk as madness and disbelieving, thus not engaging. Explanation: "Zhuāng yǔ" means grand words. People within the world沉滞 in darkness, all drowning in petty debates—not fit for grand words.
Using goblet words for endless flow, weighty words for truth, allegorical words for breadth.
Explanation: "Zhī yán" means uncertain; "mànyǎn" means mindless; "zhòng yán" means respecting elders; "yù yán" means lodging. A goblet full tilts, empty leans
A turtle is longer than a snake.

Explanation: When length and shortness are relative, there is no absolute length or shortness. To claim that snakes are long and turtles short is to be trapped by material perceptions. To dispel such confusion, it is said that a turtle is longer than a snake.
A square cannot be made with a compass, nor a circle with a square.
Explanation: Compasses for circles and squares for right angles have long been used, yet their definitions are unstable; circles and squares lack fixed essence, hence they cannot achieve this.
A mortise does not enclose the tenon.

Explanation: A mortise is a hole; a tenon is the wood inserted into it. When the tenon enters the mortise, the wood passes through the void without true connection, so it cannot be said to enclose it. This is akin to the separable linked rings.
The shadow of a flying bird never moves.

Explanation: The past has vanished, the future has not arrived; beyond past and future, there is no time of flight. Only the bird and its shadow stand still and unmoving. Thus, it is known that all things in the world are inherently tranquil. Hence, the treatise states: "The four phenomena gallop like wind, the celestial mechanism whirls like lightning, yet in grasping the subtle essence, though they shift, they do not truly move—this is what is meant by 'things do not migrate.'"
Even at the swiftest moment of an arrow's flight, there is a time when it neither moves nor stops.

Explanation: The arrow's tip, though launched with speed, does not escape the three times (past, present, future), no different from a wheel's motion or a bird's shadow. Since it neither halts nor moves, how can the arrow be said to either stop or go? It is like a sharp knife cutting three strands of silk, among which there are also past, future, and present strands.
A dog is not a canine.

Explanation: "Dog" and "canine" refer to one entity with two names. Since names are empty, a dog is not a canine. Dog and canine share the same substance but differ in name. If name and substance align, one may call it "dog" and another "canine." If they diverge, then "dog" is considered different from "canine." Mòzǐ said: "A dog is a canine, yet a dog is not a canine."
A yellow horse and a black ox make three.

Explanation: Form is not color, color is not form. Thus, one horse and one ox make two, but adding the horse's color yields three: the yellow horse, the black ox, and the yellow-black form, making three. It is like one and the word making two, and two and one making three.
A white dog is black.
Explanation: Since names and assertions are unreal, and forms and colors are empty, to overturn stubborn perceptions, white is declared black.
An orphaned colt never had a mother; a one-foot rod, halved daily, will never be exhausted.

Explanation: A rod is a staff; "take" means to break. Question: A one-foot rod, halved this morning, leaves five inches by evening. In two days, should it not be completely used up? This seems evident—how can it be inexhaustible? Answer: Names correspond to substances, substances to names. Thus, using the name to seek the thing, the thing cannot hide. Therefore, holding the name accountable to the substance, it is called a "one-foot rod." If halved each time, how could it ever be exhausted? If broken at five inches, it violates the name's logic—how can "half-foot" mean "one-foot"?
Sophists used such arguments to debate with Huì Shī, endlessly throughout their lives. Huán Tuán and Gōngsūn Lǒng were among these sophists.

Explanation: Surnamed Huán, named Tuán; surnamed Gōngsūn, named Lǒng, both from Zhào, were debaters. They traveled as guests in Lord Píngyuán's household, and Gōngsūn Lǒng authored the "White Horse Discourse," circulated in the world. Using the above rod argument, they responded in turn, thus passing their years without end.
They adorned people's minds and altered their intentions.
Explanation: Wielding such profound debates, they embellished human hearts; employing elegant rhetoric, they changed people's views.
They could overcome others' mouths but not win their hearts—this is the realm of the sophists.

Explanation: Their arguments surpassed ordinary things, so they could overpower speech; yet their words lacked true principle, thus failing to convince hearts. Sophists used this as their domain. Alternatively, "realm" means a confined area. Huì Shī's words did not align with principle, and their scope did not extend beyond this.
Huì Shī said: "Using his knowledge in debate with others, he uniquely set forth strange notions with the world's debaters—this was his foundation."

Explanation: "Uniquely" means alone; some texts read "shall." "Strange" means peculiar; "foundation" means essence. Huì Shī said: employing discriminating knowledge to critique others, he alone pitted himself against heaven and earth as extraordinary. Though cunning and varied, his fundamental essence did not go beyond this.
Yet in oral debate, Huì Shī considered himself the most worthy.
Explanation: "Yet" means thus. Huì Shī's understanding of principle was second to Zhuāngzǐ, but in debate, he deemed himself supreme among all—unlike others who merely argued.
He said: "Heaven and earth—are they not grand? Shī preserves his prowess with five methods."

Explanation: "Grand" means great; "methods" means ways. He claimed heaven, earth, and I are coeval, yet insufficient to express his intent. Aiming for heroic transcendence, he lacked humility and thus had no true way. Speaking of grandeur, it was solitary boastfulness.
In the south, there was an eccentric named Huáng Liǎo, who asked why heaven and earth do not fall or sink, and the reasons for wind, rain, thunder, and lightning.

Explanation: Residing in the south, surnamed Huáng, named Liǎo, he was unmatched by convention, detached from ordinary people, a worthy beyond the mundane. Hearing of Huì Shī's wit, he came to ask: why the two realms endure, and what causes wind, rain, thunder, and lightning to arise.
Huì Shī responded without declining, answered without pondering.
Explanation: His spirit was heroic, his speech unrestrained—thus, he replied instantly without refusal, answered without deliberation.
He elaborated on all things, spoke incessantly, endlessly, yet deemed it insufficient, adding strangeness.

Explanation: He extensively explained the roots of all things, debating the causes of the two realms and thunder, never ceasing, still finding it too brief, so he added wonders to display his ability.
He took contradicting others as substance and sought fame by overcoming them—thus, he was at odds with the multitude.
Explanation: Considering opposition to human sentiment as true principle, he always aimed to surpass the crowd and stand out, intent on reputation, so he could not harmonize with the world.
Weak in virtue, strong in things, his path was obscure.
Explanation: "Path" means way. His virtue was feeble, his focus on things extreme; he claimed his principles were profoundly abstruse.
Viewing Huì Shī's abilities through the way of heaven and earth, they are like the toil of a single mosquito or fly. What use are they to things?

Explanation: "Viewing" means considering; "use" means utility. From the generative way of the two realms, Huì Shī's power to transform things is no different from a mosquito or fly buzzing in the air, flapping wings—mere futile labor, hardly worth mentioning. His words, meant to benefit things, become useless.
To fulfill one aspect may be called improvement, but to esteem the way is nearly there.

Explanation: "Nearly" means close. Huì Shī's debates, interpreting principle not broadly, could at best count as one among many. Yet, eager to passionately honor the way and adorn his intent to approach truth, honestly assessed, it is hardly acceptable.
Huì Shī could not find peace in this, scattering himself among things without weariness, ultimately gaining fame as a skilled debater.

Explanation: "Ultimately" means in the end. He could not use this profound way to attain tranquility, but scattered his spirit, expounding on all things without preserving the way. Eyewitnesses ultimately knew him as a sophist.
Alas! Huì Shī's talent, dissipated and overflowing, failed to follow things without return—this is like exhausting an echo with sound, or the form racing with its shadow. How sorrowful!

Note: Previously, before studying Zhuāngzǐ, I heard scholars debate the meaning of the one-foot rod and linked rings, all attributing it to Zhuāngzǐ, thus classifying him among sophists. Examining this text's critique of various thinkers, up to this chapter, it says: "His way is erratic, his words miss the mark." Then I realized the harm of hearsay and groundless talk. I also deem it lacking in statecraft and genuine substance—truly useless discourse. Yet, for the refined, equally in leisure, weary of classical words, the ability to analyze names and principles to express their energy and sustain thought, passed to later ages, preventing nature from depravity—is this not better than gambling? Thus, I preserve it without further discussion, leaving it to enthusiasts. Explanation: "Dissipated" means unrestrained. Lamenting Huì Shī's talent without way, his unrestrained debates failed to reach the true source. Chasing the ends of things, he could not return to the wondrous root. To grasp principle, nothing beats forgetting knowledge; to return to the root, nothing surpasses ceasing debate. Now, Huìzǐ labored his mind, seeking the way, squandering like a river's flow to obscure truth—how unlike trying to escape an echo by raising voice, or flee a shadow by running fast. Such great talent—deeply sorrowful!
Nánhuá Zhēnjīng Commentary, Volume 35.
